docs.title: Nuclear and Particle Physics
docs.text:
Binding energy is what responsible for the difference (mass defect) between the mass of an atom and the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in it. The force responsible of it is called the strong force.

Direct calculation of binding energy is not possible because in a nucleus, the particles are tightly bounded (perturbative methods have poor convergence) and it is a many body problem with all particles of the same mass. The nucleons also move at large speeds and need to use relativistic approximation.

The usual notation for an element is $\(^A_ZX\)$ where \(A\) is the mass number (proton + neutron), \(Z\) is the number of proton and \(X\) is the elemental symbol.

Here we use the liquid drop model to approximate a formula for binding energies: $$ \begin{aligned} B(A, Z) = E_{\text{Volume}} - E_{\text{Surface}} - E_{\text{Coulomb}} - E_{\text{Asymmetry}} \pm E_{\text{Pairing}} \ = a_V A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_a \frac{(N - Z)^2}{4A} + \frac{\delta}{A^{1/2}} \end{aligned} $$

docs.title: Volume term, \(E_{\text{Volume}} = a_V A\)
docs.text:
The attractive strong force between nucleons implies that it is energetically favourable for a nucleon to surround itself with other surrounding nucleons, inducing a binding energy between them.

Since \(4\pi R^3 / 3 \propto A\), we expect this term to scale with \(A\)

docs.title: Surface term, \(E_{\text{Surface}} = a_S A^{2/3}\)
docs.text:
Here we consider the particle at the edge of the surface where are have less binding energy as compared to the ones at the centre because they are surrounded by less nucleons.

This term, following from the scaling factor as outlined in volume term, scales with \(R^2 = A^{2/3}\)

docs.title: Coulomb term, \(E_{\text{Coulomb}} = a_C Z^2/A^{1/3}\)
docs.text:
The protons have the same charge so they repel each other, implying a weaker binding energy.

Coulomb potential scales as \(V = a/r\) so we expect this term to be scaling with \(1/R = A^{-1/3}\)

docs.title: Asymmetry term, \(E_{\text{Asymmetry}} = a_a (N-Z)^2/4A\)
docs.text:
This term involves Pauli exclusion principle. Since protons and neutrons are fermions, they cannot lie in the same state. Consider that we have \(n\) protons and neutrons and each of them fill \(n\) lowest energy state. If we try to replace a neutron with a proton, it has to occupy the upper energy level, hence reducing the binding energy. In other words, the symmetric number of neutrons and protons can be packed tighter.

This term measures the difference between the number of neutrons and protons i.e. it is proportional to \(N-Z\)

docs.title: Pairing term, \(E_{\text{Pairing}} = \delta/A^{1/2}\)
docs.text: Nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons are more stable because two different nucleons with opposite spin can be on the same shell. If we have odd number of protons/neutrons, the third spin has to be in the next shell.

docs.title: About me
docs.text:
I am a physics graduate from Durham University with a strong interest in condensed matter physics (CMP). My coursework focused on CMP, Modern Atomic and Optical Physics, Statistical Physics, Nuclear and Particle Physics, and Quantum Mechanics. Additionally, I completed two final-year projects: an advanced laboratory project and a bachelor's project in CMP. Summaries of these projects can be found here.

To build on my undergraduate theoretical foundation, I am furthering my studies with a master's in Medical Physics at the University of Aberdeen. Medical physics is an interdisciplinary field that applies physical principles—such as magnetism and nuclear physics—to medicine. Examples include the development of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and the use of iodine-131 (\(I\text{-}131\)) isotopes in nuclear medicine. Given my background in condensed matter physics and my focus on magnetism, my goal is to specialise in the research and development of MRI technology.

Alongside my studies, I actively participate in various university societies to develop key transferable skills for my professional growth. For more details on my involvement, see here.

docs.title: Absorption cross section and saturation
docs.text:
Motivation:

Absorption cross-section refers to how likely an atom to absorb a photon by looking at the intensity change of a beam as it passes through a sample of atoms

Saturation here refers to how populated the excited state is.

Here we look at how intense light affects the energy levels.

We first incorporate natural broadening in rate equations as defined in Light Forces because spontaneous emission leads natural broadening.

\[ a_{21}(\omega) = A_{21} L(\omega) \] \[ b_{21}(\omega) = B_{21} L(\omega) \] \[ b_{12}(\omega) = B_{12} L(\omega) \]

where \(L(\omega)\) is normalised Lorentzian lineshape. This means that atom-light interaction is spread over a range of frequencies with a maximum on resonance \(L(\omega_{12}) = 2/\pi\Gamma\).

docs.title: Absorption cross-section
docs.text:
We want to know how the spectral intensity of the beam changes as it passes through a thin sample of atoms. Here we assume steady state (no spontaneous emission).

[!Definition] Spectral intensity: Optical power per unit area per unit angular frequency

\[ \left[ I(z + dz) - I(z) \right] A \, d\omega = \left[ N_2 B_{21} L(\omega) \rho(\omega) \, d\omega - N_1 B_{12} L(\omega) \rho(\omega) \, d\omega \right] \, \hbar \omega A \, dz \]

[!Interpretation] LHS: Optical power and it is related to the energy of the electromagnetic waves. RHS: Rate of the change in EM energy (power) due to the photons (energy of net rate of transition per unit volume)

In the limit \(dz \to 0\), $$ \frac{1}{I} \frac{dI}{dz} = \frac{\hbar \omega}{c} \left[ N_2 B_{21} - N_1 B_{12} \right] L(\omega) $$

Substitute for \(B\) coefficient using \(A_{21} = \frac{\hbar \omega_{12}^3}{\pi^2 c^3} B_{21}\) and \(g_1 B_{12} = g_2 B_{21}\), $$ \frac{1}{I} \frac{dI}{dz} = \underbrace{\frac{\pi^2 c^2}{\omega_{12}^2} A_{21} L(\omega)}_{\text{Scattering (absorption) cross section } (\sigma(\omega))} \left[ N_2 - N_1 \right] $$ (Textbook interpretation see here)

[!note] This is the result for unpolarised light. For polarised light, we have three polarisation axes so we have to multiply by three.

And the solution to this equation is the beer's law $\(I(z) = I(0)e^{\sigma(\omega)[N_2-N_1]z} = I(0)e^{-\kappa(\omega)z}\)$ Remember that we are dealing with intense light when stimulated emission is significant (which affects \(N_2\)). Unlike weak beam where \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) are roughly the same. Physical intuition: stimulated emission leads to gain in intensity.

docs.title: Saturation
docs.text:
\[ \underbrace{(N_1 - N_2) \sigma(\omega) I}_{\text{Net absorption rate}} = \underbrace{N_2 A_{21} \hbar\omega}_{\text{Rate of atoms scatter energy out of the beam}} \]

Where: - \(N_1, N_2\) = populations of ground and excited states - \(\sigma(\omega)\) = absorption cross section - \(I\) = beam intensity - \(A_{21}\) = Einstein A coefficient (spontaneous emission rate)

The power absorbed from the beam = power radiated away by atoms

\[ r = \frac{\sigma(\omega)I}{A_{21} \hbar\omega}, \quad (N_1 - N_2)r = N_2, \quad N_1 + N_2 = N \] \[ (N_1 - N_2) = \frac{N}{1 + 2r} = \frac{N}{1 + \frac{I}{I_S(\omega)}} \]

When \(I = I_S\), \(\frac{1}{4}\) of atoms are excited.

Solution method

\[ I_S(\omega) = \frac{\hbar\omega A_{21}}{2\sigma(\omega)} \]

→ Minimum value of \(I_S\) occurs on resonance when \(\sigma(\omega)\) is largest (when the interaction is very probable).

\[ I_S(\omega_0) = I_{\text{sat}} = \frac{\pi\hbar c}{3\lambda^2 \tau} \]

docs.title: Power Broadening
docs.text:
By subsituting \((N_1 - N_2)\) above into the beer's law, we get

\[\kappa(\omega,I) = \frac{N\sigma(\omega)}{1+\frac{I}{I_S(\omega)}}\]

and for whatever the fuck reason, it becomes $$ k(\omega, I) = \frac{N\sigma(\omega_{12})\frac{\Gamma^2}{4}}{(\omega - \omega_{12})^2 + \frac{\Gamma^2}{4}} \times \frac{1}{1 + \frac{I}{I_{\text{sat}}}\left(\frac{\frac{\Gamma^2}{4}}{(\omega - \omega_{12})^2 + \frac{\Gamma^2}{4}}\right)} $$

That means the absorption coefficient has a Lorentzian lineshape, implying Power Broadening. This is due to saturation which reduces absorption near resonance while far from resonance the absorption changes little.

Therefore the scattering force is generalised to $$ F = \hbar k R_{\text{scatt}} = \hbar k \frac{dN_2}{dt} $$

\[ = \hbar k \frac{\Gamma}{2} \frac{I}{I + I_{\text{sat}}\left(1 + \frac{4\Delta^2}{\Gamma^2}\right)} \]

At low intensity: \(F\propto I\) At high intensity: \(F_{max} = \hbar k\Gamma / 2\) as discussed in Light Forces

docs.title: Amplitude Mode Excitation
docs.text:
Compared to the 'rolling the gutter mode', remember that there is another mode called amplitude mode excitation where the change of order parameter requires energy. The question is what type of quantum mechanical excitation is described by this?

Note that when approaching the bottom when \(T > T_c\), the excitation behaves like a harmonic oscillator. i.e.

the excitation is oscillating in amplitude (of energy, the excitation from \(n\) to \(n+1\) becomes a particle) rather than the angles in Goldstone mode. The free energy equation is then the Ginzburg-Landau model $\(f \approx \frac{\mu^2\phi^2}{2}\)$ where it describes the particle excitations with mass. Since this excitation has mass, from the particle dispersion, the curve is the bold line where the energy is its rest mass when it is stationary. The mass of the particle is $\(m = \mu \ = \sqrt{\text{curvature of the potential well}}\)$ Since the harmonic oscillation i.e. the square term in the Ginzburg-Landau model is associated with the mass (mass = sqrt of curvature), $\(\begin{aligned} \frac{\mu^2}{2} \phi^2 \quad & \text{often called the mass term} \\ \frac{\lambda}{4!} \phi^4 \quad & \text{often called the interaction term} \end{aligned}\)$

\[ \hat{L}_y = -i\hbar \left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial x} - x \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \right) \] \[ \hat{L}_z = -i\hbar \left( x \frac{\partial}{\partial y} - y \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \right) \]

docs.title: Spatial symmetry and angular momentum
docs.text:
Angular momentum is zero for spherically symmetric wavefunction, ie only a function of the radial coordinate.

If we have \(\psi = x + iy\), the eigenvalue equation is $\(L_z (x + iy) = \hbar(x+iy)\)$ where \(x+iy\) is the eigenfunction of \(\hbar\)

docs.title: Eigenfunctions of \(L_z\)
docs.text: $$ L_z \Phi_m = m\hbar \Phi_m $$ where \(m \in \mathbb{Z}\) is the eigenvalues of the eigenfunction \(\Phi_m\) and \(\hbar\) is inserted for convenience.

docs.title: Eigenfunctions of \(L^2\)
docs.text:
Above eigenvalue equation can be replaced by spherical harmonics

$$ L_z Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi) = m\hbar Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi) $$ and the total angular momentum eigenvalue equation is

\[ L^2 Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi) = l(l+1)\hbar^2 Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi) \]

Skipping bunch of nasty steps including Legendre polynomials and shits, we get the allowed values of \(m\) to be $$ m = -l, -l+1, \ldots, 0, \ldots, l-1, l $$ (\(l\) can be obtained by solving the eigenvalue equation of total angular momentum)

docs.title: Spherical harmonics \(Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi)\)
docs.text:
This is the common eigenfunctions to \(L_z\) and \(L^2\) and from bunch of steps, we get that the possible values of \(m\) is \(-l \leq m \leq l\)

When dealing with spherical polar coordinates, we need \(r\), \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) to define a coordinate. So the time independent wavefunction turns from \(\psi(x, y, z) = X(x)Y(y)Z(z)\) to \(\psi(r, \theta, \phi) = R(r)Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi)\). Move to here for more information.

  • \(l\) is orbital quantum number, representing the total angular momentum magnitude (orbital shape)
  • \(m\) is magnetic quantum number, representing the projection of angular momentum along the \(z\)-axis (orbital orientation).

In the diagram, \(l\) is the length of the slanted side of the cone, setting the shape of the orbital, whereas \(m\) is the \(z\)-component of the angular momentum, setting the orbital orientation in 3D space ie (is it pointing along the \(x, y\) or \(z\) axis?). So height of the cone is determined by \(m\) and the slant length is determined by \(l\).

docs.title: Weiss theory of antiferromagnetism
docs.text:
Antiferromagnetic lattice can be separated into two ferromagnetic sub-lattices

and each magnetisation on each sub-lattices are equal but opposite$$ B_{\text{mf}}^+ = -|\lambda| M^- $$ $$ B_{\text{mf}}^- = -|\lambda| M^+ $$

where the up sublattice is indicated by \(+\) and down sublattice is \(-\) and the directions of the molecular field is opposite to the direction of the sublattice.

$\(\implies \frac{M^{\pm}}{M_s} = \frac{\mu_B (B + B_{\text{mf}}^{\pm})}{k_B T} = \frac{\mu_B (B - |\lambda| M^{\mp})}{k_B T}\)$ where \(M^+ = M^- = M\)

\[\implies \chi = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_B M_S}{k_B \left[ T + \frac{|\lambda| \mu_B M_S}{k_B} \right]} \propto \frac{1}{T + T_N} \]

But does the line looks like before \(T_N\) (Neel temperature)?

So the idea is to get rid of the discontinuity by replacing the pupil function \(f(x',y')\) with \(\text{apod} (x)\) which remove the side discontinuity (by using a transmission filter on the lens).

Some function are suggested:

This is therefore getting rid of the high frequency region i.e. low pass filter.

docs.title: Ramsey method
docs.text:
• Using two pulses of radio field

Sequence: 1. At T = 0, the first \(\pi/2\)-pulse is applied to the atoms to put them into a superposition state: $\(\psi(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\left|1\rangle + i|2\rangle \right)\)$ 2. Then the atoms undergo free evolution $\(\psi(T) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\left|1\rangle + ie^{-i\omega_{12}T}|2\rangle \right)\)$ 3. Then the second pulse is applied the state is then $$ \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -ie^{-i\omega T} \ -ie^{i\omega T} & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & ie^{-i\omega T} \ -ie^{i\omega T} & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$ $$ \implies \psi_{\text{final}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 - e^{i \Delta T} \right) |1\rangle - \frac{i}{2} \left(1- e^{-i \Delta T} \right) |2\rangle $$

\[ \implies |c_2|^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 + \cos \Delta T \right] = \cos^2 \frac{\Delta T}{2} \]

docs.title: Band Theory - interaction between lattice + electrons
Nearly free electrons
docs.text:
Recall that in a crystal \(\underline{k} = \underline{k} + \underline{G}\) and the energy \(E = \hbar^2k^2/2m\)

Electrons will Bragg scatter by lattice potential $\(\Delta\underline{k} = \underline{k}_j - \underline{k}_i = \underline{G}\)$ and the scattering occurs at \(|k| = \pi/a\). Its wavefunction is then $\(\Psi = A(e^{i\pi x/a}\pm e^{-i\pi x/a})\)$ However, if we consider the near Brillouin Zone where \(k = \pm \pi/a\), the free electron energies at \(k\) and \(-k\) are degenerate - they have the same energy. Hence we use the Degenerate perturbation theory.

In real crystal, electrons feel a periodic potential due to the positively charged ions. To the perturbation is then$$ \left[ - \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m} \frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}} + V(x) \right] \psi(x) = E \psi(x) $$ We consider two states $$ \psi_k(x) = e^{ikx} \quad \text{and} \quad \psi_{k-G}(x) = e^{i(k-G)x} $$ We write a trial solution as:

\[ \Psi(x) = Ae^{ikx} + Be^{i(k-G)x} $$ Refer to the definition of $W_{ij}$ in [Degenerate perturbation theory](Degenerate perturbation theory.md), the eigenvalue problem is $$ \begin{pmatrix} E_k^{(0)} & V_G \\ V_G^* & E_{k-G}^{(0)} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A \\ B \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} A \\ B \end{pmatrix} $$ And by solving it gives $$E = E_k^{(0)} \pm |V_g|\]

Physically, it means that due to the periodic potential from the positively charged ion, the energy level is splitted into two levels

where the bottom band is the valence band and the top band is the conduction band.

The valance band shapes like this because away from \(k = \pm \pi/a\), the periodic potential is weak, so it follows the original free electron parabola approximately. Near it, because of the mixing and repulsion, the energy bands downwards. The gap between the bands is the energy required for the electrons to jump from the valence band to the conduction band (forbidden band)

docs.title: Canonical Transformations and Poisson Brackets
docs.text: A transformation is by definition canonical if it preserves the structure of Hamilton's equations for all dynamical systems. Hence, for a specific dynamical system, a new Hamiltonian \(H'\) that is a function of \(Q\) and \(P\) is produced and Hamilton's equations for \(H'\), \(P\) and \(Q\) must describe the correct transformed dynamics.

docs.title: The generating function
docs.text:
\(F(q,Q,t)\) is called a generating function.

By doing this, we can get $$ \frac{\partial L'}{\partial \dot{Q}} = -\frac{\partial F}{\partial Q} \Rightarrow P = -\frac{\partial F}{\partial Q} $$ where \(P\) is the canonical momentum and \(Q\) is the generalised coordinate and \(F\) is the generating function.

Generating function interchanges the coordinates and momenta.

docs.title: Transformed Hamiltonian
docs.text:
The aim is to convert \(H(q,p,t)\) to \(H'(Q,P,t)\)

\[ \begin{align} H'(Q, P, t) &\equiv P \dot{Q} - L' \\ &= -\frac{\partial F}{\partial Q} \dot{Q} - L + \frac{\partial F}{\partial q} \dot{q} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial \dot{Q}} \dot{Q} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} \\ &= p \dot{q} - L + \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} \\ &= H(q, p, t) + \frac{\partial F(q, Q, t)}{\partial t} \end{align} \]

docs.title: Poisson Brackets
docs.text:
$$ {F, G} \equiv \sum_{k=1}^{N} \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial q_k} \frac{\partial G}{\partial p_k} - \frac{\partial F}{\partial p_k} \frac{\partial G}{\partial q_k} \right) $$ Poisson brackets of conjugate variables are

\[\{q,q\}=0, \quad \{p,p\}=0, \quad \{q,p\}=1$$ and for a transformation to be canonical, the condition is that $$\{Q,P\} = 1\]

docs.title: Poisson bracket formulation of Hamilton's equations
docs.text: The Hamilton's first two equations of motion can be written as $\(\dot{q}=\{q,H\} \quad, \quad \dot{p} = \{p,H\}\)$

docs.title: Cartesian separability
docs.text: Recall that the Fresnel diffraction integral is $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)}(x,y) &= \frac{1}{i\lambda z} e^{ik\overline{r}} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x',y') E^{(0)} e^{-\frac{ik(xx' + yy')}{z}} e^{\frac{ik\rho'^2}{2z}} dx' dy' \end{align} $$ There is a situation when the aperture function is separable i.e. \(f(x',y') = g(x')h(y')\). In that case the integral becomes $$ E^{(z)}(x,y) = \frac{E^{(0)}}{i\lambda z} e^{ikz} \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x') e^{\frac{ik(x-x')^2}{2z}} dx' \right] \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(y') e^{\frac{ik(y-y')^2}{2z}} dy' \right] $$

docs.title: Example:
docs.text:
A uniform input field in \(x'\) or \(y'\) direction, i.e. long slits.

For \(y'\) axis, \(h(y') = 1\) so the integral over \(y'\) is $$ \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ik(y-y')^2/(2z)} dy' &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ik(y'-y)^2/(2z)} d(y'-y) \quad \text{(Symmetry)} \ &= \sqrt{\frac{2z}{k}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{it^2} dt \quad \text{(Let } t = (y'-y)\sqrt{k/(2z)}) \ &= \sqrt{\frac{2\pi z}{k}} e^{i\pi/4} \quad \text{(Fresnel integral identity)} \end{align} $$ and the Fresnel diffraction integral for long slits as $$ E^{(z)}(x,y) = \frac{E^{(0)}}{\sqrt{i \lambda z}} e^{ikz} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x') e^{\frac{ik(x-x')^2}{2z}} dx' $$

docs.title: Note
docs.text: This example is for \(y'\) axis only. Be sure to know which axis to calculate in the exam.

docs.title: Two interacting bodies
docs.text: Central forces are the forces that only depend on the distance \(r\) between two bodies, directed along the line between them. The general case of 2 point masses has a Lagrangian of $$ L = \frac{1}{2} (m_1 \dot{r}1^2 + m_2 \dot{r}_2^2) - \underbrace{V_1(r_1) - V_2(r_2)} $$ and if there is no external potentials, then the Lagrangian is translationally invariant i.e. }} - \underbrace{V_{12}(|r_1 - r_2|)}_{\text{interaction potential}\(L(r_1, r_2, \dot{r}_1, \dot{r}_2) = L(r_1 + a, r_2 + a, \dot{r}_1, \dot{r}_2)\)

docs.title: Ignorable CoM Motion and conservation of momentum
docs.text:
The Lagrangian above can be rewritten in terms of \(\underline{R}\), \(R = \frac{m_1 r_1 + m_2 r_2}{m_1 + m_2}\) and the relative coordinate \(\underline{r} = \underline{r_1} - \underline{r_2}\) $$ L = \frac{1}{2} M \dot{\underline{R}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \mu \dot{r}^2 - V_{12}(r) $$ where \(M = m_1+m_2\) and \(\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1 +m_2)\). \(R\) is an ignorable coordinate as it does not explicitly appear in the Lagrangian.

If we switch to CoM frame (a frame moving with CoM), the \(\underline{R} = \underline{\dot{R}} = 0\) and thus, \(L = (1/2)\mu \underline{\dot{r}}^2 - V_{12}(r)\) (rotational invariant)

By using spherical coordinates $$ L = \frac{1}{2} \mu \left[ \dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + r^2 \dot{\phi}^2 \sin^2 \theta \right] - V_{12}(r) $$ where the angular momentum in \(z\) direction is $$ p_{\phi} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\phi}} = \mu r^2 \dot{\phi} \sin^2 \theta = \text{constant} \equiv J_z $$

For any choice of z axis, the angular momentum in that direction is constant. Without loss of generality, we can choose the coordinates such that \(J\) always lies along the z axis

docs.title: Equivalent 1D problem
docs.text: We wish to remove the \(\theta\) and \(\dot{\phi}\) term to simplify the calculation. Following the Lagrangian in the spherical coordinates, we substitute \(\dot{\theta} = 0\), \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\dot{\phi} = J/\mu r^2\) (because \(J= rp =\mu r^2\dot{\phi}\)), we get the total energy is$$ E = \frac{1}{2} \mu \dot{r}^2 + \underbrace{\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2} + V_{12}(r)}{V $$ The effective potential is the combination of the angular momentum barrier (centrifugal force since it arises from the choice of reference frame, not other physics) and interaction potential. The Euler-Lagrange equation yields $$ \mu \ddot{r} = \frac{J^2}{\mu r^3} - \frac{\partial V_{12}}{\partial r} $$ which will be used }}(r)in the next chapter

docs.title: Charge density in conductors
docs.text:
Bulk charge density in conductors are fast and we can assume that there is no bulk charge density inside conductors.

Using Ohm's law (\(\underline{E} = \underline{J}\rho_n\)), Maxwell I and the continuity equation $$ \underline{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{\underline{J}} = - \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} $$ we use dimensionality argument to find the characteristic life-time, \(\tau\) is $$ \tau = \rho_n \varepsilon_0 $$

Where: - \(\tau\): Charge relaxation time - \(\rho_n\): Resistivity of material - \(\varepsilon_0\): Permittivity of free space

Physical Meaning: Time for charge density to reduce to \(1/e\) in a conductor.

To a good approximation, we assume that \(\rho = 0\), hence $$ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0 \quad \text{(Maxwell I for conductors)} $$

docs.title: Circular aperture and Fresnel zone
docs.text:
Consider an aperture with radius \(R_A\). We use polar coordinate to simplify the problem.

Recall from Fresnel diffraction integral that the diffraction integral is $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)}(x,y) &= \frac{1}{i\lambda z} e^{ik\overline{r}} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x',y') E^{(0)} e^{-\frac{ik(xx' + yy')}{z}} e^{\frac{ik\rho'^2}{2z}} dx' dy' \end{align} $$ By using polar coordinates, the equation becomes $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)}(0,0) &= \frac{E^{(0)}}{i\lambda z}e^{ikz} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{R_A} e^{ik\rho'^2/(2z)} \rho' d\rho' d\theta \ &= \frac{E^{(0)}}{i\lambda z}e^{ikz} 2\pi \int_0^{R_A} e^{ik\rho'^2/(2z)} \rho' d\rho' \ &= \frac{E^{(0)}}{i\lambda z}e^{ikz} \pi \int_0^{R_A} e^{ik\rho'^2/(2z)} d\rho'^2 \ &= \frac{E^{(0)}}{i\lambda z}e^{ikz} \frac{2\pi z}{ik} \left[ e^{ik\rho'^2/(2z)} \right]_0^{R_A} \ &= -E^{(0)}e^{ikz} \left( e^{ikR_A^2/(2z)} - 1 \right) \ &= -2i E^{(0)} e^{ikz} e^{ikR_A^2/(4z)} \sin\left( \frac{kR_A^2}{4z} \right) \end{align} $$ where we use \(u\) substitution to get from step 2 to 3.

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
By taking the modulus squared, the intensity is $$ \begin{align} I^{(z)} &= 4 I^{(0)} \sin^2\left( \frac{k R_A^2}{4 z} \right) \ &= 4 I^{(0)} \sin^2\left( \frac{\pi R_A^2}{2 \lambda z} \right) \ &= 2 I^{(0)} \left[ 1 - \cos\left( \frac{\pi R_A^2}{\lambda z} \right) \right] \end{align} $$

The extrema (max and min) of the intensity is \(m\pi\) and by breaking up the aperture into concentric rings with radius \(\rho_m\), we can create Fresnel zones

This circles are not a screen. The wavelets from each zone interfere each other differently

docs.title: Circular basis
docs.text:
This basis is useful for light-matter interactions. We use two circularly polarised waves with opposite handedness, both with the same wavevector and angular frequency \(\omega\). The unit vectors are $$ \begin{align} \hat{\epsilon}+ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\hat{\epsilon}_1 + i\hat{\epsilon}_2) \tag{100} \ \hat{\epsilon}- &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\hat{\epsilon}_1 - i\hat{\epsilon}_2) \tag{101} \end{align} $$

They are complex and orthonormal. The coefficient is for normalisation.

Similar to Linear Basis, the most general polarised plane wave (elliptical polarisation) in the circular basis is:

\[ \underline{E} = \underline{E}_+ + \underline{E}_- = (E_+ \hat{\epsilon}_+ + E_- \hat{\epsilon}_- e^{i\varphi}) e^{i(\underline{k}\cdot\underline{r}-\omega t)} \tag{102} \]

docs.title: Circular birefringence
docs.text:
Types of circular birefringence:

  • Natural optical activity (originated from chirality of the materials)
  • Induced circular birefringence arise from Faraday effect in magnetic materials

We express the linearly polarised light in circular basis Linear polarisation in a circular basis where $\(\underline{E}^{(0)} = E_0(\hat{\epsilon_+} + \hat{\epsilon_-})e^{i\omega t}\)$ where \(\varphi = 0\) and \(\underline{r} = 0\)

Similar to Linear birefringence, the field after propagating a distance \(\underline{r}\) is $$ \begin{split} E^{(\mathcal{L})} &= E_{0}\left(e^{in_{\mathrm{L}}k\cdot r}\hat{\epsilon}{+}+e^{in}}k\cdot r}\hat{\epsilon{-}\right)e^{-i\omega t}\ &= E}\left(\hat{\epsilon{+}+e^{i\varphi}\hat{\epsilon} \end{split} $$where }\right)e^{i(n_{\mathrm{L}}k\cdot r-\omega t)\(\varphi=2\pi(n_{\mathrm{R}}-n_{\mathrm{L}})z/\lambda\) and \(\lambda\) is the vacuum wavelength. The result shows that light is still linearly polarised but the direction of polarisation is rotated by an angle \(\beta\), given by $$ \beta=-\frac{\varphi}{2}=\frac{\pi r}{\lambda}\left(n_{\mathrm{L}}-n_{\mathrm{R}}\right) $$

docs.title: Circular polarisation in a circular basis

docs.title: Circular polarisation in a linear basis
docs.text:
Circularly polarised waves are achieved by having \(\underline{E_1}\) and \(\underline{E_2}\) with equal amplitudes and a phase difference of \(\pm \pi/2\).

  • Left circularly polarised: \(\varphi = +\pi/2\)
  • Right circularly polarised: \(\varphi = -\pi/2\)

docs.title: How to define left or right circularly polarised?
docs.text:
Point the thumb in the direction of \(\underline{k}\) and the electric field rotates in the direction of the other right (left) four fingers, then it's right (left) circularly polarised.

This is left circularly polarised diagram:

Using the equation in Linear polarisation in a linear basis that $$ \begin{align} E &= E_1 + E_2 = (E_1 \hat{\epsilon}_1 + E_2 \hat{\epsilon}_2 e^{i\varphi}) e^{i(kx-\omega t+\phi_1)} \end{align} $$ we could get the circularly polarised electric field in a linear basis: $$ \begin{align} E_{\rm L}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}E_0\left(\hat{\epsilon}1+i\hat{\epsilon}_2\right)e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\ E \end{align}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}E_0\left(\hat{\epsilon}_1-i\hat{\epsilon}_2\right)e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)} $$

docs.title: Colliods I   Single colloids and van der Waals interactions
docs.text: [!Definition] Small (not significantly influenced by gravity), insoluble particles of solids or droplets of liquid dispersed into a liquid, e.g. inks and emulsions

docs.title: Single Colloids
docs.text:
A spherical colloidal particle with radius \(a\) moving with a velocity \(v\) in a liquid density of \(\rho\) and viscosity \(\eta\) is so small that inertial forces (rotating frame forces involving mass term) are negligible i.e. $$ Re = \frac{\rho v a}{\eta} = \frac{\text{inertial forces}}{\text{viscous forces}} \ll 1 $$

and the force exerted on it is dominated by viscous force \(F_s = 6\pi a \eta v\)

docs.title: Brownian motion
docs.text:
In fact Brownian motion overcomes the effect from gravity. To describe Brownian motion, we can use the random walk model similar to the one we mentioned in polymer (Flory and random walk models). Here we want to find the mean square displacement of the particle, \(\langle\vec{R}(t)^2\rangle\) due to the Brownian motion.

The equation of motion of the particle is described by $$ \underbrace{m\frac{d^2 \vec{R}(t)}{dt^2}}\text{Force} + \underbrace{\xi \frac{d\vec{R}(t)}{dt}}\text{Stokes' law} = \vec{F}{\text{random}} $$ where \(\xi = 6\pi a \eta\) . Since the directions will be independent on each other, we can just take the \(x\) direction $$ m \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + \xi \frac{dx}{dt} = F $$ $$ \implies \frac{\xi}{2} \frac{d\langle x^2 \rangle}{dt} = \langle x F_{\text{random}, x} \rangle - m \underbrace{\frac{d}{dt} \langle x \frac{dx}{dt} \rangle}_{0} + m \left\langle \left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 \right\rangle $$}, x

where \(\frac{dx^2}{dt} = 2x \frac{dx}{dt} \quad \text{and} \quad x \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = \frac{d}{dt} \left( x \frac{dx}{dt} \right) - \left( \frac{dx}{dt} \right)^2\)

We take the Equipartition Theorem which states every degree of freedom will have \(m\langle v_x^2 \rangle / 2 = k_B T / 2\), so: $$ \frac{\xi}{2} \frac{d\langle x^2 \rangle}{dt} = m \langle v_x^2 \rangle = k_B T \implies \frac{d\langle x^2 \rangle}{dt} = \frac{2k_B T}{\xi} $$

[!Results] $$ \langle x^2 \rangle = 2Dt, \quad D = \frac{k_B T}{\xi} = \frac{k_B T}{6\pi a \eta} $$

and \(\langle\vec{R}(t)^2\rangle = 2nDt\) since \(\langle\vec{R}(t)^2\rangle = n\langle x \rangle ^2\) where \(n\) is the number of dimensions in the system.

docs.title: Forces between colloidal particles
docs.text:
There are two forces acting between colloidal particles

  1. Van der Waals attraction force (\(U \propto r^{-6}\)), which is the sum of

    • Keesom Interactions
    • Debye interactions
    • London dispersion interactions

  2. Double layer repulsive force

docs.title: Keesom Interaction
docs.text: Two freely rotating permanent dipole will tend to attract each other because they preferentially orient with their opposite charges facing each other $\(U \propto r^{-6}\)$

docs.title: Debye Interaction
docs.text: A molecule with a static dipole will interact with a polarisable molecule by inducing a temporary dipole moment in the polarisable molecule. $$ U_{\text{Debye}}(r) = -\frac{p^2 \alpha}{(4\pi \epsilon \epsilon_0)^2 r^6} = -\frac{C_{\text{Debye}}}{r^6}, \quad C_{\text{Debye}} > 0 $$

docs.title: London dispersion interactions
docs.text:
• it's about local charge density fluctuations
  • When the electrons circulate around nuclei at finite frequencies, at each instant, the atom has a net dipole moment. Two atoms will therefore experience an average attractive force. $$ U_{ ext{London}}(r) = - rac{3}{2} rac{\alpha_A \alpha_B}{(4\pi \epsilon \epsilon_0)^2 r^6} rac{h u_A u_B}{ u_A + u_B} = - rac{C_{ ext{disp.}}}{r^6}, \quad C_{ ext{disp.}} > 0$$

docs.title: From molecular pairs to macroscopic forces
docs.text:
To calculate the van der Waals interaction between macroscopic objects, it is therefore essential to integrate pair molecule interactions over the whole object/particles.

Essentially, if we want to find the total interaction between two particles/objects with finite volumes, we are finding: $\(U_{\text{tot}}=\int \int U(r)\rho_1dV_1\rho_2dV_2\)$

For example, interaction between molecule and a ring of semi-infinite solid we have

$$ U_{\text{tot}}(r) = \int_{z=r}^{\infty} \int_{x=0}^{\infty} 2\pi x \, dz \, dx \, \rho \frac{-C}{\left(\sqrt{z^2 + x^2}\right)^n} $$ where \(dV = 2\pi x \ dz \ dx\) (circumference times area) and \(U(r) = -C/r^n\)

Another example is a sphere of radius \(R\) and an infinite planar surface:

Same method is used for sphere-sphere interaction. The volume is calculated by first find the area of an infinitesimally small ring \(A = 2\pi x \ dx\) and use chord theorem \(x^2 = z(2r-z)\) where \(x\) is the length of chord and \(z\) is the length from centre of chord to the circumference. Then integrate it over the radius. Remember that the \(r\) term in \(U(r)\) is defined as the distance between the (currently) interacting object. In the sphere-wall interaction case, \(r\) is from the wall to the ring.

docs.title: Colliods II   Double layer forces and the DLVO theory
Double layer forces
docs.text:
• Occur when charged solids are immersed into a liquid that contain ions.
  • When the solids are immersed into the liquid, the ionisation of the surface group or adsorption causes the surface charge imbalance.
  • To maintain the neutrality, the ions from the liquids adsorb to the surface, creating an ionic concentration gradient
  • This gradient could repel (most cases)/attract another solid in a similar condition

We try to quantify the potential and ionic density near the interface. For some reason without derivation, the ions in the presence of an electrical potential \(\psi\) has the chemical potential of $$ \mu_{\text{ion},i} = \mu_{0,i} + k_B T \ln(\rho_i) + z_i e \psi $$ where \(\rho_i\) is the concentration of ions of type \(i\) (per volume) and \(z_i\) is the valency of ions (e.g. for Ca\(^{++}\) is +2 ) .

At equilibrium \(\mu_{\text{ion},i} = cte\), we rearrange for \(\rho_i\) and this is the Boltzmann equation that describes the ionic concentration profile of the counter-ions $$ n_i = \underbrace{e^\frac{\mu_{\text{ion},i} - \mu_{0,i}}{k_B T}}{n_0} e^{-\frac{z_i e \psi}{k_B T}} $$ We also have consider the potential screening effect from the ions i.e. potential is related to the distribution of net charge (in other words, both influence each other). This is Poisson equation$$ \underbrace{ze\rho(x)}\text{total charge at \(x\)} = -\varepsilon \varepsilon_0 \frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2} $$where we consider only a dimension. Combining them gives $$ \frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2} = -\frac{z_i e \rho(x)}{\varepsilon \varepsilon_0} = -\frac{z_i e \rho_0}{\varepsilon \varepsilon_0} e^{-\frac{z_i e \psi(x)}{k_B T}} $$ (Boltzmann-Poisson equation) - This is the general case

docs.title: Example on a solid in an electrolyte of NaCl
docs.text:
Debye screening length is \(1/\kappa\) where $$ \kappa = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i \rho_{0,i} z_i^2 e^2}{\varepsilon \varepsilon_0 k_B T}} $$ is the screening effect in the electrolyte. Beyond this length, the direct electrostatic interaction between two charged objects rapidly falls to zero. Since potential is related to force, the double layer force decays exponentially with the Debye length.

\(\psi = \psi_0 e^{-\kappa x}\)

docs.title: Consequences of Symmetry Properties of Wave Functions
docs.text:
Recalling from Exchange Operators and Pauli Exclusion Principle where we discussed the wave function of the bosons: $\(\psi(r, r') = \frac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')+\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ and fermions $\(\psi(r, r') = \frac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')-\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ Here we want to investigate the quantum force which is fictitious and originates from the symmetry of the wave functions.

Starting from the distinguishable particles, we calculate for the probability for the particles to appear in the same position: $\(\psi_{\text{cl}}(\vec{r}, \vec{r}') = \phi_1(\vec{r}) \phi_2(\vec{r}')\)$ $\(\implies P(\vec{r}, \vec{r}') = |\psi_{\text{cl}}(\vec{r}, \vec{r}')|^2 = |\phi_1(\vec{r})|^2 |\phi_2(\vec{r}')|^2\)$

Now we investigate bosons, $\(|\Psi_{+1} (\vec{r}, \vec{r}')|^2= 2 |\phi_1(\vec{r})|^2 |\phi_2(\vec{r})|^2\)$

We find that the probability of those two bosons appearing at the same position is twice as much as the probability of distinguishable particles. This is quantum attractive force which is not real. We also consider fermions case where $\(|\psi_- (\vec{r}, \vec{r})|^2 = 0\)$ And this is quantum repulsive force.

docs.title: Coupled Small Oscillations
docs.text: In the coupled pendulums, the kinetic energy is given: $$ T = \frac{m l^2}{2} \left( \dot{\theta}1^2 + \dot{\theta}_2^2 \right) $$ and the potential energy due to the gravity is $$ V \left( \theta_1^2 + \theta_2^2 \right) $$ where the cosine component in gravitational potential energy is approximated using taylor series. Since the pendulums are coupled by a spring at half length of the string, so there is a elastic potential energy: $$ V_{\text{coupling}} = \frac{k}{2} \left( \frac{l}{2} \right)^2 (\theta_2 - \theta_1)^2 $$ The Lagrangian of the system is then $$ L = \frac{m l^2}{2} \left( \dot{\theta}_1^2 + \dot{\theta}_2^2 \right) - \frac{1}{2} \left( m g l (\theta_1^2 + \theta_2^2) + k \left( \frac{l}{2} \right)^2 (\theta_2 - \theta_1)^2 \right) $$ The expansion leads to awkward maths step, so we change the frame of reference to the centre of mass and relative motion, }} = \frac{m g l}{2\(\theta_c = \frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2}\), \(\theta_r = \theta_2 - \theta_1\), \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{g}{l}}\) and coupling constant, \(\eta = \frac{k l}{4 m g}\) gives the equations of motion $$ \ddot{\theta}_c + \omega_0^2 \theta_c = 0 $$ for separated pendulums where the pendulums move in phase and $$ \ddot{\theta}_r + \omega_0^2 (1 + 2\eta) \theta_r = 0 $$ for coupled pendulums where the pendulums move out of phase. This refers to the modes of vibration

docs.title: Matrix form of Lagrange equation
docs.text:
Starting with an example on free vibrations of a diatomic molecules. We define the Lagrangian coefficient matrices as $$ \tau_{jk} = \left. \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial \dot{q}j \partial \dot{q}_k} \right| $$ and $$ v_{jk} = \left. \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial q_j \partial q_k} \right|_{q=0} $$ We will arrive at an eigenvalue problem which will be discuss in }=0Normal Modes

Why should we use the matrix form? - Make the algebra easier - To decouple the term \(q_i q_j\) - More efficiency in solving

When should we use? - Coupled systems - Small oscillation around an equilibrium - More than one coordinate

docs.title: Number of states

The number of states is defined as $\(\text{No.of states} = \frac{\text{Volume of all states}}{\text{Volume of one state}}\)$

For example, for a 3D k-space sphere, the number of states is given: $\(N(k) = \frac{\frac{4\pi}{3}k^3}{(\frac{2\pi}{L})^3} = \frac{Vk^3}{6\pi^2}\)$ By considering the dispersion relation as discussed previously \(\omega = v_s k\) for condensed matter and the fact that there are 3 polarisations, we get $\(N(\omega) = \frac{V\omega^3}{2\pi^2v_s^3}\)$ where we have multiplied the whole shit by 3.

docs.title: Total number of phonons and total energy
docs.text:
With all these shit, we are able to derive another shit bunch of stuff cibai:

\[\text{Total number of phonons} = \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{\text{No. of phonons}}{\text{No. of state}} \cdot \frac{\text{no. of states}}{\Delta \omega} \Delta\omega$$ or based on [Statistical Physics](Statistical Physics.md) it's $$N = \int_0^\infty g(\omega)f_{\text{BE}}(\omega)d\omega$$$$\implies \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{1}{e^{\hbar\omega/kT}-1} g(\omega)d\omega$$ and for total energy, simply multiply the energy inside of the integral $$E = \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{1}{e^{\hbar\omega/kT}-1} g(\omega)d\omega \hbar\omega\]

By substituting the 3D sphere we did before into the formula and we get $\(E\propto T^4\)$ and that \(C = \partial E/ \partial T = 4BT^4\) where \(B\) is the coefficient of the proportionality. The Debye temperature is \(\hbar \omega_D = k_B\theta_D\) where \(\omega_D\) is the Debye angular frequency.

docs.title: Debye (cibai) approximation
docs.text:
The vibration of the particles in condensed matter is quantised into wave-like excitation, described by Bose statistic.

  • The dispersion is \(\omega = v_s |k|\) for low \(T\)
  • There is a max frequency

If \(T\ll\theta_D\), then low \(T\) limit If \(T\approx \theta_D\), then high \(T\) limit

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text: The waves keep repeating itself, say after length \(L\). Then the wavefunction is then $\(\Psi(x) = \Psi(x+L)\)$ From there, you should be able to use the trial solution and derive a boundary conditions or quantisation. The spacing \(\Delta k\) = \(k_{n+1} - k_n = 2\pi/L\)

docs.title: Number of states
docs.text:
The number of states is defined as $\(\text{No.of states} = \frac{\text{Volume of all states}}{\text{Volume of one state}}\)$

For example, for a 3D k-space sphere, the number of states is given: $\(N(k) = \frac{\frac{4\pi}{3}k^3}{(\frac{2\pi}{L})^3} = \frac{Vk^3}{6\pi^2}\)$ By considering the dispersion relation as discussed previously \(\omega = v_s k\) for condensed matter and the fact that there are 3 polarisations, we get $\(N(\omega) = \frac{v\omega^3}{2\pi^2v_s^3}\)$ where we have multiplied the whole shit by 3.

docs.title: Density of states, \(g(\omega)d\omega\)
docs.text: It is defined as the number of states between \(\omega\) and \(\omega + d\omega\) and is taken as $\(g(\omega) = \frac{dN(\omega)}{d\omega}\)$

docs.title: Total number of phonons and total energy
docs.text:
With all these shit, we are able to derive another shit bunch of stuff cibai:

\[\text{Total number of phonons} = \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{\text{No. of phonons}}{\text{No. of state}} \cdot \frac{\text{no. of states}}{\Delta \omega} \Delta\omega$$ $$\implies \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{1}{e^{\hbar\omega/kT}-1} g(\omega)d\omega$$ and for total energy, simply multiply the energy inside of the integral $$E = \int^{\omega_D}_0 \frac{1}{e^{\hbar\omega/kT}-1} g(\omega)d\omega \hbar\omega\]

By substituting the 3D sphere we did before into the formula and we get $\(E\propto T^4\)$ and that \(C = \partial E/ \partial T = 4BT^4\) where \(B\) is the coefficient of the proportionality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
1. Macrostate:

    • Specification of a system using microscopic quantities such as particle number N, volume, energy, temperature, pressure and fields

  2. Microstates

    • Complete specification of the system such as position/momentum of particle in the system

      [!note] 1. Microcanonical ensemble: systems specified by N, U, V 2. Canonical ensemble: systems specified by N, T, V 3. grand canonical ensemble: systems specified by \(\mu\) (Fermi energy), T, V

  3. Distribution

    • An intermediate state between macro and micro that can be described by some other quantity of the whole system (grouping microstate into different categories)

  4. Probability

    • For a system where we perform an experiment, an event \(i\) occurs \(n_i\) times; then the frequency of occurrence is \(\frac{n_i}{N}\). Probability is $$ P_i = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{n_i}{N} $$

docs.title: Simplifying the eigenvalue problem
docs.text:
As we can see from previously, the eigenvalue problem has a non-zero diagonal which can make the operation very messy. The idea here is to simplify by choosing a smart basis to manually make the \(W_{ab}\) terms equal zero.

So we can choose a Hermitian operator \(A\) that 1. Commutes with \(H^0\): - \([A, H^0]\) = 0, so \(A\) shares eigenfunctions with \(H^0\) (as discussed very very early in this module) 2. Lifts the degeneracy in \(A\) - \(A\psi_a^0 = \mu \psi_a^0\) and \(A\psi_b^0 = v \psi_b^0\) with \(\mu \neq v\) 3. Commutes with \(H'\) - \([A,H']\) = 0

docs.title: Higher order degeneracy
docs.text: This generalises easily to \(n\)-fold degeneracy. We form the matrix elements $$ W_{ij} = \langle \psi_i^0 | H' | \psi_j^0 \rangle $$ where we get an \(n \times n\) matrix with \(n\) separate roots.

docs.title: Degenerate perturbation theory and hydrogen II
Meaning of spin-orbit term
docs.text:
Goal: To derive spin-orbit term (perturbed energy)

Starting from the total angular momentum, we have $\(J^2 = L^2 + S^2 +2 \vec{L}\cdot \vec{S}\)$$\(\implies \boldsymbol{L} \cdot \boldsymbol{S} = \frac{1}{2} \left( J^2 - L^2 - S^2 \right)\)$ Since they are equal, the eigenvalue of \(\boldsymbol{L} \cdot \boldsymbol{S}\) and \(\frac{1}{2} \left( J^2 - L^2 - S^2 \right)\) are actually the same, i.e. the eigenvalue is$$ \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2} \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - s(s+1) \right] = \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2} \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right] $$ Recall from Degenerate perturbation theory and hydrogen that \(H'_{\text{so}} = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 c^2 m^2 r^3} \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}\) and from Time-independent perturbation theory that \(E_{nlj,\mathrm{so}}^{1} = \langle \psi_{nlj} | H_{\mathrm{so}}' | \psi_{nlj} \rangle\), we can combine them as $$ E_{nlj,\mathrm{so}}^{1} = \langle \psi_{nlj} | H_{\mathrm{so}}' | \psi_{nlj} \rangle = \frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\epsilon_{0} c^{2} m^{2}} \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2} \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right] \langle \psi_{nlj} | r^{-3} | \psi_{nlj} \rangle $$ We then evaluate the bra-ket on the RHS. Recall from Finding the Hydrogen Wavefunction that the expectation value of r, \(\langle r \rangle\) is \(\langle \psi_0^* | r | \psi_0 \rangle\), the above equation gives $$ E_{nlj,\text{so}}^{1} = \frac{e^2 \hbar^2}{16 \pi \epsilon_0 c^2 m^2} \frac{j(j+1) - l(l+1) - 3/4}{l(l+1/2)(l+1) n^3 a^3} $$ Using the definition of Bohr radius, \(a\), \(e^2/4 \pi \epsilon_0 = \hbar^2/a m\) and \(E_n^0 = -\hbar^2/2 m a^2 n^2\) (which is obtained from the unperturbed Hamiltonian in Time-independent perturbation theory where \(\hat{H} = -(\hbar^2/2\mu) \nabla^2 - e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r\) and \(H\psi = E\psi\)), the final equation is $$ E_{nlj,\text{so}}^1 = \frac{(E_n^0)^2 n \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right]}{mc^2 \, l(l + \frac{1}{2})(l+1)} $$ and this is the spin-orbit term.

docs.title: Summarising these messy shits
docs.text: So bascially we have unperturbed Hamiltonian and energy as defined as $\(H^{0} \psi_{n}^{0} = E_{n}^{0} \psi_{n}^{0}\)$ and we have a perturbed energy as defined by $\(E_{nlj,\mathrm{so}}^{1} = \langle \psi_{nlj} | H_{\mathrm{so}}' | \psi_{nlj} \rangle\)$ The goal is to derive the perturbed energy in term of unperturbed one. To start, we first realise that Hamiltonian of perturbed energy is (obtained from magnetic potential energy) \(H'_{\text{so}} = -\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s \cdot \underline{\boldsymbol{B}}\), where \(\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = -\frac{e}{m_e} \boldsymbol{S}\) and \(L = r m_e v = \frac{r m_e 2\pi r}{P} = \frac{2\pi m_e r^2}{P} = \frac{2\pi m_e r^2 I}{e} = \frac{4\pi m_e r^3 B}{\mu_0 e}\). By combining those, we have $\(H_{\text{so}}' = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 c^2 m^2 r^3} \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}\)$ What else to do? We find \(H'_{SO} \psi_{nlm} = E'_{SO} \psi_{nlm}\) by finding the eigenvalue (since \(E'\) is the eigenvalue). We do this by starting from total angular momentum \(J^2\). The eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{L}\) is then like this $\(\hat{\mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{L}} = \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2} \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right]\)$ Subs into \(H_{\text{so}}'\) and by realising the definition of perturbed energy, we do the bra-ket operation, subs in Bohr radius, find initial Hamiltonian from the defined unperturbed Hamiltonian to get the final result $$ E_{nlj,\text{so}}^1 = \frac{(E_n^0)^2 n \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right]}{mc^2 \, l(l + \frac{1}{2})(l+1)} $$

docs.title: Correction to the electron-proton potential energy (Darwin's term)
docs.text:
Very well, congrats of getting here after those messy fucking operations. I promise what you learn so far will make you easily understand this part. No surprise that other than the SOC, there is another correction (perturbation) to be considered: Darwin term defined as $$ H_D^1 = \frac{\pi \hbar^2}{2 m^2 c^2} \frac{e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \delta(\boldsymbol{r}) $$ and this only happens when the electron is at the same position as the proton

Similarly, recall that \(E_{nlj,\mathrm{so}}^{1} = \langle \psi_{nlj} | H_{\mathrm{so}}' | \psi_{nlj} \rangle\), we get $$ E_n^1 = \frac{\pi \hbar^2}{2m^2 c^2} \frac{e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \int_V \psi_{nlm}^* \, \delta(r) \, \psi_{nlm} \, dV $$ For the integral part, take a look at the behavior. Since we have said that it happens when the electron is at the same position as the proton, it only acts at the origin. So based on the Laguerre solution \(R_{nl}\) in Finding the Hydrogen Wavefunction, we look for the value of \(l\) when \(R_{nl}(r = 0) \neq 0\), which obviously only \(l = 0\) work. So $$ E_n^1 = \frac{\pi \hbar^2}{2 m^2 c^2} \frac{e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} |\psi_{n00}(0)|^2 $$ The significance is like this: there is a probability of electron appearing in the nucleus in a region very close to the nucleus and the probability density is spread out (zitterbewegung effect).

At \(r=0\), all the Laguerre polynomials for \(l=0\) are \(L_{n-1}^1(0)\) and this is the constant term in the polynomial. Hence we get \(|\psi_{n00}(0)|^2 = 1/\pi a^3 n^3\) and $$ E_n^1 = \frac{\pi \hbar^2 e^2}{2 m^2 c^2 4 \pi \epsilon_0} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi a_0^3 n^3} = \frac{\hbar^4}{2 m^3 c^2 a_0^4 n^3} $$ Recall that \((E_n^0)^2 = \hbar^4/(4m^2 a^4 n^4)\), hence $\(E_n^1 = \frac{c}{mc^2}(E_n^0)^2n\)$

docs.title: Relativistic corrections to kinetic energy
docs.text:
Right, the end of this chapter (finally). We look at relativistic corrections to kinetic energy \(E^2 = (T + mc^2)^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4\): $$ T + mc^2 = mc^2 \sqrt{1 + \frac{p^2}{m^2 c^2}} $$

We expand it (using binomial expansion or taylor series): $\(T \approx \frac{p^2}{2m} - \frac{1}{8}\frac{p^4}{m^3 c^2} = T^0 - \frac{1}{2m}(T^0)^2\)$ Here we can see that the second term \(H'_r = (T^0)^2/2m\) is the lowest order correction term. We make a little operation here: \(H'_r = (H^0 - V(r))^2/2mc^2\). Ahhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh everything is easily here: \(E_{nlj,\mathrm{so}}^{1} = \langle \psi_{nlj} | H_{\mathrm{so}}' | \psi_{nlj} \rangle\) do this shit but in integral form. If we do it correctly (dont think too much, just expand the term and then separate the integral, since you have three terms after expanding the square term), you will get $$ E_{\text{r}}^1 = -\frac{1}{2mc^2} \left[ (E_n^0)^2 - 2E_n^0 \langle V(r) \rangle + \langle V(r)^2 \rangle \right] $$

Here: - \(\langle V(r) \rangle = [-e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0)]\langle 1/r\rangle\) and \(\langle 1/r\rangle = 1/an^2\) based on virial theorem - \(\langle V(r)^2 \rangle = [-e^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0)]^2\langle 1/r^2\rangle\) and \(\langle 1/r^2\rangle = 1/[a^2 n^3 (l +1/2)]\)

Subs these, \(a\) and \(E^0\) into the corrected kinetic energy, you get $$ E^1 = -\frac{(E_n^0)^2}{2mc^2} \left[ \frac{4n}{l+1/2} - 3 \right] $$

docs.title: In summary
docs.text:
The perturbations of hydrogen atoms are: - Spin-orbit coupling - Darwin term - Relativistic kinetic energy

And their perturbed energy are: - $$ E_{nlj,\text{so}}^1 = \frac{(E_n^0)^2 n \left[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right]}{mc^2 \, l(l + \frac{1}{2})(l+1)} $$ - $\(E_n^1 = \frac{c}{mc^2}(E_n^0)^2n\)$ - $$ E^1 = -\frac{(E_n^0)^2}{2mc^2} \left[ \frac{4n}{l+1/2} - 3 \right] $$

docs.text: Energy level \(n\) in hydrogen is - \(n^2\) degenerate (without spin) - 2\(n^2\) degenerate (with spin, with additional \(m_s = \pm 1/2\))

docs.title: Spin-orbit coupling (a perturbation to energy of a particle of non-heavy elements)
Idea
docs.text:
Classically, we say the electron is orbiting the nucleus in nucleus and lab view. However, due to relativistic effect, in the electron's view, the nucleus is orbiting around the electron and hence, it experiences an electric and magnetic fields (due to moving charge particles). The magnetic field couples \(L\) and \(s\) which will perturb the energy of electrons and cause an energy level splitting.

Nuclei do not experience magnetic field like electrons do even though it sees electrons orbiting around them. This is because in lab view, nuclei are stationary and have zero spin. So they experience (if any) negligible effect of SOC

  • Heavy atoms like gold, bismuth and lead do not experience SOC as a mere perturbation. Instead, because their inner electrons move very close to the speed of light, so we should include the term in our initial Hamiltonian.

We ultimately want to find the perturbed potential due to the magnetic dipole momentum generated by electron spin i.e. $$ H'_{\text{so}} = -\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s \cdot \underline{\boldsymbol{B}} $$

docs.title: Finding \(\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s\)
docs.text: Recall that the spin angular momentum is (info here) \(\mu_s = -g_s \left( \frac{e}{2m_e} \right) S\) where the g-factor is approximately 2. So the equation is $$ \underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = -\frac{e}{m_e} \boldsymbol{S} $$

docs.title: Finding \(\underline{\boldsymbol{B}}\)
docs.text: $$ L = r m_e v = \frac{r m_e 2\pi r}{P} = \frac{2\pi m_e r^2}{P} = \frac{2\pi m_e r^2 I}{e} = \frac{4\pi m_e r^3 B}{\mu_0 e} $$ where \(B = \mu_0 I/2r\) and \(I = e/P\) where \(P = 2\pi r/v\) is the orbital period

docs.title: Combining
docs.text:
It gives $$ H_{\text{so}}' = -\boldsymbol{\mu}_s \cdot \boldsymbol{B} = \frac{e}{m} \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \left( \frac{e}{4\pi\epsilon_0 c^2 m r^3} \boldsymbol{L} \right) = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 c^2 m^2 r^3} \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{L} $$

But due to special relativity, the correct perturbation term is being approximately half in magnitude:

$\(H_{\text{so}}' = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 c^2 m^2 r^3} \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}\)$and it matches with the experimental findings. This effect is called Thomas' precession and takes into account relativistic time dilation between the electron and the nucleus.

docs.title: Commutation properties
docs.text:
Remember the smart operator we mentioned in Degenerate perturbation theory II? We are going to use the total angular momentum \(\boldsymbol{J} = \boldsymbol{L} + \boldsymbol{S}\) where \(J^2\) and \(J_z\) commute with all of our original operators and with the perturbation

\[ [J^2, \boldsymbol{L} \cdot \boldsymbol{S}] = 0 $$ $$ [J^2, \boldsymbol{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{L}] = 0 \]

So we are going to use joint eigenfunctions of operators \(H^0, \quad L^2, \quad J^2, \quad S^2, \quad J_z\)

docs.title: Maximum and minimum values of \(m_J\)
docs.text:
Recall that - \(m_l = -l, -l+1, ..., 0, ..., l-1, l\) - \(m_s = -s, ..., s\) - \(s = 1/2\) for electron

Hence the maximum value of \(m_J\) is \(m_J = l + s\) and minimum value is \(m_J = -l-s\). The range runs in integer steps, the eigenvalue is \(j(j+1)\hbar^2\)

Basically: - Eigenvalue of \(L^2\) is \(l(l+1)\) - Eigenvalue of \(S^2\) is \(s(s+1)\) - Eigenvalue of \(J^2\) is \(j(j+1)\)

The range of \(j\) is \(|l-s| < j < l+s\) and \(-j < m_j < j\)

docs.title: Twofold degeneracy
docs.text:
Let's say there are two orthogonal states \(\psi_{a}^{0}\) and \(\psi_{b}^{0}\) that have the same energy \(E^0\), then the linear combination $$ \psi^{0} = \alpha \psi_{a}^{0} + \beta \psi_{b}^{0} $$ is also have the same energy as \(E^0\)

Then we introduce a perturbation \(\lambda H'\) to break the degeneracy, causing \(E^0\) to split into two values, \(E^0 + \lambda E^1\) with two values of \(E^1\) (the perturbation cause the initial energy level to break into two, one higher and another one lower). Our task is to find \(H^1\) and \(\alpha\), \(\beta\).

Remember that $$ H^0 \psi^1 + H' \psi^0 = E^0 \psi^1 + E^1 \psi^0 $$as found in the previous session. By multiplying that shit by the conjugate of one of our states \(\psi_a^{0*}\) gives $$ \langle \psi_{a}^{0} | H' | \psi^{0} \rangle = E' \langle \psi_{a}^{0} | \psi^{0} \rangle $$$\(\implies \alpha \langle \psi_a^0 | H' | \psi_a^0 \rangle + \beta \langle \psi_a^0 | H' | \psi_b^0 \rangle = E^1 \alpha\)$ by substituting \(\psi^0\) by \(\psi^{0} = \alpha \psi_{a}^{0} + \beta \psi_{b}^{0}\)

Now we interested in matrix form. We could express it as $$ \alpha W_{aa} + \beta W_{ab} = \alpha E^{1}, \quad \text{where} \quad W_{ij} = \langle \psi_{i}^{0} | H' | \psi_{j}^{0} \rangle $$ $$ \implies \begin{pmatrix} W_{aa} & W_{ab} \ W_{ba} & W_{bb} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \ \beta \end{pmatrix} = E^1 \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \ \beta \end{pmatrix} $$

This is just a eigenvalue equation. The only non-trivial solutions are where the determinant = 0 (so it cannot be inverted): $$ \left( W_{aa} - E^1 \right) \left( W_{bb} - E^1 \right) - W_{ab} W_{ba} = 0 $$ and as \(W_{ab} = W_{ba}^*\) so $\((E^1)^2 - (W_{aa} + W_{bb}) E^1 + (W_{aa} W_{bb} - |W_{ab}|^2) = 0\)$ Then we can solve for \(E^1\) (it has two values, yes). And to get the values of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), simply substitute this into the matrix equation.

docs.title: Density of States, Expectation Values and DeBroglie Thermal Wavelength
Derivation and Understanding
docs.text:
For a Fermi sphere with quantum states residing in it, the density of state can be easily obtained:

$$ g(k) \, \delta k = \frac{\text{Volume of shell}}{\text{Volume of quantum state}} = \frac{4 \pi k^2 \delta k}{(\pi/a)^3} \frac{1}{8} $$ where \(\delta k\) is the thickness of the shell and the quantum states are arranged periodically. The reason why it is \((\pi /a)^3\) is because of boundary condition

The 1/8 contribution on the RHS is because we are considering only the positive \(k_x, k_y, k_z\) so we are using the first octant (quadrant in 2D, imagine you have a sphere and cut it with vertical and horizontal planes). If we use different boundary condition, i.e. \(2\pi / a\) , we do not need the factor because we accounted all plane waves state

We can also express it in terms of \(\varepsilon = \hbar^2 k^2/2m\) and we find that

[!Result] \(g(k) \sim k^2\) \(g(\varepsilon) \sim \sqrt{\varepsilon}\) For doubly occupied states such as spins, multiply them by 2

docs.title: Expectation value
docs.text:
[!note] We define the expectation value of quantity \(Q\) as $\(\langle Q \rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_j n_jQ_j\)$ just like \(U = \sum_j n_j \varepsilon\)

In previous chapter, we mention that \(n_j=f_j g_j\) . Subs \(f\) (e.g. MB) into the equation above and we have $$ \frac{ \sum_j g_j e^{-\beta \epsilon_j} Q_j}{\sum_j g_j e^{-\beta \epsilon_j}} = \frac{Z(Q_j)}{Z} $$

If we deal with macroscopic continuum, we have

[!Result] $$ \langle Q \rangle = \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty} g(\varepsilon) e^{-\beta \varepsilon} Q(\varepsilon) \, d\varepsilon}{\int_{0}^{\infty} g(\varepsilon) e^{-\beta \varepsilon} \, d\varepsilon} $$ which is similar to the expectation value in Quantum Mechanics (bra-ket notation in integral format). But note that this is the average i.e. total / number of particle. Be careful if you want the total or the average.

docs.title: Dilution Limit in terms of DeBroglie Wavelength
docs.text:
In Introduction to Density of States and Fermi-Dirac Curve, we mentioned that when \(f_j = n_j / g_j \ll 1\), the quantum phenomena is negligible and the BE and FD distributions approximate to MB distribution.

Following from \(f = e^{-\alpha} e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}\) for MB, we must have \(e^{-\alpha} \ll 1\) because \(e^{-\beta \varepsilon_j}\) is a constant for any \(j\). $\(\implies Z = \sum_j g_j e^{-\beta \varepsilon_j} = \int_0^\infty g(k) e^{-\beta E(k)} \, dk = \int_0^\infty \frac{V}{2\pi^2} k^2 e^{-\beta \left( \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m} \right)} \, dk\)$ Using the Gaussian integral: $$ \int_0^\infty x^2 e^{-\lambda x^2} \, dx = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\lambda^3}} $$ we get

[!note] $$ Z = V \left( \frac{2\pi m}{\beta h^2} \right)^{3/2} = \frac{V}{\lambda_D^3} $$

where \(\lambda_D = h \sqrt{\frac{\beta}{2\pi}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2\pi m k_B T}}\) is the DeBroglie Wavelength (characteristic length associated with dilute limit).

Here to justify this is the characteristic length, we use equipartition theorem to find $$ \left\langle \frac{p^2}{2m} \right\rangle = \frac{3}{2} kT \implies \left\langle p^2 \right\rangle = 3mkT $$ and we then use de Broglie \(\lambda = h/p\) to get the exact same thing as \(\lambda_D\). So the Gaussian integral is consistent with the de broglie wavelength

[!note] - If \(\lambda_D < a\) (interparticle spacing), particles are further apart than this classical measure, hence dilute. - If \(\lambda_D > a\), particles are close together, closer than classical measure. Are they dilute? No → Quantum

Remember the mean speed of particles and Root mean square speed is different. Mean speed is the average speed of the particles and root mean square speed, \(v_{RMS} = \sqrt{\langle v^2 \rangle}\) is the characteristic speed associated with the thermal energy of the system.

docs.title: Diamagnetism
docs.text:
Diamagnetism has a negative susceptibility as mentioned in Fundamental Equations for Magnetism, it implies that the \(B\)-field of the solid is smaller than the \(B\)-field of the vacuum, causing it to repel from a magnetic substance.

As stated in Hund's Rule, diamagnetic substances have full shell (no unpaired electron), so it does not have magnetic moment without external field. Therefore we are calculating the susceptibility based on the fact (in quantum mechanics) that the external field will distort the orbital motion of electrons.

docs.title: Classical Physics
docs.text:
We revisit the Larmor precession in Fundamental Equations for Magnetism and the basic equation of magnetic moment $\(\mu = I\mathbf{A} = -\frac{eB}{4\pi m} \pi \langle\rho^2\rangle\)$ where \(\langle \rho^2\rangle\) is the mean square radius and \(I = e/T = e/ (2\pi/\omega)\). Here we assume a spherically symmetric atom \(\langle r^2 \rangle = \langle x^2 \rangle + \langle y^2 \rangle + \langle z^2 \rangle\) and since \(\mu_z\) is unchanged, we have only two direction components \(\langle \rho^2 \rangle = \frac{2}{3} \langle r^2 \rangle\).

Subs into the magnetic moment equation and assuming there are \(n\) atoms/ions per unit volume, each with \(Z\) electrons, we have $\(M = -\frac{n e^2 Z B \langle r^2 \rangle}{6m}\)$ For weak magnetisation, we have \(B = \mu_0 (H + M) \approx \mu_0 H \implies \chi = M/H = M/(B/\mu_0)\), giving $$ \chi = -\frac{n e^2 \mu_0 Z \langle r^2 \rangle}{6m} $$ Fucking ppiece of shittzshu nugget

docs.title: Quantum Mechanics
docs.text:
We start from the electron Hamiltonian in a magnetic field $$ \hat{H} = \frac{(\mathbf{p} + e\mathbf{A})^2}{2m} + V + g_s \gamma \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{s} $$which will essentially give $$ \hat{H} = \left( \frac{\mathbf{p}^2}{2m} + V \right) + \underbrace{\gamma \mathbf{B} \cdot (\mathbf{L} + g_s \mathbf{s})}{\text{paramagnetic term}} + \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{8m} (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{r})^2} $$}

After identifying the diamagnetic term inside, we use first order perturbation theory to find the energy change to the ground state wavefunction $$ \Delta E = \frac{e^2}{8m} \langle 0 | (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{r})^2 | 0 \rangle = \frac{B^2 \langle 0 |(x^2 + y^2) | 0 \rangle}{8m} $$ Since \(\langle x^2 \rangle = \langle y^2 \rangle = \frac{\langle r^2 \rangle}{3}\), we have $$ \Delta E = \frac{e^2 B^2}{12m} \langle r^2 \rangle $$ For \(\mu = -\frac{d(\Delta E)}{dB}\), we have $$ M = -\frac{n e^2 Z B}{6m} \langle r^2 \rangle $$ $$ \chi = \frac{\mu_0 M}{B} = -\frac{n e^2 \mu_0 Z \langle r^2 \rangle}{6m} $$

docs.title: Diatomic Molecules
docs.text: In diatomic molecules, there are four degree of freedom - translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic. Their partition function is $\(Z = Z_{\text{cm}} Z_{\text{rot}} Z_{\text{vib}} Z_{\text{elec}}\)$

docs.title: Electronic
docs.text:
\[ Z_{\text{elec}} = \sum_j e^{-\beta \epsilon_j} = e^{-\beta \epsilon_0} \left( 1 + e^{-\beta (\epsilon_1 - \epsilon_0)} + e^{-\beta (\epsilon_2 - \epsilon_0)} + \dots \right) \]

Second order (first excitation) of \(Z_{\text{elec}}\) gives the 'active' temperature for electronic degree of freedom is around \(T \sim 10^5\)K . Just equate the energy to \(k_B T\)

If we take the first order, there is zero heat capacity, meaning that the system is not absorbing energy and it is true only if \(T < 10^5\)K

docs.title: Vibration
docs.text:
We treat diatomic molecule as a SHO where $\(\varepsilon_n = (n+1/2) \hbar\omega\)$ For ground state, the partition function is obtained by substituting the energy above to \(Z\) and use geometric series $$ Z_{\text{vib}} = \frac{e^{-\beta \hbar \omega / 2}}{1 - e^{-\beta \hbar \omega}} $$

giving $$ U_{\text{vib}} = -N \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z_{\text{vib}} = \frac{N \hbar \omega}{2} + \frac{N \hbar \omega}{e^{\beta \hbar \omega} - 1} $$

The temperature for this to occur is \(T \sim 5000\) K. Therefore for low temperature limit, we can just use the second order

But we use need high temperature limit, we need to include higher order terms $$ Z_{\text{vib}} = e^{-\beta \hbar \omega / 2} \left( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} e^{-\beta \hbar \omega n} \right) $$

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
The angular momentum of a diatomic molecule is quantised $\(L^2=l(l+1)\hbar^2\)$ $\(L_z = m\hbar\)$

The energy is then obtained from the quantum rigid motor where Hamiltonian \(H = L^2/2I\) $$ \varepsilon_l = \frac{1}{2}\frac{L^2}{I} = \frac{\hbar^2}{2I} l(l+1) $$ and it gives $$ Z_{\text{rot}} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} g(l) e^{-\beta \varepsilon_l} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (2l+1) e^{-\beta \left( \frac{\hbar^2}{2I} l(l+1) \right)} \approx \int_{0}^{\infty} (2l+1) e^{-\beta \left( \frac{\hbar^2}{2I} l(l+1) \right)} \, dl $$ at high temperature where we replace summation with integral and using a fucking computer, we have

[!Partition Function of Vibrational State] $\(Z_{\text{rot}} = \frac{2I}{\hbar \beta}\)$

At low temperature limit, we just have to take \(l=0,1\) from the partition function and it gives $\(Z_{\text{rot}} = 1 + 3e^{-\beta\hbar^2/I}\)$

docs.title: Dielectric Function
docs.text: We first consider the Claussius-Mossotti relationship between relative permittivity to the polarisability. Let's start with polarisation (analogous to magnetisation)$\(P = N\mu = N\alpha E_{\text{local}}\)$ where \(\mu = \alpha E_{\text{local}}\) and \(E_{\text{local}} = E_{\text{macro}} + \frac{P}{3\epsilon_0}\) as derived here. From definition of electric displacement \(D = \epsilon_0 E_{\text{macro}} + P = \epsilon_0 \epsilon_r E_{\text{macro}}\): $\(\frac{\epsilon_r - 1}{\epsilon_r + 2} = \frac{N\alpha}{3\epsilon_0} \quad \text{(Claussius-Mossotti)}\)$ Here the \(E_{\text{macro}}\) is the internal macroscopic field i.e. sum of external and depolarising fields

docs.title: Electronic Polarisation and Clausius-Mossotti Relation
docs.text:
Let's us take a look at one of the mechanism.

When there is an oscillating local electric field: $\(\mathbf{E}_{\text{local}}(\omega) = \mathbf{E}_0 \exp(i\omega t)\)$ the electron position will be shifted in sync with the electric field: $\(\mathbf{r}(\omega) = \mathbf{r}_0 \exp(i\omega t)\)$ but since the nucleus of the atom is trying to pull the electron back to equilibrium $\(K = m\omega_0^2\)$ Now we write the force equation involving only two forces:

[!note] $\(m \mathbf{\ddot{r}} = -K\mathbf{r} - e\mathbf{E}_{\text{local}}\)$

By substituting the electric field and the electron position into the differential equation and solve it and consider the polarisability we get

[!note] $\(\alpha(\omega) = \frac{e^2}{m(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)}\)$ where \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{K/m}\)

By using the Clausius-Mossotti we have $\(\epsilon_r(\omega) = 1 + \frac{Ne^2}{m\epsilon_0(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2) - (Ne^2/3)}\)$

but in reality thats not very accurate, there suppose to have a term of \(i\gamma\omega\) to get the experimental graph

where the change is maximum at natural frequency.

docs.title: Diffraction
docs.text:
We need to consider diffraction if the assumption \(D\ll d\), where \(D\) is the diameter of the holes and \(d\) is the separation between the holes, does not hold.

Huygens-Fresnel principle states: Every point on a wavefront is itself the source of spherical wavelets and the secondary wavelets emanating from different points mutually interfere. The sum of these spherical wavelets forms a new wavefront. $$ \tilde{U}(P) = \oint_{\Sigma} d\tilde{U}(P) $$ Where: - \(\tilde{U}(P)\) is the complex amplitude (electric field \(E\)) at observation point \(P\) - \(d\tilde{U}(P)\) is the contribution from a secondary wavelet originating at infinitesimal area \(d\Sigma\) on surface \(\Sigma\) - The integral is taken over any closed surface \(\Sigma\) separating the source and observation point

Here, we take the limit \(N \to \infty\) where \(N\) is the number of holes.

docs.title: Dimensionality
docs.text:
We use exchange interaction between spins as example on how dimensionality will affect the presence of phase transition.

Recall that the exchange interaction term is $\(\hat{H}_{\text{mag}} = \sum_{i,j} -J_{ij} \mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j\)$ We also define \(D\) as the dimension of the spin and \(d\) as the dimension of the lattice. In \(d= 1, D=1\) (1D Ising model) case, when \(N\) spins are all aligned, we have the energy as $\(E = -(N-1)\frac{J}{4}\)$ If we flip one spin, the energy cost i.e. change in energy is $\(E = \frac{J}{2}\)$ Future me: you might get \(-J/4\) because you should consider change. Initially it was \(-J/4\) but you flip from negative to positive, so the change is \(J/2\).

We also have to consider the entropy due to the change. As there are \(N-1\) ways to put the wall, we have $\(k_BT \ln(N-1)\)$ So the free energy of the system is then $$ F_1 = -(N-1)\frac{J}{4} + \frac{J}{2} - k_B T \ln(N-1) $$

docs.title: Dispersion Relation and Slow, Fast Light
docs.text:
Recall from Optical Beats and Frequency Comb that the group velocity is \(\Delta \omega/\Delta k = c\), we are going to explain and derive the group velocity. Consider the Taylor expansion of dispersion relation $$ \omega(k) = \omega_c + \frac{d\omega}{dk} \bigg|_{k=k_c} (k-k_c) + \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2\omega}{dk^2} (k-k_c)^2 + \cdots $$ We then subs this, up to first order into the Hedgehog equation we get $\(\mathcal{E}(z,t) = e^{i(k_c z - \omega t)} \underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} A(k) \exp \left[ i(k-k_c) \left( z - \frac{d\omega}{dk}t \right) \right] dk}_\text{treat this as an envelope function}\)$ Since we treat the integral as an envelope function and we can see that this is a Fourier integral where the peak occurs when the phase factor is zero i.e. $\(\left(\frac{d\omega}{dk}\right)_{k_c} t = z \implies v_{gp}=\frac{d\omega}{dk}\)$

From here, we can also derive the group velocity in terms of dispersion relation by noting that \(ck = n(\omega)\omega\) $\(\implies v_g = \frac{c}{n + \omega \frac{dn}{d\omega}}\)$

docs.title: Slow Light
docs.text: Using this formula, we can modify the dispersion relation to slow the light. For example, the noble winning cold Cs atom that slows the light to 600ms\(^{-1}\). This is achieved by turning a 2-level atom to 3-level by introducing a probe laser to induce EIT. By using a probe laser, we change the dispersion relation of the ultracold atom

docs.title: Fast Light
docs.text: It is possible for the wave packet to travel faster than light if we look at the formula closely. However, it is possible because the transfer of information cannot be faster than light

docs.title: Group Velocity Dispersion
docs.text:
The third term of Taylor expansion $\(\frac{d^2\omega}{dk^2} (k-k_c)^2\)$ is the dispersion of the group velocity i.e. it changes the shape change as the wave packet propagates. See Electromagnetic waves. This is the main effect of long-distance communication where the information will be spread and merge with other information.

To quantify the broadening, we have $\(\Delta t = |D| z \Delta \lambda\)$ where \(|D|\) is the temporal broadening and \(z\) is the propagation distance.

docs.title: Displaced slit
docs.text:
THe Fraunhofer diffraction formula predicts the translational invariance (constant diffraction pattern when we translate the position of the field/aperture within the input plane).

In this example, we will displace the slit to \(x' = d\) rather than the origin. $$ g(x') = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x' \in (-\infty, d - a/2] \ 1 & \text{if } x' \in (d - a/2, d + a/2] \ 0 & \text{if } x' \in (d + a/2, \infty) \end{cases} $$ Using the Fraunhofer integral, we get $$ \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x') e^{-i 2 \pi x x' / (\lambda z)} dx' &= \int_{d-a/2}^{d+a/2} e^{-i 2 \pi x x' / (\lambda z)} dx' \ &= \frac{e^{-i 2 \pi x x' / (\lambda z)} \big|_{d-a/2}^{d+a/2}}{-i 2 \pi x / (\lambda z)} \ &= e^{-i 2 \pi x d / (\lambda z)} \cdot a \operatorname{sinc}\left(\frac{\pi a x}{\lambda z}\right), \end{align} $$ and

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
Fraunhofer diffraction formula becomes $$ I^{(z)}(x,y) = I_0 \frac{a^2}{\lambda z} \operatorname{sinc}^2\left(\frac{\pi a x}{\lambda z}\right) $$

This gives the same result as before. The translational displacement \(d\) of the aperture induces an additional path length, \(dx/z\), resulting in a global phase of \(2\pi xd/z\). This suggests that under Fraunhofer approximation, the additional path length is the same for all points on the slit.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
Based on Boltzmann, the entropy of a system is $$ S({n_j}) = k_B \ln \Omega({n_j}) = k_B \ln \left( \frac{N!}{\prod_j n_j!} \right) $$ where $$ \Omega({n_j}) = \frac{N!}{n_1! \, n_2! \, \dots} = \frac{N!}{\prod_j n_j!} $$ is the microstate. Here we can use this to find the most probable distribution, given that the system will tend to maximise its entropy.

To maximise the entropy, use Lagrangian multiplier where $$ L = N \ln N - \sum_j n_j \ln n_j - \alpha \sum_j n_j - \beta \sum_j n_j \epsilon_j $$ given the constraints $$ N = \sum_j n_j, \quad U = \sum_j n_j \varepsilon_j $$ and it yields the results of internal energy of the system:

[!Internal Energy] $$ U = -N \frac{d}{d\beta} \ln Z $$

where \(Z\) is the partition function $$ e^{-\alpha} = \frac{N}{\sum_j e^{-\beta \epsilon_j}} = \frac{N}{Z} $$

docs.title: Vortices
docs.text: This is the defect for 2d material e.g. superfluid. To quantify the properties of vortices, we need to define a few physical properties $\( egin{aligned} & ext{Velocity} \qquad \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r}) = rac{\hbar}{m} \mathbf{ abla} heta \qquad \qquad \mathbf{ abla} imes \mathbf{v} = 0 \[1.5em] & ext{Circulation} \qquad \kappa = \oint \mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{l} \ &\phantom{ ext{Circulation} \qquad \kappa} = rac{\hbar}{m} \oint \mathbf{ abla} heta \cdot d\mathbf{l} \ &\phantom{ ext{Circulation} \qquad \kappa} = rac{\hbar}{m} \Delta heta \end{aligned}\)$ where \(\Psi = \sqrt{n}e^{i heta}\). And from the form of \(\Psi\), we have to have \(\Delta heta = 2\pi w\) where \(w\) is the winding number (how many times arrows rotate through \(2\pi\) as you traverse a loop around the defect). From the range of \(\Delta heta\), we can redefine those formulae above: $\( egin{aligned} &\kappa = rac{h}{m}w \[2em] &\mathbf{v} = rac{\kappa}{2\pi r} \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi \ &= rac{w\hbar}{mr} \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi \end{aligned}\)$ where \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi\) is the unitary vector.

docs.title: Double slit revisited
docs.text:
Recall Double slit that we looked before.

Based on Fraunhofer diffraction as Fourier transform that the aperture function can be written as the convolution of single aperture and the sum of delta function: $$ g(x^{\prime})=\text{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)\ast\left[\delta\left( x^{\prime}+\frac{d}{2}\right)+\delta\left(x^{\prime}-\frac{d}{2}\right)\right] $$ and the Fourier transform of the aperture function is then $$ \mathcal{F}\left[g(x^{\prime})\right]=\mathcal{F}\left[\text{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)\right]\mathcal{F}\left[\delta\left(x^{\prime}+\frac{d}{2}\right)+\delta\left(x^{\prime}-\frac{d}{2}\right)\right] $$ where $$ \mathcal{F}\left[\delta\left(x^{\prime}+\frac{d}{2}\right)+\delta\left(x^{\prime}-\frac{d}{2}\right)\right] =e^{i\pi ud}+e^{-i\pi ud}=2\cos(\pi ud) $$ and $$ \begin{align} \mathcal{F}\left[\text{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)\right] &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\text{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)e^{-i2\pi ux^{\prime}}dx^{\prime} \ &= \int_{-a/2}^{a/2}e^{-i2\pi ux^{\prime}}dx^{\prime} \ &= a sinc(\pi au), \end{align} $$ where \(u = x/\lambda z\)

docs.title: Tip
docs.text: The Fourier transform of a rect function is sinc function.

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text: Use the intensity in Fraunhofer diffraction as Fourier transform it becomes $$ \begin{align} I^{(z)} &= \frac{4I_{0}}{\lambda z}a^{2}\cos^{2}(\pi ud) sinc^{2}(\pi au) \ &= \frac{4I_{0}}{\lambda z}a^{2}\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\pi xd}{\lambda z}\right)sinc ^{2}\left(\frac{\pi xa}{\lambda z}\right) \end{align} $$ which gives the same result as quoted in Double slit

docs.title: Oscillator driven by an external force
docs.text:
Consider an undamped oscillator, driven by a time-dependent external force, \(F(t)\) with no spatial dependence. The Lagrangian is $$ L = \frac{m \dot{q}^2}{2} - \left( \frac{m \omega^2 q^2}{2} - F(t) q \right) $$ which yields a differential equation: $$ \ddot{q} + \omega^2 q = \frac{F(t)}{m} $$ We want to split the driving force into an infinite number of impulsive forces and sum up the displacements caused by each of these impulsive forces to find \(q(t)\) using Dirac-\(\delta\) Function: $$ f(t') = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \delta(t - t') f(t) \, dt $$ where \(\delta(t-t')\) is the zero-width limit of a function/distribution of \(t\) and have inverse dimension.

With the tool, we can work out what the system was doing before an impulse, how the system responds to an impulse (\(G(t)\) is the solution when \(F(t)/m\) is replaced by \(\delta(t)\)) and how it continues after.

docs.title: Response of an oscillator to a \(q\)-independent Impulse force
docs.text:
With \(F(t) = K\delta(t-t')\) where \(K\) is the total impulse provided, integrating around \(t=t'\) gives $$ \int_{t'-\epsilon}^{t'+\epsilon} (\ddot{q} + \omega^2 q) \, dt = \int_{t'-\epsilon}^{t'+\epsilon} \frac{K}{m} \delta(t - t') \, dt $$ $$\implies \underbrace{\dot{q}(t'+\epsilon) - \dot{q}(t'-\epsilon)}{\text{Velocity jump}} + \underbrace{\omega^2 \int $$ $}^{t'+\epsilon} q(t) \, dt}_{\text{Vanishes as } \epsilon \to 0} = \frac{K}{m\(\implies \dot{q}(t'+\epsilon) = \dot{q}(t'-\epsilon) + \frac{K}{m}\)$

Hence, there is an instantaneous change in the velocity where $$ t'{\pm} = \lim t' \pm \epsilon $$ which is the definition of an impulsive force.

This is the time-evolution sequence of a SHO with an impulsive force. This can be explained that the delta function in \(F(t) = K\delta(t-t')\) is zero when \(t\neq t'\) so when they are the same, there is a velocity jump.

docs.title: Green's function \(G\)
docs.text:
The solution to the differential equation mentioned previously is called the Green's function $$ \ddot{G}(t - t') + \omega^2 G(t - t') = \delta(t - t') $$ scaled as \(G(t-t') = q(t)m/K\)

\[\implies G(t-t') = 0 , t-t' \leq 0\] \[\implies G(t - t') = \frac{1}{\omega} \sin\big(\omega [t - t']\big)\]

docs.title: General driving force \(F(t)\)
docs.text: The differential equation can be rewritten as $$ \ddot{q} + \omega^2 q = \left(\frac{1}{m}\right) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dt' \, F(t') \delta(t - t') $$ By subsituting the Green's function, we can get the equation of \(q(t)\): $$ q(t) = \frac{1}{m} \int_{-\infty}^{t} F(t') G(t - t') \, dt' $$
