docs.title: Earnshaw's Theorem
docs.text: • Point charges can't stay in stable equilibrium position using solely electrostatic forces

docs.title: Understanding
docs.text:
This theorem follows from Gauss law. Normally ions are trapped in vacuum so we expect the divergence of electric field is zero: $$ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0 $$ or $$ \oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 $$

Here we use the fact that the charge density is zero because 1. Ions are trapped in vacuum so there is no interacting free charge 2. Ions themselves cannot be considered as interacting free charge because this equation assumes free charges as the external factors that act on the ions

Here we consider the scalar potential:

To form a trap, we need a local minimum \(\nabla^2\Psi < 0\) but here we get zero that means we only have saddle point.

docs.title: Ladder Operators
docs.text:
For \(H\psi(x) = E\psi(x)\), the step-up operator is moving up the ladder in energies: $\(H(a_+\psi_n) = (E_n+\hbar\omega)a_+\psi_n\)$ and the step-down operator is moving down the ladder in energies: $\(H(a_-\psi_n) = (E_n-\hbar\omega)a_-\psi_n\)$ However, there is a bottom rung, i.e. \(a_-\psi_0 = 0\) where there is no more to move down.

Here, the Hamiltonian \(H\) is \(\hat{H} = \hbar\omega \left( \hat{a}_+ \hat{a}_- + \frac{1}{2} \right)\)

[!note] \(\hat{a}_{\pm} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\hbar m\omega}}(\mp i\hat{p} + m\omega \hat{x})\)

If operators commute, then they share a common set of eigenfunctions, so measuring one does not disturb the wavefunction for the measurement of the next.

docs.title: Elastic vs Inelastic Scattering
docs.text:
We want to investigate if a scattering event is elastic or not. If the collision is elastic then the momentum are fully conserved i.e. $\(w^\mu = p^\mu_e + p^\mu_P - p'^\mu_e = p_p^\mu + q^\mu\)$ where \(q^\mu = p^\mu_e - p_e'^\mu\).

We want to find \(Q^2\) and plot a graph to see what is the difference between elastic and inelastic scattering. We first define the velocity of proton: $$ u = rac{p_P^\mu \cdot q^\mu}{M_P} = rac{(M_P, \mathbf{0}) \cdot (E - E', \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}')}{M_P} = rac{E - E'}{M_P} $$

and we find $\({(w^\mu)}^2 = {(p^\mu_e + p^\mu_P - p'^\mu_e)}^2 = {p_p^\mu}^2 + 2M_p u - Q^2\)$

For elastic scattering, \((w^\mu)^2 = M_p^2 = (p_p^\mu)^2 \implies 2M_p u - Q^2 = 0\)

For inelastic scattering, proton absorbs energy from electron to excite and accelerate: \((w^\mu)^2 > M_p^2 = (p_p^\mu)^2 \implies 2M_p u - Q^2 > 0\)

Experimentally, the inelastic lineshape will be just a peak but since the energy of the electron will be used to excite the protons, so there will be many resonances. \(\Delta^+\) resonance is the first excited state of proton.

It will be great to quantify if the scattering is elastic or not. Using the fact that \(2M_p u - Q^2 = 0\) for elastic and \(2M_p u - Q^2 > 0\) for inelastic scattering. We define:

$\(\chi = rac{Q^2}{2M_p u}\)$ where \(0 \leq X \leq 1\) . Therefore, the Rosenbluth cross-section can be modified to include \(X\) $$ rac{d^2\sigma}{d(Q^2) d\chi} = rac{4\pi\alpha^2}{Q^4} \left[ \left(1 - y - rac{M_p^2 y^2 \chi^2}{Q^2} ight) rac{F_2(\chi, Q^2)}{\chi} + y^2 F_1(\chi, Q^2) ight] $$ where \(y = (P_P \cdot q)/(P_p \cdot P_e)\) and \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are analogous to \(g_E\) and \(g_M\). Oh for fuck sake.

If we have \(Q^2\) large enough, we can do scattering off of one of the constituents of proton which carries some fraction \(\eta\) of the proton 4-momentum. Given the conservation of momentum \(k^2 = (\eta P_p + P_e - P')^2\), we have $$ egin{aligned} 0 = (\eta P_P - q)^2 &= \eta^2 P_P^2 + 2\eta P_P \cdot q + q^2 = \eta^2 M_p^2 + 2\eta P_P \cdot q - Q^2 \ \[1em] &\Rightarrow \eta = rac{Q^2}{2P_P \cdot q} = rac{Q^2}{2M_p u} = X \end{aligned} $$ and if we plot the graph, we get

there is 1/3 chance of scattering elastically and 2/3 chance of not. The reason why experimentally we get broadening is that Toy model is not accurate as there are more quarks in proton.

We can do the same for magnetic scattering i.e. spin. We have relationships $$ oxed{ egin{aligned} ext{Spin } rac{1}{2} &: \quad 2X F_1 = F_2 \ \[0.5em] ext{Spin } 0 &: \quad 2X F_1 = 0 \end{aligned}} $$ Experimentally, we get

This implies that the constituents have spin-1/2 which are fermions

Each particle will have its contribution to the total scattering as governed by $$ rac{d^2\sigma}{dX \, d(Q^2)} = \sum_{\substack{ ext{constituents} \ c}} f_c(X) imes \underbrace{\left( rac{d^2\sigma}{dX \, d(Q^2)} ight)c} $$ The individual scattering is proportional to the charge of the constituents. For proton, we see 2 constituents have twice charge than the others, so we know those are 2/3 and another one has 1/3. }

docs.title: Electrons and Holes In Semiconductors
docs.text:
Compared to free electrons, the electrons in a semiconductor is subjected to periodic potential due to the ion cores. The response to an external force is therefore different to an electron in free space, i.e. the mass is modified: $\(F=m^*a\)$ where \(m^*\) is the effective mass. Without proof, here are some results for the properties of electrons.

\[v = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \frac{1}{\hbar} \frac{dE}{dk} \quad \text{(Group Velocity)}\] \[\mathbf{F} = \hbar \frac{d\mathbf{k}}{dt}\quad \text{(Force)}\] \[F = m^*a = m^* \left( \frac{dv}{dt} \right)\] \[m^* = \hbar^2 / \frac{d^2E}{dk^2} \quad \text{(effective mass of isotropic semiconductor)}\] \[m_{ij}^* = \hbar^2 / \frac{d^2E}{dk_i dk_j} \quad \text{(effective mass of anisotropic semiconductor)}\]

docs.title: Conduction at \(T=0\) under an electric field
docs.text:
Initially the valence band of the semiconductor is full and when we apply an electric field, we apply a force in opposition to electric field (\(\vec{F}=q\vec{E} = \hbar d\vec{k}/dt\)).

Here due to the force, the electron will be shifted but since \(k\)-space is periodic, we can effectively treat the electron which is moved to the next brillouin zone as the LHS-most electron

Therefore, at \(T=0\), semiconductor is not conducting electricity.

docs.title: Conduction of perfect crystals at finite temperature
docs.text:
This is different case as there are some electrons being promoted to the conduction band. So after the electric field is applied to the semiconductors, we have instantaneous current in the field direction

But time averaged velocity of the electron is zero because \(v = dE/\hbar dk\) so eventually the electrons will come again from the RHS to the LHS again. Therefore perfect crystal with nearly empty band does not carry a current for any appreciable time.

docs.title: Conduction of real crystals at finite temperature
docs.text:
In perfect crystals, the dispersion curve is perfectly symmetry i.e. the sum of \(k\) and velocity are zero

To break the symmetry, in real materials at finite temperature with electric field, scattering occurs as electrons moving across the ion cores, causing a net displacement from the starting, S and ending, F .

That means the electrons are drifted with $\(\mathbf{v}_d = -\mu\mathbf{E}\)$

In \(k\)-space, it means that the Fermi sphere is shifted

This shift causes the \(\sum \mathbf{k} \neq 0\) as the sphere is no longer symmetrical at the centre. After the shift, the total momentum is then shifted to \(-\mathbf{k}_e\) and a hole is formed there when the electron is being promoted there: i.e. \(\mathbf{k}_h = -\mathbf{k_e}\)

The holes have similar properties as electrons just that it has negative energy and negative effective mass. But it is still moving at the same velocity as electron.

docs.title: Elliptical polarisation in a circular basis
docs.text:
Same with Linear Basis

\(E_+ \neq E_-\) and they are finite.

docs.title: Elliptical polarisation in a linear basis
docs.text:
In Linear polarisation in a linear basis we show that $$ \begin{align} E &= E_1 + E_2 = (E_1 \hat{\epsilon}_1 + E_2 \hat{\epsilon}_2 e^{i\varphi}) e^{i(kx-\omega t+\phi_1)} \end{align} $$ and in Circular polarisation in a linear basis we let the magnitudes of the electric fields \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) the same.

If they are not the same, and the phase difference is \(\varphi\), we get the most general form of polarised light - elliptical light.

docs.title: Efficiency and effectiveness of a process
docs.text:
Effectiveness is how well the system achieves its specific purpose compared to the theoretical maximum $\(\eta_{\text{rev}} = \frac{\left| \text{Best possible Work} \right|}{\left| \text{Heat input} \right|}\)$

The second law efficiency is the ratio of these $\(\eta_{\text{2nd}} = \frac{\text{Actual efficiency}}{\text{Effectiveness}} = \frac{\eta_{\text{actual}}}{\eta_{\text{rev}}}\)$ where \(\eta_{actual}\) is the efficiency

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Amount of available useful work a system can provide and in spontaneous processes, \(A\) will tend towards a minimum. $\(A = U + p_0 - T_0S\)$

and the irreversibility of the processes $\(I = T_0\Delta S_{universe}\)$

docs.title: Exchange Interaction and Ferromagnetism
docs.text:
So far we have considered a Hamtiltonian that deals only with paramagnetic and diamagnetic terms, in fact we should also consider the interaction between atoms in a multi-electron systems.

The medium between interaction can be: 1. Superexchange in ionic solids, e.g. MnO neighbouring \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) interact via \(\text{O}^{2-}\) 2. RKKY interaction: alignment of spins in ferromagnetic metals via conduction electrons

docs.title: Weiss model of Ferromagnetism
docs.text:
Now we include the exchange term in the magnetic part of the Hamiltonian $$ \hat{H}{\text{mag}} = \sum_i)^2 $$ where } -J_{ij} \mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j + \sum_i \gamma g_j \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{J}_i + \sum_i \frac{e^2}{8m} (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{r\(J_{ij}\) is the exchange coefficient and it is - Positive if it is ferromagnetic (positivity indicates \(s_i \cdot s_j\) is negative i.e. two spins have the same sign) - Negative if it is antiferromagnetism (negativity indicates the spins have different signs)

\[ -J_{ij} \mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3J_{ij}\hbar^2}{4} & (\text{singlet}) \\[10pt] -\dfrac{J_{ij}\hbar^2}{4} & (\text{triplet}) \end{cases} \]

To simplify the calculation and explanation of ferromagnetism, we define a fictitious field called molecular field, \(\mathbf{B}_{\text{mf}}\) $$ \mathbf{B}{\text{mf}} = \frac{1}{\gamma g_J} \sum} -J_{ij} \mathbf{Sj = \lambda \mathbf{M} $$ and it is the magnetic field formed by the magnetic field from the magnetic moment. Assuming identical atoms/ions with \(\mathbf{L} =0\) and \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{J}\), we have $$ \hat{H} $$}} = \sum_i \gamma g_J (\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{B}_{\text{mf}}) \cdot \mathbf{J

This form is similar to the one with Paramagnetism and from there, remember that $$ \frac{M}{M_s} = B_J(y) \quad ; \quad B_J(y) = \frac{2J + 1}{2J} \coth\left(\frac{2J + 1}{2J}y\right) - \frac{1}{2J} \coth\left(\frac{y}{2J}\right) $$ Here, since we just introduce the molecular field, we simply include \(\lambda M\) term into the solution \(y\) $$ y = \frac{g_J \mu_B J ( \cancel{B} + B_{\text{mf}})}{k_B T} = \frac{g_J \mu_B J ( \cancel{B} + \lambda M)}{k_B T} $$ where we assume \(B\) is neglegible. If we rearrange this to find the relationship between \(M\) and \(y\), we get a straight line which represent different temperature.

This solution suggests that as the temperature decreases until it reaches a certain critical temperature (Curie temperature), the ferromagnets will have a spontaneous magnetisation. (Phase Transition). This is due to the presence of the molecular field.

The result is similar to Paramagnetism except there is an additional term: $$ \frac{M}{M_s} = \frac{\mu_B (B + \lambda M)}{k_B T} $$ $$ \implies \chi = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_B M_s}{k_B \left[ T - \frac{\lambda \mu_B M_s}{k_B} \right]} \propto \frac{1}{T - T_C} $$

for small magnetisation \(\chi = \mu_0M/B\)

docs.title: Helimagnetism
docs.text:
The exchange energy is $\(E = -2NS^2(J_1\cos\theta+J_2\cos2\theta)\)$ where \(N\) is the number of atoms in the plane. The minimum energy condition is \(dE/d\theta = 0\) $\((J_1+4J_2\cos\theta)\sin\theta = 0\)$

\[ \sin \theta = 0 \begin{cases} \theta = 0^\circ \text{ (ferromagnetic)} \\ \theta = 180^\circ \text{ (antiferromagnetic)} \end{cases} \] \[ \cos \theta = -\frac{J_1}{4J_2} \text{ (helimagnetism)} \]

docs.title: Exchange Operators and Pauli Exclusion Principle
docs.text:
Here we introduce the exchange operator and how it relates to Pauli Exclusion Principle.

Consider a system of two identical, indistinguishable particles described by $\(\psi(\underbrace{\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1}_{1}; \underbrace{\vec{r}_2, \sigma_2}_{2}) \equiv \psi(1, 2)\)$ If we introduce an exchange operator on the wave function, we, mathematically, exchange the label of the particles, i.e. the positions, momenta and spins of the particles. $\(P_{12}\psi(1,2)=\psi(2,1)\)$

docs.title: Properties of \(P\) on Hamiltonian
docs.text:
Since the particles are identical, the Hamiltonian has to be invariant under the exchange of particle labels \(\psi(1,2)=\psi(2,1)\). Therefore if we apply the exchange operator on both sides and multiply both sides by \(P_{12}\), we get

\[P_{12}H(1,2) \cancelto{\mathbb{I}}{P_{12}^{-1}P_{12}} = H(2,1)P_{12}$$ $$\implies [P_{12}, H(1,2)] = 0\]

The commutativity implies that we can find a common eigenvector for \(P\) and \(H\): $\(P_{12}\psi=\lambda\psi\)$

To find the eigenvalue of \(P_{12}\), we use the fact that \(P^2 = \mathbb{I}\) (I have proven it) as exchanging twice gives doesn't do shit on the original wavefunction. $\(P \cdot P \psi = P \lambda \psi \implies \mathbb{I}\psi = \lambda(\lambda\psi)\)$ $\(\implies \lambda^2 = 1\)$

docs.title: Bosons and Fermions
docs.text:
If \(\lambda =1\) (exchanging labels don't affect their wave function) then we have \(P_{12} \psi(1,2) = \psi(2,1) = \psi(1,2)\). If we construct a wavefunction consisting two states in the system, we have $\(\psi(r, r') = \frac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')+\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ where \(\phi_i\) is the wavefunction of individual particle. They are allowed to be in the same state i.e. BOSONS

If we have \(\lambda = -1\) (exchanging labels makes the wavefunction antisymmetric) then we have $\(\psi(r, r') = \frac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')-\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ which gives zero wave function i.e. FERMIONS (Pauli Exclusion principle)

In summary: exchanging the labels of two indistinguishable particles can have two impacts on the wavefunction. 1. Nothing 2. Make the total wavefunction anti-symmetric

docs.title: Excitation of Electrons via Electromagnetic Field   Absorption and Stimulated Emission
docs.text:
• In non-relativistic quantum mechanics and in an isolated system, an electron remains in the excited state indefinitely unless it is disturbed by some external influence.
  • The transition is balanced by absorption rate = spontaneous + stimulated emission

Here different derivation approach is used as compared to atomic physics course and we will focus on the absorption and spontaneous emission.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The electric field of the electromagnetic field is given by $\(\vec{E} = \vec{E}_0 \cos(\omega t)\hat{z}\)$ and the Hamiltonian includes only the potential energy of the electric field: $$ H'(\vec{r}, t) = -q z E_0 \cos(\omega t) = -p_zE_0 \cos(\omega t) =V(z) \cos(\omega t) $$

where \(p_z\) is the electric dipole

docs.title: Absorption of Radiation
docs.text:
With the knowledge in Perturbation Theory, we work out the probability of transition by finding the square of modulus $$ P_{a \to b}(\omega, t) = |c_b(t)|^2 = \frac{|V_{ba}|^2 \sin^2\left[\frac{(\omega - \omega_0)t}{2}\right]}{(\omega_0 - \omega)^2} = \frac{|\langle b | p_z | a \rangle|^2 E_0^2 \sin^2\left[\frac{(\omega - \omega_0)t}{2}\right]}{(\omega - \omega_0)^2} $$ where $$ c_b(t) = -\frac{V_{ba}}{\hbar} \left[ \frac{e^{i(\omega_0 + \omega)t} - 1}{\omega_0 + \omega} + \frac{e^{i(\omega_0 - \omega)t} - 1}{\omega_0 - \omega} \right] $$ where \(V_{ba}\) is the matrix element that represents the strength of the interction between the electron's dipole moment and the electric field.

You can do the derivation, it is not hard but a lot of algebra. Just remember that the Hamiltonian matrix is \(\langle f | H' | i \rangle\) where \(f\) is the final state and \(i\) is the initial state. So for absorption of radiation we are finding \(\langle \psi_b | H' | \psi_a \rangle\) .

docs.title: Stimulated Emission of Radiation
docs.text:
Everything is the same except we have to flip \(b\) with \(a\) in the Hamiltonian matrix and it gives $$ P_{b \to a} = |c_a(t)|^2 = \frac{|V_{ab}|^2 \sin^2 \left[ \frac{(\omega - \omega_0)t}{2} \right]}{(\omega - \omega_0)^2} = \frac{|\langle a | p_z | b \rangle|^2 E_0^2 \sin^2 \left[ \frac{(\omega - \omega_0)t}{2} \right]}{(\omega - \omega_0)^2} $$where $$ c_a(t) = -\frac{V_{ab}}{\hbar} \left[ \frac{e^{i(-\omega_0 + \omega)t} - 1}{-\omega_0 + \omega} + \frac{e^{i(-\omega_0 - \omega)t} - 1}{-\omega_0 - \omega} \right] $$

Here when we swap \(a\) and \(b\), we have to swap \(\omega_0\) to \(-\omega_0\)

docs.title: Spontaneous emission
docs.text: See Absorption cross-section and saturation and the next notes

docs.title: Excitation
docs.text:
Recall from Superfluidity that the broken symmetry potential is a Mexican hat. There are two types of excitation here: 1. Amplitude excitation where it costs the order parameter energy to be excited (from the bottom of the potential to the maximum), creating massive particles. 2. Goldstone mode where it rolls around the gutter (breaking of continuous symmetry because phase changes but not for amplitude excitation where the energy changes instead of the phase) and it takes less energy. It only happens in broken symmetry state with 2D or 3D order parameter case.

Here we use magnetism to show that when we break the global symmetry (introducing flipped spin), we create an [[Setup/Magnon|excitation]]. We will construct more than one energy state and find the lowest energy state. We will use Heisenberg model where \(D= 3\). We will use different method to derive the [[Setup/Magnon|Magnon]].

We start from [[Setup/Exchange Interaction and Ferromagnetism|interaction energy]] $$ \hat{H} = -\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} J \hat{S}i \cdot \hat{S}_j = -J \sum_i \left[ S_i^z S^+) \right] $$ We have a ground state of [[Setup/Exchange Interaction and Ferromagnetism|ferromagnetism]] when }^z + \frac{1}{2} (S_i^+ S_{i+1}^- + S_i^- S_{i+1\(T < T_c\) and all spins are aligned. $\(|\Phi\rangle=|\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\cdots\rangle\)$where the energy is $$ E = -\frac{NJ}{4} $$ Let's find an excited state. We want to find a correct excited state when the symmetry is broken. We try first by flipping a spin at \(j\) position: \(|j\rangle = |\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\cdots\rangle\). We apply the Hamiltonian to this state $$ \hat{H}|j\rangle = \left(-\frac{NJ}{4} + J\right)|j\rangle - \frac{J}{2}|j+1\rangle - \frac{J}{2}|j-1\rangle $$ To future me: you might wonder how \(j-1\) araised. Note that index \(i\) is arbitrary. For the \(|j-1\rangle\) part, we define \(i = j-1\). Back to the topic, we find that \(|j\rangle\) is not an eigenstate of \(H\). We then try introducing spin waves by defining a new state $\(|q\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_j e^{iqja}|j\rangle\)$ where \(q\) is the wave vector and \(a\) is the lattice spacing. We will get $\(\hat{H}|q\rangle = \hat{H} \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_j e^{iq j a} |j\rangle = \left( -\frac{NJ}{4} + \underbrace{J (1 - \cos q a)}_\text{energy cost} \right) |q\rangle\)$ which is an eigenstate of \(H\).

docs.title: Energy of the Excitation
docs.text:
We can find the energy cost using dispersion relation $\(\hbar\omega(q) = J(1 - \cos(qa))\)$ And we can find that \(q \rightarrow 0\), \(\omega \rightarrow 0\), meaning that if we have large wave vector, we have large wavelength and the excitation costs basically no energy.

For small \(q\), we have the dispersion relation \(\omega \approx q^2\), from there we can get the [[Setup/Density of States, Expectation Values and DeBroglie Thermal Wavelength|density of state]] \(g(q) \propto q^2 dq\) and the energy \(g(\omega) d\omega \approx \omega^{1/2} d\omega\) just like phonon.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• \(S=1/2 - (-1/2) = 1\) as we flip one spin i.e. boson
  • Massless
  • Goldstone mode

docs.title: Goldstone's theorem
docs.text: • Whenever a continuous symmetry is broken, we get a new massless excitation i.e. a pseudo-particle.

docs.title: Experimental Significance and Particles
docs.text: When we plot the [[Setup/Exchange Interaction and Ferromagnetism|temperature dependence of magnetisation of ferromagnets]] we get [[Setup/Magnon|Bloch's law]] instead of Weiss-Curie curve where it drops more rapidly. [[Setup/Magnon|Magnon]] then comes into play. Each magnon reduces magnetisation by one unit (spin). By using the [[Setup/Density of States, Expectation Values and DeBroglie Thermal Wavelength|approach in statistical physics]], we can get $\(n_{\text{magnon}} = \int \left[ \frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{kT}\right) - 1} \right] g_m(\hbar\omega) \, d(\hbar\omega) \propto T^{3/2}\)$ which is Bloch's law where the expected energy of magnon is $\(E_{\text{magnon}} = \int \left[ \frac{\hbar\omega}{\exp\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{kT}\right) - 1} \right] g_m(\hbar\omega) \, d(\hbar\omega) \propto T^{5/2}\)$ and the specific heat is $\(C_{\text{magnon}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \propto T^{3/2}\)$

docs.title: Dimensionality
docs.text:
Does dimensionality of the lattice affect the results that we get in the section above? Yes. If we change the density of states above to 1d or 2d i.e. $\(\begin{aligned} \text{2d:} \quad & g(\omega) = \text{const.} \\ \text{1d:} \quad & g(\omega) \propto \omega^{-1/2} \\[1em] & N \propto \int \frac{g(\omega)d\omega}{e^{\hbar\omega/k_BT} - 1} \to \infty \end{aligned}\)$

We realise that the number of magnon approaches infinity i.e. there is no magnetisation if we treat the spin as 1d or 2d. (d because we are dealing with dimension of the lattice, not spin).

This is called the Mermin-Small Wienner - Kolo Mee (Coleman-Mermin-Wagner) Theorem.

docs.title: Measuring Spin Waves
docs.text: We use [[Setup/Scattering Techniques|inelastic neutron scattering]] to detect spin waves where we utilised the conservation of momentum and energy. $\(\begin{aligned} \text{Energy Conservation:} \quad & E_i = E_f + \hbar\omega \\ & \text{\small (initial neutron)} = \text{\small (final neutron)} + \text{\small (magnon energy)} \\[1.5em] \text{Momentum Conservation:} \quad & \mathbf{k}_i = \mathbf{k}_f + \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{G} \\ & \text{\small (initial neutron)} = \text{\small (final neutron)} + \text{\small (magnon)} + \text{\small (reciprocal lattice vector)} \end{aligned}\)$

docs.title: Extrinsic Semiconductors
docs.text:
In previous note we talked about the intrinsic semiconductors being the pure, undoped semiconductors. Now we want to discuss about doping and it will be extrinsic semiconductors.

There are two types of doping: 1. Donors (n-type) 2. Acceptor (p-type)

docs.title: Donor impurities
docs.text:
$$E_D = \frac{e^4 m_e^}{2(4\pi \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 \hbar)^2} = \underbrace{\frac{m_e^}{m \varepsilon_r^2}}{\sim \frac{1}{100}} \left[ \underbrace{\frac{e^4 m}{2(4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar)^2}}{13.6 \text{ eV (Rydberg energy, \(E_H\))}} \right]$$ The fact that the ratio is 1/100 causes the donor energy level to be lower than that of conduction band.

\[r = \frac{4\pi \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e^* e^2} = \frac{\varepsilon_r m}{m_e^*} \left( \frac{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m e^2} \right)\]

The donor level between the CB and VB will start to be excited at low T, increasing the electron density \(n\) as indicated as the Freeze-out region. At the room temperature, the donors are fully ionised so \(n\) plateau (saturation region). If we put in more temperature, the VB electrons will start to be promoted to CB (intrinsic range).

Here we want to (no we don't) deduce the new electron density \(n\) after introducing the dopants at saturation regime (when the electrons of the donors are activated). For intrinsic semiconductor, \(n = p = n_i\), when we introduce the dopant, we are effectively just introduce some more electrons. Therefore $\(n = p + N_D\)$ where \(N_D\) is the donor concentration. By using completing the square method and combine this with the fact that \(np = n_i^2\) for intrinsic semiconductor we get $\(n = \frac{N_D}{2} + \sqrt{\left( \frac{N_D}{2} \right)^2 + n_i^2}\)$

docs.title: Chemical potential
docs.text: The chemical potential should lie in between the CB and DB because at \(T=0\), VB and DB have to be full and CB has to be empty.

docs.title: p-type semiconductor
docs.text:
The energy level is close to VB

and the chemical potential is in between AB and VB because same reason, VB has to be full and AB is a part of CB now as it is accepting.

docs.title: Far field
docs.text: Fraunhofer diffraction is in the far-field regime where Fraunhofer approximation holds (see Young's double slits E^{(0)} e^{-ik(xx' + yy')/z} dx'dy' $$ This is different than Focal plane of a lens because in that example, the terms cancel because we use \(z=f\).

docs.title: How far should a far field be to use Fraunhofer diffraction?
docs.text:
We require $$ \frac{k\rho_{\max}^2}{2z} \ll \frac{\pi}{4} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad z \gg \frac{4\rho_{\max}^2}{\lambda} $$ where \(\rho_{max}'\) is the maximum \(\rho'\) that contributes. We use \(\pi/4\) because we want the angle between \(k\) and the axis to be far less than \(45\degree\) For circular aperture with diameter \(a\) or a rectangular aperture with width \(a\), we can write \(\rho_{max}' = a/2\)

$$ z \gg d _ { \mathrm { R } } = \frac { a ^ { 2 } } { \lambda } $$where \(d_R\) is the Rayleigh distance and this inequality defines far-field regime.

We can work out the relationship between the internal energy of Fermion and temperature by considering $\(U = \int_0^\infty \varepsilon(k)g(k)f_{\text{FD}(k)} dk\)$ with energy \(\varepsilon = \hbar^2 c^2 k^2\) from Einstein's energy formula

docs.title: The radial equation for a spherical potential
docs.text: Based on the spherical polar, the Schrodinger equation now becomes $$ \frac{1}{R(r)}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^{2}\frac{dR(r)}{dr}\right) - \frac{2mr^{2}}{\hbar^{2}}\left(V(r) - E\right) = \frac{L^{2}Y(\theta,\phi)}{\hbar^{2}Y(\theta,\phi)} $$ By using the eigenvalue equation of total angular momentum and substituting \(U_{nl} = rR_{nl}\) we find that the radial equation $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2 U_{nl}}{dr^2} + \left[ V(r) + \frac{\hbar^2 l(l+1)}{2mr^2} \right] U_{nl} = E U_{nl} $$ is analogous to that of 1D Schrodinger equation with the potential replaced by \(V(r) + \hbar^2 l(l+1)/2mr^2 = V(r) + {L^2}/2mr^2\). \(n\) in this case is the principle quantum number. The additional term behaves like a contribution to the potential can be appreciated by considering an electron on a circular orbit.

docs.title: The hydrogen atom
docs.text:
For a hydrogen atom with a proton and an electron, the coulomb potential \(V(r) = -Ze^2/(4\pi \epsilon_0 r)\), by substituting this into the radial equation above: $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\frac{d^2U_{nl}}{dr^2} + \left[\frac{l(l+1)\hbar^2}{2\mu r^2} - \frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}\right]U_{nl} = EU_{nl} $$ where \(\mu = M_p m_e / (M_p + m_e)\) is reduced mass. Solving the Laguerre equation with \(\rho = kr\) and \(k = \mu Z e^2 / (4\pi \epsilon_0 \hbar^2 n)\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3 ...\) yields $$ E \approx -13.6 \, \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \left( \frac{\mu}{\mu_H} \right) \, \text{eV} $$ For hydrogen, \(\mu_H = \mu\) and \(Z = 1\)

Through the derivation of this energy equation, \(l\) can be linked to \(n\) by $\(l = 0, 1, ..., n-1\)$

The Laguerre equation gives solutions of \(R_{10}(r) = 2 a^{-3/2} e^{-r/a}\) \(R_{20}(r) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} a^{-3/2} \left(1 - \frac{r}{2a} \right) e^{-r/2a}\) \(R_{21}(r) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{24}} a^{-3/2} \frac{r}{a} e^{-r/2a}\)

docs.text: For a slit like this, the aperture function is $$ g(x^{\prime}) = \mathrm{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x^{\prime}| > a/2 \ 1 & \text{if } |x^{\prime}| \leq a/2 \end{cases}. $$ Recognising that this is a long split with uniform electric field in \(y\) direction, the intensity derived in Far field $$ I ^ { ( z ) } ( x , y ) = \frac { I _ { 0 } } { \lambda z } \left| \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } g ( x ^ { \prime } ) e ^ { - i 2 \pi x x ^ { \prime } / ( \lambda z ) } d x ^ { \prime } \right| ^ { 2 } $$ becomes $$ I^{(z)}(x,y)=\frac{I_{0}}{\lambda z}\left|\int_{-a/2}^{a/2}e^{-i2\pi xx^{\prime}/(\lambda z )}dx^{\prime}\right|^{2} $$ By solving the equation, we get $$ \begin{align} I^{(z)}(x,y) &= \frac{I_{0}}{\lambda z}\left|\frac{e^{-i2\pi xx^{\prime}/(\lambda z)}|^{a/2}{-a/2}}{-i2\pi x/(\lambda z)}\right|^{2} \ &= \frac{I \ &= \frac{I_{0}}{\lambda z}\left|\frac{\sin\left[\pi xa/(\lambda z)\right]}{\pi x/(\lambda z)}\right|^{2} \ &= I_{0}\frac{a^{2}}{\lambda z} \sin c^{2}\left(\frac{\pi a x}{\lambda z}\right). \end{align}}{\lambda z}\left|\frac{e^{-i\pi xa/(\lambda z)} - e^{i\pi xa/(\lambda z)}}{-2i\pi x/(\lambda z)}\right|^{2} $$

docs.title: Form Factor
docs.text:
In Rutherford's model, it is assumed that the nucleus and the particle are point-like. Instead we have to account for the fact that the nucleus has a distribution or density of charge. This induces an additional term which I don't care about and it gives $$ \left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)\rho = |F(q^2)|^2 \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right) $$ where $$ F(q^2) = \int d^3y \, e^{i\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{y}} f(y) $$ is the form factor. We can infer the size of the nucleus using the form factor by investigating the probability density of proton }\(f(y)\) through inverse Fourier transform.

Consider a spherical uniform distribution at the nucleus and the charge distribution is $$ f_{\text{Sph}}(y) = \frac{3}{4\pi R^3} \begin{cases} 1 & r < R \ 0 & r > R \end{cases} $$ i.e. it is the normalisation condition of \(\int d^3 f(y) =1\) and by subs into the form factor, we have $$ F(q^2) = \frac{3}{4\pi R^3} \int_0^R r^2 \, dr \, (2\pi) \frac{e^{iqr} - e^{-iqr}}{iqr} = \frac{3}{(|q|R)^2} \left( \frac{\sin |q|R}{|q|R} - \cos(|q|R) \right) $$ Here we can separate it into two cases: 1. In low energy limit \(qR \ll 1\), we don't have enough energy to resolve the size of nucleus. So the form factor becomes one, which is essentially the Rutherford's model 2. In high momentum regime, there is some angles \(|q|R = \theta\) that gives zero form factor and those angles are due to the destructive interference in diffraction pattern, i.e. \(\theta = 1.22\lambda/D\) .

Here when we plot the form factor and find the first zero point, that point is due to the interference.

docs.title: Frequency Time Fourier Pairs and Mode Locked Pulse Trains
docs.text:
Beginning from here we are looking at the time dependent phenomena where the the light have different wavelength

And the Fourier transform we are using is frequency dependent $\(\begin{aligned} F(\omega) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{i\omega t} dt = \mathcal{F}[f(t)](\omega) \\ f(t) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F(\omega) e^{-i\omega t} \frac{d\omega}{2\pi} \end{aligned}\)$ To understand the optical pulse, we start by investigating the rectangular pulse

The cosine fringes are in the rectangular envelope and the transmission function can be modelled as $\(f(t) = \cos(\omega_ct) \times \text{rect}\left(\frac{t}{\tau}\right)\)$ where \(\tau\) is the length of the envelope. The Fourier transform gives two sinc function in the positive and negative frequencies

where the spectral width is proportional to \(1/\tau\). Using this, we can extend this to \(N\) pulses by including the comb function: $\(\begin{aligned} f(t) &= \left( \text{rect} \left( \frac{t}{\tau} \right) * \text{III}_{T}^{(N)} \right) \cos(\omega_c t) \end{aligned}\)$ and the Fourier transform of this piece of shit is $\(\mathcal{F}(\omega) = \tau\text{sinc}\left[\frac{(\omega - \omega_c)\tau}{2}\right] \text{III}_{1/T}^{(N)} \ * \ \text{sinc}\left[\frac{(\omega + \omega_c)NT}{2}\right]\)$

The square of fourier transform shows that the cos fringes in the sinc envelopes get thinner and thinner as \(N\) increases. The discrete, equally spaced frequency lines are called optical frequency combs and it is used for precision measurements.

Mode locked pulse train?

However, in actual lasers, the transmission profile is not rectangular. It will be Gaussian due to Doppler broadening so we can construct the Fourier spectrum as $\(F(\omega) = \text{III}_{\omega_1} (\omega) \ G_0 \ \text{exp}\left[-\frac{(\omega - \omega_c)^2}{\Delta \omega^2}\right]\)$ By inverse Fourier transform, we have $\(\begin{aligned} \frac{\Delta \omega G_0}{4 \pi^{3/2}} \exp(-i \omega_c t) \text{III}_T(t) * \text{gauss} \left( \frac{\Delta \omega t}{2} \right) \end{aligned}\)$

docs.title: Fresnel diffraction integral
docs.text: To tackle this problem, recall from Paraxial Spherical waves, the equation of the spherical waves in paraxial regime can be modified by Fresnel approximation (in Paraxial optics) $$ dE^{(z)}(x,y) = \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikr_P} d\Sigma = \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikz} e^{\frac{ik\left[(x-x')^2 + (y-y')^2\right]}{2z}} d\Sigma $$ Note that this is the secondary wave because we use the infinitesimal area here based on Huygen-Fresnel principle. We then take the [[Surface integral]] of the equation above $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)}(x,y) &= \frac{1}{ikz} \iint_{(S_A)} A e^{ik r_P} d\Sigma \ &= \frac{1}{ikz} e^{ikz} \iint_{(S_A)} A e^{\frac{ik[(x-x')^2 + (y-y')^2]}{2z}} dx' dy' \end{align} $$ To solve a specific question, we consider the aperture function \(f(x',y')\) that determines what fraction of the input light is transmitted at the location \((x',y')\). For 100\% transmissive aperture (light is fully transmitted if it passes through the area of aperture) $$ \begin{align} f(x',y') = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } (x',y') \in S_A \text{ (aperture region)} \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{align} $$ By multiplying the integral with the aperture function, the equation becomes $$ E^{(z)}(x,y) = \frac{1}{ik z} e^{ikz} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x',y') A e^{\frac{ik[(x-x')^2 + (y-y')^2]}{2z}} dx' dy' $$

docs.title: Value of \(A\)
docs.text:
We apply this equation to plane wave to calculate \(A\). For a plane wave, \(E^{(z)}\), \(E^{(0)}\) and \(A\) are independent of the position on their wavefronts $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)} &= \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikz} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ik(x'^2 + y'^2)/(2z)} dx' dy' \ &= \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikz} \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ikx'^2/(2z)} dx' \right) \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{iky'^2/(2z)} dy' \right) \ &= \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikz} \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ikt^2/(2z)} dt \right]^2 \end{align} $$ Solving the integral using Fresnel integral gives $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)} &= \frac{A}{ikz} e^{ikz} \left( \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}} e^{i\pi/4} \right)^2 \ &= \frac{A}{ikz} \frac{i\pi}{a} e^{ikz} \ &= \frac{A}{ikz} \frac{2i\pi z}{k} e^{ikz} \ &= \frac{A}{ikz} i\lambda z e^{ikz} \ \end{align} $$ Comparing to the solution of \(E^{(z)} = E^{(0)}e^{ikz}\) we have: $\(A = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda^2}E^{(0)}\)$ Plugging this into the original equation gives $$ \begin{align} E^{(z)}(x,y) &= \frac{1}{i\lambda z} e^{ik\overline{r}} \iint_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x',y') E^{(0)} e^{-\frac{ik(xx' + yy')}{z}} e^{\frac{ik\rho'^2}{2z}} dx' dy' \end{align} $$

This equation is called the Fresnel diffraction integral.

docs.title: Fundamental Equations for Magnetism
docs.text:
Consider an electron moving in a circular loop, current is generated and it creates the magnetic field through the normal of the plane of the plane. The magnetic field acts as a magnetic dipole and it has a magnetic moment of $\(\mathbf{{\mu}} = I\mathbf{A}\)$ and the angular momentum of the electron is then (solved classically): $$ \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} = m(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}) $$ where \(\mathbf{p}\) is the momentum. The magnetic moment can also be written as $\(\mathbf{\mu} = -\gamma \mathbf{L}\)$ where \(\gamma = e/2m\) is the gyromagnetic ratio.

The energy of the magnetic moment is then $\(E = -\mathbf{\mu} \cdot \mathbf{B}\)$ - Since in quantum mechanics, the angular momentum is \(\mathbf{L}=m_l\hbar\) we have $$ E_L = \gamma L_z B = \underbrace{\gamma \hbar}_{\mu_B} m_L B $$ - For spin, \(\mu_s = -g_s\gamma \mathbf{s}\), we have spin energy $\(E_s=-\mu_s\cdot\mathbf{B} = g_sm_s\mu_BB = \pm\mu_B B\)$ for electron with \(g_s \approx 2\) and \(m_s = \pm 1/2\)

docs.title: Aside:
docs.text: For spin-orbit interaction, the energy is \(\Delta E \propto (dV/dr) (\mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{L})\). As the atomic number increases, \(dV/dr\) increases and hence the strength of S-O coupling. For the total angular momentum, the magnetic moment is then $\(\mu_J = -g_J\gamma J\)$ where $\(g_J = \frac{3}{2}+\frac{s(s+1)-l(l+1)}{2j(j+1)}\)$

docs.title: Bohr Magneton
docs.text:
• Fundamental unit for expressing magnetic moments
  • Magnetic moment for an electron in a circular loop $\(\mu_B = IA = \frac{ev}{2\pi r} \cdot \pi r^2 = \frac{e}{2m} (mvr) = \frac{e}{2m} L = \gamma L\)$ where \(I = e/T\) is current (rate of flow of charge) and \(L = mvr\) is the angular momentum.

docs.title: Magnetic fields
docs.text:
In magnetism, we use \(\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) regularly. \(\mathbf{B}\) is the magnetic field and acts as a 'output' field while \(\mathbf{H}\) is the magnetic field from the outside to magnetise something.

In vacuum, $\(\mathbf{B}=\mu_0 \mathbf{H}\)$ where \(\mu_0\) is the permeability of free space.

In solid, $$ \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 (\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{M}) $$ where \(\mathbf{M}\) is the magnetisation (net magnetic moment per unit volume and is how strongly the material is magnetised by \(\mathbf{H}\)). In general, the relationship between \(\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) fields is $$ \mathbf{M} = \chi \mathbf{H} $$ where \(\chi\) is the susceptibility.

  • If diamagnet, \(\chi < 0\)
  • If paramagnet, \(\chi > 0\)
  • If ferromagnet, \(\chi \gg 0\)

docs.title: Contradiction
docs.text: If we consider the energy per unit volume of the magnetic moment, we have $$ M = -\frac{dE_{\text{vol}}}{dB} $$ but based on the Lorentz force \(\mathbf{F} = -e(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\), the force is normal to the velocity of the electron, it does not do work on the electron, so the magnetisation should be zero.

docs.text:
\[ f(x) = f(x + d) = a_0 + \sum_{j=1}^\infty a_j \cos(2\pi u_j x) + \sum_{j=1}^\infty b_j \sin(2\pi u_j x) $$ where $$ a_0 = \frac{1}{d} \int_{0}^{d} f(x) \, dx \] \[ a_j = \frac{2}{d} \int_{0}^{d} f(x) \cos\left(\frac{2\pi j x}{d}\right) \, dx \] \[ b_j = \frac{2}{d} \int_{0}^{d} f(x) \sin\left(\frac{2\pi j x}{d}\right) \, dx \]

and the cos and sin in the coefficients are the basis functions (to show how the function \(f(x)\) modifies the basis functions). We can simplify this by using complex notation:

$$ f(x) = \sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty} c_j e^{i\frac{2\pi j x}{d}} $$ where $$ c_j = \frac{1}{d} \int_0^d f(x) e^{-\frac{2\pi i j x}{d}} \, dx $$ and the real part of this coefficient is the 'amount' of cos we need and complex part is the 'amount' of sin we need

docs.title: Dirac Delta Function
docs.text:
\[ \delta(x) = \begin{cases} \infty & x = 0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0 \end{cases} $$ It pick out values of a function $$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x) f(x) \, dx = f(0) \] \[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x - x_1) f(x) \, dx = f(x_1) \]

Intuitively, since the delta function is a vertical, infinite straight line at origin, when multiplied to a function, it gives the value at the origin. If the \(\delta(x)\) is shifted by a finite amount, it gives the value of the function at that position.

docs.title: Gauge Freedom I
docs.text:
To demonstrate the Gauge freedom, we have to have a Hamiltonian. We consider the Hamiltonian for particles with charge and mass in \(E\) and \(B\) fields.

And I thought the lecture notes started with the proof so I followed it step by step, but at the end it says a big fuck off 'without proof'. Fuck you. Anyways,

The Hamiltonian is given by $$ H = \underbrace{ rac{1}{2m} \left( -i\hbar abla - q\vec{A}(\vec{r}, t) ight)^2}{ ext{Kinetic energy}} + \underbrace{q\phi(\vec{r}, t)} $$}

where $$ \vec{E} = - abla \phi(\vec{r}, t) - rac{\partial \vec{A}(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t} $$ $$ \vec{B} = abla imes \vec{A}(\vec{r}, t) $$ and \(\phi\) is the scalar potential and \(\vec{A}\) is the vector potential. By considering the vector potential $\(\vec{A} = rac{B}{2} \hat{z} imes \vec{r} , \quad \vec{A}' = -By\hat{x} \ \ ext{(Landau Gauge)}\)$ we can find that they give the same \(\vec{B}\) values.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
By finding the difference between two gauges, we find that $$ \vec{A}' - \vec{A} = -By\hat{x} - \frac{B}{2}(-y\hat{x} + x\hat{y}) = -\frac{B}{2}(y\hat{x} + x\hat{y}) = \underbrace{\nabla \left( -\frac{Bxy}{2} \right)}_{\Lambda(\vec{r})} $$

where \(\Lambda(\vec{r})\) is a scalar function. If you take the curl of the gradient of any scalar function, you get 0 (basically saying there is no difference). In general, consider the gauge transformation: $$ \begin{cases} \phi(\vec{r}, t) \ \vec{A}(\vec{r}, t) \end{cases} \to \begin{cases} \phi'(\vec{r}, t) = \phi(\vec{r}, t) - \frac{\partial \Lambda(\vec{r}, t)}{\partial t} \ \vec{A}'(\vec{r}, t) = \vec{A}(\vec{r}, t) + \nabla \Lambda(\vec{r}, t) \end{cases} $$

that gives you Gauge freedom, where \(\phi\) transformation can be obtained from the \(E\) equation. Subs the transformed one into the \(E\) equation and you get the same equation.

docs.title: Landau Levels in a Uniform Magnetic Field
docs.text:
By using the Landau gauge and solve for Hamiltonian. We get the energy levels of the system. This is called the Landau levels.

Here the solution is $$ H = \frac{1}{2m} \left( -\hbar^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} - 2i\hbar q B y \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + q^2 B^2 y^2 - \hbar^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2} \right) $$ where the Hamiltonian does not depend explicitly on \(x\). Therefore it is safe to say that the wave function (solution) is variable separable: $$\psi(x,y) = \underbrace{e^{-ikx}}{\text{Plane wave}} \ \underbrace{\phi(y)}{\text{Function dependent on \(y\)}}$$

docs.title: Gauge Freedom II
docs.text:
Following from Gauge Freedom I that the solution to the Hamiltonian for a charged particle with mass in \(E\) and \(B\) field is separable. For solving for the Hamiltonian $$ \left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2} + \underbrace{\frac{m}{2} \underbrace{\frac{q^2 B^2}{m^2}}{\omega_c^2} \left( y - \underbrace{\frac{\hbar k}{qB}} \right] \phi(y) = E \phi(y) $$ where the second term is potential energy of a SHO (} \right)^2}_{\text{potential for SHO}\(U = m\omega^2 x^2 /2\) centred at \(y_0\) with the cyclotron frequency \(\omega_c = qB/m\) . The energy of this system is quantised so when we solve for energy, we have $\(E_n = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar \omega_c = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\hbar qB}{m}\)$

Note that gauge freedom will change the Hamiltonian but will not change the observable, i.e. the observables are gauge invariant.

docs.title: \(y_0\) periodicity
docs.text:
Now we investigate the value of \(y_0\). We first trap the motion of the charged particle in a 2D square plane with \(L\) on each side and a \(\mathbf{B}\)-field out of the page.

Since \(y_0 = \hbar k / qB\) is dependent on \(k\), alongside with the fact that the energy is quantised, it means that these wave vectors shows the number of independent quantum states.

Since the motion is constraints in \(L\) and can be repeated on an infinite 2D plane, we expect a periodicity in \(y_0\) $$ e^{-ik(x+L)} = e^{-ikx} \implies e^{-ikL} = 1 \implies kL = 2\pi l \quad \text{where } l \in \mathbb{Z}_+ $$

and we find $$ y_0 = \frac{\hbar k}{qB} = \frac{\hbar \cdot 2\pi l}{qBL} \quad \forall l \in \mathbb{Z_+} $$ We realise \(y_0\) is constrained between \(0\) to \(L\) so: $$ 0 < \frac{\hbar \cdot 2\pi l}{qBL} < L $$

By rearranging for \(l\), we have $$ 0 < l < l_{\text{max}} = \frac{\Phi}{\frac{h}{q}} $$ and this is the range of allowed values for \(y_0\) where \(\Phi = B\cdot L^2\) is the magnetic flux.

docs.title: Aharanov-Bohm Effect
docs.text:
In quantum mechanics, it is the scalar and vector potentials that describe the behaviour of particles as compared to the \(E\) and \(B\) in classical mechanics.

To see this we compare two situations:

docs.title: \(B\)-field without constraint
docs.text: Consider a particle moving circularly with a \(B\)-field in the \(z\) axis. We use cylindrical coordinates (\(\rho, \phi, z\)) and express Hamiltonian as $$ H = -\frac{\hbar^2 \nabla^2}{2m} $$ where $$ \nabla^2 = \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} \left( \rho \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} \right) + \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \phi^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2} $$ By solving it we get $$ \psi(\phi) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{in\phi}, \quad E_n = \frac{\hbar^2 n^2}{2mb^2}, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z} $$

docs.title: Constrained \(B\)-field
docs.text:
Now we constrain the \(B\)-field in a solenoid of radius \(a\) at the centre of the particle orbit. The \(B\)-field is non-zero only in the solenoid. Then the Hamiltonian is modified to $$ H = rac{1}{2m} \left( -i\hbar abla - q\vec{A} ight)^2 $$ where we need \(\vec{A}\) to be zero outside because \(\vec{B} = abla imes \vec{A}\), therefore we need $$ \vec{A} = A_\phi( ho)\hat{\phi} = egin{cases} \dfrac{\Phi ho}{2\pi a^2}\hat{\phi} = \dfrac{B ho}{2}\hat{\phi} & ext{if } ho < a, \[10pt] \dfrac{\Phi}{2\pi ho}\hat{\phi} = \dfrac{Ba^2}{2 ho}\hat{\phi} & ext{if } ho \geq a. \end{cases} $$ where $$ \vec{B} = abla imes \vec{A} = egin{cases} B\hat{z} & ext{if } ho < a, \ 0 & ext{if } ho \geq a. \end{cases} $$

By solving for this Hamiltonian, we get $$ E_n = rac{\hbar^2}{2mb^2} \left[ n - rac{\Phi}{(h/q)} ight]^2 $$ Note that how the energy level depends on magnetic flux even though there is no magnetic field outside the solenoid.

docs.title: Gauge Theory and Higgs Mechanism
docs.text: Recap for Mass of Excitation where we proved Goldstone theorem using the minimum \(\phi_1 = \left( rac{6\mu^2}{\lambda} ight)^{1/2}, \qquad \phi_2 = 0\). Here we will do the same but in polar coordinate \(\phi = ho e^{i heta} \implies abla \phi = e^{i heta} ( abla ho) + i ho e^{i heta} ( abla heta)\). By substituting this into the free energy gives $$ f = ( abla \phi)^\dagger \cdot ( abla \phi) - \underbrace{\mu^2 (\phi^\dagger \phi) + \lambda (\phi^\dagger \phi)^2} ext{potential term, \(U\)} = ( abla ho)^2 + ho^2 ( abla heta)^2 - \underbrace{\mu^2 ho^2 + \lambda ho^4} ext{potential term, \(U\)} $$ Now when we break the symmetry by choosing the minimum $$ ho_0 = \left( rac{\mu^2}{2\lambda} ight)^{1/2}, \quad heta_0 = 0 $$ and expand around the minimum where \( ho' = ho - ho_0\) and \( heta' = heta - heta_0 \; (\equiv heta)\) $$ U( ho') \approx U( ho_0) + \left( rac{\partial^2 U}{\partial ho^2} ight){ ho_0} rac{ ho'^2}{2!} + \left( rac{\partial^3 U}{\partial ho^3} ight) + \cdots $$ and another one for } rac{ ho'^3}{3!\( heta\) (which gives zero) we get $$ f = \left( rac{\mu^2}{2\lambda} ight) ( abla heta')^2 + ( abla ho')^2 + 2\mu ( ho')^2 + 4 \left( rac{\mu^2 \lambda}{2} ight)^{1/2} ( ho')^3 + \lambda ( ho')^4 $$ we see there is no dependence on \( heta\) i.e. it is a massless excitation (Goldstone mode). Same proof as in Mass of Excitation where we use \(\phi_2 = 0\).

docs.title: Gauge field
docs.text:
Now we use the gauge field described in Superfluid and Superconductivity $$ f = (D\phi)^\dagger \cdot (D\phi) - \mu^2 (\phi^\dagger \phi) + \lambda (\phi^\dagger \phi)^2 $$ where \(D\phi = abla \phi + iq A \phi = ( abla ho) e^{i heta} + i ( abla heta + q A) ho e^{i heta}\). This is the key: we then define a few gauge field to replace \(A\) by $$ C = \left( A + rac{1}{q} abla heta ight) $$ where this is a gauge field for \(A\) so whatever local changes in phase will modify \(A\) and reflected in \(C\). This make $$ (D\phi)^\dagger \cdot (D\phi) = ( abla ho)^2 + ho^2 q^2 C \cdot C $$ $\(\implies f = ( abla ho)^2 + ho^2 q^2 |C|^2 - \mu^2 ho^2 + \lambda ho^4\)$

WE do the same break the symmetry and expand around the minimum but instead of using \( ho' = ho - ho_0\) we use $\( ho - ho_0 = rac{\chi}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ for I dont give a fuck anymore reason. We then get $$ f = rac{( abla \chi)^2}{2} + \mu^2 \chi^2 + \sqrt{\lambda} \mu \chi^3 + rac{\lambda}{4} \chi^4 + \underbrace{ rac{1}{2} \left( rac{q^2 \mu^2}{\lambda} ight) |C|^2}_ ext{C field is massive} + \left( rac{\mu^2}{\lambda} ight)^{1/2} q^2 \chi |C|^2 + rac{1}{2} q^2 \chi^2 |C|^2 + \cdots $$

where \({ rac{1}{2} \left( rac{q^2 \mu^2}{\lambda} ight) |C|^2}\) with mass = \(\left( rac{q^2 \mu^2}{\lambda} ight)^{1/2}\) (square root of curvature which is the coefficient of the \(C\) field. As C field incorporate the \( heta\) field i.e. replace the \( heta\) field or the goldstone mode, we have no goldstone mode.

This idea is then applied to other particles i.e. neutrinos, photons, Higgs, \(W\), \(Z\) bosons. They are believed to be the excitation to their own fields. And it is the symmetry breaking of Higgs field that gives the particles mass except photons because of a more complicated field theory.

docs.title: Gaussian beam
docs.text:
Light can propagate thousands of kilometres without changing significantly in a laser cavity or a waveguide such as optical fibre.

\[ E^{(0)}=E_{0}e^{-x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-y^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}} $$ and the aperture function is $$ f\left(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\right)=e^{-x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-y^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}} \]

The Fourier transform of the aperture function is $$ \begin{align} \mathcal{F}\left[f\left(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\right)\right] &=\iint_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-y^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-i2\pi(ux^{\prime}+vy^{\prime})}dx^{\prime}dy^{\prime} \ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-i2\pi ux^{\prime}}dx^{\prime}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-y^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-i2\pi vy^{\prime}}dy^{\prime} \end{align} $$ The integrals are the same, the \(x^\prime\) integral is $$ \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}}e^{-i2\pi ux^{\prime}}dx^{\prime} &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}+i2\pi ux^{\prime})}dx^{\prime} \ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(x^{\prime 2}/\omega_{0}^{2}+i2\pi ux^{\prime}-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2})-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}}dx^{\prime} \ &=e^{-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(x^{\prime}/\omega_{0}+i\pi u\omega_{0})^{2}}dx^{\prime} \ &=\omega_{0}e^{-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(x^{\prime}/\omega_{0}+i\pi u\omega_{0})^{2}}d(x^{\prime}/\omega_{0}+i\pi u\omega_{0}) \ &=\omega_{0}e^{-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}}dt \ &=\omega_{0}e^{-\pi^{2}u^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}}\sqrt{\pi} \end{align} $$

Hence the final fourier transform is $$ \mathcal{F}\left[f\left(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\right)\right]=\pi\omega_{0}^{2}e^{-\pi^{2}(u^{2}+v^{2})\omega_{0}^{2}}=\pi\omega_{0}^{2}e^{-\pi^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})/(\lambda^{2}z^{2})}=\pi\omega_{0}^{2}e^{-\pi^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}\rho^{2}/(\lambda^{2}z^{2})} $$

docs.text: The Fourier trans form of gauss\((x/\omega_0) = \sqrt{\pi}\omega_0\)gauss\((\pi \omega_0 u)\) where gauss\((x) = e^{-x^2}\)

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
\[ I^{(z)}=\frac{I_{0}}{\lambda^{2}z^{2}}\pi^{2}\omega_{0}^{4}e^{-2\pi^{2}\omega_{0}^{2}\rho^{2}/(\lambda^{2}z^{2})}=I_{0}\frac{\pi^{2}\omega_{0}^{4}}{\lambda^{2}z^{2}}e^{-2\rho^{2}/\omega^{2}} \]

where \(\omega = \lambda z/\pi \omega_0\) is the far-field beam radius.

The angular spread of the beam is $$ \Delta\theta=\frac{\omega}{z}=\frac{\lambda}{\pi\omega_{0}} \quad \text{(92)} $$

As for the case of a single slit, the Fraunhofer approximation is valid only when the width of the light distribution is much larger than the initial size. The cross over beywee initial size dominating and diffraction dominating occurs at the Rayleigh range, \(z_R = \omega_0/\Delta \theta\) which gives $$ z_{R}=\frac{\pi\omega_{0}^{2}}{\lambda} \quad \text{(93)} $$ It basically means that the beam travels at a distance of \(z_R\) in parallel (collimated) with minimal spread and starts to spread after \(z_R\).

Rayleigh range is greater than Rayleigh distance due to Gaussian function. The far field condition for Gaussian beams like laser beams is \(z\gg z_R\).

docs.title: Degree of freedom
docs.text: A system of \(M\) point masses has \(N = 3M\) DoF and due to contraints, \(j\) the DoF is reduced by \(N = 3M - j\)

docs.title: Types of constraints
docs.text:
• Holonomic: constraints that can be expressed in the form of $\(f(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_M, t) = 0\)$

    • Rheonomic: constraints that have explicit time dependence
    • Scleronomic: constraints that do not have time dependence

  • Nonholonomic: constraints involve either differential equations or inequalities (rather than algebraic equations)

docs.title: Generalised coordinates \(q_k\)
docs.text:
The existence of \(j\) constraints means that the coordinates are no longer independent. We require as many coordinates as there are DoF, i.e. if the constraints are holonomic, then we can express the position of the \(i\)th part of a system as $\(\vec{r}_i = \vec{r}_i(q_1, \ldots, q_k, \ldots, q_N, t)\)$ The \(t\) dependence is only when the constraints are rheonomic.

When we use generalised coordinates in the operation then the generalised velocities are \(\dot{q_k} = dq_k/dt\) and they are independent variables (this is a defined concept and is necessary to make sense of variational calculus where the components need to be independent to be worked out), meaning that \(\partial q_k / \partial \dot{q}_k = \partial \dot{q}_k / \partial q_k = 0\)

docs.title: Preview of spin concept
docs.text:
Spin is introduced in the early development of quantum mechanics to refer to the intrinsic angular momentum (like the spin of a planet). This word is kept until now even though an electron does not spin physically.

For now, spin is actually intrinsic angular momentum of an electron.

docs.title: Angular momentum ladder operators
docs.text:
The angular momentum ladder operators are similar to that of ladder operators of a and is defined as: $$ L_{\pm} = L_{x} \pm i L_{y}. $$

\(L_+\) is a step-up operator and can be observed from $$ L^2(L_+f_{\lambda,\mu})=\lambda\hbar^2(L_+f_{\lambda,\mu}) $$ and $$ L_z \left( L_+ f_{\lambda,\mu} \right) = (\mu + 1) \hbar \left( L_+ f_{\lambda,\mu} \right) $$ Note: - The operator only affects \(L_z\) instead of \(L^2\) because \(L^2\) commutes \(L_+\) but \(L_z\) does not commute with \(L_+\) - This is because \(L^2\) depends only on \(l\) while the operator only affect \(m\). The ladder operators rotate the state within the same \(l\)-subspace, altering its orientation but not its total angular momentum magnitude.

docs.title: Properties of the ladder operators
docs.text: There is a top and bottom rung to this ladder, where at the top and bottom rung, the operator (acting on a function) gives zero

docs.title: Overview of general angular momentum
docs.text:
• \[ [J_x, J_y] = i\hbar J_z, \quad [J_y, J_z] = i\hbar J_x, \quad [J_z, J_x] = i\hbar J_y, $$ $$ [J^2, J_x] = [J^2, J_y] = [J^2, J_z] = 0 \]
  • \[ J^2 f_{j,m_j} = j(j+1) \hbar^2 f_{j,m_j} \quad \text{and} \quad J_z f_{j,m_j} = m_j \hbar f_{j,m_j} \]
  • $$ J_z J_+ f_{j,m_j} = (m_j + 1) \hbar J_+ f_{j,m_j}, \qquad J_z J_- f_{j,m_j} = (m_j - 1) \hbar J_- f_{j,m_j} $$

So basically the generalised angular momentum is \(J\). Here \(m_j\) is magnetic quantum number and \(j\) is orbital quantum number.

docs.title: Giant Rydberg Excitons in the Copper Oxide   Letter
docs.text:
• We can find the average radius of an orbital \(<r_n>\) with principle quantum number \(n\) and angular momentum \(\ell\) by $\(<r_n> = \frac{1}{2}a_B(3n^2-\ell(\ell+1))\)$ where \(a_B\) is Bohr radius and \(\ell =1\) for P-state
  • The absorption lines exhibit an asymmetry with a stepper slope on the high energy flank because of interference of a discrete excitonic state and a continuum of states from interaction with optical phonons.
  • Binding energy: $\(E_n = E_g - \frac{\text{Ry}}{(n-\delta_\ell)^2}\)$ and the quantum defect can be found by plotting \(E_n - E_g\) against \(n^2\) graph
  • The areas under the absorption peak corresponds to the absorption strength and is determined by the exciton oscillator strength. The area is decreasing as \(n\) increases is due to Rydberg blockade.
  • Broadening effects observed in the optical density peak and can be quantified and analysed using FWHM.

docs.title: Ginzburg Landau Theory For Superconductivity
docs.text:
There are currently two theories for superconductivity: 1. BCS theory (microscopic theory of superconductivity) 2. Ginzburg-Landau Theory (Phenomenological/macroscopic theory of superconductivity)

GL postulated that something will change from normal metallic state to superconducting state and it is called the order parameter. The order parameter is either non-zero or 0 depending on the critical temperature $\(\psi(T) = \begin{cases} \psi(T)\neq 0 & T < T_c \\ 0 & T > T_c \end{cases}\)$ They also postulated that order parameter is a complex number and the real-valued free energy is a smooth function of order parameter. So if we Taylor expand the free energy in terms of the order parameter, the only possible case is $\(G_s(T) = G_N(T) + a(T) |\psi|^2+\frac{b(T)}{2}|\psi|^4\)$

where \(a(T)\) and \(b(T)\) are coefficients that depend on \(T\). This is because even power terms can cancel the imaginary part of \(\psi\). In superconductivity, the order parameter is the cooper pairs where \(|\psi|^2 = n_s/2\) where \(n_s\) is the density of superconducting electrons.

In normal state, \(a(T) > 0\) where it is a parabolic shape

But in superconducting state, \(a(T) < 0\)

In both cases, the coefficient \(b(T) >0\) to make sure the curves have a minimum. To simplify the equation, we take the Taylor expansion of the coefficients. Since the coefficients are arbitrary, we can define the order of expansion such that it simplifies the equations: $\(\begin{aligned} a(T) &\approx \dot{a}(T - T_c) + \dots \quad (\dot{a} > 0) \\ b(T) &\approx b + \dots \quad (b > 0) \end{aligned}\)$

where the first order of \(a(T)\) is zero and only keep the first order of \(b(T)\). The stable point is \(\Delta G = \dot{a}(T-T_c) + b|\psi|^2 =0 \implies\) $\(|\psi|^2 = \begin{cases} \frac{\dot{a}(T_c - T)}{b} & T < T_c \\ 0 & T > T_c \end{cases}\)$

We eventually get $\(\begin{aligned} G_n(T) - G_s(T) &= -a(T)|\psi|^2 - \frac{b(T)}{2}|\psi|^4 \\ &= \frac{[\dot{a}(T - T_c)]^2}{2b} \quad \text{(Condensation energy)} \end{aligned}\)$

Recall from Meissner Effect that $\(G_N[0] - G_s[0] = \frac{B_c(T)^2}{2\mu_0}\)$

We can eventually work out \(B_c(T)\) in terms of temperature and the entropy change which is \(S = - (dG/dT)\) to see that there is no latent heat/entropy change at \(T_c\) i.e. second order transition.

docs.title: Inhomogeneous Systems
docs.text:
Order parameters can depends on the position \(\mathbf{r}\) if the surfaces/systems are inhomogeneous $\(G_s(T, \mathbf{r}) = G_N(T, \mathbf{r}) + rac{\hbar^2}{2m} | abla \psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + a(T) |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + rac{b(T)}{2} |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^4\)$ where the \(m\) term is the energy associated with the gradient of the order parameter and it is readily reduce to the homogeneous case by setting it to constant \(\psi(\mathbf{r}) ightarrow \psi\) . Since a system will have the tendency to stay in its lowest energy, we minimise the energy $\(G_s(T) = G_N(T) + \int \left( rac{\hbar^2}{2m} | abla \psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + a(T) |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 + rac{b(T)}{2} |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^4 ight) d\mathbf{r}\)$ and we get the nonlinear Schrodinger equation: $\(\Rightarrow rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 \psi(\mathbf{r}) + \left[ a(T) + rac{b(T)}{2} |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 ight] \psi(\mathbf{r}) = 0\)$

By solving this we get a solution $\(\psi(x) = \psi_0 anh \left( rac{x}{\sqrt{2} \xi(T)} ight)\)$ where $\(\xi(T) = \left( rac{\hbar^2}{2m |a(T)|} ight)^{1/2}\)$ is the coherence length. Physically, consider an interface between the normal metal and superconducting states. The order parameter \(\psi\) has to be zero before \(x = 0\) (normal metal state) and non-zero after. To stay continuous, it has to be like this described by the tanh equation.

This coherence length is the separation of the Cooper pair electrons.

Using this knowledge with energy we can differentiate type I or II superconductors. Here we consider two energies:

  1. Magnetic energy
  2. Condensation energy

docs.title: Magnetic energy
docs.text: Recall from Meissner Effect that the magnetic field decay rapidly. If we plot the energy graph \(=B^2/2\mu_0\) we have

docs.title: Condensation energy
docs.text:
When we plot the order parameter graph, we get the coherence length where cooper pair starts to form. The formation of cooper pair will take up the free energy of the system

In a system, these two energies are in competition.

docs.title: Case I: \(\lambda_L \ll \xi\)
docs.text: The interfacial energy is high (the interception point). That means this system is not favourable for an interface to form: i.e. no metal and superconductor interface \(\implies\) type I

docs.title: Case II: \(\xi \ll \lambda_L\)
docs.text: The interfacial energy is low and it is favourable for an interface to form \(\implies\) type II

docs.title: Ginzburg Landau Theory of Ferroelectrics
docs.text:
This is a similar note for Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity but for ferroelectrics. The concept of ferroelectrics and paraelectrics are exactly the same as ferromagnetism and Paramagnetism i.e. after critical temperature, ferroelectrics will turn into paraelectrics and the dielectric constant will be largely increased.

The order parameter of ferroelectrics is the spontaneous polarisation (analogous to magnetisation). In Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity, we mentioned that the GL theory is $\(G_s(T) = G_N(T) + a(T) |\psi|^2+\frac{b(T)}{2}|\psi|^4\)$ where \(|\psi|\) is the order parameter for superconductivity.

docs.title: Second Order Transition
docs.text:
Here we extend this theory for a bit. For ferroelectrics, $\(\begin{aligned} G_{FE}(T) &= G_{PE}(T) + \frac{1}{2} g_2 P^2 + \frac{1}{4} g_4 P^4 \end{aligned}\)$ where \(G_{FE}\) is the ferroelectric free energy and \(G_{PE}\) is the paraelectric free energy. This equation is sufficient if \(g_4 > 0\) which guarantee stable minimum points. Here the even power is due to the fact that the transition has to be invariant in polarisation direction.

Similar approach is used to obtain the dependence of \(P\) and \(T\). We find the minimum point and Taylor expand \(g_2\) around the critical point. Eventually we get $\(\begin{aligned} \text{(i) } P_s &= 0 \quad \text{(Paraelectric)} \\ \text{(ii) } P_s &= \left( -\frac{g_2}{g_4} \right)^{1/2} = \left( \frac{\gamma}{g_4} \right)^{1/2} (T_o - T)^{1/2} \quad \text{(Ferroelectric)} \end{aligned}\)$ This is called the second order transition where there is no discontinuity and no latent heat is produced.

docs.title: Applied Electric Field
docs.text: In an applied electric field, just like inhomogeneous system where there is a perturbation, we include the perturbation energy into the GL theory: $\(G_{FE}(T) = G_{PE}(T) - EP + \frac{1}{2} g_2 P^2 + \frac{1}{4} g_4 P^4\)$ By minimising the system energy and using the fact that \(D = \epsilon_0 E + P = \epsilon_0\epsilon_rE\) we get $\(\epsilon_r = 1 + \frac{1}{\epsilon_o} \left( \frac{P}{E} \right) = 1 + \frac{1}{\gamma \epsilon_o (T - T_o)}\)$

docs.title: First Order Transition (Extension)
docs.text:
When \(b(T) < 0\), the system can no longer have stable minimum points, we have to add sixth power: $\(G_{FE}(T) = G_{PE}(T) + \frac{1}{2} g_2 P^2 + \frac{1}{4} g_4 P^4 + \frac{1}{6}g_6P^6\)$ Using similar method to find the relationship between \(P\) and \(T\) we actually get a discontinuity and a release of latent heat after critical temperature.

\[\begin{aligned} \text{(i) } P_s &= 0 \quad \text{(paraelectric state)} \\ \text{(ii) } P_s^2 &= \frac{-g_4 \pm \sqrt{g_4^2 - 4g_6g_2}}{2g_6} \quad \text{(ferroelectric state; select solution)} \end{aligned}\]

docs.title: Heat Engines and the Carnot cycle
docs.text:
Systems operating in a cyclic process (returns to initial state) to convert some (not 100% efficient) heat into work

  1. Transfer heat \(Q_H\) from hot source to engine
  2. Engine converts some heat to work \(-w\)
  3. Waste heat \(-Q_l\) is transferred to cold sink
  4. Return engine to initial state

docs.title: Efficiency
docs.text: Ratio of what we want to get and what we input $\(\eta = \frac{|w|}{|Q_H|} = \frac{|Q_H - Q_l|}{|Q_H|} = 1 - \frac{|Q_l|}{|Q_H|}\)$

docs.title: Carnot cycle
docs.text:
Most efficient engines we can design, described by 4 reversible steps

  1. A to B: Isothermal expansion (no change of temperature and is in thermal contact with heat source)
  2. B to C: Adiabatic expansion (no heat exchange and is thermally isolated)
  3. C to D: Isothermic compression (in thermal contact with cold source)
  4. D to A: Adiabatic compression (thermally isolated)

[!caution] Isothemal process -> \(dU = 0\) also when it's a cycle Adiabatic process -> \(dQ = 0\)

From the efficiency equation and the ratio of \(Q_H\) and \(Q_l\) in the isothermic processes in the Carnot cycle, the efficiency is then $\(\eta_{Carnot} = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H}\)$

docs.text:
There are two factors that determine the electronic configuration in an atom/ion 1. Coulomb repulsion energy between electronics 2. Spin-orbit coupling energy

For light atoms, the coulomb repulsion energy is dominant (as mentioned in Fundamental Equations for Magnetism) and has to be minimised. It has two contribution:

docs.title: Spin contribution

docs.title: Orbital contribution

docs.title: Hund's rule

With that, we see $$ E \right] \right) $$ and this term is fine structure term.} = E_n^0 + E_n^0 \alpha^2 \frac{mc^2}{2n^2 2mc^2} \left[ -3 + \frac{4n}{(j + 1/2)} \right] = E_n^0 \left( 1 + \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2} \left[ \frac{n}{(j + 1/2)} - \frac{3}{4

docs.title: Ground state of hydrogen
docs.text: The ground state of hydrogen is \(n=1 \implies l=1\), \(j = |l-s|\) and \(j=l+s\), which there is only a value \(s = j =1/2\), so $$ \frac{\Delta E_1}{E_1^0} = \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2} \left( \frac{n}{j + 1/2} - \frac{3}{4} \right) = \alpha^2 \left( 1 - \frac{3}{4} \right) = \frac{\alpha^2}{4} $$

docs.title: Quantum number sets
docs.text:
Very messy notation right? Here is the sum-up

Initially, without perturbations, we are using \(n, l, m_l, m_s\) which corresponds to \(H^0, L^2, L_z, S_z\) where we ignore \(S^2\) because it has only one value which is \(s(s+1)\) (where \(s = 1/2\)) so it's not very useful.

With perturbation, we are using \(n,l,j,m_j\) corresponding to \(H^0, L^2,J^2, J_z\) (ignoring \(S^2\)) since we are considering spin + orbital angular momentum. \(J^2\) has eigenvalues of \(j(j+1)\hbar^2\) and \(J_z\) has \(m_j\hbar\) ( where \(-j < m_j < j\) and \(|l-s| < j < l+s\))

docs.title: Balmer line energies
docs.text:
Balmer line is from \(n = 3\) to \(n=2\) and by accounting the fine structure, we have

Note that how \(n=3\) has five different labels with only three distinct \(j\) values (representing distinct energies). Based on Degenerate perturbation theory and hydrogen, the degeneracy is \(2n^2\) with perturbation, so we have 18 degeneracies with 3 different energies.

For \(n=2\), there are 3 different labels, with 2 different \(j\) values and has 8 degeneracies.

\(\implies\) there are 6 possible different transition energy. But we can only observe two strong spectral lines because it needs to follow the conservation of angular momentum:

  • Photon is a spin-1 particle, i.e. it removes or add a unit of angular momentum in our old system (atom before emiting or absorbing photon). So the system (atom) has to gain or lose a unit of angular momentum (\(\Delta j = 0, \pm1\))
  • For \(\Delta l = \pm 1\), it's because of electric dipole operator (dont know in details, left to be asked)
  • The transitions outside this requirement is forbidden

This requirement removes some of the possibilities, leaving only with 7 labels with 5 energies. As the energy split gets smaller with increasing \(n\), they form 2 set of near degenerate lines \(n = 3 \rightarrow 2, 1/2\) (two lines) and \(n = 3 \rightarrow 2, 3/2\) (three lines). This is doublet.

docs.title: Lamb shifting
docs.text: Our calculation gave \(2p_{1/2}\) and \(2s_{1/2}\) as the same energy value but there is a very small difference due to lamb shift (an interaction between the electron and the vacuum fluctuations of the quantised electromagnetic fi eld) - degeneracy lifting

docs.title: Hyperfine splitting
docs.text:
There is a even smaller energy shift of \(E^1_{n,\text{hyperfine}} \propto \alpha^4 m_e/m_p\) which arises because of proton's spin.

The proton's spin gives a magnetic dipole of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_p = g_p e/2 m_p \boldsymbol{S}_p\) and magnetic field of $$ \boldsymbol{B}_p = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3} \left[ 3(\boldsymbol{\mu}_p \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}) \hat{\boldsymbol{r}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_p \right] + \frac{2\mu_0}{3} \boldsymbol{\mu}_p \delta(\boldsymbol{r}) $$ Recall from Degenerate perturbation theory and hydrogen that \(\underline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = -e/m_e \boldsymbol{S}\), there is an additional contribution to the potential energy given by \(H' = \underline{\mu_e} \cdot B_p\)

docs.title: Imaging Systems
docs.text:
Abel realised the important of having wide aperture to improve the diffraction limit of a lens i.e. the resolution of the lens $\(\Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{2NA}\)$ where \(NA = n \sin \Lambda\) is the numerical aperture, \(n\) is the refractive index and \(\Lambda\) is the fringe separation.

The physical reasoning behind this is that the lights from \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) paths interfere each other to form \(\cos\) fringes. In order to increase the resolution, we need small fringes i.e. \(\Lambda \downarrow \implies \alpha \uparrow \implies k_1 \ \text{and} \ k_2 \ \text{larger} \implies D \uparrow\)

Due to this finite size of aperture, our image is not 100% sharp. Hence instead of \(f(x',y')\) which we learnt in Intensity and Angular Spectrum, we need to include an additional transmission term after the lens \(t(x',y')\): $\(\begin{aligned} f(x', y') &= f_i(x', y') \cdot t(x', y') \ E^{(f)} \\ \implies&\propto \mathcal{F}[f_i(x', y')] * psf(u, v) \end{aligned}\)$ where \(psf(u,v) = \mathcal{F}[t(x',y')]\) is the point spread function of the lens. Therefore the goal is to make the point spread function as small (close to Dirac-delta) as possible to make the image to be what it supposed to be.

Since normal people will use a circular lens with diameter \(D\), we model our transmission \(t(x',y')\) function as a circ function and hence the point spread function is $\(psf = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} \text{jinc} \left( \frac{\pi D \rho}{\lambda f} \right)\)$ Why don't we de-convolve the \(psf\) to get the real image? It is hard, that's it.

docs.title: Angular Resolution
docs.text:
[!Definition] Resolving power of a circular instrument

For two distant objects, we approximate the the lights travelling from there to our lens are plane waves. As they are focussed to the Fourier plane, they are a dirac-delta function shifted by some distances from the centre.

As the \(psf\) is a jinc function, the result is a convolution of the \(psf\) and and delta function, which produces Airy disk and the images are said to be just 'resolved' when the second image is at the first minima of the first image i.e. $\(\theta_R = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D}\)$ This is the Rayleigh criterion.

docs.title: Induced circular birefringence   the Faraday effect

  • Causes a polarisation rotation, which is proportional to the projection of the magnetic field along the direction of the light propagation: $\(\beta = VBl\)$ where \(V = \pi(n_L - n_R)/\lambda B\) is the Verdet coefficient and is wavelength dependent and small in most materials. It is the strongest in substances containing paramagnetic ions such as terbium.

The Faraday rotation of polarisation is non-reciprocal unlike as discussed previously in natural optical activity.

An optical isolator allows the transmission of light in only one direction. For each pass, the Faraday rotation of the Faraday rotator is \(\pi/4\) Made up of: - input polariser - Faraday rotator - Analyser.

docs.title: Procedure for determining a local coordinate system
Inertial forces in the local coordinate system
docs.text:
Note that in the derivation of centrifugal, coriolis and Euler force terms as mentioned in the previous section assumes \(\underline{r}\) to be defined with repect to a point on the axis of rotation

The displacement of the local coordinate system origin (in the section above) means the associated position vector \(\underline{r}'\) does not begin on the axis of rotation. So we need to substitute \(\underline{r} = \underline{r}' + \underline{R}\) into inertial force terms. \(\underline{r}\) term is the position vector associated with the coordinate system.

docs.title: Centrifugal force
docs.text: The direction is easy to determine, just follow the cross product rule. Hence the centrifugal force points directly away from the axis of rotation.

docs.title: Coriolis Force
docs.text: $$ -2m\underline{\omega} \times {\underline{\dot{r}}}' = -2m\omega (\dot{z}\sin\theta - \dot{y}\cos\theta, \dot{x}\cos\theta, -\dot{x}\sin\theta) $$ It is proportional to velocities, so only comes into play when there is motion. We consider phenomena whe motion is effectively constrained to be in plane, when we ignore the z dimension. so \(\dot{z} = z = 0\)

docs.title: Loose ends
docs.text:
Euler force is not zero on earth but is commonly taken to be negligible.

In a rotating reference frame that is also accelerating translationally with acceleration \(\vec{\ddot{R}}\), the general EOM is given by

\[ m\ddot{\vec{r}} = \vec{F} - 2m\vec{\omega} \times \dot{\vec{r}} - m\vec{\omega} \times (\vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}) - m\dot{\vec{\omega}} \times \vec{r} - m\vec{R}. \]

docs.title: Parton distribution functions (PDFs)
docs.text:
Let \(f_c(X)\) for a given \(Q^2\) be number of density/fraction of a given constituent of \(X\). Based on charge conservation, the sum of the functions will be $$ \int_0^1 \sum_c f_c(X) \, (\text{charge})_c^2 \, dX = \begin{cases} 1 & (\text{proton}) \ 0 & (\text{neutron}) \end{cases} $$ Remember that \(X\) is the fraction of proton's 4-momentum that is stolen by the parton. If we plot the function of proton (with the broadening effect) and log it, we get

The distribution of quarks and antiquarks are, from the plots, $$ \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow f_q(X) &= f_q^V(X) + f_q^S(X) \ \Rightarrow f_{\bar{q}}(X) &= 0 + f_q^S(X) \end{aligned} $$

where the superscript \(V\) means valence quarks and \(S\) means sea quarks.

The parton distribution function in electron-proton scattering is then $$\boxed{ F^{e-p}(X) = X \sum_q \sum_{y=s,v} (\text{charge})q^2 \left[ f_q^y(X) + f $$ Here the }}^y(X) \right]\((\text{charge})_q^2\) is the interaction strength and it can be generalised to other scattering. For example, for proton/electron-neutrino scattering, we use weak coupling constant.

Using PDF, we can add up the total 4-momentum in a nucleon: $$ P_{\text{total}} = \int_0^1 X \sum_c c(X) P_c \, dX $$ where \(P_c\) is the 4-momentum stolen by the particle \(c\). But experimentally, the value is half of the theoretically value so we are missing something i.e. gluons.

docs.title: Introduction To Dielectrics
docs.text:
[!Definition of Dielectrics] Dielectrics are insulator materials that can be polarised by an applied electric field. $\(C= \frac{Q}{V} = \epsilon_0\epsilon_r\frac{A}{d}\)$ where \(\epsilon_r\) is the dielectric constant

This is the electric analogue of diamagnets with equations here. When an atom is being polarised by an electric field, it forms an electric dipole moment by deforming its electron cloud, governed by formula $\(|\mu| = qd\)$ and torque $\(\mathbf{\tau} = \mu \times \mathbf{E}\)$ and potential energy due to electric field $\(U = -\mu \cdot \mathbf{E}\)$

docs.title: Dielectric Media In An Electric Field
docs.text:
The torque induces rotations in the dipole such that the positive side aligns with the electric field

and the polarisation (magnetisation in magnetism) is defined as the dipole moment per unit volume $\(\mathbf{P} = N\mu\)$ The electric field due to a single dipole is $\(\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{3(\boldsymbol{\mu} \cdot \mathbf{r})\mathbf{r} - r^2 \boldsymbol{\mu}}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r^5}\)$ and the uniform polarisation \(\mathbf{P}\), the collective effect of all dipoles is the surface charge density $\(\sigma = \mathbf{P} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{n}}\)$ The polarisability, \(\alpha\) (sensitivity of a dipole to external electric field) of a single dipole is $\(\mu = \alpha\mathbf{E}_{\text{local}}\)$

docs.title: Local Electric Field Of a Dipole
docs.text:
To calculate this, we need to cut a spherical segment of dipole and calculate this separately.

Given that the Lorentz field is $\(\mathbf{E}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{P}}{3\epsilon_0}\)$ and atomistic field is, as suggested above, $\(\begin{aligned} \mathbf{E}_3 &= \sum_{\text{dipoles } i} \frac{3(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \cdot \mathbf{r}_i)\mathbf{r}_i - r_i^2 \boldsymbol{\mu}_i}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r_i^5} \\ &= \mu \sum_{i} \frac{3x_i^2 - r_i^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r_i^5} = 0 \end{aligned}\)$ where we have assume \(\mu_i = \mu\) is parallel to the \(x\) axis and $\(\sum_{i} x_i^2 = \sum_{i} y_i^2 = \sum_{i} z_i^2 = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{i} r_i^2\)$ Therefore we have $\(\mathbf{E}_{\text{local}} = \mathbf{E}_{\text{ext}} - \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} + \frac{P}{3\epsilon_0}\)$
