docs.title: Covalent Bonding
docs.text:
The electron density for pure covalent bond is symmetrical. When the electron density cloud for two atoms overlap, it forms a region with less/more electron density depending on the type of interference.

For destructive interference, the centre region has less electron density and hence forming antibonding molecular orbital

Otherwise, the centre region has more electron density and form a bonding molecular orbital

The quantum mechanical derivation is outlined in Bonding. The extend of interaction and stabilisation of the bonding combination depends on the energy difference between the antibonding and bonding energy levels. For example

HF has a larger energy difference between the antibonding \(3\sigma^*\) and \(2\sigma\) and the former is closer to the 1s atomic orbital while the latter is closer to the 2p atomic orbital. This means that there is less mixing between states and more of ionic property and it will be discussed below.

In contrast, HCl has less energy difference and more mixing between states.

These molecular orbital will overlap each other in solids and form a band where the bonding levels will overlap to form valence band and antibonding forms conduction band.

Since the band gaps and the widths of the conduction band depend on the interatomic distance, it allows us to find which elements are metals or insulator or semiconductor

docs.title: Ionic Bonding
docs.text:
When the relative energy between the interacting atoms becomes large, the covalent bonding is effectively turning into ionic bonding.

Since all interactions are attractive in close range and repulsive in long range, ionic bonding is attractive in close range because of Coulomb force and repulsive because of the electronic repulsion.

Therefore we are looking for the equilibrium between these two forces i.e. the overall lattice energy is $\(U_{\text{lattice}} = U_{\text{Mad}} + U_{\text{rep}} = \alpha \frac{N_A Q_+ Q_-}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r} + m N_A B e^{\frac{-r}{\rho}}\)$ where \(U_\text{Mad}\) is Madelung attractive energy and \(U_\text{rep}\) is the Born-Mayer repulsive energy. \(N_A\) is the Avogadro's constant, \(B\) and \(\rho\) are the constants to be determined.

docs.title: Electronegativity
docs.text:
To classify the bonding of two elements, it is easier to define a new concept: electronegativity which means the ability of an atom to attract draw electron cloud towards itself.

Bonding between atoms with very different electronegativities will be predominantly ionic.

docs.title: Hydrogen Bonding
docs.text: • Interaction between an positive dipole \(\delta^+\) and the lone pair of electrons in very electronegative elements such as FON (Fluorine, Oxygen and Nitrogen).

docs.title: van Der Waals
docs.text:
This is common in soft matter physics.

  • Temporary dipole-dipole interaction
  • Fluctuating electron density induces transient dipole

This dipole from species 1 has an electric field of $\(E=\frac{p_1}{2\pi\epsilon_0r^3}\)$ Depending on the polarisability of species 2 which described by \(p_2 = \alpha E\) the potential energy is then $\(U = \frac{-|p_1| |p_2|}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r^3} = \frac{-|p_1| \chi E}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r^3} = \frac{-|p_1|^2 \chi}{(4\pi \epsilon_0 r^3)^2}\)$ Thus the force of this is \(f\propto r^{-7}\). This is then balanced with the repulsive force described by Lennard-Jones potential which arised from the cohesive energy i.e. energy needed to separate constituent pairs of species. $\(U_{LJ Cohesive} = -2E_0 \left[ A_6 \left( \frac{\sigma}{r_{ij}} \right)^6 - A_{12} \left( \frac{\sigma}{r_{ij}} \right)^{12} \right]\)$

docs.title: Introduction to Atomic Clock
docs.text: Small width because $\(\sigma \propto \frac{\Delta \omega}{\omega_{12}}\)$

docs.title: Introduction to Coherence
docs.text:
Coherence is all about phase. - Coherent light has a well-defined phase and we can sum the electric field \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2\) - Incoherent light doesn't have a well-defined phase and we can sum the intensity \(I = I_1 + I_2\)

The reasoning is here.

docs.title: Measurement of Coherence
docs.text:
• Use interference

Coherent light will have a defined phase interference pattern with 100% visibility, otherwise the light is incoherent.

When we say phase interference, we are using one single light source, spread them into two paths with one of the path having delayed phase and make them interfere. This can be achieved using Young double slit or Michaelson interferometer.

docs.title: Introduction to Density of States and Fermi Dirac Curve
docs.text:
Following from last chapter we see that \(e^\alpha e^{\beta\varepsilon}\) can be written in terms of $$ e^{\alpha + \beta \epsilon_j} = e^{\beta (\varepsilon - \mu)} $$ by defining \(\alpha = \beta \mu\) where \(\mu\) is the Fermi level. We can determine if the energy levels are below or above the Fermi level by looking at the sign of \(\varepsilon - \mu\) .

In the context of Fermi-Dirac distribution, at \(T=0\), all states with \(\varepsilon < \mu\) are filled and states with \(\varepsilon>\mu\) are empty.

docs.title: Dilution Limit
docs.text:
The system becomes classical when the states are more than the particles themselves, i.e. low density. As the quantum phenomena such as Pauli exclusion principle and the exchange terms can be neglected as the particles are very 'weakly' interacting with each other.

Therefore, Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions become Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution when the states are far more than the particles, i.e. \(g\gg N\), this is dilution limit.

Therefore, we need to formulate a concept of density of states to justify if the system is at the dilution limit.

docs.title: Introduction to Lasers and Cavities
docs.text:
Lasers require two mirrors reflecting lights back and fourth but most of the field distribution light will not fold back on themselves i.e. mess in the cavity. Therefore we need to use modes (field distributions that propagate without change in shape), e.g. gaussian.

How you go and find modes? We use paraxial wave equation (differential equation) for low-loss cavity and gaussian beam is the simplest solutions, but it depends on the shape of your lenses. And we don't want high order mode because they tend to spread out (we want to confine the light in the cavity).

The intensity of the laser outside the cavity is $\(I = I_0 \exp \left\{ -\frac{2(x^2 + y^2)}{W^2} \right\}\)$

There are ways to quantify the waist of the laser beam 1. \(1/e^2\) for laser community 2. FWHM 3. Standard Deviation

docs.title: Propagation of Beam From Waist \(w_0\)
docs.text:
At waist $\(\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{E}_0 e^{-\frac{x^2}{w_0^2}} \cdot e^{-\frac{y^2}{w_0^2}}\)$

The distribution of light or the angular spectrum is then $\(A^{(0)} = \mathcal{F}[\mathcal{E}^{(0)}](u, v) = \pi w_0^2 \mathcal{E}_0 e^{-\pi^2(u^2 + v^2)w_0^2}\)$ Using radial wave vector \(k_\rho^2 = 4\pi^2(u^2 + v^2)\), we have $\(A^{(0)} = \pi w_0^2 \mathcal{E}_0 \exp \left\{ -k_\rho^2 \frac{w_0^2}{4} \right\}\)$ Under paraxial limit \(k_z = \sqrt{k^2 - k_\rho^2} \approx k - \frac{k_\rho^2}{2k}\) and throw it into the hedgehog equation gives $\(\mathcal{E}^{(z)} = e^{ikz} \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left[ e^{- \frac{ik_\rho^2 z}{2k}} \mathcal{F}[\mathcal{E}^{(0)}] \right]\)$ which gives $\(= \frac{z_R}{iq} \mathcal{E}_0 e^{ikz} e^{i \frac{k \rho^2}{2q}}\)$ where \(q = z - iz_R\) is a complex beam parameter and \(z_R = \pi w_o^2/\lambda\) is the Rayleigh range i.e. how far you have to go to reach Fraunhofer regime.

docs.title: Introduction to Superconductivity
docs.text: When a metal is cooled below the critical temperature (phase transition), the resistivity drops to zero. It can be modelled as $\(\rho(T) = \underbrace{\rho_0}_\text{Impurity effects} + \underbrace{aT^2}_\text{electron-electron scattering} + \underbrace{bT^5}_\text{electron-phonon scattering}\)$

docs.title: Persistent Currents
docs.text:
The idea is that when a metal ring is immerse in a magnetic field at finite temperature, electric field is produced in the ring according to the maxwell equation. If it is immediately cool to below \(T_c\) and the magnetic field is switched off, the supercurrent will flow indefinitely.

The decay of current density is $\(J(t) = J_0 \ \text{exp}(-t/\tau)\)$ where \(\tau\) is the average time between scattering events. For superconductors, there is no noticeable decay in current even after several years as compared to metal that decays to only 1% of its starting value within 1 ps.

docs.title: Meissner effect
docs.text: As the superconductors will repel the magnetic fields, it can be described as a perfect diamagnet with a magnetic susceptibility of $\(\chi = \frac{M}{H} = -1\)$ However the questions why it is a perfect diamagnet and what is the connection between this and 0 resistivity are still unknown.

docs.title: Type I Superconductors
docs.text:
We increase the H field and measure the M field (which gives negative gradient because susceptibility is -1). The superconductor is doing work against the magnetic field to repel it so it increases the free energy of the system. At some point (the critical H field), it is no longer favourable so the system gives up the superconducting state.

The phase diagram is as such and the empirical formula for Type I is $\(B_c(T) = B_c(0) \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{T}{T_c} \right)^2 \right]\)$

If we have a superconducting, current-carrying wire, the maximum allowed current is $\(I_{max} = \frac{2\pi R B_c(T)}{\mu_0}\)$

where we can derive this equation from \(B = \mu_0 I/2\pi R\)

docs.title: Type II Superconductors
docs.text:
The vortex state is the mixture of normal and superconducting states. And it can be visualised below.

The pores are the normal state where the magnetic flux penetrates through it and the 'blocks' between pores are the superconducting state where no field penetrates.

The magnitude of flux through the filament is constant \((= h/2e)\) and they are called fluxons. As the magnetic field increases, the spacing between filaments decreases i.e. the filaments become denser.

docs.title: Macrostate
docs.text:
• Average properties such as \(p, V, T\) and average velocity are defined by macrostate
  • Composed of microstates (precise configuration)

docs.title: Multiplicity
docs.text: • Number of microstates to make up a macrostate $\(\Omega = \frac{N!}{\prod_i n_i!}\)$ where \(N\) is the number of objects and \(n_i\) is the number of possible states. If there are only 2 possible states then the equation becomes $\(\Omega = \frac{N!}{r!(N-r)!}\)$

docs.title: Boltzmann distribution (statistical definition of temperature)
docs.text: $\(\frac{1}{k_B T} = \frac{d\ln \Omega}{dE} = \beta\)$ where \(\beta\) is Boltzmann factor

docs.title: Introduction, heat and temperature
docs.text:
[!Assumption of Ideal gas] - Negligible volume - Spherical particles - Elastic collision - No interaction between particles $\(pV = nRT = nkT\)$

[!Definitions of thermodynamical processes] 1. Diathermal: Heat transfer 2. Adiathermal: No heat transfer 3. Adiabatic: Reversible no heat transfer, ie \(dQ = 0\)

  • For adiabat, the equations governs \(pV^{\gamma} = constant = TV^{\gamma -1}\)
  • For isotherm, constant T \(\implies pV = constant\), \(dU = 0\) (T is constant but dQ is not because there is heat exchange to keep the temperature constant. The confusion araises from the integral definition of dQ where it assumes no work done on the system, unlike in isothermic system.)
  • For isochoric, constant volume
  • For isobar, constant pressure

[!Definition of Heat capacity] $\(C_{\alpha} = \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial T}\right)_\alpha\)$ \(C_p\) is larger than \(C_v\) because the heat you put in in \(C_p\) will put a work to increase the temperature.

docs.text: • Two systems independently in thermal equilibrium with a third system, are also in thermal equilibrium themselves

docs.title: Kink and Topological Objects
docs.text:
Most systems break symmetry in the same way:

They either choose one side or two sides at \(-v\) and \(v\). These kind of breaking of symmetry is called wall or kink (for Quantum Field Theory) or soliton (for classical mechanics).

Vortices are said to be topologically equivalent if the winding number is the same.

docs.title: Energy of a kink
docs.text:
Remember that the free energy has kinetic and potential term: $\(f = f_0 + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{\nabla}\phi)^2}_{\text{"Kinetic energy" } K} \pm \underbrace{\frac{\mu^2}{2}\phi^2 + \frac{\lambda}{4!}\phi^4}_{\text{"Potential energy" } U}\)$

Suppose kink is of size \(l\): The energy cost for the kinetic term is $\(\begin{aligned} &\int dx \, \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} \right)^2 \approx l \left( \frac{v}{l} \right)^2 = \frac{v^2}{l} \end{aligned}\)$ where we used dimensional analysis and neglecting the prefactor. \(\partial \phi\) is related to \(v\) based on the alternative graph shown in the figure above and \(\partial x\) is related to \(l\) i.e. length of the wall. To let this to be roughly equal to the equation in Magnetic Domain, we need to minimise the cost by smearing out the wall.

The energy cost for the potential term is $\(\int dx \, U(\phi) \approx l \lambda v^4\)$ where \(l\) comes from \(dx\) and \(\lambda v^4\) comes from the \(U\). Therefore the total energy is $$E \approx \frac{v^2}{l} + l \lambda v^4 $$ where it has a similar form as Magnetic Domain (one term is inversely proportional to \(l\) and another one is linearly proportional to \(l\)). The minimum of this energy is then $\(\frac{\partial E}{\partial l} = -\frac{v^2}{l^2} + \lambda v^4 = 0 \implies l = \left( \frac{1}{\lambda v^2} \right)^{1/2}\)$ or $\(l \sim \frac{1}{\mu}\)$ Therefore it requires a finite length and energy to form kinks/walls.

The energy will be centred at the centre of the kink because that is where the total spin is zero and it can be anywhere. It costs semi-infinite amount of energy to remove it i.e. it is stable.

docs.title: Kink - anti-kink pair
docs.text:
Aside: Skyrmions are the squashing of monopoles

But vortices are not stable on their own even though one vortex costs infinite amount of energy because of their swirliness at infinity. This is because they can be cancelled via a vortex-antivortex annihilation, time dependence and be bound by a boundary (add a field that cancels the effect of the swirliness).

Derrich's theorem: Time-independent topological objects are impossible in more than one spatial dimension for this theory.

docs.title: Lagrange's formulation of mechanics
docs.text: Assumptions: - Holonomic constraints (not expressed in differential equations or inequalities) - Contraining forces do no virtual work - Applied forces are conservative (no dissipative forces)

docs.title: Generalised equations of motion
docs.text:
(A bunch of derivation in front, i will only quote the result)

The defining Lagrangian is $\(L = T - V\)$ where \(T\) is the kinetic energy and \(V\) is the potential energy. The Euler-Lagrange equations is $$ \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_k} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k} = 0 $$ where $\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q_k}} = p_k\)$ and $\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k} = F_k\)$

docs.title: Ignorable coordinates
docs.text: A coordinate is \(q_k\) is ignorable if: $\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k} = 0\)$ Implications: - The conjugate momentum is then a constant since \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k} = 0 = constant\)

docs.title: Landau Theory Of Phase Transition
docs.text:
This is the basics of Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity and here we will add some extra stuff as an extension.

Recall that the Ginzburg-Landau Theory is $\(G_s(T) = G_N(T) + a(T) |\psi|^2+\frac{b(T)}{2}|\psi|^4\)$ where there is no odd power to ensure the function is symmetrical. There are two remarks to take away:

  1. Phase transitions are sharp at \(T = T_c\) i.e. the symmetry is either broken or not, not gradually.
  2. The consequences of broken symmetry are
    • Phase transitions: Mathematical singularity at \(T_c\)
    • Rigidity: Property to transmit forces
    • Excitations: Creation of new particle
    • Defects: Walls that separate different order in different places

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Maxwell-Boltzmann curve gives the probability-velocity curve. Laser cooling the velocity of the distribution to 'cool' the temperature. Note that we always want the atoms to decay from the excited to ground state i.e. closed loop transition without needing a repumping laser.

Consider atom travelling in \(+z\) direction towards a laser beam with \(\omega_L\).

The frequency experienced by atom is $$ \omega = \omega_L \left( 1 + \frac{v_z}{c} \right) $$

To slow the atom, we red detune the laser so that the atom will reach resonance with the laser frequency, described by formula: $$ \Delta = \omega_{12} - \omega_L = \frac{\omega_L v_z}{c} = k v_z $$

[!Definition] Red detuning: Setting the laser frequency to slightly below the resonance frequency

However, the atom will slow down when in resonance with the laser, causing it to shift away from the red-detuning laser.

docs.title: Compensation
docs.text:
1. Change the laser frequency over time (Chirp cooling) but this can only work with pulses of atoms, not continuous beams.
  2. Shift the resonance frequency with position to keep the atoms in resonance as they slow down (Zeeman Deceleration)

[!Zeeman Deceleration] - To compensate Doppler shift, a position-dependent magnetic field is applied to Zeeman-shift the atomic resonance. - The magnetic field is set such that $\(\omega_{12} + \underbrace{\frac{\mu_B B(z)}{\hbar}}_{\text{frequency of the magnetic field } (\hbar\omega = \mu_B B(z))} = \omega_L + kv_z\)$ - Another equation can be derived $\(B(z) = B_0 \left( 1 - \frac{z}{L_0} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} + B_{\text{bias}}\)$ - Without \(B_{bias}\), the magnetic field will go to zero at the end so we need to ensure a nonzero magnetic field everywhere. So we set \(\mu_B B_{bias} \approx \hbar\omega_L - \hbar\omega_{12}\), then the atoms come to rest at \(z=L_0\) - Achieved experimentally with a tapered solenoid - Useful for cooling fast atoms such as He/Li and atoms with low vapour pressure

Recall the scattering force in Light Forces $$ F = \frac{\Gamma}{2} \frac{I}{I + I_{\text{sat}} \left( 1 + \frac{4\Delta^2}{\Gamma^2} \right)} $$

If the atom has velocity \(v_z\) we need to include the doppler shift in the detuning term $$ F_\pm = \pm \frac{\hbar k \Gamma}{2} \frac{I}{I + I_{\text{sat}} \left( 1 + \frac{4(\Delta I k v_z)^2}{\Gamma^2} \right)} $$

Then the total force (\(F = F_+ +F_-\)) on atom is shown in with capture range \(\approx \pm \Delta/k\)

docs.title: Doppler cooling limit
docs.text:
• Lowest temperature can possibly achieve

Diffusion: $$ T_{\text{min}} = \frac{\hbar \Gamma}{2k_B} \frac{1 + \left( \frac{2\Delta}{\Gamma} \right)^2}{-2\Delta / \Gamma} $$ Minimum is at \(\Delta = -\Gamma/2\) so we have $\(T_{min}= \frac{\hbar\Gamma}{2k_B}\)$

docs.title: Doppler velocity
docs.text:
• Velocity corresponding to a Doppler shift equal to natural linewidth \(\Gamma\)
  • Beyond this velocity, the atom is significantly off resonance
  • Equate Kinetic energy to \(\hbar\Gamma/2\)

docs.title: Recoil velocity
docs.text:
• Velocity an atom acquires from absorbing or emitting a single photon

Calculated from using the conservation of momentum $\(mv_r = \hbar k\)$

docs.title: Capture velocity
docs.text:
• Maximum initial velocity at which an atom can still be slowed and trapped by a given laser-cooling configuration
\[v_c \approx \frac{\Gamma}{k}\]

docs.title: Lasers Beams
docs.text:
The electric field of the laser beams evolves as $\(\mathcal{E}^{(z)} = \mathcal{E}_0 \underbrace{\frac{w_0}{w}}_{\text{Amplitude Scaling}} \ \underbrace{e^{-i\alpha}}_{\text{Gouy Phase}} \ \underbrace{e^{ikz}}_{\text{Plane wave}} \ \underbrace{e^{i \frac{k \rho^2}{2R}}}_{\text{Wavefront Curvature}} \ \underbrace{e^{-\frac{\rho^2}{W^2}}}_{\text{Gaussian Profile}}\)$ where \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}(z/z_R)\) evolves from \(-\pi/2 \ \text{to} \ \pi/2\) as \(z/z_R \rightarrow \pm\infty\) and it is a phase shift of \(\pi\) as it propagates through space. It describes the difference between curved and plane wavefronts i.e.

and \(R = z + z_R^2/z\) . Rearranging this gives $\(w = w_0 \left( 1 + \frac{z^2}{z_0^2} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\)$

For large \(z/{z_R} \text{ , } \quad w = w_0 z/{z_R}\) and therefore the diffraction angle is $\(\Delta\theta = \frac{w}{z} = \frac{w_0}{z_R} = \frac{\lambda}{\pi w_0}\)$ where \(z_R = w_0^2/\lambda\). Remember, smaller waist spreads more, larger waist spreads less. Just remember this as \(\Delta \theta = \lambda / D = \lambda / w_0\) which the missing factor is 1.22 for circular aperture and \(1/\pi\) for gaussian beam spread. (end of this page summary)

docs.title: Lattices and Symmetry Operations
docs.text: A solid is a crystal is its atoms, ions and molecules form, on average, a long-range ordered arrangement i.e. periodic array governed by the rules of translational symmetry i.e. they have to obey symmetry operations: transformations that leave object indistinguishable from its initial state

docs.title: Symmetry Operations
docs.text:
Here we are focusing so far on point group symmetry operation which is defined as

[!Definition] Operations carried out on with respect to a point that does not move during the operation.

Mathematically, it transforms basis \(\mathbf{r}\) to a new basis \(\mathbf{r'}\) through a transformation matrix \(\mathbf{R}\): $\(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{r'}\)$

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Transformation that leaves the object unchanged.
  • Transformation matrix is an identity matrix

docs.title: Proper Rotation \(n\) or \(C_n\)
docs.text:
• Rotates an object by \((360/n)\degree\)
  • Transformation matrix is a rotational matrix with trigs
  • Principle rotation axis is defined as the rotation with highest \(n\)

docs.title: Rotoinversion \(\bar{n}\)
docs.text:
• Rotates an object by \((360/n)\degree\) and invert it with respect to the centre of symmetry.
  • \(\bar{1}\) (or sometimes \(i\)) is inversion operation alone
  • \(\bar{2}\) (or sometimes \(\sigma\) or \(m\)) is rotation by \(180\degree\) followed by inversion

docs.title: Improper Rotation \(S_n\)
docs.text: • Rotates an object by \((360/n)\degree\) and reflect it

docs.title: Left brain vs right brain
docs.text:
Corpus callosum (nerve in between right and left brain) was cut to treat epilepsy in the past. But the patients could use their brain separately, each with its own strengths and weaknesses.

It is oversimplified to say left brain is for logical and right brain is for creativity. One could say it is left brain is, dominantly, for logics.

Remember that brain is a network of wires, talking to each other with corpus callosum. When cut, the task cannot be executed perfectly. For example, when cut, when a patient is given a picture on their left side, the right hemisphere registers it but the information cannot be sent to left hemisphere, causing the patient to not being able to name the pic.

docs.title: Length Scales
docs.text:
This can be investigated by pair distribution functions. Here, we take liquid, crystalline solids and amorphous solids as example.

In solids, the crystal structures repeat themselves over specific points in the lattice so they have a well-defined long length scale. In amorphous solids, the positions of atom are disordered and there is a distribution of distances between the atoms.

To quantify this, we use probability to find atoms in a certain radius from the atom, \(g_{kl}(r)\) or pair distribution function $\(n_{kl} = 4\pi r^2 \rho_l g_{kl}(r) dr\)$ where \(n_{kl}\) is the number of atoms of type \(l\) within a shell thickness of \(dr\) at a distance \(r\) from atom \(k\). The behaviour of the pair distribution function is that: $$ g_{kl}(r) = \begin{cases} 0 & r < \text{bond length} \ \text{oscillations/peaks} & \text{intermediate } r \ 1 & r \rightarrow \infty \end{cases}$$

Here, \(g_{kl}(r)\) in intermediate \(r\) has different behaviour i.e. - \(g_{kl}(r) < 1\) when fewer atoms than expected from uniform arrangement (\(g_{kl}(r) =1\)) - \(g_{kl}(r) > 1\) more atoms than expected from uniform arrangement

For solids, there will be defined peaks over a large distance but not amorphous solids as there is no well-defined repeating lattice structure.

i.e. amorphous solids seem similar to gases and liquids at longer length scales.

docs.title: Stress, Strain and Timescales
docs.text:
This section particularly focuses on using viscosity to categorise the state of matter. In [[Physics/Physics/Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics|Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics]] we mentioned that everything is viscoelastic depending on the timescales. Here the shear viscosity is $\(\eta = \frac{\sigma}{\dot{e}}\)$ where \(\sigma\) is shear stress and \(\dot{e}\) is the shear rate. Liquids respond more quickly to shear stresses (obviously) than solids.

Under stress (which results in strain): 1. Van Der Waals bonding will undergo deformation because it is weak and the layers are slipping over one another 2. Covalent bonding will break as it is fragile due to its directional property and being stronger than other bonds 3. Metallic bonding: metals are elastic at low stresses and undergo plastic deformation at high stresses described in [[Physics/Physics/Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics|Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics]]

docs.title: Lens applications Imaging
docs.text: Suppose there is a spherical wave at \(-s_1\) and converge to \(s_2\). The input field is $$ E^{i(0)} = \frac{E_{s1}}{i k s_1} e^{i k s_1} e^{i k \rho^2 / (2 s_1)} $$ and in the thin lens which we discussed in Paraxial optics example Lenses, the field is $$ E^{(L)} = E^{i(0)} e^{-i k \rho'^2 / (2 f)} = \frac{E_{s1}}{i k s_1} e^{i k s_1} e^{i k \rho'^2 / (2 s_1)} e^{-i k \rho'^2 / (2 f)} $$ The outgoing wave is then $$ E^{o(0)} = -\frac{E_{s2}}{i k s_2} e^{-i k s_2} e^{-i k \rho'^2 / (2 s_2)} $$ Due to the continuity equation, the incoming and outgoing fields are the same $$ \frac{E_{s1}}{i k s_1} e^{i k s_1} e^{i k \rho'^2 / (2 s_1)} e^{-i k \rho'^2 / (2 f)} = -\frac{E_{s2}}{i k s_2} e^{-i k s_2} e^{-i k \rho'^2 / (2 s_2)} $$ and we get $$ \frac{E_{s1}}{i k s_1} e^{i k s_1} = -\frac{E_{s2}}{i k s_2} e^{-i k s_2} $$ which results in thin lens equation $$ \frac{1}{s_1} - \frac{1}{f} = -\frac{1}{s_2} $$

docs.title: Mechanism of Light Forces
docs.text:
1. When atom absorbs a photon, it receives a momentum kick in the direction of the incoming path
  2. The atom spontaneously decay at a rate of \(\Gamma = 1/\tau\). Photons are emitted in a random direction with the atom receiving a momentum kick in the opposite direction to the photon emission.
  3. The spontaneous emission is isotropic and the momentum average to zero. Each cycle on average transfers \(\hbar k\) to the atom.

docs.title: Force exerted on atom
docs.text:
The atom experiences force $\(\underline{F}=\hbar\underline{k}R_{\text{scatt}} = \hbar \underline{k} \frac{dN_2}{dt}\)$ The maximum scattering rate (minimum time to excite the atom and decay again) is \(R_{\text{max}} = 1/2\tau\)

\(\implies\) $\(\underline{F}=\frac{\hbar k}{2\tau}\)$ Since the decay time is related to the linewidth \(\Gamma\), it explains why we need to use laser to cool the atoms, instead of a white light source.

docs.title: Einstein treatment of absorption and emission
docs.text:
[!Important] with scattering rates \(R_{\text{{scatt}}}\): - Spontaneous emision: \(A_{21}\) - Absorption: \(B_{21}\rho(\omega_{12})\) - Simulated emisssion: \(B_{21}\rho(\omega_{21})\)

where \(\rho(\omega)\) is the spectral energy density (defined: energy density per unit angular frequency range at \(\omega_{12}\)).

We need to include the spectral energy density for the absorption and simulated emission, not for spontaneous emission, because we need an external electromagnetic field to drive the transitions.

docs.title: Finding Einstein-B coefficient
docs.text:
Since it is in the same system, we realise that the scattering rate and the total population densities are the same i.e. \(N_1 + N_2 = N\) and $$ \frac{dN_2}{dt} = -\frac{dN_1}{dt} $$ $$ \implies N_1 B_{12} \rho(\omega) = N_2 A_{21} + N_2 B_{21} \rho(\omega) $$

\[ \implies \rho(\omega) = \frac{N_2 A_{21}}{N_1 B_{12} - N_2 B_{21}} = \frac{A_{21}/B_{21}}{\frac{N_1}{N_2} \frac{B_{12}}{B_{21}} - 1} $$ Using the statistical physics approach (remember to give link when done): $$ \frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{g_2}{g_1} e^{-\frac{\hbar \omega_{12}}{k_B T}} \] \[ \implies \rho(\omega) = \frac{A_{21}/B_{21}}{\frac{g_1 B_{12}}{g_2 B_{21}} \exp\left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{12}}{k_B T}\right) - 1} \]

Compare it to Plank's blackbody spectrum \((g_1B_{12} = g_2B_{21})\) and

[!note] $$ \rho(\omega) = \frac{\hbar \omega^3}{\pi^2 c^3} \frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{\hbar \omega}{k_B T}\right) - 1} $$

$$ \implies A_{21} = \frac{\hbar \omega_{12}^3}{\pi^2 c^3} \, B_{21} $$ Remember the form of A coefficient in Linewidth and Broadening.

docs.title: Population densities of state 1 and 2
docs.text:
Using the first two equations on this page, we find

\[ \frac{dN_2}{dt} = N B_{12} \rho(\omega) - \left( A_{21} + B_{21} \rho(\omega) \right) N_2 \]

Then we solve for this differential equation and obtain: $$ N_2 = \frac{N B_{12} \rho(\omega)}{A_{21} + 2 B_{12} \rho(\omega)} \left[ 1 - \exp\left[-(A_{21} + 2 B_{12} \rho(\omega)) t\right] \right] $$

docs.title: Equilibrium
docs.text: Reminder: there are stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium and they occur when the generalised forces vanish.

docs.title: Simple harmonic motion
docs.text: For a simple harmonic oscillator, the Lagrangian is $$ L = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{q}^2 - \frac{1}{2} k q^2 $$ which matches the form above. If \(D/F < 0\), then it's simple harmonic motion, or stable equilibrium. If \(D/F > 0\), it's unstable. The characteristic frequency is \(\omega = \sqrt{-D/F}\). The equation can be solved to give $$ q(t) = q(0) \cos(\omega t) + \frac{\dot{q}(0)}{\omega} \sin(\omega t) $$ where \(\omega = \sqrt{k/m}\)

docs.title: Damping force
docs.text: Dissipative force is expressed as $$ F_d = -\gamma \dot{q} = -\left( \frac{m \omega}{Q} \right) \dot{q} $$ from Stoke's law where \(Q\) is the dimensionless quality factor of the oscillator. Equate this to the Euler equation with the Lagrangian of simple harmonic oscillator and solve it gives $$ \ddot{q} + \frac{\omega}{Q} \dot{q} + \omega^2 q = 0 $$ The trial solution to this differential equation is \(q = e^{\lambda t}\) and it gives $$\lambda = \frac{\omega}{2Q} \pm \frac{\omega}{2Q} \sqrt{1 - 4Q^2} = \frac{\omega}{2Q} \pm \omega' $$ along with the full equation of $$ q(t) = A e^{-\left(\frac{\omega}{2Q} + \omega'\right)t} + B e^{-\left(\frac{\omega}{2Q} - \omega'\right)t} $$

docs.title: \(Q > 1/2\) (high quality)- underdamped
docs.text:
The value of \(\lambda\) becomes imaginary and it becomes $$ \lambda = -\frac{\omega}{2Q} \pm i\omega' $$ \(\implies\)

The value of \(Q\) can determine the amplitude of the peak and higher \(Q\) can lead to longer time to decay.

docs.title: \(Q<1/2\) (low quality) - overdamped
docs.text: \[\lambda = -\frac{\omega}{2Q}\pm\omega'\]

docs.title: Linear birefringence
docs.text:
The two orthogonal axes are called fast and slow axes, with refractive indices \(n_f\) and \(n_s\) (as the names suggest, the light passes more slowly in slow axis) where \(n_f > n_s\) since \(n = c/v\). They are also called extraordinary and ordinary axes.

If the input polarisation in the \(z = 0\) plane is linearly polarised with a direction at \(\pi/4\) to the slow axis, we can write

\[ E^{(0)}=\frac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{f}}+\hat{\epsilon}_{\mathrm{s}}\right)e^{-i\omega t} \]

and after distance \(z\) $$ \begin{split} E^{(z)}&=\frac{E_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(e^{in_{\mathrm{f}}kz}\hat{\epsilon}{\mathrm{f}}+e^{in}}kz}\hat{\epsilon{\mathrm{s}}\right)e^{-i\omega t}\ &=\frac{E}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{\epsilon{\mathrm{f}}+e^{i\varphi}\hat{\epsilon}, \end{split} \tag{104} $$ where }}\right)e^{i(n_{\mathrm{f}}kz-\omega t)\(\varphi=2\pi(n_{\mathrm{s}}-n_{\mathrm{f}})z/\lambda\)

\(\implies\) Polarisation state varies with \(z\) and \(\lambda\)

docs.title: Linear polarisation in a circular basis
docs.text:
To turn the circular basis back to linear basis, plugging (100) and (101) to (102) from Circular basis, gives $$ \begin{align} \underline{E} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} [E_+ (\hat{\epsilon}1 + i\hat{\epsilon}_2) + E- (\hat{\epsilon}1 - i\hat{\epsilon}_2) e^{i\varphi}] e^{i(\underline{k}\cdot\underline{r}-\omega t)} \ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} [(E+ + E_- e^{i\varphi}) \hat{\epsilon}1 + i (E+ - E_- e^{i\varphi}) \hat{\epsilon}_2] e^{i(\underline{k}\cdot\underline{r}-\omega t)} \ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (E_1 e^{i\phi_1} \hat{\epsilon}_1 + E_2 e^{i\phi_2} \hat{\epsilon}_2) e^{i(\underline{k}\cdot\underline{r}-\omega t)} \end{align} $$ where linear polarisation requires \(\phi_1 = \phi_2\).

The phases are be $$ \begin{align} \phi_1 &= \arctan \frac{E_- \sin \varphi}{E_+ + E_- \cos \varphi} \ \phi_2 &= \arctan \frac{E_+ - E_- \cos \varphi}{E_- \sin \varphi} \end{align} $$

Combining the information mentioned previously, we get that $$ \begin{align} \frac{E_{-} \sin \varphi}{E_{+} + E_{-} \cos \varphi} &= \frac{E_{+} - E_{-} \cos \varphi}{E_{-} \sin \varphi} \ \Rightarrow E_{-}^{2} \sin^{2} \varphi &= E_{+}^{2} - E_{-}^{2} \cos^{2} \varphi \ \Rightarrow E_{+}^{2} &= E_{-}^{2} \ |E_{+}| &= |E_{-}| \end{align} $$ Hence the expression for a linearly polarised wave in a circular basis is $$ E = E_{0} (\hat{\epsilon}{+} + \hat{\epsilon} $$ where } e^{i\varphi}) e^{i(\underline{k}\cdot\underline{r}-\omega t)\(E_0 = E_+ = E_-\) and the angle \(\alpha\) is $$ \begin{align} \alpha &= \arctan \left( \frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}} \right) \ &= \arctan \left[ \frac{E_{0} \sqrt{(1 + \cos \varphi)^{2} + \sin^{2} \varphi}}{E_{0} \sqrt{\sin^{2} \varphi + (1 - \cos \varphi)^{2}}} \right] \ &= \arctan \left( \sqrt{\frac{2 - 2 \cos \varphi}{2 + 2 \cos \varphi}} \right) \ &= \arctan \left[ \sqrt{\frac{\sin^{2} (\varphi/2)}{\cos^{2} (\varphi/2)}} \right] \ &= \arctan [\tan (\varphi/2)] \ &= \frac{\varphi}{2} \end{align} $$

docs.title: Linear polarisation in a linear basis
docs.text:
In the linear basis, two linearly polarised plane waves - both with the same \(\underline{k}\) and \(\omega\) - are used to construct polarised light. The electric fields associated with the two plane waves point along directions specified by the unit vectors \(\hat{\epsilon_1}\) and \(\hat{\epsilon_2}\). As plane waves are perfectly transverse, we have: $$ k \cdot \hat{\epsilon}_1 = k \cdot \hat{\epsilon}_2 = 0 $$ and we can choose for our basis vectors: $$ \hat{\epsilon}_1 \cdot \hat{\epsilon}_2 = 0, \quad \text{and} \quad \hat{\epsilon}_1 \times \hat{\epsilon}_2 = \hat{k} $$

The the arbitrary electric field of a light wave can be written as $$ \begin{align} E &= E_1 + E_2 = E_1 \hat{\epsilon}_1 e^{i(kx-\omega t+\phi_1)} + E_2 \hat{\epsilon}_2 e^{i(kx-\omega t+\phi_2)} \ &= (E_1 \hat{\epsilon}_1 + E_2 \hat{\epsilon}_2 e^{i\varphi}) e^{i(kx-\omega t+\phi_1)} \end{align} $$ where \(\phi_{1,2}\) are the initial phases for two components and \(\varphi = \phi_2 - \phi_1\) is the relative phase (can help determine what kind of polarisation \(\underline{E}\) has) between \(\underline{E_1}\) and \(\underline{E_2}\).

docs.title: Linear polarisation in a linear basis
docs.text:
Linearly polarised wave is obtained by choosing the relative phase \(\varphi = 0\).

Definition: Plane of polarisation - Plane containing the wavevector \(\underline{k}\) and electric field \(\underline{E}\)

The magnitude of electric field is $$ E_0 = \sqrt{|E_1|^2 + |E_2|^2} $$ Hence, for a linearly polarised wave, the electric field becomes $$ \begin{align} E &= (E_1 \hat{\epsilon}_1 + E_2 \hat{\epsilon}_2) e^{i(kx-\omega t)} \tag{96} \ &= E_0 (\cos \alpha \hat{\epsilon}_1 + \sin \alpha \hat{\epsilon}_2) e^{i(kx-\omega t)} \tag{97} \end{align} $$ where \(\alpha =\) arctan\((E_2/E_1)\) is the angle of plane of polarisation with respect to \(\hat{\epsilon_1}\) and \(\phi_1\) is omitted. docs.title: Linewidth and Broadening
docs.text: The aim of this is to minimise the spread of this graph (Probability of the atom to be in excited state vs the detuning frequency \(\Delta\) ).

docs.title: Interpretation of this graph
docs.text:
Detuning frequency (\(\Delta\) = \(\omega - \omega_{12}\)) measures how well the oscillator (laser/microwave) frequency is to match the natural resonance frequency of the atom.

[!Goal] To minimise the spread of this graph so that we know the real natural resonance frequency for laser calibration.

This graph is basically telling us how well does the atom response to the oscillator when the frequency of oscillator is slightly off the natural resonance frequency. A broad line means the atom responses to a range of wavelengths, which makes us difficult to determine the real resonance frequency.

docs.title: Problems When Narrowing the Line
docs.text:
1. Transit time broadening
  2. The atoms move pass the oscillator quickly and the time for interacting with the light field is limited

[!Solution] - Use laser cooling to slow down the atoms when passing through the oscillator - Use magneto-optical trap to trap the atoms

  1. Doppler Broadening
  2. The atoms could be moving towards or away from the oscillator
  3. When moving towards, the atoms see higher frequency (\(\omega = \omega_{12} \left( 1 + \frac{v_z}{c} \right)\))

  4. When moving away, the atoms see lower frequency (\(\omega = \omega_{12} \left( 1 - \frac{v_z}{c} \right)\))

  5. Broadening areas due to Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of velocities $$ P(v_z) \, dv_z = \left( \frac{M}{2\pi k_B T} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \exp\left(-\frac{Mv_z^2}{2k_BT}\right) \, dv_z $$

→ Distribution of frequencies $$ P(\omega) \, d\omega = \frac{c}{\omega_2} \left( \frac{M}{2\pi k_B T} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \exp\left(-\frac{Mc^2}{2k_BT} \frac{(\omega - \omega_2)^2}{\omega_2^2}\right) \, d\omega $$

→ FWHM $$ \Delta \omega_D = \frac{2\omega_2}{c} \left( \frac{2k_B T}{M} \ln 2 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} $$

\[ = 7.16 \times 10^{-7} \omega_2 \left( \frac{I}{M_A} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \]

mass in a.m.u

[!Solution] Use laser cooling, magneto-optical trap or optical tweezer

  1. Natural Broadening
  2. The atoms will spontaneously de-excite from the excited state

[!Solution] - Use a longer half-life atom - Low freq magnetic dipole transition - hyperfine structure transition

The decay rate of the excited state is given by Einstein A-coefficient Rate, \(A_{21}\)

\[ A_{21} = \frac{d^2 \omega_{12}^3}{3\pi \epsilon_0 \hbar c^3} \left( \frac{g_1}{g_2} \right) $$ where $d^2 = | \langle 1|er|2\rangle|^2$ and $r$ is the radius of atom. The *natural lifetime* is then $$\tau = \frac{1}{\Gamma} = \frac{1}{A_{21}}\]

docs.title: Liquid Crystal II   Phase Transitions and Elasticity
docs.text:
Recall that in Liquid Crystals I - Introduction and Fundamental Concepts, we mentioned that if we turn isotropic to nematic, we have to decrease the entropy and increase the free energy which is not favourable.

In Maier Saupe Theory, it says there is an attractive force between the LC which decreases internal energy. It assumes that the energetic interaction between LC follows a simple quadratic function: $$ U_{MS} = -\frac{uQ^2}{2} $$ where \(u\) is interaction parameter. Subs this into Helmholtz free energy gives $$ F_{MS} = U_{MS} - TS_{\text{orient}} = -\frac{uQ^2}{2} + k_B T \int_{\Omega} f(\theta) \ln[f(\theta)] \, d\Omega $$ where \(S_{\text{orient}}\) is defined in Liquid Crystals I - Introduction and Fundamental Concepts. Therefore in Maier Saupe, it is a competition between LHS and RHS as LHS favours the transition and RHS disfavours the transition.

For a transition to occur, it must have maximum entropy, therefore we have to maximise the \(f(\theta)\) using Lagrangian multiplier with the constraints: $$ Q = \int_{\Omega} \frac{3}{2} \left( \cos^2 \theta - \frac{1}{3} \right) f(\theta) \, d\Omega $$ $\(\int_\Omega f(\theta)d\Omega = 1\)$

and it gives $$ f(\theta) = C e^{\frac{3\lambda}{2} \cos^2 \theta} $$ where \(C\) and \(\lambda\) are determined by normalisation.

The min point is Nematic where the free energy is minimised. - At the transition between the two regimes (\(u/k_B T \approx 4.55\), obtained numerically), the system admits two minima, at \(Q = 0\) and \(Q > 0\) (inset in right-hand side of previous figure). This indicates a coexistence of isotropic and nematic phases at the transition. This occurs at the critical transition temperature \(T_c\) which satisfies \(T_c \approx 4.55 \, k_B / u\). The transition is, in fact, a first order transition, albeit 'weakly first order'.

While good at capturing the behavior of transition, Maier-Saupe limitations are: 1. Neglect temperature dependent of \(u\) 2. Neglect correlations in the particle fluctuations

docs.title: Rigidity and elasticity of nematic LC
docs.text:
• Nematic LC has a preferential orientation implies that it can resist imposed strains, exhibiting an elastic response to small deformations.

The elastic energy of distortion per unit volume is $$ F_d = \underbrace{ rac{K_1}{2} [ abla \cdot \vec{n}(r)]^2}{ ext{Splay deform}} + \underbrace{ rac{K_2}{2} [\vec{n}(r) \cdot ( abla imes \vec{n}(r))]^2} ext{Twist deform} + \underbrace{ rac{K_3}{2} [\vec{n}(r) imes ( abla imes \vec{n}(r))]^2}_ ext{Bend deform} $$

docs.title: Liquid Crystals I   Introduction and Fundamental Concepts
docs.text:
• Liquid Crystal is a state of matter which is an intermediate between a liquid and crystal.
  • It has some form of order and possesses fluidity
  • E.g. colloidal suspensions, polymers, amphiphilic systems
  • LC forming materials are called mesogens

docs.title: Liquid crystal phases
docs.text:
1. Nematic (common): Orientational order but no positional order
  2. Smectic: Orientational and 1D positional order
  3. Columnar: Orientational order and 2D positional order
  4. Cholesterics: formed by chiral molecules.

The initial state is called isotropic and it can phase transition to ordered LC phases by decreasing temperature (thermotropic) or increasing molecular density (lyotropic)

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: To understand LC, we have to understand some technical terms:

docs.title: Director
docs.text:
• Unit vector \(\vec{n}\) pointing to the average molecular direction
  • To describe the group alignment of the LC, we introduce the orientation function \(f(\theta)\); \(f(\theta)d\Omega\) is the fraction of molecules in a solid angle \(d\Omega\) that are oriented \(\theta\) from the director. Therefore, for a more ordered LC, the LCs will mostly distributed at \(\theta = 0, \pi\)

docs.title: Order parameter
docs.text:
See Broken Symmetry as well.

  • Order parameter is a parameter that changes its value during phase transition.
  • Here, we defined it, \(\overline{\overline{Q}}\) as average alignment of the molecules to the director.
  • This is a tensor order parameter

For the case of uniaxial (molecular distribution function for the LC molecules has an axial symmetry) nematic LC (which is the focus in this course), the order parameter is $$ Q_{\alpha \beta} = \left\langle u_{\alpha} u_{\beta} - \frac{1}{3} \delta_{\alpha \beta} \right\rangle = Q \left( n_{\alpha} n_{\beta} - \frac{1}{3} \delta_{\alpha \beta} \right) $$ where \(\vec{u}\) is the unit vector, \(Q\) is the largest eigenvalue/scalar order parameter of \(\overline{\overline{Q}}\) and \(\vec{n}\) is the eigenvector of \(\overline{\overline{Q}}\) with the largest eigenvalue. Intuitively, the largest eigenvalue is the most probable/aligned LC to the director.

For a nematic with an angle distribution \(f(\theta)\) between \(\langle \vec{r} \rangle\) and \(\vec{n}\), the scalar order parameter is then $$ Q = \frac{3}{2} \left\langle (\vec{u} \cdot \vec{n})^2 - \frac{1}{3} \right\rangle = \frac{3}{2} \langle \cos^2 \theta - \frac{1}{3} \rangle = \int_{\Omega} \frac{3}{2} \left( \cos^2 \theta - \frac{1}{3} \right) f(\theta) \, d\Omega $$

[!note] Note that the expectation value is $\(\langle x\rangle = \int xf(\theta)d\theta\)$ for a real-valued \(f(\theta)\)

docs.title: Nematic-Isotropic transition
docs.text:
Here we use Helmholtz free energy instead of Gibbs free energy, since pressure is not necessarily conserved but the volume is conserved $\(F=U-TS\)$

When transition from nematic to isotropic, since the LC is becoming more orientated, the entropy decreases and it causes an increase in the Helmholtz free energy. This is unfavourable. There are two possible factors:

  1. Maier-Saupe theory: LC molecules have attractive interaction and they have lower internal energy when the molecules are aligned.

  2. Onsager theory: When the LC molecules are aligned, there are more ways to arrange these rod-like molecules, which gives a higher entropy.

docs.title: Orientational entropy
docs.text:
To derive an expression for Helmholtz free energy, we need to calculate the orientational entropy. We assume:

  • uniaxial nematic: only depends on the polar angle \(\theta\)
  • \(f(\theta)\) is normalised: \(\int f(\theta) d\Omega =1\)

Using Boltzmann's formula, we obtain i.e. $\(S_{\text{orient}} = - k_B\sum P_i \text{ln}P_i = - k_B \int_\Omega f(\theta) \ \text{ln} \ (f(\theta))\)$ where we have a continuous distribution of \(\theta\) (turning summation into integration).

docs.title: Magnetic Domain
docs.text:
To satisfy Maxwell equation $$ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{M} = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{H} $$ the creation of magnetisation will have to result in a demagnetising field \(\mathbf{H}\) in the opposite direction.

To minimise the wasted energy, the configuration has to be rotating

Here, we are looking for a method to quantify domain wall energy and width and there are two factors affecting these:

  1. Exchange energy
  2. Anisotropy energy density

docs.title: Exchange energy
docs.text:
For \(N\) perfectly aligned spins: $$ E_0 = -2J_{\text{ex}} N S^2 $$

and for \(N\) spins at angle \(\Delta \theta\) $$ E_1 = -2J_{\text{ex}} N S^2 \cos \Delta\theta $$

\[\implies \Delta E = E_1 - E_0 = -2J_{\text{ex}} N S^2 (\cos \Delta\theta - 1) \]

For small angle:

\[ \Delta E \approx J_{\text{ex}} \frac{\pi^2 S^2}{N} \]

If the spins are arranged in a square lattice i.e. one spin per unit area \((1/a^2)\), then the energy per unit area is $\(\sigma_1 = \frac{\Delta E}{a^2}\)$

docs.title: Anisotropy energy density
docs.text:
Recall that anisotropy energy density is \(K\sin^2\alpha\) where \(K = \text{anisotropy constant}\) and \(\alpha\) is the angle with respect to easy axis.

\[ \Delta E = \sum_{i=1}^N K \sin^2(i\Delta\theta) \quad (\text{NB: } N\Delta\theta = \pi) \] \[ \approx \frac{1}{\Delta\theta} \int_0^{\pi} K \sin^2\theta \, d\theta = \frac{N}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} K \sin^2\theta \, d\theta = \frac{NK}{2} \quad (\text{for } \Delta\theta \to 0) \]
  • \(\Delta E\) is an energy density which is already the energy per unit volume
  • Anisotropy energy for a given spin is defined over a distance \(a/2\) either side of the spin
\[\implies a\Delta E = \frac{NKa}{2}\]

docs.title: Classical
docs.text:
We start this topic by investigating the Larmor precession, dont know why it is here as well but yes we will start. It is mentioned in Fundamental Equations for Magnetism so here we will quote the results.

we have a magnetic moment \(\vec{{\mu}}\) which is proportional to the spin \(S\) $\(\vec{\mu} = \gamma S\)$ where \(\gamma\) is the gyroscopic ratio. For electron, we have $\(\mu = g_s \gamma S = g_s \mu_B S/ \hbar\)$ and because of the torque from the magnetic moment itself, it causes the magnetic moment to precess around the direction of magnetic field.

docs.title: Quantum
docs.text:
The Hamiltonian of the system is given by $$ H = -\vec{\mu} \cdot \vec{B} = -\gamma \mathbf{S} \cdot B\hat{z} = -\gamma B S_z = -\gamma B \frac{\hbar}{2} \sigma_z = \frac{\hbar \omega_L}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} $$ where the Hamiltonian has only one potential term \(E = -\vec{\mu} \cdot \vec{B}\). Solve this Hamiltonian using eigenvalue problems with the spin states as the eigenvectors with their respective eigen-energies gives $$ H \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar \omega_L}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad H \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} = -\frac{\hbar \omega_L}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} $$

At time \(t=0\), the state is in superposition of spin-up and -down, $$ \chi(t=0) = \begin{pmatrix} a \ b \end{pmatrix} = a \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} + b \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \cos\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \sin\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix} $$ where the coefficients are expressed in terms of angles to visualise the spinning of the magnetic moment. This is converted to the time-dependent: $$ \chi(t) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) e^{-i\frac{\omega_L t}{2}} \ \sin\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) e^{+i\frac{\omega_L t}{2}} \end{pmatrix} $$

Here, we can calculate the expectation value of the spin operator under the influence of magnetic field $\(\langle \chi(t) | S | \chi(t) \rangle = \langle \chi(t) | S_x + S_y +S_z | \chi(t) \rangle\)$ where we can solve each component individually using Pauli Matrices and the spin states. The results $$ = \frac{\hbar}{2} \sin(\alpha) \cdot [\cos(\omega_L t) \, \hat{x} + \sin(\omega_L t) \, \hat{y}] + \frac{\hbar}{2} \cos(\alpha) \, \hat{z} $$ and the magnetic moment is precessing at a frequency of \(\omega_L = E / \hbar = \mu_B B/\hbar = \gamma B\)

docs.title: Hilbert Space and Total Spins of two spin-1/2 particles in a system
docs.text:
Consider two spin-1/2 particles in a system. Each one of them have their individual Hilbert space with their individual spins. In this case the total Hamiltonian is the tensor product of their Hamiltonian.

\[ H_{\text{total}} = H_1 \otimes H_2 \]

The spin for each particles are $$ S_{jz} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)} = \frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)}, \quad S_{jz} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)} = -\frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)}, \quad j = 1, 2 $$ where \(j\) is the index for the particles. We simplify the notation by $$ \alpha(j) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)}, \quad \beta(j) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}^{(j)} $$ therefore it gives $$ S_{jz} \alpha(j) = \frac{\hbar}{2} \alpha(j), \quad S_{jz} \beta(j) = -\frac{\hbar}{2} \beta(j), \quad j = 1, 2 $$ These form the basis states for the two-particle system in this box $$ \alpha(1) \alpha(2), \quad \alpha(1) \beta(2), \quad \beta(1) \alpha(2), \quad \beta(1) \beta(2) $$

docs.title: \(S_z\) and the magnetic quantum number
docs.text:
The spin operator to the basis states, $\(S_z \alpha(1)\alpha(2)=(S_{1z} + S_{2z})\alpha(1)\alpha(2)\)$ we can get the magnetic quantum number of the system.

[!note] $\(\alpha(1)\alpha(2) \quad |S = 1, M = 1\rangle\)$ $\(\alpha(1)\beta(2) \quad |S = ?, M = 0\rangle\)$ $\(\beta(1)\alpha(2) \quad |S = ?, M = 0\rangle\)$ $\(\beta(1)\beta(2) \quad |S = 1, M = -1\rangle\)$

docs.title: \(S^2\) and \(S(S+1)\) eigenvalues
docs.text:
Instead of directly adding \(S_{1z} + S_{2z}\) we have \(S^2 = (S_1+S_2)^2\) where \(S = S_x +S_y +S_z\)

The results are stated above. For the question marks ones, the eigenvalues are not in the eigenstates. In fact, they are in superposition i.e. indistinguishable. We can distinguish two possibility based on symmetry:

  1. Symmetric combination
  2. Antisymmetric combination

These two combinations could be a result in \(S\)

[!note] $\(\alpha(1)\alpha(2) \quad \rightarrow |S = 1, M = 1\rangle\)$ $\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\alpha(1)\beta(2) + \beta(1)\alpha(2)) \quad \rightarrow |S = 1, M = 0\rangle\)$ $\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\alpha(1)\beta(2) - \beta(1)\alpha(2)) \quad \rightarrow |S = 0, M = 0\rangle\)$ $\(\beta(1)\beta(2) \quad \rightarrow |S = 1, M = -1\rangle\)$

Note that the total spin in the box is either 0 or 1. For \(S=1\) states, the particles are symmetric under exchange i.e., it will be indistinguishable and you don't know if they are swapped. They have different values of \(M\) which have different projection of the total spin along the \(z\)-axis

These three \(S=1\) states are called triplet states while the one \(S=0\) state is called the singlet state.

docs.title: Another approach
docs.text:
The other approach to express the basic states in terms of \(|S, M\rangle\) is to use the raising/lowering operators: $\(S_\pm = S_{1\pm} + S_{2\pm}\)$ where they raise/lower the magnetic quantum number (for the spin case, it increases/decreases the spin by one unit i.e. decrease \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\)). We can start from \(\alpha(1)\alpha(2)\) $$ S_- \alpha(1) \alpha(2) = (S_1^- + S_2^-) \alpha(1) \alpha(2) = (S_1^- \alpha(1)) \alpha(2) + \alpha(1)(S_2^- \alpha(2)) = \hbar \underbrace{(\beta(1)\alpha(2) + \alpha(1)\beta(2))}_{\propto |1,0\rangle} $$ where it can be shown that $\(|1,0\rangle = \frac{\alpha(1)\beta(2) + \beta(1)\alpha(2)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$

We can do the same for the other combinations. For the \(|0,0\rangle\) state, it will be orthogonal to the triplet states. And it can be proven that it is in the eigenstate of total spin in the box \(S_z\).

docs.title: Magnetic Structure
docs.text:
Recall that charge density form factor and Rutherford cross section that $\(\left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)_\rho = |F(q^2)|^2 \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right)_{\text{Ruth}}\)$

Now we want to include the magnetic and electric form factor to account for the charge of the magnetic structure: $$ \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right){\text{Rosenbluth}} = \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right) \right] $$ where }} \left[ \frac{g_E^2(Q^2) + \tau g_m^2(Q^2)}{1 + \tau} + 2\tau g_m^2(Q^2) \tan^2 \frac{\theta}{2\(g_E\) is the electric form factor (FT of electric field), \(g_M\) is the magnetic form factor, \(\tau = Q^2/4M_p\) and \(Q^2 = (q^{\mu}_p)^2\) is the four momentum difference before and after the scattering of proton.

To find the form factor, we set \(A = (g^2_E + g^2_M) / (1+\tau)\) and \(B = 2\tau g^2_M\) and find the relationship between Rosenbuth and cross section and \(\tan^2 (\theta/2)\). We obtain a straight line. From there we can get the gradient and y-intercept to calculate the form factor.

There is the problem: the measurements of $$ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} g_E^P(0) &= 1 \ g_M^P(0) &= 2.79 \end{aligned} } $$

are reasonable because proton has charge and therefore magnetic field (non-zero magnetic form factor). But $$ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} g_E^N(0) &= 0 \ g_M^N(0) &= -1.99 \end{aligned} } $$ is problematic because the neutron does not have electric field but it has a magnetic field. This suggests that the neutrons must have a charged substructure.

docs.title: Magnetism in Metals
docs.text:
For noble metals and some alkali metals, they have delocalised electron in the free space. The magnetic response originates from the interaction between the spin of the electrons and the magnetic field.

The energy of a single spin in magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) is $$E =\mu_s B = g_s \gamma \mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B} = \mp \gamma \hbar B = \mp \mu_B B $$ The change in number of spin down electrons is (?) $$ \Delta n_{\downarrow} = -\frac{1}{2} g(E_F) \mu_B B $$ and it causes the increase of spin up electron by the same amount $$ \Delta n_{\uparrow} = -\Delta n_{\downarrow} = \frac{1}{2} g(E_F) \mu_B B $$

The magnetisation is then $$ M = \mu_B (\Delta n_{\uparrow} - \Delta n_{\downarrow}) = g(E_F) \mu_B^2 B $$ $$\implies \chi = \frac{M}{H} \approx \frac{\mu_0 M}{B} = g(E_F) \mu_0 \mu_B^2 $$ The density of state is calculated using the same method as in Statistical Physics

NOTE: the susceptibility is no longer temperature dependent.

docs.title: Stoner criterion
docs.text:
However, it is not possible to keep moving the spin down electron to spin up. It has to balance the

  1. Increase in kinetic energy of transferred electrons
  2. Decrease in magnetic potential energy

(i.e. the transfer of electron which increases kinetic energy causes the magnetic potential energy to decrease)

docs.title: Increase in kinetic energy
docs.text:
Spin down electrons over energy range \(\delta E\) near \(E_F\) are transferred to spin up band. The increase in kinetic energy is then:

\[ \Delta E_{KE} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} g(E_F) \delta E}_\text{number of electrons} \underbrace{\delta E}_\text{energy increase}\]

docs.title: Decrease in potential energy
docs.text:
$$ \Delta E_{PE} = -\int_0^M \mathbf{B}\text{mf} \cdot d\mathbf{M} = -\int_0^M \lambda M' \, dM' = -\frac{\lambda M^2}{2} $$ Using the previous analysis on Pauli paramgnetism, $$ M = \mu_B (\Delta n) = g(E_F) \mu_B (\mu_B B) $$ by subs in the potential energy term we can find the expression for decrease in potential energy. } - \Delta n_{\downarrow

For stable ferromagnetism where the potential is greater than kinetic, the spin down electrons are transferred to spin up because of the minimum energy configuration (the molecular field aligns with spin up). As they both balance, the molecular field stops the spin up to transfer to spin down. So the potential energy dominates: \(\Delta E<0\) (minimise energy)

\[\implies Ug(E_F) > 1\]

where \(U = \lambda\mu_B^2\) is the coulomb interaction. This condition means ferromagnetism is more likely in transition metals because \(g(E_F)\) is large due to a narrow energy \(d\) band.

docs.title: Magneto Optical Trap
docs.text:
We want to accumulate many atoms so we need to make a trap. The MOT uses 6 circularly polarised laser beams and spatially dependent magnetic field to shift atoms into resonance when they move away from trap centre.

This trick is discussed in Laser Cooling where spatially dependent magnetic field is used in Zeeman cooling.

docs.title: Magnetic field
docs.text:
• Created using two coils with currents passing in opposite directions - Anti-Helmholtz
  • Quadrupole field is zero at the origin and increases in magnitude in all direction
  • As \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0\) $$ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial B_x}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial B_y}{\partial y} = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z} $$

docs.title: MOT
docs.text:
Mechanism: The \(\sigma^\pm\) lasers provides photons with momentum \(\pm h\) and can excite the atoms to \(\Delta m_F = \pm1\) state.

The magnetic field splits the state into substates. One of the states (in pic) is closer to the resonance frequency. As the atoms are displaced to the \(+z\) direction, they get resonated to the \(\sigma^-\) laser which is red-detuned and hence absorbed the photons which carry momentum \(-h\), kicking the atoms back to the center.

docs.title: Maths
docs.text:
The magnetic interaction has the form $\(U=m_Fg_f\mu_B B\)$ at low field.

And we need to introduce the Zeeman shift into the detuning term in Light Forces and Laser Cooling of scattering force.

\[ F = F_1 - F_2 \] \[ F_{12} = \frac{\hbar k \Gamma}{2} \frac{I/I_s}{1 + 2\frac{I}{I_s} + 4(\Delta \pm k v \pm b' z)^2 / \Gamma^2} \]

where \(\hbar k \Gamma = g_f \mu_B B\)

For small velocities, where \(kv < \Gamma\) & small displacement \(b'|z| < \Gamma\) we expand to find

[!MOT forces] $\(F = -\alpha v - \beta z\)$

where \(\alpha\) is the friction coefficient and \(\beta = \frac{b' \alpha}{k}\) is a spring constant.

docs.title: Side note
docs.text:
• Atoms motion in MOT is like a over-damped oscillator
  • The capture velocity of MOT is 10x greater than optical molasses so we can load it directly from thermal vapour
  • An MOT accumulates up to \(10^{10}\) atoms with typical radius of 1 mm and \(T\approx 100 mK\)

docs.title: Cycling transition
docs.text: Laser cooling works because we scatter lots of photons - this only works for closed transitions

docs.title: Magnon
docs.text:
Recall that the shape of the Curie-Weiss graph, in fact in experiment the magnetisation decreases more rapid with respect to \(T\).

As the temperature increases, instead of one of the spin fully flipped, they precess about the equilibrium as it is the minimum energy configuration.

Consider a chain of 1D chain of atoms (Ising model),

The exchange energy at \(j\) is $\(E = \sum_i -J_{ij}\mathbf{S_i} \cdot \mathbf{S_j}\)$ but here we only care about the nearest neighbours: $$ E = -2 J_{ex} \mathbf{S}j \cdot (\mathbf{S}} + \mathbf{S{j+1}) $$ As \(E = \boldsymbol{\mu}_j = g_s \gamma \mathbf{S}_j\) , we have $$ \Rightarrow E = -\boldsymbol{\mu}_j \cdot \underbrace{\left[ \frac{-2 J}}{g_s \gamma} (\mathbf{S{j-1} + \mathbf{S}}) \right]{\mathbf{B}\text{eff}} $$

as \(E = -\mu_j \cdot \mathbf{B}_\text{eff}\) .

Since the spins are precessing about the equilibrium position, we then consider the torque: $$ \frac{d\mathbf{S}j}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\mu} \times \mathbf{B}}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d\mathbf{Sj}{dt} = 2 J} \mathbf{Sj \times \left[ \mathbf{S} \right] $$ The solutions are: } + \mathbf{S}_{j+1

  1. \(A=iB\) and it shows the cyclic rotation of spin in \(xy\)-plane
  2. \(\hbar\omega = 4J_{\text{ex}}S(1-\cos qa)\) the spin waves are quantised

(Broken Symmetry workshop)

docs.title: Bloch's law
docs.text:
• Magnons are the reason why the Curie-Weiss law drops more rapidly at the start.

Excitation of a single magnon will reduce the net magnetic moment by 1 unit. Therefore we need to work out the number of magnons created.

\[n_{\text{magnon}} = \int \left[ \frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{kT}\right) - 1} \right] g_m(\hbar\omega) \, d(\hbar\omega)\]

See Statistical Physics.

From the quantisation we see last lecture:

\[\hbar\omega = 4 J_{\text{ex}} S \left[1 - \cos(qa)\right] \propto q^2$$ for small $q$. Be reminded that $q$ is the momentum like $k$ for phonons. That means $$g(\varepsilon) \propto \sqrt{\varepsilon}\] \[\implies n_{\text{magnon}} \propto \left( \frac{kT}{\hbar} \right)^{3/2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\sqrt{x} \, dx}{e^x - 1} \propto T^{3/2} \]

docs.title: Make it attractive
docs.text:
1. Make the habit attractive so that the expectation of a rewarding experience motivates us through temptation bundling

[!Temptation Bundling] Do favourite things with the things you need to do at the same time

This is due to Premark Principle: most probable things enforce less probable things

  1. Imitating the close, the many and the powerful because of you will have a sense of approval

[!The close] Join a culture where your desired behavior is the normal behavior

[!The many] - Rewards of being accepted overrides the rewards of winning an argument. - Join tribe with habits that you are trying to fit in

[!The powerful] Explaination: fitting in implies wanting to stand out

docs.title: Make it difficult
docs.text:
1. Make bad habits more difficult by creating commitment device

[!Commitment device] Choice to make in the present that controls your actions in the future

  1. Change the task such that it requires more work to get out of the good habit
  2. Automate your habits by using technology
  3. Get onetime choices ie things that can be bought once and is able to build your good habit forever.

docs.title: Make it easy
docs.text:
1. Key to master a habit is to start with repetition, not perfection (helps to develop long term potentiation or the strengthening of connections of neurons in brain based on recent patterns of activity)

[!Law of least effort] - Get rid of frictions/troubles that can hinder your way to progress - Combining environment we talked in Make it obvious, we can make use of environment to get least effort to do something eg prep for the next action - Or prime the environment to make bad behavior difficult

[!Two-minute rule to avoid procrastination] When starting new habit, it should take less than two minutes to do, ie make the habit as easy as possible - Habit shaping helps to scale your habit back to towards your ultimate goal. Start by mastering the rule, then advance to an intermediate step and repeat.

Cue implies Prediction which causes Feelings and leads to Behavior. Behavior depends heavily on prediction

Feelings: - Transforms cues to application - Desire (difference between where you are now and where you was) - Craving (sense that something is missing)

These are the underlying natures of habits

So we need: - Associate hard habits with positive experience - Reframing habits to highlight benefits

[!Motivation ritual] - Associating habits with something you enjoy - We need to highlight benefits of avoiding bad habit to make it seem unattractive

docs.title: Make it obvious
docs.text:
1. Using pointing-and-calling method, make your cue and what you are doing now obvious, reminding yourself what you are doing.
  2. Use implement intension - make a clear plan, stating where, when, what

[!Diderot effect] Obtaining new possession creates spiral of consumption which induce additional purchase

Using Diderot effect, we can use another method called habit staking.

  1. Stake new habit to the previous one, make it smooth in transition and immediate actionable.
  2. Make each part of room to have their own functionality to make the cue obvious (designing environment is important)

docs.title: Make it satisfying
docs.text:
Pleasure teaches your brain that a behavior is worth remembering and repeating.

  1. Make the experience more satisfying (Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change) and it needs to be immediate satisfaction

[!Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change] What is immediately rewarded is repeated and what is immediately punished is avoided.

[!Time Inconsistency/Hyperbolic Discounting] The way your brain evaluates rewards is inconsistent across time. You value the present more than the future.

  • Good habit is unattractive because the immediate outcome is bad but the ultimate outcome is good

  • Make avoidance visible ie make the outcome of the avoidance visible

  • Use habit tracking to motivate yourself because it has visual evidence of progression (tracking your progress)
  • Dont miss the habit twice

docs.title: Make it unattractive
docs.text: Reframe your mindset and highlight the benefits of avoiding your bad habits

docs.title: Making Heavy Particle
docs.text:
Here we can make new particles by colliding two particles together but to do so we need a very high centre of mass (COM) 4-momentum $\(S = (P_1+P_2)^2 = 4E^2\)$

Before that, we need to make particles to be injected into the accelerator.

We can make heavy particle if 1. COM energy is high enough 2. Probability is controlled by vertices

Recall from Quantum Field Theory that probability amplitude is governed by the vertices of the Feynman diagrams. This probability amplitude gives rise to probability (definition of cross section)

$$ \sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{hadrons}) = \sum_f^{4M_q^2 \approx S} \sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow q_f \bar{q}f) $$ where \(f\) is the quark flavour. We can do the same for lepton production $\(\sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{charged leptons}) = \sum_f^{4M_q^2 \approx S} \sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow \ell \bar{\ell})\)$ From this, we define a quantity called the \(R\)-ratio $$ R = \frac{\sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{hadrons})}{\sigma(e^+ + e^- \rightarrow \mu^+ + \mu^-)} = \frac{3 \sum_f Q_f^2}{\sum\ell Q_\ell^2} $$ where the factor of 3 is due to the colour charge. This ratio tells us how likely is the collision between electron and positron to produce hadrons compared to muon pairs.

This is the plot for the \(R\)-ratio. The peak is due to the resonance of \(S\) and \(M_{z^0}\) . As the collision is mediated not only by photon, but \(Z^0\) is possible as well. Recall from Quantum Field Theory, the propagator for weak interaction is $\(M\sim \frac{g_w}{S-M_{z^0}}\)$ where \(g_w\) is the weak coupling constant. When \(S\) is large and resonate with \(M_{z^0}\), the strength spikes up. It is a sweet spot where the weak interaction becomes strong.

To produce a higher energy collision, we can use proton-antiproton collisions. LHC detected Higgs boson by colliding gluons

docs.title: Many Electron Systems
docs.text:
In general, following from the two electron systems last chapter, we can generalise the slater determinant for \(N\) electrons: $$ \begin{aligned} \psi(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1; \vec{r}_2, \sigma_2; \dots; \vec{r}_N, \sigma_N) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1) & \psi_1(\vec{r}_2, \sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_1(\vec{r}_N, \sigma_N) \ \psi_2(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1) & \psi_2(\vec{r}_2, \sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_2(\vec{r}_N, \sigma_N) \ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \psi_N(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1) & \psi_N(\vec{r}_2, \sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_N(\vec{r}_N, \sigma_N) \end{vmatrix}

\[1.5em] &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r}_1)\chi_1(\sigma_1) & \psi_1(\vec{r}_2)\chi_1(\sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_1(\vec{r}_N)\chi_1(\sigma_N) \ \psi_2(\vec{r}_1)\chi_2(\sigma_1) & \psi_2(\vec{r}_2)\chi_2(\sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_2(\vec{r}_N)\chi_2(\sigma_N) \ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \psi_N(\vec{r}_1)\chi_N(\sigma_1) & \psi_N(\vec{r}_2)\chi_N(\sigma_2) & \dots & \psi_N(\vec{r}_N)\chi_N(\sigma_N) \end{vmatrix} \end{aligned} $$

However slater determinant does not include the interaction between electrons, which is significant in a multi-electron systems. The Hamiltonian for the multi-electron systems is $$ \left{ \underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \nabla_i^2}{T} + \underbrace{\sum}^{N} v(\vec{ri)}}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \sum_{i \neq j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{|\vec{ri - \vec{r}_j|}}_N, \sigma_N) $$}} \right} \psi(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1; \dots; \vec{r}_N, \sigma_N) = E \psi(\vec{r}_1, \sigma_1; \dots; \vec{r

and solving this for large \(N\) is not possible so approximation has to be used. The common one is called the Hartree-Fock approximation.

This approximation is used to form the expectation value of the total Hamiltonian with a slater determinant wave function and vary the single-electron wave functions to minimise this expectation value.

docs.title: Mapping the brain
docs.text:
Glossary 1. Connectome - Map of all connections in brain

  1. Electroencephalography (EEG)
  2. The practice of detecting electric field in brain, which are produced by the activity of underlying neurons in cortex. It is accurate in time domain but poor in the localising activity in space

  3. Similar method is Magnetoencephalography (MEG) which is more complex and expensive

  4. fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging)

  5. Extension of MRI which is based on blood oxygenation which goes along the neutral network.

  6. Good in localising in space but not in time resolution compared to EEG.

  7. Transcranial magnetic stimulation

  8. A technique that sends pulses of magnetic fields to the cortex through the scalp

  9. Used to perturb the brain activity in specific region and observe what happens (used to determine what region does what function)

  10. Default mode network (DMN)

  11. Brain regions (mainly in cortical midline) that go less active when doing externally directed task and more active in wakeful rest and mind wandering, i.e. self-related processing.
  • Neuropsychology
  • Brain imaging
  • Optogenetics
  • Left brain vs right brain

People

  • Wilder Penfield

docs.title: Amplitude mode (Non-continuous symmetry breaking)
docs.text:
Recall that the Ginzburg-Landau model is $\(f = f_0 + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{\nabla}\phi)^2}_{\text{"Kinetic energy" } K} \pm \underbrace{\frac{\mu^2}{2}\phi^2 + \frac{\lambda}{4!}\phi^4}_{\text{"Potential energy" } U}\)$ For amplitude modes when \(T>T_c\) the potential is $\(U(\phi) = \frac{\mu^2}{2} \phi^2 + \frac{\lambda}{4!} \phi^4 \approx \frac{\mu^2}{2} \phi^2\)$ where \(\mu = m\). For \(T<T_c\) we have $\(U(\phi) = \frac{\mu^2}{2} \phi^2 + \frac{\lambda}{4!} \phi^4\)$ Now we want to prove that this excitation requires energy. We first find the minimum point: $\(\left. \frac{\partial U}{\partial \phi} \right|_{\phi_0} = -\mu^2 \phi_0 + \frac{\lambda}{3!} \phi_0^3 = 0 \implies \phi_0 = \left( \frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda} \right)^{1/2}\)$ and expand around it $\(\begin{aligned} U(\phi) &\approx U(\phi_0) + \frac{1}{2} \left. \left( \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi^2} \right) \right|_{\phi_0} (\phi - \phi_0)^2 + \cdots \\[1em] \left. \left( \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi^2} \right) \right|_{\phi_0} &= -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\phi_0^2 = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\left( \frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda} \right) = 2\mu^2 \\[1em] \implies U(\phi) &\approx U(\phi_0) + \mu^2 (\phi - \phi_0)^2 + \cdots \end{aligned}\)$

By comparing this to the case where \(T>T_c\) i.e. it turns from \(\mu^2/2\) to \(\mu^2\): $\(\frac{m^2}{2} = \mu \implies m = \sqrt{2}\mu\)$ i.e. the excitation causes increase in mass by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

docs.title: Goldstone mode (continuous symmetry breaking)
docs.text:
Goldstone mode is a different story as it is the rolling the gutter mode. We therefore have to look at two directions: \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\)

Note that this has a rotational symmetry i.e. we can obtain our free energy from there. At high temperature, $\(\begin{aligned} &\begin{pmatrix} \phi'_1 \\ \phi'_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 \\ \phi_2 \end{pmatrix} \\[1em] &f(\phi'_1, \phi'_2) = f(\phi_1, \phi_2) \qquad \qquad \text{['SO(2)' symmetry]} \\[1em] &\boxed{f = \frac{1}{2}\left[ (\mathbf{\nabla}\phi_1)^2 + (\mathbf{\nabla}\phi_2)^2 \right] \pm \frac{\mu^2}{2}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) + \frac{\lambda}{4!}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2)^2} \end{aligned}\)$

At low temperature, we have $\(U = -\frac{\mu^2}{2}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) + \frac{\lambda}{4!}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2)^2\)$ By letting \(x^2 = \phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2\), we express the global minimum in terms of \(x\): $\(\left. \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} \right|_{x_0} = -\mu^2 x_0 + \frac{\lambda}{3!} x_0^3 = 0\)$Here we choose a minimum to simplify the calculation: $\(\phi_1 = \left(\frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda}\right)^{1/2}, \qquad \phi_2 = 0\)$

Again, we expand around the chosen minimum point $\(\begin{aligned} &U(\phi) \approx U(\phi_0) + \frac{1}{2} \left. \left( \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi^2} \right) \right|_{\phi_0} (\phi - \phi_0)^2 + \cdots = \\[1em] &\implies \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi_1^2} = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{3!} (\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) + \frac{2\lambda}{3!} \phi_1^2 = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \phi_1^2 + \frac{\lambda}{3!} \phi_2^2 \\[1em] & \qquad\implies \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi_1^2} = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda} = 2\mu^2 \qquad \text{Evaluate at the minimum, } \left[ \left(\frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda}\right)^{1/2}, 0 \right] \\[1em] &\implies \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi_2^2} = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\phi_2^2 + \frac{\lambda}{3!}\phi_1^2\\[1em] & \qquad \implies \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial \phi_2^2} = -\mu^2 + \frac{\lambda}{3!}\frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda} = 0 \qquad \text{Evaluate at the minimum, } \left[ \left(\frac{6\mu^2}{\lambda}\right)^{1/2}, 0 \right] \end{aligned}\)$ By comparing it to high temperature where $\(U = -\frac{\mu^2}{2}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2) + \frac{\lambda}{4!}(\phi_1^2 + \phi_2^2)^2\)$ we realise that the \(\phi_1\) mode (amplitude mode) has an increase of mass i.e. $\(\frac{m^2}{2} = \mu^2\)$ consistent with the results we had in amplitude mode. And the \(\phi^2\) excitation have zero mass

This is the result of Goldstone's theorem i.e. breaking a continuous symmetry leads to massless excitations.

Personal statement

Healthcare quality is often regarded as one of the clearest indicators of a nation’s development. In many developing countries, including my home country Malaysia—particularly in East Malaysia—limited access to advanced medical treatment and the rising incidence of cancer remain deeply concerning issues. According to the Global Cancer Observatory of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, the age-standardised mortality rate for cancer in Malaysia is 86.3 per 100,000 population. This statistic reflects not only a public health challenge but also the urgent need for more trained professionals in medical physics and cancer treatment.

As a physicist with a strong interest in biology and medicine, I have long sought opportunities to merge my academic background with my desire to contribute to healthcare. Medical physics, especially in the context of cancer treatment, provides the ideal pathway for me to apply my scientific training in a way that directly benefits patients. I am motivated by the responsibility—and privilege—of helping individuals who may view a cancer diagnosis as a death sentence, and I aspire to play a meaningful role in improving their treatment outcomes.

The University of Manchester stands out to me because of its close integration with The Christie, the largest single-site cancer centre in Europe. Studying in an environment where physicists, clinicians, and interdisciplinary researchers work side by side will be invaluable for my development as a medical physicist. I am particularly drawn to the programme’s emphasis on clinical relevance and its strong research culture, both of which align with my ambition to contribute to the advancement of cancer treatment technologies.

Although my current studies lean towards ‘hard’ condensed matter physics, my education at Durham University has equipped me with a broad and rigorous foundation across multiple areas of physics. My exposure to soft matter physics has strengthened my understanding of physical processes in biological systems, while my training in nuclear physics has given me insight into the behaviour and interaction of radiation—central knowledge in medical physics. Furthermore, my A-level physics background provided me with introductory familiarity with medical imaging technologies, including MRI, PET, ultrasound and CT scanning. Together, these experiences have prepared me to approach medical physics with both confidence and curiosity.
