docs.title: Meissner Effect
docs.text: To describe the Meissner effect, we need two equations 1. Continuity equation that conserve charge 2. London equation that describe the magnetic field

docs.title: Continuity Equation
docs.text:
This is governed by the London gauge \(\mathbf{ abla} \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0 \implies \mathbf{ abla} \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0\) where \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{ abla} \cdot \mathbf{A}\). Assume that we have a superconducting cube with a width of \(\Delta x\) and a current density of \(J(x)\) is passing through it.

The charge passing through the cube per unit time is propertional to the change of current density $\( rac{\partial n_s}{\partial t} = rac{1}{e} rac{dJ}{dx} = rac{1}{e} abla\cdot \mathbf{J} =0 \quad ext{(in 3D steady state)}\)$

docs.title: London Equation
docs.text: We are given an equation that cannot be derived, very good: $\(\mathbf{J} = -\frac{1}{\mu_0 \lambda_L^2} \mathbf{A}\)$ By considering the curl of Maxwell's 4th equation at steady state i.e. \(\partial \mathbf{E} / \partial t =0\) we have $\(\nabla^2 \mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\lambda_L^2} \mathbf{B}\)$

docs.title: London Penetration Depth
docs.text:
The magnetic field energy penetrating through the superconductor rapidly decreases until it is no longer appreciable and this length is London penetration depth

$\(\lambda_L = \sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu_0 n_s e^2}}\)$ where \(n_s\) is the density of superconducting electrons that behave very differently than fermionic electrons. How different? The entropy of the electrons in normal state and superconducting state is plotted

It can be seen that the electrons in superconducting state are more ordered than the normal state. So it can be treated as the order parameter.

docs.title: Free Energy Difference Between Superconducting And Normal Metal States
docs.text: What is the change of free energy when the magnetic field is increased from \(B_c = 0\) to \(B_c(T)\)? As the magnetic field is applied, the magnetic moment in the superconductor is created and the energy is $\(dW = -\mathbf{M(B)} \cdot d\mathbf{B}\)$ The energy change is purely because of the energy of the magnetic moment, therefore the Gibbs free energy is $\(\begin{aligned} G_s[B_c(T)] - G_s[0] &= -\int_{0}^{B_c(T)} \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{B}) \cdot d\mathbf{B} \\ &= \int_{0}^{B_c(T)} \frac{B}{\mu_0} dB = \frac{B_c(T)^2}{2\mu_0} \end{aligned}\)$ where \(\mathbf{M} = -\mathbf{H} = -\mathbf{B}/\mu_0\). At normal state where the metal is not interacting with the magnetic field, \(G_N[B_c(T)] = G_N[0]\), therefore at the boundary where the normal and superconducting states meet (phase boundary), $\(G_N[B_c(T)] = G_B[B_c(T)] = G_N[0]\)$ It implies $\(G_N[0] - G_s[0] = \frac{B_c(T)^2}{2\mu_0}\)$ Recall that $\(B_c(T) = B_c(0) \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{T}{T_c} \right)^2 \right]\)$ We have $$\text{condensation energy} \propto \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{T}{T_c} \right)^2 \right]^2 $$ At \(T = T_c\), no condensation energy \(\implies\) no entropy change \(\implies\) no latent heat \(\implies\) second order phase transition

docs.title: Meson
docs.text:
The state notation for a particle is $\(n^{2s+1} \ L_J\)$ where \(n\) is the principle quantum number, \(s\) is the spin, \(L\) is the orbital angular momentum and \(J\) is the total angular momentum just like atomic physics notation

The excitation of meson can occur in many ways, e.g. increase in \(L, n\) and spin flip

where the individual spin is \(s =1\) when spins are aligned, otherwise \(s=0\).

docs.title: Parity of Meson
docs.text:
The parity of the meson can be evaluated as $\(P(\text{meson}) = P(q)P(\bar{q})\underbrace{(-1)^L}_{\text{orbital contribution}} = (-1)(-1)^L\)$

Note that the parity will always be opposite in a quark and antiquark i.e. one of them must be opposite to another. The contribution of the orbital quantum number is from the symmetricity of the spherical harmonics: even \(L\) symmetrical, odd \(L\) antisymmetric.

docs.title: Excitation
docs.text:
How much energy should we input to excite a meson? Let's take the spin flip case as an example. The potential for strong interaction $$ V_{\text{spin-spin}}(q \bar{q}) = \frac{32\pi}{9} \left( \mathbf{S}1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2 \right) \ \alpha_s \ \delta(x) $$ and it gives $$ \begin{aligned} E = \langle \psi | V | \psi \rangle \[1.5em]}

= \frac{32\pi}{9} \alpha_s \frac{S_q \cdot S_\bar{q}}{M_q M_\bar{q}} \psi(0) \end{aligned} $$

Therefore the interaction between spins is $\(\Delta E \propto \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2\)$Just remember from spins in magnetism course. To evaluate this, we find the total spin of a meson $$ \langle S^2 \rangle = \langle (S_q + S_{\bar{q}})^2 \rangle = \langle S_q^2 \rangle + \underbrace{\langle 2 \mathbf{S}q \cdot \mathbf{S}}} \rangle\text{what we want} + \langle S^2 \rangle $$ Using the fact that }\(\hat{S^2} = S(S+1)\hbar\) and for fermions, \(s= 1/2\) we have $$ \langle \hat{S}^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} + 1 \right) + \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} + 2 \right) + 2 \langle \hat{S}q \cdot \hat{S}_q \rangle $$ Now remember that: individual spin is \(s =1\) when spins are aligned, otherwise \(s=0\) so we have $$ \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) + 2\langle \hat{\mathbf{S}}_q \cdot \hat{\mathbf{S}} \rangle $$}

and it gives $$ \langle \hat{S}q \cdot \hat{S} \rangle = \begin{cases} -\frac{3}{4} & , \quad \langle S^2 \rangle = 0 \quad \text{(Spin misaligned)} \ \[0.5em] +\frac{1}{4} & , \quad \langle S^2 \rangle = 2 \quad \text{(Spin aligned)} \end{cases} $$}

PS: when evaluating the wave function and you are trying to work from a symmetric to anti-symmetric wave function, just remember it is symmetric times an anti-symmetric component.

docs.title: Phenomenology of metals and properties of Drude model
Drude model
docs.text:
A model that is used as a model for metal. In Drude model, electrons in a metal are treated as a free Fermi gas, occupying states up to the Fermi energy. The occupied states then form a sphere called Fermi sphere in k-space.

Resistivity: $\(\rho = \frac{RA}{L}\)$ Similar to Ohm's law \(V=IR\), the current density is $\(J = \sigma E\)$ where \(\sigma\) is the conductivity and \(E = J\rho = J/\sigma\) is electric field.

For Drude model, we can modify \(I = nAqv\) into \(J = nqv_d\) where \(v_d\) is the drift velocity and $\(F = qE = ma = \frac{mv_d}{\tau}\)$ where \(\tau\) is the collision time between the electrons and the atoms. From these we get $\(J = \frac{nq^2\tau E}{m} = \sigma E\)$ where \(\sigma = nq^2\tau /m\)

docs.title: Thermal conductivity
docs.text:
Drude model predicts thermal conductivity using the kinetic theory of gases. We have \(\underline{J}_q = -\kappa \underline{\nabla}T\) where \(\kappa = (1/3) nC\lambda <v> = (1/3) nC<v>^2 \tau\) . Using \(C_v = \frac{3}{2} nk_B\) (from classical equipartition) and \(v_{d}^2 = \frac{3k_B T}{m}\), we get:

\[ \kappa = \frac{n k_B^2 T \tau}{m} \]

Wiedemann - Franz ratio: $\(\frac{\kappa}{\sigma T} = \text{const} \approx \frac{3}{2}\frac{k_B^2}{e^2} = L\quad(\text{Lorentz number)}\)$ This matches the experiments surprisingly well, even though the Drude model's assumptions are oversimplified. However, the reality is actually larger, showing the inadequate accuracy of Drude model (because two errors cancel out)

docs.title: Heat Capacity
docs.text: Phonons contribute \(AT^3\) and electron contribute \(\gamma T\). However, Drude model can't explain this phenomena so it fails. Drude model also gets the mean free path of electron and magnetic susceptibility wrong.

docs.title: Free electron model: Fermi gas model
docs.text:
We consider this model.

It's the combination of electrons in a box + Pauli principle where there is no interactions with others.

By solving the Schrodinger equation, we know $\(E = \frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\)$ and \(p = \hbar k\)

We then use Pauli principle to visualise the energy of the electrons where \(E_F = \hbar^2k_F^2/2m\) is the Fermi energy.

docs.title: Density of states
docs.text: Similar to the density of states we mentioned previously, for a Fermi sphere, the number of states is $\(N(k) = \frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi k^3}{(\frac{2\pi}{L})^3} \times 2 = \frac{Vk^3}{3\pi^2}\)$ The 2 is because of two spin states. Given that the energy is \(E = \hbar^2k^2/2m\), the number of states in term of energy is $$ N(E) = \frac{V}{3\pi^2} \left( \frac{2mE}{\hbar^2} \right)^{\frac{3}{2}} $$ and the density of state is the derivative of \(N\) with respect to energy.

This is slightly different

The \(\mu\) is whatever number that can be used for this value to be true. docs.text: Fermi energy is a chemical potential at temperature \(T=0\) and you can (not in all cases) call it the energy level of the most occupied state.

docs.title: Michaelson Morley interferometry
docs.text:
No matter you use plane or spherical waves, they end up the same.

The beam splitter splits the intensity of the light rays into 50:50, i.e. \(I_1^{(0)} = I_2^{(0)} = I_0^{(0)}/2\) and recalling that \(I = (1/2) \epsilon_0 c E^2\), we get that the fields after the beamsplitter is $$ E_1^{(0)} = E_2^{(0)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} E^{(0)} $$ and we neglect the reflection of the light ray. After splitting, the wavevectors become $$ \begin{align} \mathbf{k}_1 &= (0, k, 0), \ \mathbf{k}_2 &= (k, 0, 0) \end{align} $$ With the reflection mirror at \(\mathbf{r}_1 = (0, l_1, 0),\mathbf{r}_2 = (l_2, 0, 0)\), before the recombination, the electric fields of the waves at the back of the beamsplitter are $$ \begin{align} E_1^{(BS)} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} E_1^{(0)} e^{i(2k l_1 - \omega t)} = \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} e^{i(2k l_1 - \omega t)} \ E_2^{(BS)} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} E_2^{(0)} e^{i(2k l_2 - \omega t)} = \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} e^{i(2k l_2 - \omega t)} \end{align} $$ where another factor of \(1/\sqrt{2}\) is introduced because they pass through the beamsplitter before they recombine (basically got splitted again). The combined field is then $$ \begin{align} E^{(BS)} &= E_1^{(BS)} + E_2^{(BS)} \ &= \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} \left[e^{i(2k l_1 - \omega t)} + e^{i(2k l_2 - \omega t)}\right] \ &= \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} e^{-i \omega t} \left(e^{2i k l_1} + e^{2i k l_2}\right) \end{align} $$ We can simplify the expression by defining $$ \bar{l} = \frac{l_1 + l_2}{2}, \quad \Delta l = l_1 - l_2 $$ so it becomes $$ \begin{align} E^{(BS)} &= \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} e^{-i \omega t} \left[e^{2i k (\bar{l} + \Delta l/2)} + e^{2i k (\bar{l} - \Delta l/2)}\right] \ &= \frac{1}{2} E^{(0)} e^{-i \omega t} e^{2i k \bar{l}} \left(e^{i k \Delta l} + e^{-i k \Delta l}\right) \ &= E^{(0)} e^{-i \omega t} e^{2i k \bar{l}} \cos(k \Delta l) \end{align} $$

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text: The intensity of the un-simplified field is $$ \begin{align} I &\propto |E^{(BS)} E^{(BS)}| \ &= \frac{1}{4} |E_0^{(0)} E_0^{(0)}| \left(e^{2i k l_1} + e^{2i k l_2}\right) \left(e^{-2i k l_1} + e^{-2i k l_2}\right) \ &= \frac{I_0}{4} \left[2 + e^{2i k (l_1 - l_2)} + e^{-2i k (l_1 - l_2)}\right] \ &= \frac{I_0}{2} \left{1 + \cos\left[2k (l_1 - l_2)\right]\right} \ &= I_0 \cos^2\left[k (l_1 - l_2)\right] \ &= I_0cos^2(k\Delta l) \quad \text{(from the defining \(l\))} \end{align} $$

docs.title: Mixtures 1   Regular Solution Model
docs.text:
So far we have seen the application of Gibbs free energy in particles at the interface and nucleation. And we have been dealing with various platforms, solids, liquids and gas.

Here, we take a closer look at the mixing between liquids and we want to predict if two liquids mix or not.

docs.title: Reminder and terminology
docs.text:
Recall that $$ \Delta G_{mix} = G_{mix} - G_{unmix} = \Delta H_{mix} - T\Delta S_{mix} $$ where \(\Delta G_{mix} < 0\) means mixing and \(\Delta G_{mix} > 0\) means demixing.

Throughout the note, we will use 1. \(N_A\) and \(N_B\) are the number of molecules A and B respectively. 2. \(\mu = \bar{G} = G/N\) as chemical potential or the Gibbs free energy per molecules 3. \(\phi_A = N_A/N, \phi_B = N_B/N\) where \(N=N_A + N_B\) as the fraction of molecules A and B, respectively.

docs.title: Entropy term
docs.text: Recall from Statistical physics that $$ \bar{S} = -k_B \sum_i \phi_i \ln(\phi_i) $$ $$\implies \bar{S} = -k_B [\phi_A \ln(\phi_A) + \phi_B \ln(\phi_B)] $$ That implies the Gibbs free energy is lowered

docs.title: Enthalpy term
docs.text:
If you take some molecules A and put into B, you need energy to break the bond between them. When you put A into a pile and B into another pile, you form new bonds between A and B. That change of energy affects the internal energy of the system.

\[ \Delta \bar{U}_{mix} = \bar{U}_{mixed} - \bar{U}_{unmixed} = \begin{pmatrix} \text{energy change per} \\ A - B \text{ bond relative} \\ \text{to } A - A \text{ or } B - B \end{pmatrix} (\# A - B \text{ contacts}) \]

The probability of A-B contact is given by \(P \sim Z\phi_A \phi_B\) therefore

$$ \Delta \bar{U}_{mix} = \kappa \phi_A \phi_B $$ where \(\kappa\) is interaction parameter (J/molecule). - If \(\kappa > 0\) disfavour mixing (because it increases free energy) - If \(\kappa<0\) favour mixing

By definition $$ H \equiv U + PV $$ $\(\implies \Delta \bar{H}_{mix} = \Delta \bar{U}_{mix} + P \underbrace{\Delta V_{mix}}_{\sim 0 (Z = cte)} + V \Delta \underbrace{P_{mix}}_{=0 (P=cte)} = \kappa\phi_A\phi_B\)$

docs.title: Regular solution model
docs.text:
Based on the thermodynamical model above, we have $$ \Delta \bar{G}{mix} = \Delta \bar{H} = \kappa \, \phi_A \phi_B + k_B T [\phi_A \ln(\phi_A) + \phi_B \ln(\phi_B)] $$ i.e. } - T \Delta \bar{S}_{mix\(\Delta H\) increases energy of the system but entropy always decreases the energy.

Remember that for mixing, \(\Delta G <0\)

  • In almost all cases \(\kappa > 0\) we have two minima and a maximum at \(\phi = \phi_B = 1-\phi_A = 1/2\) because it disfavour mixing. At \(\phi = 1/2\) it is a stable point, from the formula.

docs.title: Mixtures II   Stability and Phase Diagram
docs.text: As a summary of the last note: We have initially a straight line if we dont consider the interfacial energy and the solution is not mixed. We then have a curve with two minima and a maximum when \(\phi = 1/2\) if we consider the interfacial energy.

docs.title: Demixing under the Regular Solution model
docs.text:
There are two variable that oppose each other

  1. \(\kappa\)
  2. \(T\)

The goal of this chapter is to find the mixture compositions at \(\phi_{\text{min1}}\) and \(\phi_{\text{min2}}\)

At \(\phi_{\text{min1}}\) and \(\phi_{\text{min2}}\) , there must be specific mixture compositions that are particularly stable. We expect the mixture to decompose from \(\phi^*\) to \(\phi_{\text{min1}}\) and \(\phi_{\text{min2}}\) $$ \phi^ = \alpha \, \phi_{min1} + (1 - \alpha) \, \phi_{min2}, \quad 0 < \alpha < 1 $$ From there, we can calculate the decreases of free energy upon demixing $$ \bar{G}_{demix}^ = \alpha \, \bar{G}_1 + (1 - \alpha) \, \bar{G}_2 $$ and it can be shown that \(\bar{G}_{demix}^*\) is lower than the free energy of the unmixed system at the same composition. That's why there are dips (decrease from the pure A or pure B). Hint in the lecture note. From the graph, it also shows that the demixing in pure A and B is more energetically favourable than the mixing at \(\phi = 1/2\)

Just remember - Free energy higher than the straight line is mixing, - Below than is mixing

docs.title: Mode of demixing and composition stability
docs.text: More complex stuff can happen and using free energy to determine the mixing/demixing processes of liquids is not enough. Sometimes it is possible for a system to exhibit \(\Delta \bar{G}^*_{mix} < 0\) but still demix.

docs.title: Demixing from a concave (with respect to the x-axis) region
docs.text:
By looking at the region \(\phi^* \pm d\phi\) and analyse the trend, we can see if the free energy is locally convex, it can undergo spontaneous demix due to small fluctuation (note the position of the straight line in \(\phi^* \pm d\phi\)) as the free energy is decreasing locally.

This spontaneous demixing process is called a spinodal decomposition

docs.title: Demixing from a convex (with respect to the x-axis) region
docs.text:
By looking at the region \(\phi^* \pm d\phi\) and analyse the trend, we can see if the free energy is locally concave, it cannot undergo spontaneous demix (note the position of the straight line in \(\phi^* \pm d\phi\)) as the free energy is increasing locally.

When it eventually takes place, the resulting spontaneous demixing process is called nucleation.

docs.title: Formalism
docs.text:
If we are looking for a global favourable, we can just use the free energy. If we are looking for the stability (how the change in energy occurs with perturbation) of each state, we need second derivative. Because there exist a metastable state that is stable but not global minimum.

The second derivative test comes from the Taylor expansion where \(\phi \rightarrow \phi+d\phi\) and \(\Delta f = \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2 f}{d\phi^2}(\delta \phi)^2\)

Unstable system have a decrease in energy $$ \frac{\partial^2 \Delta \bar{G}{mix}}{\partial \phi^2} = \frac{\partial^2 \bar{G} < 0 $$ For metastable (convex) $$ \frac{\partial^2 \Delta \bar{G}}}{\partial \phi^2{mix}}{\partial \phi^2} = \frac{\partial^2 \bar{G} > 0 $$ The inflexion point $}}{\partial \phi^2\(\frac{\partial^2 \Delta \bar{G}_{mix}}{\partial \phi^2} = \frac{\partial^2 \bar{G}_{mix}}{\partial \phi^2} = 0\)$ is called the spinodal

docs.title: N identical aperture
docs.text:
Generally,

[!note] $$ I^{(z)} = \frac{I_0}{(\lambda z)^2} \left[ \mathcal{F} f(x', y') \right]^2 \times \underbrace{\left( \frac{\sin(N \pi u d)}{\sin \pi u d} \right)^2}_{\text{interference term}} $$

Derivation

This involves summing the individual slits up and calculate the geometric series from the delta function. It is exactly the same form as modelling a finite diffraction grating by convolving a comb function with a rectangular function.

The result is that there will be \(N-2\) subsidiary peaks between major peaks in intensity curve

docs.title: Barbinet's Principle
docs.text:
[!Definition] Every complimentary function \(f_c(x',y') = 1 - f(x',y')\) has the identical diffraction intensity pattern as their corresponding function in the far field, except at the centre.

At the centre of the intensity curve, it is a \(\delta(x)\) function but the patterns for the rest will just be the squared modulus of transmission function.

Intuitively, it means if you have a slit (any aperture) and an opaque surrounding, it's diffraction intensity pattern is the same as making the slit opaque but the removing the surrounding

docs.title: N phasor sum
docs.text:
For \(N\) phasor sum, similarr to the three-hole example, we can extend the above analysis to the general case of a \(N\)-hole case to work out the intensity profile of a diffraction grating.

Again, we take the middle point as the reference point, so we have \(M = (N-1)/2\) holes on each side. We can easily extend the equation in Three phasor sum $\(E = \overline{E}_s e^{ik\overline{r}}\left(e^{-ikdx/z} + e^0 + e^{ikdx/z}\right)\)$ to $$ E = \overline{E}s e^{i k \overline{r}} e^{-i M k d x / z} \sum $$ and by using the solution to the summation term: $}^{2M} e^{i n k d x / z\(S = \frac{1-r^{P+1}}{1-r}\)$ we can obtain $$ E = \overline{E}_s e^{i k \overline{r}} \frac{\sin\left[N k d x / (2 z)\right]}{\sin\left[k d x / (2 z)\right]} $$

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text: The intensity, using the formula, can be calculated as $$ I = I_s \frac{\sin^2\left[\frac{N k d x}{2 z}\right]}{\sin^2\left[\frac{k d x}{2 z}\right]} $$

docs.title: Intensity at principal maxima
docs.text:
The principal maxima occurs when the detominator is zero (giving the intensity infinity): $$ \begin{align} &\sin^2\left[\frac{k d x_{pm}}{2 z}\right] = 0, \ \Rightarrow &\frac{k d x_{pm}}{2 z} = n\pi, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}, \ \Rightarrow &x_{pm} = \frac{2 n \pi z}{k d} = \frac{n \lambda z}{d}, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z} \end{align} $$ The intensity of the principal maxima can be calculated by taking the limit of \(kdx/2z \to 0\):

\[ \begin{align*} \frac{I_{pm}}{I_s} &= \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{\sin^2 (N\alpha)}{\sin^2 \alpha} \\ &= \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos (2N\alpha)}{1 - \cos (2\alpha)} \\ &= N^2 \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Zero intensity

docs.title: Noether's Thorem
docs.text:
If the Lagrangian is invariant under a continuous symmetry transformation, then there are conserved quantities associated with that symmetry, one for each parameter of the transformation.

These can be found by differentiating each coordinate with respect to the parameters of the transformation in the immediate neighbourhood of the identity transformation, multiplying by the conjugate momentum, and summing over the degrees of freedom.

docs.title: Legendre transform
docs.text: It is possible to map two equivalent functions \(A(x,y)\) and \(B(x,z)\) which represent the same information in different ways. $\(B(x,y) = yz - A(x,y)\)$ where \(z = \partial A/\partial y|_x\)

docs.title: The Hamiltonian
docs.text: By applying Legendre transform to the 1DoF Lagrangian \(L(q, \dot{q})\) where the active variable is the velocity \(\dot{q}\) $\(H(q,p) = p\dot{q} - L(q,\dot{q})\)$ where \(p = \partial L/\partial \dot{q}|_q\) . By differentiating this equation and using the Euler-Lagrange equation, we have $$ \frac{\partial H}{\partial p} \bigg|q = \dot{q}, \quad \frac{\partial H}{\partial q} \bigg|_p = -\left. \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} \right| $$ Or more generally, if we consider the time-dependence: $}} = -\left. \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}} \right|_q = - \dot{p\(H(q,p,t) = \sum_i p_i \dot{q_i} - L(q, \dot{p},t)\)$ then, we have $$ \dot{q}_k = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_k}, \quad \dot{p}_k = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_k}, \quad \frac{dH}{dt} = -\frac{\partial L}{\partial t} $$

docs.title: Nuclear Masses and Binding Energies
docs.text:
Binding energy is what responsible for the difference (mass defect) between the mass of an atom and the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in it. The force responsible of it is called the strong force.

Direct calculation of binding energy is not possible because in a nucleus, the particles are tightly bounded (perturbative methods have poor convergence) and it is a many body problem with all particles of the same mass. The nucleons also move at large speeds and need to use relativistic approximation.

The usual notation for an element is $\(^A_ZX\)$ where \(A\) is the mass number (proton + neutron), \(Z\) is the number of proton and \(X\) is the elemental symbol.

Here we use the liquid drop model to approximate a formula for binding energies: $$ \begin{aligned} B(A, Z) = E_{\text{Volume}} - E_{\text{Surface}} - E_{\text{Coulomb}} - E_{\text{Asymmetry}} \pm E_{\text{Pairing}} \ = a_V A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_a \frac{(N - Z)^2}{4A} + \frac{\delta}{A^{1/2}} \end{aligned} $$

docs.title: Volume term, \(E_{\text{Volume}} = a_V A\)
docs.text:
The attractive strong force between nucleons implies that it is energetically favourable for a nucleon to surround itself with other surrounding nucleons, inducing a binding energy between them.

Since \(4\pi R^3 / 3 \propto A\), we expect this term to scale with \(A\)

docs.title: Surface term, \(E_{\text{Surface}} = a_S A^{2/3}\)
docs.text:
Here we consider the particle at the edge of the surface where are have less binding energy as compared to the ones at the centre because they are surrounded by less nucleons.

This term, following from the scaling factor as outlined in volume term, scales with \(R^2 = A^{2/3}\)

docs.title: Coulomb term, \(E_{\text{Coulomb}} = a_C Z^2/A^{1/3}\)
docs.text:
The protons have the same charge so they repel each other, implying a weaker binding energy.

Coulomb potential scales as \(V = a/r\) so we expect this term to be scaling with \(1/R = A^{-1/3}\)

docs.title: Asymmetry term, \(E_{\text{Asymmetry}} = a_a (N-Z)^2/4A\)
docs.text:
This term involves Pauli exclusion principle. Since protons and neutrons are fermions, they cannot lie in the same state. Consider that we have \(n\) protons and neutrons and each of them fill \(n\) lowest energy state. If we try to replace a neutron with a proton, it has to occupy the upper energy level, hence reducing the binding energy. In other words, the symmetric number of neutrons and protons can be packed tighter.

This term measures the difference between the number of neutrons and protons i.e. it is proportional to \(N-Z\)

docs.title: Pairing term, \(E_{\text{Pairing}} = \delta/A^{1/2}\)
docs.text: Nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons are more stable because two different nucleons with opposite spin can be on the same shell. If we have odd number of protons/neutrons, the third spin has to be in the next shell.

docs.text:
The uranium sample used in nuclear fission is mainly the \(^{235}_{92}U\) which is not common in natural uranium ore. It contains less than a percent in natural-occuring uranium ore. The reason why uranium ore does not undergo fission reaction in earth crust is because of the low concentration of \(U-235\) and the fact that nuclear fission requires a much higher energy neutrons (up to MeV) which are produced in a nuclear fission.

Fission reaction produces a lot of nuclear waste which last for thousands of years and some retards do not manage it properly. So fussion, in theory, is a good replacement of fission. The proposed reaction is $$ {}^{3}{1}\text{H} + {}^{2} + n $$ The problem with the fusion reaction is that to use tritium and deuterium in the reaction, we have to heat them up to a temperature of KeV, forming plasma to overcome the electromagnetic repulsion between them. The plasma is then handled by magnetic fields. We currently do not have the technology to settle the problems we have.}\text{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He

docs.title: Nuclear Stability and Types of Decays
docs.text:
We characterise how long does a nucleus live by the frequency of decays or activity

$$ A =\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N(t) \quad \Rightarrow \quad N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} $$ Here we can work out the halflife of a sample, i.e. the time for a sample to decay to half of the number of atoms: $$ \begin{aligned} N(t_{1/2}) = \frac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda t_{1/2}} \ \implies t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda} \end{aligned} $$ where the mean lifetime (average time for a nucleus in the sample to decay) is given by \(\tau = t_{1/2}/\text{ln}2\)

docs.title: \(\beta^-\) decays
docs.text:
This process occurs when the nucleus has more neutrons than protons. It converts neutrons to protons through $$ n \to p + e^- + \bar{\nu}e $$ and the resulting equation in terms of the proton and neutron number will be $$ ^A_ZX_N \rightarrow ^A_e $$} Y_{N-1} + e^- + \bar{\nu

The initial energy is used to create an electron and 'make' the element \(Y\) to lack of an electron, there is no additional energy required for the neutron to be converted to proton i.e., the only requirement is that the energy of the mother nucleus has to be greater than the daughter nucleus: $$ M(A, Z) > M(A, Z+1) $$

docs.title: \(\beta^+\) decays
docs.text:
This process occurs when the protons are more than the neutrons in the nucleus and the process is described by $$ p \to n + e^+ + \nu_e $$ where the equation of proton and neutron numbers is $$^A_Z X_N \rightarrow ^A_{Z-1}Y_{N+1} + e^+ + \nu_e $$ Note that the initial energy is used to create a positron and 'make' the daughter nucleus to have one excess electron, so additional energy is required for this process to be feasible: $\(M(A,Z) > M(A,Z-1) + 2m_e\)$

Therefore, there is no free neutrons even though there are free protons (free neutrons do not need additional energy to decay).

docs.title: Electron Capture
docs.text:
This process is only feasible when the wave function of the electron overlaps with the nucleus and it is typically \(s\)-shell electron because its radial wave function is non-zero at the centre of the atom.

The process is $$ p + e^- \rightarrow n + \nu_e, $$ with $$ ^A_Z X_N + e^- \rightarrow ^A_{Z-1} Y_{N+1} + \nu_e $$ No energy is needed to produce a positron or electron, only negligible energy for the neutrino is needed: $$ M(A, Z) > M(A, Z - 1) + \epsilon $$ The binding energy of a nucleus is the difference between the atomic constituents and the atomic mass $$ B(A, Z) = \underbrace{Z M(^1\text{H}) + (A - Z) M(n)}_\text{mass of the atomic constituents} - M(A, Z) $$ where \(M(^1H) = M_p + m_e\) , \(M(n)\) is the mass of neutron and \(M(A,Z)\) is the mass of mother nucleus. Since \(A\) does not change we can combine this with the binding energy discussed in Nuclear Masses and Binding Energies to form $$ M(A, Z) = (A - Z)M_n + Z(M_p + m_e) - a_V A + a_s A^{2/3} + a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} + a_a \frac{(A - 2Z)^2}{4A} - \frac{\delta}{A^{1/2}} $$ For odd \(A\), we have only one parabola. Only one isobar is the lowest and is \(\beta\)-stable. Akk other isobars can decay to that stable isobar

For even A, we have two parabolas (because of pairing term i.e. $$ \delta = \begin{cases} +\delta_p & \text{even-even nucleus} \ 0 & \text{odd-even nucleus} \ -\delta_p & \text{odd-odd nucleus} \end{cases} $$

docs.title: \(A\) changing decays
docs.text:
As discussed above, the \(\beta\) decay does not change \(A\) but they can occur in 3 processes.

  1. Proton and neutron emission: Proton-, or neutron-rich nuclei emit a single proton or neutron first before decaying.
\[ \text{Neuton emission:} \quad^{A}_{Z} X_N \rightarrow ^{A-1}_{Z} Y_{N-1} + n $$ $$ \text{Proton emission:} \quad ^{A}_{Z} X_N \rightarrow ^{A-1}_{Z-1} Y_N + p \]

where $$ \text{Neutron emission:} \quad M(A, Z) > M(A - 1, Z) + M_n $$

\[ \text{Proton emission:} \quad M(A, Z) > M(A - 1, Z - 1) + M(^1\text{H}) \]
  1. \(\alpha\)-decay: This typically happens in a heavy nucleus.
\[ ^{A}_{Z} X_N \rightarrow ^{A-4}_{Z-2} Y_{N-2} + ^{4}_{2} \text{He}_2 \]

where energy has to fulfil $$ M(A, Z) > M(A - 4, Z - 2) + M(4, 2) $$ We can predict the probability of the nucleus of emitting an \(\alpha\) particle. We first construct the potential wall which consists of coulomb interaction outside of the atomic radius and strong force inside ![[Pasted image 20260417090002.png]]

By solving the Schrodinger equation, we get the probability of the particle tunnels out through the thin wall $$ \Psi(x) = \exp \left( -\int_{0}^{x} dx \sqrt{2m(V(x) - E)} \right) \equiv e^{-G} $$ where \(G\) is the Gamow factor.

  1. Nuclear fission:

If we look that the energy as we pull two parts of a nucleus apart in this graph, we notice that we have to overcome an activation energy before splitting the nucleus. As we put energy into the nucleus via neutrons, we reach an unstable equilibrium point where the energy we put into (to overcome surface energy by 'stretching' it out) is balanced with the electromagnetic interaction whose force tries to push the two same-charge daughter nuclei apart.

docs.title: Optical Beats and Frequency Comb   Copy
docs.text: Beginning from here, we will be using the inverse fourier to find the Fourier spectrum from the time dependence of frequency $\(f(t) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[F(\omega)]\)$

docs.title: Optical Beats
docs.text:
Optical beats are the results of addition of two waves with slightly different frequency and momentum.

$\(\begin{aligned} \mathcal{E} &= \mathcal{E}_0 \left[ \cos(k_1 x - \omega_1 t) + \cos(k_2 x - \omega_2 t) \right] \\ &= 2\mathcal{E}_0 \cos(\bar{k} z - \bar{\omega} t) \underbrace{\cos\left( \frac{\Delta k}{2} x - \frac{\Delta \omega}{2} t \right)}_\text{envelope} \end{aligned}\)$ where $\(\begin{aligned} \bar{k} &= \frac{1}{2}(k_1 + k_2) \\[1.5em] \bar{\omega} &= \frac{1}{2}(\omega_1 + \omega_2) \\[1.5em] \Delta k &= k_2 - k_1 \\[1.5em] \Delta \omega &= \omega_2 - \omega_1 \end{aligned}\)$ The velocity of the envelope is $\(\frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta k} = c\)$ The medium where all frequencies propagate at the same speed is known is dispersionless and the [[Physics/Scientific words and definitions/Dispersion Relation|dispersion relation]] is a constant.

docs.title: Many Frequencies
docs.text:
This can be generalised to many frequencies. We first look at an example of laser. In a Fabry-Perot cavity, we have two mirrors confining some modes of frequencies. To satisfy the boundary condition of the electric field where the field has to be zero on the surface of the mirror, the modes have to be $\(\omega = \frac{m\pi c}{L}\)$ where \(m \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(L\) is the length of the cavity. Therefore the Fourier spectrum of the laser will be

By doing the inverse Fourier transform, we can find the time dependence of the transmission function: $\(f(t) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[F(\omega)] = F_0 \text{III}_T(t) \frac{1}{2\pi}\)$ where \(T = 2\pi/\omega = 2L/c\) is the round trip time of the cavity

However, laser has a finite bandwidth i.e. it is encapsulated in an envelope like in previous chapter

So we introduce a gauss function into our Fourier spectrum: $\(F(\omega) = F_o \ \text{III}(\omega) \ \text{gauss}\left( \frac{\omega}{\Delta \omega} \right)\)$ and the inverse Fourier \(f(t) \propto \text{III}_T(t) * \text{gauss}(\Delta \omega /2)\)

It will be useful to derive a Hedgehog equation in time domain. We are summing over plane waves with different frequencies so $\(\mathcal{E}(z,t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} A(k) e^{i[kz - \omega(k)t]} dk\)$ where \(A(k)\) is Fourier spectrum of wave vector. We then have $\(\mathcal{E}(z,t) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left[ e^{-i\omega(k)t} \mathcal{F} \left[ \mathcal{E}(z,0) \right] \right]\)$

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The atomic clock has systematic error such as 2nd order Zeeman see Zeeman effect part 2, blackbody radiation and relativistic.

The fractional uncertainty is given by $$ \sigma = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\omega_{12}} \sqrt{\frac{T_c}{N\tau}} $$

where \(T_c\) is the time for single measurement, \(N\) is the number of atoms per measurement and \(\tau\) is the averaging time.

To reduce \(\sigma\), we need to increase \(N\) and \(\tau\). However, it is hard to achieve both. Now both of these method use optical transitions as the frequency reference. (will be discussed in Trapped Ion and [[Optical Trap]])

Question: How do we measure optical frequencies?

docs.title: Optical frequency comb
docs.text:
We use pulsed femtosecond laser where the output looks like a ruler teeth of a comb and it can provide a relative frequency measurement but not an absolute measurement because we dont know the origin.

[!note] The frequency of the \(n^{th}\) comb tooth is $\(\omega_n = \omega_{\text{CE}} + n\Delta\omega\)$ where \(\omega_{\text{CE}}\) is the carrier envelope offset frequency which can be found using octave spanning comb in PD2 parts in the setup diagram

The setup is as such: we break this diagram into 3 parts: PD1, PD2 and PD3

docs.title: PD2
docs.text:
Here is the part where we find \(\omega_{\text{CE}}\) using octave spanning comb. The input signal after the fibre is splitted into two parts, with one passing with the doubling crystal (nonlinear material which gives second harmonic generation) giving $\(\overline{\omega} =2\omega_n=2\omega_{\text{CE}}+2n\Delta\omega\)$ and another one passing right through the medium, maintaining the same \(\omega_{\text{CE}}\) and \(\Delta\omega\): $\(\omega_n' = \omega_{\text{CE}} +n'\Delta\omega\)$ The light then mixes and passes through the diffraction grating before reaching the photodiode 2 which measure the beat frequency (frequency between two teeth):

[!note] $\(\omega_{\text{beat}} = \overline{\omega_n} - \omega_n' = 2\omega_n-\omega_n'=\omega_{\text{CE}}\)$ where we set \(n'=2n\) (?)

Now we can measure optical frequency. We can use laser as oscillator in atomic clocks but the laser needs to be stable

docs.title: PD1
docs.text:
• This is used to measure \(\Delta\omega\) and it is maintained constant by electronic feedback from the frequency counter to the laser.
  • 'Locking' laser to ultra stable reference cavity.

docs.title: PD3
docs.text:
The laser with unknown frequency is introduced to the path to allow the mixing of light. A part of the light is used for experiments and another one is to measure the frequency of the laser.

The laser frequency is then: $\(\omega_L = \omega_{\text{CE}} + n'' \Delta\omega +\omega_{\text{beat}}\)$ This can be derived from \(\omega_{\text{beat}}\)

docs.title: Optogenetics
docs.text:
A scientist had used a virus to smuggle a virus carrying algal light-sensitive gene inro rat neurons. When exposed to blue light, the neuron fired.

It is a field of study involving manipulating lights to switch on and off the neurons. It could be used to treat photosensitive epilepsy or Parkinson's disease (by targeting the movement-controlling neurons) using micro-flashlight. But safety concerns have to be met before clinical trials on humans.

docs.title: PN Junction   Equilibrium
docs.text:
Now we have p-type and n-type semiconductors and we could make a diode by combining them. Here we take a close look at the depletion region i.e. the pn junction

Recall that the donor concentration is \(n\sim N_D\) and \(p = n_i^2/N_D\) for the donor dopant and it's the other way round for the acceptor dopant. Here we ignore the electron in CB and holes in VB and focus only on the ionised donors and acceptors.

docs.title: Electric field
docs.text:
Gauss's law says $\(\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{\mathcal{E}} = \frac{d\mathcal{E}}{dx} = \frac{\rho(x)}{\epsilon_r \epsilon_0}\)$ where \(\rho(x)\) is the charge density and we care about the \(x\) axis. Given that the depletion region with length from \(-w_p\) to \(w_n\), has no charge so we have $\(\rho(x) = \begin{cases} -eN_A & -w_p < x < 0 \\ eN_D & 0 < x < w_n \\ 0 & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}\)$ where for the region \(-w_p < x < 0\), the depletion zone is negative because the electron from the n-Si flows to that region; for the region \(0 < x < w_n\), the region is positive because the holes from p-Si flows to that region.

Through integration, we get the electric field $\(\mathcal{E}(x) = \begin{cases} -\frac{eN_A}{\epsilon_r \epsilon_0}(x + w_p), & -w_p < x < 0 \\ \frac{eN_D}{\epsilon_r \epsilon_0}(x - w_n), & 0 < x < w_n \end{cases}\)$ Solving the boundary condition (where we use continuity of electric field at the boundary) gives \(N_Aw_p = N_Dw_D\)

docs.title: Electric potential
docs.text:
The potential is defined as $\(\vec{\mathcal{E}} = -\vec{\nabla}\phi \quad (\phi = \text{electrostatic potential})\)$

By more integration, we get $\(\phi(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{eN_A}{2\epsilon_r\epsilon_0}(x + w_p)^2 & -w_p < x < 0 \\ \phi_{bi} - \frac{eN_D}{2\epsilon_r\epsilon_0}(x - w_n)^2 & 0 < x < w_n \end{cases}\)$ where \(\phi_{bi}\) is the build-in potential (potential difference) and it is the solution of the boundary condition.

docs.title: Energy level diagram for pn-junction
docs.text:
Before contacting,

After contact the energy level \(E_c\) and \(E_v\) follows the electron energy lineshape

From here we can calculate \(\phi_{bi} = (\mu_n - \mu_p)/e\) where $\(\begin{aligned} \mu_n &= E_c - kT \ln \left( \frac{N_c}{N_D} \right) \\ \mu_p &= E_v + kT \ln \left( \frac{N_v}{N_A} \right) \end{aligned}\)$ as can be derived from the results in Statistical Mechanics for Semiconductors and Intrinsic Semiconductors and Extrinsic Semiconductors. We get $$ \phi_{bi} = \frac{kT}{e} \ln \left( \frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2} \right)$$ and by considering the potential is continuous at \(x=0\), we get $\(\begin{aligned} w_n &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 \phi_{bi}}{e} \left( \frac{N_A}{N_D} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \\ w_p &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 \phi_{bi}}{e} \left( \frac{N_D}{N_A} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \end{aligned}\)$

docs.title: PN Junction   Non Equilibrium
docs.text:
Electrically bias means that an electric field is applied to the pn-junction so that the depletion region spatially shifted.

Forward bias means that the electric field is aligned such that the negative is toward the n-type Si Otherwise it is reverse bias. Considering from PN Junction - Equilibrium that $$\begin{aligned} \phi_{bi} &= \frac{kT}{e} \ln \left( \frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2} \right)\

w_n &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 \phi_{bi}}{e} \left( \frac{N_A}{N_D} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \

w_p &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 \phi_{bi}}{e} \left( \frac{N_D}{N_A} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \end{aligned}$$

we are essentially just include the potential of the electric field in the energy term. $\(\begin{aligned} w_n &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 (\phi_{bi} - V_{ext})}{e} \left( \frac{N_A}{N_D} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \\ w_p &= \left[ \frac{2\epsilon_r \epsilon_0 (\phi_{bi} - V_{ext})}{e} \left( \frac{N_D}{N_A} \right) \left( \frac{1}{N_A + N_D} \right) \right]^{1/2} \end{aligned}\)$ Since for forward bias, \(V_{ext}\) is positive and negative for reverse bias. This means that the space charge region is narrower under forward bias and wider for reverse bias.

Note that the electric field and its potential are also changed because they are dependent on \(w_n\) and \(w_p\). For forward bias, \(E_c\) decreases because \(w_p\) decreases.

docs.text:

This creates excess minority carriers in the quasi-neutral regions. Recombination occurs and light is emitted.

  • AlGaInP alloy: red emission
  • InGaN: green-blue emission

docs.title: Paramagnetism
docs.text:
• Paramagnetism has a positive magnetic susceptibility \(\chi> 0\) and it has unfilled atomic/ionic shell as mentioned in Hund's Rule

Therefore we calculate the susceptibility using the fact that paramagnets do have magnetic moments due to the unpaired electrons and they have random directions. And we extract certain magnetic moments

docs.title: Classical (Langevin's theory) for \(J = \infty\)
docs.text:
Here we consider magnetic moments lying in the area of \(\theta\) to \(d\theta\). The probability of a moment at angle \(\theta\) is given by Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution \(\exp(-E/k_B T) = \exp(\mu B \cos \theta / k_B T)\) and the distribution is given by the area of the loop, \(\text{distribution} = 2\pi\sin \theta d\theta\) where \(d\theta\) is the thickness of the loop.

The expectation value of \(\langle\mu_z\rangle\) is then $$ \langle \mu_z \rangle = \frac{\int_0^\pi (\mu \cos \theta) e^{\frac{\mu B \cos \theta}{k_B T}} (2\pi \sin \theta) \, d\theta}{\int_0^\pi e^{\frac{\mu B \cos \theta}{k_B T}} (2\pi \sin \theta) \, d\theta} = \mu \frac{\int_{-1}^1 x e^{yx} \, dx}{\int_{-1}^1 e^{yx} \, dx} $$ where \(y = \mu B / k_B T\) and \(x = \cos \theta\). The solution is then

[!Results] $$ \frac{\langle \mu_z \rangle}{\mu} = \left( \coth y - \frac{1}{y} \right) = \underbrace{L(y)}_\text{Langevin function} $$

As \(y \rightarrow 0\) $$ \frac{\langle \mu_z \rangle}{\mu} =\frac{M}{M_s} = \frac{y}{3} = \frac{\mu B}{3k_B T} $$

where \(M_s\) is saturation magnetisation (when all magnetic moment are aligned in \(z\) axis). Using the definition of \(\chi\) and treat the paramagnet as a weak magnetic material where \(M\) can be neglected we get

[!note] $$ \chi = \frac{n \mu_0 \mu^2}{3 k_B T} $$

docs.title: Quantum Mechanical for \(J = 1/2\)
docs.text:
Remember from Fundamental Equations for Magnetism that \(\mu_z = -g_J\gamma J_z\).

We have $\(g_J = \frac{3}{2}+\frac{S(S+1)-L(L+1)}{2J(J+1)} =2\)$ Given that \(L=0, S=1/2\) and therefore \(J=1/2\), we have \(J_z=m_J \hbar = \hbar/2\), we have discrete values of $\(\mu_z = \pm\gamma\hbar=\pm\mu_B\)$

Using expectation value of \(\mu_z\) like previously, we have $$ \langle \mu_z \rangle = \frac{\mu_B e^{\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}} - \mu_B e^{-\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}}}{e^{\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}} + e^{-\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}}} = \mu_B \tanh\left(\frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T}\right) $$ $$\implies \frac{M}{M_s} = \frac{\langle \mu_z \rangle}{\mu_B} = \frac{\mu_B B}{k_B T} $$

[!Results] $\(\chi = \frac{n \mu_0 \mu_B^2}{k_B T}\)$

For arbitrary \(J\), we have Brillouin function $$ \frac{M}{M_s} = B_J(y) $$ where $$ B_J(y) = \frac{2J + 1}{2J} \coth\left(\frac{2J + 1}{2J}y\right) - \frac{1}{2J} \coth\left(\frac{y}{2J}\right) $$

docs.title: Paraxial Spherical waves
docs.text: By using the Fresnel approximation discussed in Paraxial optics, we can simplify our spherical waves solution to $$ \mathbf{E} = \frac{\mathbf{E}_s}{i k z} e^{i k r_p} = \frac{\mathbf{E}_s}{i k z} e^{i k z} e^{i k \rho^2 / (2 z)} $$ where $$ \rho = \left[ (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 \right]^{1/2} $$ The \(r\) in denominator and the exponent are replaced by \(z\) and \(r_p\) respectively because it can minimise the errors. The details can be found in lecture note, page 16.

docs.title: Paraxial optics example Lenses
docs.text:
We let $$ \rho' = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/2} $$ and the lens has a local thickness $$ \begin{align} t &= t_0 - \ell \ &= t_0 - \left(R_{\mathrm{L}} - \sqrt{R^2_{\mathrm{L}} - \rho'^2}\right) \ &= \sqrt{R^2_{\mathrm{L}} - \rho'^2} - (R_{\mathrm{L}} - t_0) \end{align} $$ We use the paraxial regime \(\rho' \ll R_L\) as approximation (binomial expansion and we get) $$ \begin{align} t &= R_{\mathrm{L}}\sqrt{1-\frac{\rho'^2}{R_{\mathrm{L}}^2}} - (R_{\mathrm{L}}-t_0) \ &\approx R_{\mathrm{L}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\rho'^2}{R_{\mathrm{L}}^2}\right) - (R_{\mathrm{L}}-t_0) \ &= t_0 - \frac{\rho'^2}{2R_{\mathrm{L}}} \end{align} $$

The incident plane wave is \(E = E^{(0)}e^{ikz}\) and after the lens is given by $$ E^{(L)} = E^{(0)} e^{i k (t_0 - t)} e^{i n k t} $$ where the first exponential term is due to the air-gap between the lens and the \(x',y'\) axis and the second exponential term is due to the propagation through the thickness of the lens, \(t\). Plugging in, we get $$ E^{(L)} = E^{(0)} e^{i k \rho^2 / (2 R_{\mathrm{L}})} e^{i n k t_0} e^{-i n k \rho^2 / (2 R_{\mathrm{L}})} = E^{(0)} e^{i n k t_0} e^{-i (n - 1) k \rho^2 / (2 R_{\mathrm{L}})} $$

Comparing to and dropping the first exponential term due to thin lens approximation$$ \mathbf{E} = \frac{\mathbf{E}_s}{i k z} e^{i k r_p} = \frac{\mathbf{E}_s}{i k z} e^{i k z} e^{i k \rho^2 / (2 z)} $$ in the Paraxial Spherical waves, we see the wave converging into a point $\(f = \frac{R_L}{n-1}\)$

docs.title: Paraxial optics
docs.text:
In the derivation of the equation of circular wavefronts, we assumed \(r \gg \lambda\) and applied approximations that works in the region close to a specific propagation direction. This region is called paraxial regime.

  • It is a regime when light rays travel close to the optical axis, usually the \(z\) axis.

In this diagram the region is $$ |x - x'| \ll z \quad \text{and} \quad |y - y'| \ll z $$ In this region, we can use - Small angle approximation - Ajibala approximation

Since \(\theta\) is small, \(k_x = ksin\theta \ll k_z = kcos\theta\) and \(k_y \ll k_z\) where we express them in $\(\frac{k_x}{k} \ll 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{k_y}{k} \ll 1\)$ Then we write the axial component of the wavevector as $\(k_z = \sqrt{k^2 - k_x^2 - k_z^2} = k\left(1-\frac{k_x^2+k_y^2}{k^2}\right)^{1/2}\)$ from Binomial expansion

  • Fresnel approximation

Using the fact that $$ |x - x'| \ll z \quad \text{and} \quad |y - y'| \ll z, $$ Use the similar approach (Binomial expansion) as discussed previously, we will get $$ r' = z + \frac{(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2}{2z} = z + \frac{\rho^2}{2z}= r_{\mathrm{p}} $$

docs.title: Sidenote
docs.text: In Fraunhofer approximation, the \(\rho^2\) dependence will be ignored due to far field assumption. It will be discussed in Fraunhofer diffraction

docs.title: Parity
docs.text: The action of parity is a transformation: it is an inversion around the origin (transforming coordinate vector from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{-x}\)). Here we define an operator called parity operator that do: $$ \hat{P} \psi(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(-\mathbf{x}) $$ We can determine the parity of the operator by investigating the eigenvalue, i.e. $\(\hat{P} \psi(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda \psi(\mathbf{x})\)$ If we equate these two equation we get $\(\psi(-\mathbf{x}) = \lambda \psi(\mathbf{x})\)$ so if \(\lambda =1\) the operator is even, otherwise it is odd. If the parity operator and the Hamiltonian commute: $\([P,H]=0\)$ then the system does not evolve with time, implying that the parity does not change with time. As a result, the parity is conserved.

docs.title: Angular Momentum
docs.text:
For hydrogen atom, the parity and angular momentum is linked via $$ \hat{P} Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi) = Y_{lm}(\pi - \theta, \phi + \pi) = (-1)^l Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi) $$

The selection rule says: for a transition to occur then there has to be a change in parity and the angular momentum, \(\Delta l = \pm 1\) (see selection rules)

The notation of angular moment and parity in nuclear physics is $\(J_e^P\)$ where \(J\) is the total angular momentum, \(e\) is the excited/ground state and \(P\) is the parity.

docs.title: Perturbation Theory
docs.text:
Following from Time-Dependent Schrodinger Equation we derived the transition rate in a two-level system. Now to approximate the evolution of the system, we can introduce a small parameter \(\lambda\) to scale the perturbation. Here we see that for a small perturbation, the transition rate of the system is approximately unchanged up to the first order of perturbation.

Now we modified the Time-Dependent Schrodinger Equation to $$ i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi^{(\lambda)}(t)}{\partial t} = \left[ H^0 + \lambda H'(t) \right] \psi^{(\lambda)}(t) $$ where the solution is $$ \psi^{(\lambda)}(t) = c_a^{(\lambda)}(t) \psi_a e^{-iE_a t/\hbar} + c_b^{(\lambda)}(t) \psi_b e^{-iE_b t/\hbar} $$ By substituting this solution to the Schrodinger equation and do all the fuck off algebra we get $$\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \dot{c}a^{(\lambda)}(t) = -\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar} c_b^{(\lambda)}(t) H' \}(t) e^{-i\omega_0 t

\dot{c}b^{(\lambda)}(t) = -\frac{i\lambda}{\hbar} c_a^{(\lambda)}(t) H' \end{aligned} }$$}(t) e^{+i\omega_0 t

Now we power expand the coefficients: $$\begin{aligned} c_a^{(\lambda)}(t) = c_a^{(0)}(t) + \lambda c_a^{(1)}(t) + \lambda^2 c_a^{(2)}(t) + O(\lambda^3) \

c_b^{(\lambda)}(t) = c_b^{(0)}(t) + \lambda c_b^{(1)}(t) + \lambda^2 c_b^{(2)}(t) + O(\lambda^3)\end{aligned}$$

docs.title: \(c_a\) term
docs.text: We subs the power expanded coefficients into the transition rate equation and group the terms in powers of \(\lambda\), we get $$ \dot{c}a^{(1)}(t) = -\frac{i}{\hbar} c_b^{(0)}(t) H' $$ We assume that, initially at }(t) e^{-i\omega_0 t\(t=0\), \(c_a = 1\) since the population will be in the ground state, so based on the power expansion, we have $$ c_a^{\lambda} (t=0) = 1 = c_a^{(0)}(0) + \lambda c_a^{(1)}(0) + \dots $$ Here, note that \(c_a^{(0)} (0)\) will be a constant in time because if you subs \(\lambda = 0\) in the transition rate equation, you will get 0. Additionally, all values of \(\lambda\) have to fulfil this equation. Therefore \(c_a^{(0)} (0) = 1\), \(\lambda c_a^{(1)}(0) = 0\)

docs.title: \(c_b\) term
docs.text: Similar approach for \(c_b\) term and we find \(c_b^{(0)} (0) = 0, \lambda c_b^{(1)}(0) = 0\) since \(c_b^{(\lambda)} = 0\)

docs.title: Time evolution of transition
docs.text:
We can also derive an equation for the time evolution of the transition. Recall that $$ \dot{c}b^{(\lambda)}(t) = -\frac{i}{\hbar} H $$}'(t) e^{+i\omega_0 t} \implies c_b^{(\lambda)}(t) = -\frac{i}{\hbar} \int_0^t dt' \, H_{ba}'(t') e^{+i\omega_0 t'

Just subs into $\(\psi^{(\lambda)}(t) = c_a^{(\lambda)}(t) \psi_a e^{-iE_a t/\hbar} + c_b^{(\lambda)}(t) \psi_b e^{-iE_b t/\hbar}\)$

and gives $$ \psi(t) = \psi_a e^{-iE_a t/\hbar} - \frac{i}{\hbar} \psi_b e^{-iE_b t/\hbar} \int_0^t dt' \, H_{ba}'(t') e^{+i\omega_0 t'} $$

docs.title: Transition Probability
docs.text:
The transition probability can be evaluated using the fact that the probability is the modulus square of the coefficient:

\[P_{a\rightarrow b} = |c_b^{(1)}(t)|^2\]

For example, in the previous example} + e^{i \mathbf{k} \cdot (\mathbf{r}2' - \mathbf{r}')} \right] \end{align*} $$ in general. This equation can be extended to \(N\) hole case: $$ E = \overline{E}_s e^{i k \overline{r}} \sum $$}^N e^{i \mathbf{k} \cdot (\mathbf{r}_m' - \mathbf{r}')

docs.title: Rubber
docs.text:
We want to investigate the free energy when the rubber is stretched. We first consider that the incompressibility of rubber:

$$ \lambda_x \lambda_y \lambda_z = 1 $$

where \(\lambda_i\) is the stretching factor and stretching means the cross-link points upon deformation are$$ r_0^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \quad \mapsto \quad r_1^2 = \lambda_x^2 x^2 + \lambda_y^2 y^2 + \lambda_z^2 z^2 $$ From Polymer - Introduction, we know from random walk model that $$S = -k_B \frac{3r^2}{2Na^2} + \cancelto{0}{\text{constant}}= \Delta S_{\text{strand}} = -\frac{3k_B}{2Na^2} (r_1^2 - r_0^2) $$ by substituting the stretching factor into the entropy above, we get $$ \Delta S_{\text{volume}} = -\frac{nk_B}{2} (\lambda_x^2 + \lambda_y^2 + \lambda_z^2 - 3) $$ where \(n\) is the number of polymers per unit volume. Assuming the deformation is along the \(x\) direction, using the incompressibility identity, we get $$ \Delta G = T \Delta S_{\text{volume}} = -\frac{n k_B T}{2} \left( \lambda^2 + \frac{2}{\lambda} - 3 \right) $$ where we assume \(H =0\) at this moment as the interactions can be assumed unchanged.

docs.title: Tensile stress
docs.text:
The tensile stress is then $$ \sigma_T = -\frac{\partial G_T}{\partial e_T} = n k_B \left[ 1 + e - \frac{1}{(1 + e)^2} \right] $$ where \(\lambda = 1 + e\) . From here we can find Young modulus for small \(e\) $$ E = 3nk_B T $$

and the shear modulus $$ G = nk_B T = \frac{\rho RT}{M} $$

docs.title: Viscoelasticity in Polymers
docs.text:
We can also find the viscoelasticity in polymer, given that in [[Physics/Setup/Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics|Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics]] we mentioned that everything is viscoelastic in a given timescale.

To find the evolution of stress after a given strain, \(e\), we can define a stress relaxation function, \(G(t)\) $\(\sigma(t) = e_0 G(t)\)$

and to find the evolution of strain after a given stress \(\sigma\), we can define a strain relaxation function, \(J(t)\) $\(e(t) = \sigma_0J(t)\)$

and they (stress example in this case) can be generalised to

[!note] $$ \sigma(t) = \int_{t'=t_0}^t G(t-t') \, d[e(t')] = \int_{t_0}^t G(t-t') \dot{\epsilon}(t') \, dt' $$

where we are looking for a small change in \(e(t)\) with respect to time and the stress or strain while the stress relaxation function is the same.

From there, we can define the complex modulus

[!Definition] $\(G^*(\omega) = i\omega \int_0^\infty e^{-i\omega s} \, G(s) \, ds = \underbrace{G'(\omega)}_{\substack{\text{storage modulus:} \\ \text{elastic behaviour} \\ \text{of the system}}} + i \underbrace{G''(\omega)}_{\substack{\text{loss modulus:} \\ \text{viscous behaviour} \\ \text{of the system}}}\)$

where \(\omega = 2\pi/\tau\) is the shearing/stressing frequency corresponding to the relaxation timescale \(\tau\) .

For a system relaxing exponentially, $\(G(t) \propto e^{-t/\tau}\)$ is the Maxwell's model

docs.title: Experimental Investigation of Relaxation Function with respect to time
docs.text:
This is a graph for linear polymers where the distribution of relative molecular mass is narrow.

There are 3 stages:

  1. Early relaxation which does not depend on the degree of polymerisation
  2. Plateau stage where the polymer behave like an elastic solid and it does not depend on the degree of polymerisation
  3. Late relaxation which depends on the degree of polymerisation where plateau ends at the terminal, relaxation timescale \(\tau\) and has a relationship $\(\tau \sim N^{3.4}\)$ At this stage, the polymer behaves like viscous liquid

In fact the plateau can be explained by the entanglement and reptation model. Entanglement model originates from the fact that the polymers cannot intersect each other when stretched so local entanglement points will be created temporarily. But when it comes to disentanglement, we have to use reptation model which is not trivial.

docs.title: Polymer   Introduction
docs.text:
• Polymer is a giant molecule made up of many repeating units covalently joined together in the form of a long chain

  • Homopolymer: Polymer composed of only one type of molecule

  • Copolymer: Two more more repeat units

  • Block copolymer: repeating units are arranged in blocks

  • Degree of polymerisation: number of repeat units present in a chain

At a given temperature, polymeric materials are in one of the following states:

  • Liquid
  • Glass
  • Crystalline
  • Liquid Crystalline: Kevlar

docs.title: Dimension of Polymer Chains
docs.text:
We are using random walk model to describe the relationship between degree of polymerisation \(N\) and the overall dimensions of the polymer chain.

Assuming each link \(i\) is defined by a vector \(\vec{a}_i\) and the polymer end-to-end vector \(\vec{r}\) is $$ \vec{r} = \vec{a_1} + \vec{a_2} + \cdots + \vec{a_N} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{a_i} $$ $\(\implies \langle \vec{r} \cdot \vec{r} \rangle = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{a_i} \right) \cdot \left( \sum_{j=1}^N \vec{a_j} \right) = N a^2 + \underbrace{\left( \sum_{i \neq j} \vec{a_i} \cdot \vec{a_j} \right)}_{= 0 \text{ (random orient.)}}\)$

In fact, the summation term is finite and negligible in real polymer chains. See lecture note.

Using this along with the probability distribution of end-to-end distances $$ P(N, r) = \left( \frac{2\pi N a^2}{3} \right)^{-3/2} e^{-\frac{3r^2}{2Na^2}} $$ and Boltzmann entropy $$ S(r) = k_B \ln P(N, r) = -k_B \frac{3r^2}{2Na^2} + \text{constant} $$

We get $\(G_{el}(r) = \cancel{H(r)} - T S(r) = k_B T \frac{3r^2}{2Na^2} + \text{constant}\)$ where \(H(r) =0\) because enthalpic contribution is negligible (we will include this later) as 1. freely jointed chain model does not take into account any molecular interactions 2. the polymer with multiple segments are able to occupy the same space

docs.title: Revision of Random Walk Model (Flory's model)
Theoretical value
docs.text: We, so far, do not care about the volume occupied by the polymer. The chain can actually overlap itself $$ R = \sqrt{\langle \vec{r}^2 \rangle} = a\sqrt{N} $$ with a density of $$ \rho \sim \frac{N}{R^3} \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} = N^{-1/2} $$

docs.title: Real life
docs.text:
In reality, the polymer cannot intersect themselves. So 'self-avoiding walk' model should be used.

The derivation of free energy of Flory model is far from trivial. We will quote the results and assumptions:

  • Each monomer occupies a small volume \(v\sim a^3\)
  • The concentration of the segments is \(c \sim N/r^3\)

The Gibb's free energy is $$ G_{\text{excl}}(r) = -T S_{\text{excl}}(r) = k_B T v \frac{N^2}{2r^3} > 0 $$ where \(S = k_Bv N/V\)

Combining this with the random walk model gives the total expression for the Gibbs free energy:

$$ G(r) = k_B T \frac{3r^2}{2Na^2} + k_B T v \frac{N^2}{2r^3} + \text{cte} $$

Therefore the equilibrium end-to-end distance is, in practice, $$ \sqrt{\langle \vec{r}^2 \rangle} = aN^\nu $$ where \(\nu = 3/5\).

docs.title: Second correction to random-walk model (Molecular interactions and interfacial energy)
docs.text:
In random walk model, we mentioned that the enthalpic contribution is zero but it is not correct in reality. We have to consider:

  1. polymer-polymer contact
  2. polymer-solvent contact
  3. solvent-solvent contact

docs.title: Polymer-polymer contact
docs.text: $$ N_{pp} = \frac{1}{2} z N v c $$ with - \(z\) the number of nearest monomer neighbours - \(c\) the concentration of polymer segments - \(v\) is the volume of a monomer so \(v c\) is the probability of seeing another monomer along the chain

docs.title: Polymer-solvent contact
docs.text: $$ N_{ps} = z N v (\rho_s - c) $$ with - \(\rho_s\) is the concentration of solvent molecules in the bulk liquid

docs.title: Solvent-solvent contact
docs.text:
$$ N_{ss} = N_{ss}^0 - N_{ps} - N_{pp} $$ where - \(N_{ss}^0\) is the number of solvent-solvent contacts in the absence of the polymer

The total enthalpy of the system is then $$ U_{\text{int}} = N_{pp} \epsilon_{pp} + N_{ps} \epsilon_{ps} + N_{ss} \epsilon_{ss} $$ $$ \implies \frac{1}{2} z N v c (\epsilon_{pp} + \epsilon_{ss} - 2 \epsilon_{ps}) + \underbrace{z N v (\epsilon_{ps} - \epsilon_{ss}) + N_{ss}^0 \epsilon_{ss}}_{cte} $$

$$ \implies U_{\text{int}} = -2 \chi v \frac{N^2}{2 r^3} + \text{constant} = H < 0$$ where \(c \sim N/r^3\) and \(\chi = zNvc(\varepsilon_{ps}-\varepsilon_{pp}-\varepsilon_{ss})/2\) and the pressure is constant.

Combining the enthalpy and entropy from Flory model derived above, we have

[!note] $$ G = H - TS = \underbrace{k_B T v \left( 1 - \frac{2 \chi}{k_B T} \right) \frac{N^2}{2 r^3}}{G}} + \underbrace{\frac{3 k_B T}{2 N a^2} r^2{G $$}} + \text{constant

We can distinguish the behaviour of the polymer solution - If \(\chi < k_B T/2\) , it becomes Flory model as polymer extended in solvent good solvent (because \(G_{excl} > H\) so entropy increases) - If \(\chi = k_B T/2\), \(G_{excl}\) cancels with \(H \implies\) theta condition where all corrections can be ignored - If \(\chi < k_B T/2\), \(H > G_{excl}\), the interfacial energy between the polymer and solvent dominates, hence poor solvent

[!Free Energy] $$ U - TS = -N k_B T \ln Z = F $$

docs.title: Properties Difference between Indistinguishable and Distinguishable Particle
docs.text:
In Probability and List of Formulae, we mentioned that for \(N\)-particle system with \(n\) dimension, we have for a set of distinguishable particles $\(Z_n=(Z_1)^n\)$ $\(Z_N = \frac{(Z_1)^N}{N!}\)$

For indistinguishable particles, $\(Z_N^{(\text{IN})} = (Z_1)^N\)$ We also mentioned in Density of States, Expectation Values and DeBroglie Thermal Wavelength that $\(Z_1 = \gamma\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta h^2}\right)^{3/2}\)$

To see the difference between the free energy of indistinguishable and distinguishable particles, we need to remember the free energy equation.

[!Result] For indistinguishable particle: $$ F = -k_B N T \left[ \ln\left(\frac{N}{V}\right) + 3 \ln \lambda_z + 1 \right] $$

[!Result] For distinguishable particle $$ F=-k_B N T \left[ \ln(V) + 3 \ln \lambda_p \right] $$

If you double the \(V\) and \(N\), you don't get doubled free energy (get more than double) in distinguishable

Which one is correct? Answer is indistinguishable. Think of a box with two same species of gas separated by a wall. If the wall is removed and the gas is allowed to mix, the entropy from distinguishable model is non-zero which is false because there should be no entropy since two gases are of the same species. Indistinguishable model is better because it best predicted the result.

docs.title: Transport (shift of Fermi sphere)
docs.text:
Recall from here that \(J = \sigma E\) , \(\sigma = 1/\rho\) and \(F = \Delta p/\Delta t = \hbar dk/dt = -|e|E\), we get $\(\hbar dk = -|e|Edt\)$This means that we shift the Fermi sphere by a little bit when an electric field is applied to the Fermi sphere. Due to the impurities and phonons that cause scattering, there is a tendency of Fermi sphere to go back to equilibrium by randomising electron momenta.

The mean free path is \(\lambda \approx V_F \tau\)

Recall also that \(J = -n|e|V_d\) here and by substituting \(V_d = -|e|E\tau/m\) (get from \(\Delta p = mV_d\)), we recognise that $\(J = \sigma E = \frac{n|e|^2\tau}{m}E\)$ This step shows that the electric field creates a net momentum for electron (first step) and that net momentum can be converted to drift velocity and from the formula \(J = -n|e|V_d\), we know that the drift velocity can can cause the metal to be conductive. Hence the shift in Fermi sphere can be used to explain why metals are conductive.

Metals have a partially filled Fermi sphere, so a small shift creates current. Insulators/semiconductors have a fully filled valence band, so the Fermi sphere cannot shift meaningfully.

However, Drude has no explaination of electron scattering. It assumes that the scattering time is constant. However, the scattering time depends on electron energy and is caused by phonons and impurities.

docs.title: Quantum Field Theory
docs.text:
To explain the phenomena that cannot be explained solely by special relativity and quantum mechanics, we have to use quantum field theory where we quantise the field to form virtual particles such as photons, gluons. The interaction is visualised by Feynman Diagram.

Here the wiggly line is the force mediator i.e. the quantised field and the solid lines are the four momentum. The energy is not conserved at the centre.

We can find a mathematical function that describes the probability amplitude (strength of interaction, represented by the vertices) for a virtual particle to travel from one point to another point as propagator: $\(\mu \propto \frac{1}{q^2-M^2 + i\Gamma}\)$ where \(M\) is the mass of virtual particle and \(\Gamma\) is the natural linewidth. The likelihood of the the interaction as $\(\frac{\alpha^2}{q^2 - M^2 + i\Gamma}\)$ where \(\alpha\) is the interaction constant: - EM: fine structure constant (\(e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0 \hbar c\)) - Strong force: not really constant (\(\sim 1/\log(Q^2\)) - Weak: Fermi constant (depending on \(W^{\pm}\) or \(Z^0\) bosons)

From here, we see that strong force is away stronger than the rest, so if strong force is in play then it will always be the most probable interaction. If not then EM will be more probable.

  2. Wiggly for EM or weak bosons

This concept is introduced here first because we will be using Feynman diagrams in this course.

docs.title: Feynman Diagrams
docs.text:
• 2D: spatial on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis
  • Line: fermions (travel forward in time) and anti-fermions (travel backward in time)
  • Wiggly lines: interaction (strong, weak and EM). \(g\) can only interact with quarks and \(\gamma\) can only interact with electric charge. Both LHS and RHS have to be quarks for \(g\) and charged particles for \(\gamma\)
  • Vertices: contain at most 3 lines

Note that the energy on the LHS is \(\geq\) to energy on the RHS as the mass is not necessary conserved. The energy is not conserved at the centre.

Also note that \(W^\pm\) can mix different particle generation but not \(g, \gamma, Z^0\) i.e. it can produce a quark of other family when interacting with a quark e.g. \(\bar{s}\) to \(u\) or \(t\). It can also do intra-generation like \(\bar{s}\) to \(c\).

Using the resonance of the Gallilean moons to predict the effect of Jupiter on the abnormal apsidal precession rate of Mercury modelled by Peturbation Theory

[!Question:] - What is the significance of investigating the orbit resonance - How much does G.R. and the solar oblateness contribute to Mercury's abnormal apsidal precession? - If we are comparing the amount of the influences on Mercury's orbit i.e. how much solar oblateness, gravitational force from Jupiter or/and the Sun and GR, should we include the Sun's mass into the gravitational force formula? If yes, then refer to the 4th reference. If not, then refer to the 2nd reference.

[!info] - Orbit resonance occurs when the orbiting bodies exert a regular, periodic gravitational influence on each other, usually because their orbiting periods are related by a ratio of integers - Orbit resonance can either stabilise a system or destabilise a system - Jupiter's perturbation can push Mercury into a secular orbit (type of orbital resonance between two bodies with synchronized precessional frequencies), increasing the eccentricity of the orbit

[!hint] The resonance of the moon alters Jupiter's quadrupole, which will change its gravitational potential. This, in turn, will affects its gravitational influence on Mercury, i.e. perturbation. - The idea is Gallilean's moons -> Jupiter Quadrupole -> Apsidal precession (slow rotation of perihelion of a body around a massive body) of Mercury orbit (which is affected by general relativity, grvaitational perturbation and solar oblateness.)

docs.title: Rayleigh Ritz Variational Principle
docs.text: Rayleigh-Ritz Variational principle states that the expectation value of Hamiltonian i.e. $$ \frac{\langle \phi | H | \phi \rangle}{\langle \phi | \phi \rangle} = \langle \psi | H | \psi \rangle \geq \epsilon_0 $$ where LHS shows the unnormalised expected Hamiltonian.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text: Recall that $\(|\psi\rangle = \sum_{n} c_n |\psi_n\rangle, \quad \langle\psi| = \sum_{m} c_m^* \langle\psi_m|.\)$ $\(H|\psi_n\rangle = \epsilon_n |\psi_n\rangle\)$ Combine these into \(\langle \psi | H | \psi \rangle\) and do some algebra. Abstracting both side by ground state energy and it gives $\(\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle - \epsilon_0 = \sum_{n} |c_n|^2 \epsilon_n - \epsilon_0 \cdot \underbrace{1}_{\sum_n |c_n|^2}\)$ where the RHS can only be positive or zero when \(\epsilon_n = \epsilon_0\) $\(\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle \geq \epsilon_0\)$

docs.title: Example using RR principle: Particle in a 1D box
docs.text:
Here we can estimate the ground state energy of a particle in a 1D box where the potential is zero. Recall that the ground state energy of the particle is $\(E_1 = \frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\)$

Here we set up a trial wave function with boundary condition \(\phi(0) = \phi(L) =0\) and is symmetrical at the centre of the box. One of the examples is $\(\phi(\lambda; x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \leq 0 \\ x(L-x) [1 + \lambda(x - L/2)^2] & 0 < x < L \\ 0 & x \geq L \end{cases}\)$

where \(\lambda\) is the variational parameter. The Hamiltonian of the system is (just) the kinetic energy of the system, hence $\(\frac{\langle \phi | H | \phi \rangle}{\langle \phi | \phi \rangle} = E(\lambda)\)$ and we get $\(E(\lambda) = \frac{3\hbar^2}{mL^2} \frac{11a^4 \lambda^2 + 14a^2 \lambda + 35}{a^4 \lambda^2 + 6a^2 \lambda + 21}\)$ We minimise this to get the energy by differentiating it with respect to \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Group Theory
docs.text:
Here we are going to use group theory in our character tables. The definition of group is that:

  1. Group is closed: \(\text{if} \ a\in V, b\in V, \text{then} ab\in V \text{and} a^2, b^2 \in V\)
  2. Commutative and existence of identity \(E\)
  3. Associative: \(A(BC) = (AB)C = ABC\)
  4. Reciprocal: \(1/a \in V, 1/b \in B\)
  5. Subgroup of a group is a subset of parent group that is also a group

However, operations are not commutative i.e. the order matters.

docs.title: Character Tables
docs.text:
• \(h\) is the order of group i.e. the sum of operations.
  • Irreps is irreducible representation i.e. the basis for the linear combination of reducible representation.
  • The right hand column \(z\), \(R_z\), \(x, R_y\) and \(y, R_x\) is the vectors that are affected by symmetry operations
  • The right-most column are the quadrupole
  • Characters (irreps) describe how basis functions are affected by operations

docs.title: Characters
docs.text: There are several ways to find characters i.e. reducible representation

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text:
1. Pick the atoms or bonds as the basis for the operation
  2. Figure out the symmetry operations of the point group
  3. +1 if the basis is mapped onto itself; 0 if basis rotates into others; -1 if the vector is being reflected

Example: Track the coordinate of each atoms in each transformation and you will get this: the factor of 3 is due to presence of 3 atoms.

docs.title: Traces of Transformation Matrices
docs.text:
1. Find a basis (a bond)
  2. Identify the transformation matrix
  3. Find the trace

Example: $$\begin{aligned}

\text{Identity matrix} \quad I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \

\text{Rotation around \(z\) axis} \quad M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

\end{aligned}$$

docs.title: Orbital
docs.text:
When tracking orbital we can use the formula:

  • For a rotation by an angle \(\alpha\) about the \(z\) axis for an orbital with quantum number \(l\): $\(\chi^l_\alpha = \begin{cases} \frac{\sin\left[ \left( l + \frac{1}{2} \right) \alpha \right]}{\sin\left( \frac{\alpha}{2} \right)} & \text{for } \alpha \neq 0 \\ 2l + 1 & \text{for } \alpha = 0 \end{cases}\)$
  • For a roto-inversion operation: $\(\chi^l_{\bar{n}} = \chi^l(n \otimes \bar{1}) = (-1)^l \frac{\sin\left[ \left( l + 1/2 \right) \alpha \right]}{\sin\left( \frac{\alpha}{2} \right)}\)$

docs.title: Reducible Representation
docs.text:
After finding the reducible representation such as \(\Gamma_z\) and \(\Gamma_x\) above, we want to express this in terms of linear combination of irreps on the character table to find the symmetrical axes and properties.

We use the reduction formula in group theory: $\(n\Gamma_i = \frac{1}{h} \sum N_C \chi^\Gamma_C \chi^i_C\)$ where - \(h\) is the order of group (defined above), - \(N_C\) is the number of operation within the class (number beside the operation like 8 in \(8C_3\)) , - \(\chi^\Gamma_C\) and \(\chi_C^i\) are the characters in the reducible and irrep respectively.

docs.title: Application: Crystal Field Splitting for Transition Metal Ions
docs.text:
Transition metal ions have their valence electrons partially occupying d orbitals which are strongly affected by their environment. This is because the orbitals extend sufficiently from the nucleus and the interaction with the wave functions of the surrounding species are significant.

Many transition metal cations occupy octahedral environment i.e. \(O_h\) group. When we reduce the reducible representation, we find that \(\Gamma_{3d} = e_g + t_{2g}\) , meaning that the five 3d orbitals are no longer of the same symmetry and no longer degenerate in this octahedral site. They are, instead be described by triply-degenerate \(t_{2g}\) and doubly-degenerate \(e_g\) and these two sets of orbitals will have different energies.

docs.text: The aperture function is $$ f\left(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\right)=\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{y^{\prime}}{b}\right) $$ By using the fact that the f.t. of rect function is sinc as discussed in Double slit revisited and scaling property, the f.t of the aperture function is $$ \begin{align} \mathcal{F}\left[f\left(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\right)\right] &=\mathcal{F}\left[\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right)\right]\mathcal{F}\left[\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{y^{\prime}}{b}\right)\right] \ &=ab\operatorname{sinc}(\pi au)\operatorname{sinc}(\pi bv) \end{align} $$ where \(u = x/\lambda z\) and \(v = y/\lambda z\)

docs.title: Replicators and Phase Contrast Imaging
docs.text: By using a comb function filter i.e. a diffraction grating, we can get replications of the object at \(-2f\) $\(\begin{aligned} f(x, y) &\rightleftharpoons g(x, y) \\ g'(x, y) &= g(x, y) \times \text{comb}\left( \frac{x}{d} \right) \\ h(x, y) &= \mathcal{F}\left( g(x, y) \times \text{comb}\left( \frac{x}{d} \right) \right) \\ &= \mathcal{F}\left[ \mathcal{F}(f(x, y)) \right] * d \cdot \text{comb}(du) \\ &= f(-x, -y) * d \cdot \text{comb}(du) \quad \longrightarrow \text{copies of original function} \end{aligned}\)$ ![[Pasted image 20260423114213.png]]

docs.title: Phase-contrast imaging
docs.text:
Most of the times, microscopy involves transparent or semi-transparent materials which induce only a phase shift in the light waves and this cannot be detected as an intensity change in the output.

The solution is to phase shift the low spatial frequency (surrounding light) by \(\pi/2\) amount with respect to the high spatial frequency (light after the structure of the material). In this case, the initial phase variation is mapped into an intensity variation in the image and can be detected directly.

docs.title: Resolution of a microscope
docs.text:
For a plane wave incident on a circular lens with diameter \(D\), the aperture function is given by a circ-function:

\[ f(\rho') = \text{circ} \left( \frac{\rho'}{D} \right) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \rho' > D/2 \\ 1 & \text{if } \rho' \leq D/2 \end{cases} \]

The f.t. of the aperture function is $$ \mathcal{F} \left[ \text{circ} \left( \frac{\rho'}{D} \right) \right] = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} \text{jinc}(\pi wD) $$ where the jinc function is the cylindrical analogue of sinc function.

docs.title: Intensity
docs.text:
$$ \begin{align} I^{(f)} &= \frac{I_0}{\lambda^2 f^2} \left| \mathcal{F} \left[ \text{circ} \left( \frac{\rho'}{D} \right) \right] \right|^2 \ &= I_0 \frac{\pi^2 D^4}{16 \lambda^2 f^2} \text{jinc}^2 (\pi w D) \ &= I_0 \frac{\pi^2 D^4}{16 \lambda^2 f^2} \text{jinc}^2 \left( \frac{\pi D \rho}{\lambda f} \right) \end{align} $$ The intensity distribution is known as Airy pattern and is plotted in the following figure:

The first zero of the intensity is at \(\rho = 1.22f\lambda/D\) known as the diffraction limit in [[Astronomy]] module. The ratio of \(f/D\) is called the f-number in photograph which need to be small to resolve finer detail.

docs.title: Euler's equations of motion
docs.text:
We consider \(N\) mass point subject to rigid-body constraints and take the time derivative of the angular momentum vector \(\underline{J}=\sum_{k=1}^N m_k (\underline{r}_k \times \underline{\dot{r}}_k)\) as discussed here we get

$$ \dot{J} = \sum_{k=1}^N m_k (\dot{\mathbf{r}}k \times \mathbf{\dot{r}}_k) + \sum}^N m_k (\mathbf{rk \times \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_k) = \underbrace{\sum}^N \mathbf{rk \times \mathbf{F}_k}{\text{total torque \(\underline{N}\)}} $$ So, we can say, viewing the rigid body from outside (space axes/coordinate system) \((dJ/dt)_S = \underline{N}\)

Recall from Rotating Reference Frames, \(\left(\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt}\right)_B = \left(\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt}\right)_S - \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{a}\), viewing the rigid body while travelling with its rotational motion (body axes/coordinate system) we can say that $\(\left(\frac{d\underline{J}}{dt}\right)_B + \underline{\omega}\times \underline{J} = \underline{N}\)$ Using this, alongside with \(\underline{J} = (I_1\omega_1, I_2\omega_2, I_3\omega_3)\), we have the Euler's equation of motion: $$ \begin{align} I_1 \dot{\omega}_1 - \omega_2 \omega_3 (I_2 - I_3) &= N_1, \[6pt] I_2 \dot{\omega}_2 - \omega_3 \omega_1 (I_3 - I_1) &= N_2, \[6pt] I_3 \dot{\omega}_3 - \omega_1 \omega_2 (I_1 - I_2) &= N_3. \end{align} $$

docs.title: Torque-free motion
docs.text:
If there are no external torques, i.e. a freely spinning object moving through the Earth's gravitational field, then we can set \(N_1 = N_2 = N_3 =0\)

\(J^2 = J_1^2 + J_2^2 + J_3^2\) describes a sphere in angular momentum space and \(T = \frac{J_1^2}{2I_1} + \frac{J_2^2}{2I_2} + \frac{J_3^2}{2I_3}\) describes an ellipsoid where the sphere and ellipsoid intersect shows the possible trajectories for the angular momentum components \(J_k = \omega_k I_k\)
