docs.title: Accelerating reference frames
docs.text:
We can specify the position of a point mass \(\underline{r}_S\) with respect to a chosen reference frame \(S\).

However, in another reference frame \(B\), we can specify the position \(\underline{r}_B\) of the same point mass, displaced by \(\underline{R}\) from \(S\). So the position with respect to two frame are then \(\underline{r}_B = \underline{r}_S - \underline{R}\)

If \(S\) is an inertial frame, then \(B\) is not as it is attached to an accelerating body. So in frame \(S\), $\(m \ddot{\underline{r}} _ { S } = \underline{F}\)$ but in frame \(B\),

\[m \ddot{\underline{r}}_B = m (\ddot{\underline{r}}_S - \dot{\underline{R}}) = \underbrace{\underline{F}}_{\text{true force}} - \underbrace{m \ddot{\underline{R}}}_{\text{fictitious force}}\]

docs.title: Inertial forces in a rotating frame
docs.text:
\[ m\ddot{\underline{r}} = \underline{F} - \underbrace{2m\underline{\omega} \times \dot{\underline{r}}}_{\text{Coriolis force}} - \underbrace{m\underline{\omega} \times (\underline{\omega} \times \underline{r})}_{\text{centrifugal force}} - \underbrace{m\dot{\underline{\omega}} \times \underline{r}}_{\text{Euler force}} \]

[!NOTE] Derivation Consider a point fixed in frame \(S\) at \(\underline{t}_S = \underline{r}\). If frame \(B\) is infinitesimally rotated w.r.t. \(S\) by \(d\theta\), then \(\underline{t}_B = \underline{r} + d\underline{r} \iff d\underline{r} = \underline{t}_B - \underline{t}_S\). Taking the small-angle limit (i.e. \(\theta = d\theta\)), the rotation formula transforms to \(\underline{r} + d\underline{r} = \underline{r} + (\underline{r} \times \underline{n})d\theta\).

Hence, (noting that for any two vectors \(\underline{U} \times \underline{V} = -\underline{V} \times \underline{U}\)) the velocity of the point in reference frame \(B\) relative to that in frame \(S\) is given by: $$ \left[ \frac{d\underline{r}}{dt} \right]{in \, B} = -\left( \underline{u} \frac{d\theta}{dt} \right) \times \underline{r} = -\underbrace{\underline{\omega}}. $$ Note that even if }} \times \underline{r\(\underline{r}\) is constant in reference frame \(B\), it is time dependent if viewed from reference frame \(S\).

docs.text: If the vector \(\underline{r}\) does have a time-dependence in reference frame \(S\) (e.g. represents the position of a moving particle), then this must also be accounted for: $$ \left[ \frac{d\underline{r}}{dt} \right]{in \, B} = \left[ \frac{d\underline{r}}{dt} \right]} - \underbrace{\underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}{\text{velocity in } B} \quad \text{(velocity in } S\text{)} $$ This equation is completely general for any vector \(\underline{A}\), so: $$ \left[ \frac{d\underline{A}}{dt} \right] \right]} = \left[ \frac{d\underline{A}}{dt{in \, S} - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{A}. $$ We can use the operator: $$ \left[ \frac{d}{dt} \right] \right]} = \left( \left[ \frac{d}{dt{in \, S} - \underline{\omega} \times \right) $$ in conjunction with \(\underline{v}_B = \underline{v}_S - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}\) to determine the acceleration in the non-inertial frame \(B\): $$ \left[ \frac{d\underline{v}_B}{dt} \right] \right]} = \left( \left[ \frac{d}{dt{in \, S} - \underline{\omega} \times \right) \underline{v}_B $$ $$ = \left[ \frac{d}{dt} \right]. $$} (\underline{v}_S - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}) - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{v}_B $$ $$ = \underline{a}_S - \underline{\dot{\omega}} \times \underline{r} - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{v}_S - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{v}_B $$ $$ = \underline{a}_S - \underline{\dot{\omega}} \times \underline{r} - \underline{\omega} \times (\underline{v}_B + \underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}) - \underline{\omega} \times \underline{v}_B $$ $$ = \underline{a}_S - 2\underline{\omega} \times \underline{v}_B - \underline{\omega} \times (\underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}) - \underline{\dot{\omega}} \times \underline{r

docs.title: Moment of Intertia \(I\) about an axis of rotation
docs.text: The direction of the axis of rotation is defined by the unit vector \(\underline{n}\). Each mass point has a moment of inertia that is the square of its distance between the axis of rotation multiplied by its mass \(m\). The sum of such terms is called \(I\) $$ \begin{align} I &= \sum_{k=1}^N m_k |(\underline{r}k \cdot \underline{n}) \underline{n} - \underline{r}_k|^2 \ &= \sum)^2] \end{align}^N m_k [r_k^2 - (\underline{r}_k \cdot \underline{n} $$

docs.title: Definition of inertia tensor
docs.text:
From the definition of total angular momentum \(\underline{J} = \sum_{k=1}^N m_k \left[r_k^2 \underline{\omega} - (\underline{r}_k \cdot \underline{\omega})\underline{r}_k\right]\), we can show that

$$\begin{align} I_x &= \sum_{k=1}^N m_k (r_k^2 - x_k^2) \omega_x - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k x_k y_k \omega_y - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k x_k z_k \omega_z, \ I_y &= \sum_{k=1}^N m_k (r_k^2 - y_k^2) \omega_y - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k y_k x_k \omega_x - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k y_k z_k \omega_z, \ I_z &= \sum_{k=1}^N m_k (r_k^2 - z_k^2) \omega_z - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k z_k x_k \omega_x - \sum_{k=1}^N m_k z_k y_k \omega_y, \end{align} $$ and use the linear transformation relating \(\underline{\omega}\) to \(\underline{J}\) to define the inertia tensor \(\hat{I}\) $$\begin{align} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} I_x \ I_y \ I_z \end{pmatrix}}{\mathbf{\underline{J}}} &= \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} I \ I_{yx} & I_{yy} & I_{yz} \ I_{zx} & I_{zy} & I_{zz} \end{pmatrix}}} & I_{xy} & I_{xz{\mathbf{\hat{I}}} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \omega_x \ \omega_x \ \omega_y \end{pmatrix}} \end{align}} $$ with \(I_{\alpha\beta} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_k (r_k^2 \delta_{\alpha\beta} - r_{k,\alpha} r_{k,\beta})\). When we are dealing with continuous rigid bodies, we can replace the summation with integral in cartesian coordinates \((dx, dy, dz)\) and \(m_k\) with mass density \(\rho(x,y,z)\).

docs.text: \[ \begin{align*} T &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^N m_k \underline{\dot{r}}_k^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^N m_k \underline{\dot{r}}_k \cdot (\underbrace{\underline{\omega} \times \underline{r}_k}_{\text{velocity due to rotation}}) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\underbrace{\underline{\omega} \cdot \left[\sum_{k=1}^N m_k (\underline{r}_k \times \underline{\dot{r}}_k)\right]}_{\text{angular momentum}} \end{align*} \]

docs.title: Rutherford Experiment
docs.text: The goal of this chapter is to derive the Rutherford cross-section. If you get the cross section, you can get the number of scattering events by multiplying it by the luminosity.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
When a gold atom is bombarded with an alpha particle, a number of alpha particles are backscattered and most of them are scattered in a large angle. That means there has to be something at the centre of the atom. We want to know the cross section of that 'something' at the centre of the atom.

Starting from the Hamiltonian, we know that the energy experienced by the alpha particle is the potential generated by the core of the gold atom: $$ H_{\text{int}}(\mathbf{x}) = V_{\text{Coulomb}} = \frac{Z_{\text{He}} Z_{\text{Au}} e^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} $$ with \(r = |\mathbf{x}|\). Recall that the probability of the momentum transition is $$ P_{p \to p'} = 2\pi \delta(E_p - E_{p'}) t \left| \langle \Psi_{p'} | \mathcal{H}_{\text{int}} | \Psi_p \rangle \right|^2 \frac{V \, d^3p'}{(2\pi)^3} $$

docs.title: Mott cross section
docs.text:
Rutherford cross section works for particles travelling at low speed. In relativistic case, the formula will be modified as $$ \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right){\text{Mott}} = \left( \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \right) \left(1 - v^2 \sin^2(\theta/2)\right) $$}

    • photon-photon quantum gate?

  • Polariton

    • transmission very high to 17 states but got catch: no coupling strength (cavity loss, not enough field)
    • Solution:

  • Liam's fellowship goal: find other material to replace cuprite that has less cavity loss

    • Why is cuprite special? - high binding energy, band structure (nice parabolic bands, look like hydrogen ones, symmetry of bands, same parity)
    • TMDC was the choice, (huge binding, but dipole-allowed bandgap)
    • So ZnP_2 follow 1/n^2 relation, 50 times lower loss, but it's not a cubic system, so different exciton spectrum

The wavelength to excite cuprite is lower so common lasers can be used

docs.title: Scattering Experiment
docs.text:
The units in nuclear physics sucks. The unit of the cross-section, defined as the characteristic area for interaction with the incident particles.

The number of incident particles per unit area per unit time is flux $$ \text{Flux} = \frac{\text{Number of incoming particles}}{(\text{Area}) \times (\text{time})} = \frac{N_{\text{in}}}{A \times t} = F $$ Note that this formula is similar to intensity but for intensity, solid angle is accounted.

Then the number of particles scattered off the target i.e. number of particles hit the target, is then $$ N_{\text{scat}} = \frac{\text{Number of incident particles}}{(\text{Area}) \times (\text{time})} \times \text{cross section} \times \text{time interval} = F \times \sigma \times \Delta t $$ In practice, we need a lot of targets to increase the observed dataset so we modify the formula such that $$ \frac{N_{\text{scat}}}{\Delta t} = F \times N_{\text{targ}} \times \sigma \equiv \mathcal{L} \times \sigma $$ where \(\mathcal{L}\) is luminosity and it is the generalisation of flux for scattering experiments. It is measured in inverse barn per second.

(Dear future me, if you are depressed when reading the notes here, remember this is Ifan hughes after Fourier transformed filtering, please laugh).

docs.title: Scattering Techniques
docs.text: We will be working in reciprocal space which is Fourier transform of the real space plane to reciprocal space plane.

docs.title: X-rays
docs.text:
• To induce electronic excitations
  • Strongly scattered by the electron cloud in a material
  • Heavy elements scatter more strongly than light elements

docs.title: Neutrons
docs.text:
• To induce phonon and magnon excitations
  • Wavelength is comparable to typical interatomic spacing i.e. suitable for diffraction
  • Strongly scattered by nuclei of the atoms but many neutrons can pass through the material without being scattered so more sample is required

docs.title: Electrons
docs.text:
• Scattered by the electric potential in the material via strong interactions
  • But may only probe the surface of a sample

docs.title: Diffraction
docs.text:
We use Bragg's law for diffraction. For constructive interference, $\(n\lambda = 2r\sin\theta\)$

Depending on the lattice parameter and the values of \(h, k, l\) (useful to read how to do the table) each materials give different peaks at different wave length. The intensity (probability) of scattering is the square of scattering amplitude/transition rate described by Fermi's Golden Rule is then $\(\begin{aligned} I(\mathbf{Q}) = |F(\mathbf{Q})|^2 &= \left| \sum_j \exp(i\mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{r}_j) \right|^2 \\ &= \sum_{i,j} \exp[i\mathbf{Q} \cdot (\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j)] \end{aligned}\)$ where \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{k}_i -\mathbf{k}_s\) originates from the transition matrix (i.e. FT of potential), \(|F(Q)|^2 \in \mathbb{R}\) is the transition rate and \(\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\) is the relative positions of atoms as found in pair distribution function. As different particles \(j\) has different \(\mathbf{Q}\), so we need to have form factor in calculation of \(|F(Q)|^2\) $$ F(\mathbf{Q}) = \sum_j f_j \exp(i\mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{r}j) $$ For x-ray diffraction, since it diffracts off of the electron cloud, recall from Form Factor that the form factor depends on the electron density \(\rho_{\text{el}}(\mathbf{r})\) so that $$ f(\mathbf{Q}) = \int \rho $$ and if }}(\mathbf{r}) \exp(i\mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \, d\mathbf{r\(\mathbf{Q}\) is a reciprocal lattice vector, we have $$ \mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{r}_j = 2\pi (h\mathbf{a}^ + k\mathbf{b}^ + l\mathbf{c}^*) \cdot (x_j \mathbf{a} + y_j \mathbf{b} + z_j \mathbf{c}) $$ which gives the structure factor

[!note] $$ F(hkl) = \sum_j f_j(\mathbf{Q}) \exp\left(2\pi i (hx_j + ky_j + lz_j)\right) $$

where \(h, k, l\) is the coordinate in reciprocal space and \(x_j, y_j, z_j\) is the coordinate in real space.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: The combination of \(h, k,l\) of different lattice type is different!

docs.title: Scattering from Fermi's Golden Rule
docs.text:
In Scattering Experiment we mentioned that the number of scattering events is given by \(\mathcal{L}\) and the cross section \(\sigma\). Here we want to calculate the transition probability of the momentum states of the target when it is bombarded by a much lighter particle. As the target is much heavier, we assume that the target is not recoiled.

We recall from transition probability of two level system and Fermi's Golden rule that the Fermi's Golden rules for a two-level system is $$ P_{p \to p'} = \left| \frac{2 \sin[(E_{p'} - E_p)t/2]}{E_{p'} - E_p} \langle \Psi_{p'} | H_{\text{int}} | \Psi_p \rangle \right|^2 $$ for large \(t\) we can simplify it to $\(P_{p \to p'}= 2\pi t \, \delta(E_{p'} - E_p) \left| \langle \Psi_{p'} | H_{\text{int}} | \Psi_p \rangle \right|^2\)$ But since we have a distribution of momentum states, we need to integrate it over a continuum of states, as discussed in Selection Rules and Fermi's Golden Rule $$ P_{p \to p'} \, dn = 2\pi \delta(E_p - E_{p'}) t \left| \langle \Psi_{p'} | \mathcal{H}_{\text{int}} | \Psi_p \rangle \right|^2 g(p) \, dp $$ In 3D, we have to consider \(n_x, n_y, n_z\) so instead we have to find \(P_{p \to p'} \, d^3n\). Using the fact that for momentum states in a box, the length \(L\) of the box can only contain integer number of wavelength

so the equation is $$ p_x = \frac{h}{\lambda_x} = \frac{2\pi\hbar}{L/n_x} = \frac{2\pi}{L} n_x \implies d^3n = \left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^3 d^3p $$

so the equation is $$ P_{p \to p'} = 2\pi \delta(E_p - E_{p'}) t \left| \langle \Psi_{p'} | \mathcal{H}_{\text{int}} | \Psi_p \rangle \right|^2 \frac{V \, d^3p'}{(2\pi)^3} $$

docs.title: Expression of cross-section
docs.text:
The experimental probability is given by $\(P = \frac{\sigma}{A} = \sigma \frac{L}{V} = \frac{\sigma v t}{V}\)$ i.e. probability of collision with the target is the cross-section over the entire area and \(L\) and \(V\) are the length and volume of the interacting section and \(v\) is the velocity of the particle.

This is readily to be equated with the equation found from the Fermi's golden rule.

docs.title: Selection Rules and Fermi's Golden Rule
Selection Rules
docs.text:
So far we have been looking at the case where the wavelength of the radiation field is greater than that of atomic size. This approximation is called the dipole approximation and we can consider the electric field over the extent of the atom to be spatially uniform.

Recall that the Hamiltonian of the interaction of the atom with the electromagnetic field is $\(H'(\vec{r},t)=q\vec{r} \cdot \vec{E} \cos(\omega t)\)$

and by taking the expected value of Hamiltonian, we get the dipole matrix element $$ \langle \psi_b | \mathbf{r} | \psi_a \rangle \quad \text{or} \quad \langle \psi_b | x | \psi_a \rangle, \quad \langle \psi_b | y | \psi_a \rangle, \quad \langle \psi_b | z | \psi_a \rangle $$ From here, we are able to derive the selection rules of transition:

docs.title: Magnetic quantum number \(m\)
docs.text:
We have the commutative relation where $$ [L_z, z] = 0, \quad L_z |nlm\rangle = \hbar m |nlm\rangle, \quad L_z |n'l'm'\rangle = \hbar m' |n'l'm'\rangle $$

Thus:

\[ \langle n'l'm' | \underbrace{L_z z - z L_z}_{0} |nlm\rangle = \hbar (m' - m) \langle n'l'm' | z |nlm\rangle = 0 \] \[ \langle n'l'm' | z |nlm\rangle = 0 \quad \text{if } m' \neq m $$ that means we have non-zero dipole matrix element even if the change of $m$ is zero. To prove $p_x$ and $p_y$, the procedure is the same but use the commutation relation: $$ [L_z, x] = i\hbar y, \quad [L_z, y] = -i\hbar x, \] \[ [L_z, x + iy] = \hbar (x + iy), \quad [L_z, x - iy] = -\hbar (x - iy) \]

docs.title: Orbital quantum number \(l\)
docs.text: $$ \langle n'l'm' | \mathbf{r} | nlm \rangle = 0 \quad \text{if } l' \neq l \pm 1 $$ The matrix element \(\langle n'l'm' | \mathbf{r} | nlm \rangle\) is only nonzero for: \(l' - l = \pm 1\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: \[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \Delta l = \pm 1 \\ \Delta m = 0, \pm1 \end{aligned} } \]

docs.title: Fermi's Golden Rule and Total Transition Probability
docs.text:
In atomic level where the energy level is discrete, we have $\(P_{b \to a}(\omega, t) = \frac{2|p_z|^2}{\epsilon_0 \hbar^2} \rho(\omega) \frac{\sin^2[(\omega - \omega_0)t/2]}{(\omega - \omega_0)^2}\)$

but in solids or molecules, the energy levels are overlapped, forming a window, continuum of energy from \(E\) to \(E+dE\). Now we want to calculate the total transition probability in this system. We realise that we first have to find the number of states in that continuum via density of states. $\(dN = \underbrace{\frac{dN}{dE}}_{g(\varepsilon)} \cdot dE\)$ where \(g(\varepsilon)\) is the density of states. The total transition probability is then the single transition probability times the number of states:

\[ P_{i \to n} \cdot dN(E_n) = \frac{|V_{in}|^2 \sin^2\left[\frac{(\omega_0 - \omega)t}{2}\right]}{\hbar^2} g(E_n) \cdot dE_n $$ and **Fermi Golden rule** is that $$P \propto |\langle f | H'| i \rangle|^2 \rho(E)\]

docs.title: Selection Rules and Properties of Broken Symmetry
Selection Rules
docs.text:
We discussed transition metal cation in Reading Character Tables and we saw in a diagram that the Cr\(^{+3}\) ions have a 3d\(^3\) structure with 3 valence electrons occupying the d state (which is further splitted into 5 due to the magnetic quantum number). In octahedral site, this state splits into \(t_{2g}\) , \(e_g\) and \(eg^*\) (antibonding).

For the transition between \(t_{2g}\) to \(eg^*\) possible, selection rules apply i.e. the transition matrix is non zero. $\(\mu_{if} = \langle f_{l, m_l} | \mu | i_{l, m_l} \rangle \neq 0\)$ In this case, \(\mu_{if}\) is only non-zero if the integrand is symmetrical. we can consider the relationship between parity and angular momentum for the selection rule.

For inversion, the parity of \(\mu\) is (-1), therefore the parity of the integrand is then $\(P = (-1)^{l_i}(-1)(-1)^{l_f}\)$and the integrand can be zero iff the \(l_i\) and \(l_f\) are of different parity. This is Laporte Selection Rule.

This selection rule is confirmed by the character table. 1. \(\mu\) is described by vectors along \(x, y, z\) and so is described by \(T_{1u}\) 2. The highest occupied state in chromium-III is \(T_{2g}\) 3. By taking the product and reduce it, we get $\(T_{1u} \otimes T_{2g} = A_{2u} + E_u + T_{1u} + T_{2u}\)$

As observed, the allowed transitions are those 4 states, not \(E_g\) which is forbidden in Laporte selection rules.

docs.title: Anisotropy
docs.text:
This is an extension of Antiferromagnetism and Anisotropy that uses character table and tensor to qualitatively discuss anisotropy.

Properties can be described using either polar or axial tensors. The rank \(N\) of a tensor can indicate the number of directions involved in measuring a property e.g. - Direction of heat flow: 1st rank polar tensor - Thermal conductivity: 2nd rank tensor.

The tensor coefficients describe the anisotropy of the property and the effects of symmetry operations on tensors indicates whether a property might be observed. Here we look at some properties that appear when we break the symmetry.

docs.title: Pyroelectricity
docs.text:
• Change in polarisation resulting from a change in temperature which then results in a dielectric displacement (displacement of cations relative to anions in the material).
  • 1st rank polar tensor (sign changes as direction changes)
  • The material must have polar axis i.e.
    • No mirror planes \(\perp\) to it
    • No \(C_2\) axes \(\perp\) to it
    • and the material has to be non-centrosymmetrical

docs.title: Piezeoelectricity
docs.text:
• Coupling between mechanical stress and electric polarisation
  • 3rd rank tensor
  • Material has to be non-centrosymmetrical

docs.title: Enantiomorphism
docs.text:
• Chirality (Cis-Trans in Chemistry)
  • Chiral objects must have no improper rotation \(S_n\)

docs.title: Optical Activity/Circular Dichroism
docs.text:
• Circularly birefringence
  • This can be used to test enantiomorphism because chirality induces circularly birefringence.

docs.title: Self control
docs.text:
• It is a temporary strategic to avoid bad habit
  • It will be the best to avoid temptation, rather than to control yourself

[!Avoid Temptation] Reduce the exposure to cue as discussed in Make it obvious section

docs.title: Self assembly   Aggregates, Micelles, Bilayers
docs.text: Self assembly is a process when the molecules arrange themselves to form a complex structure like aggregation and formation of micelles and bilayers. Such arrangement is mainly driven by the free energy of the system, like nucleation and mixing and demixing

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
Consider a solute dissolving into a liquid, we want to predict it the aggregates form in the liquid. We have a volume fraction (fraction of the volume of solutes and the total contents in the liquid) of the solutes, \(\phi\).

Say if aggregates form, each of them have exactly \(N\) solutes and occupies \(X_N\) volume fraction. We then have a relation: \(\sum_N X_N = \phi\) . For some reason and derivation is not known yet, the Gibb's free energy per molecule is $$ G_N = \mu_N = \epsilon_N + \frac{k_B T}{N} \ln \left( \frac{X_N}{N} \right) $$ where \(\varepsilon_N\) is the energy change per molecule when moving from bulk to an aggregate of size \(N\). Rearranging this gives $$ X_N = N \exp\left(\frac{N(\mu - \varepsilon_N)}{k_B T}\right) $$ By equating this to the case where \(N = 1\) and the equilibrium case where \(\mu = \mu_N = \mu_1 = \mu_2 = ...\)

[!General Expression of Aggregates' Fraction Volume] $\(\implies X_N = N \left( X_1 e^{\frac{\epsilon_1 - \epsilon_N}{k_B T}} \right)^N\)$

where \(\varepsilon_1 = \mu_N\) and \(X_1\) is the fraction of free solution molecules.

  • If \(\varepsilon_N > \varepsilon_1\), exponential term becomes negative and \(X_N\) decreases with energy, implying aggregates do not (primarily) form
  • If \(\varepsilon_N < \varepsilon_1\), aggregates form

docs.title: Another approach?
docs.text:
Using the symbols with usual meanings in this note $$Nv = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \implies r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3v}{4\pi} N} $$ and $$ \epsilon_N = \frac{4 \pi r^2 \gamma}{N} + \epsilon_{\infty} $$ where \(v\) is the volume of solute and \(\varepsilon_\infty\) is introduced to avoid \(\varepsilon_N \rightarrow 0\) when \(N\) is large. Then by subs into \(X_N\) we get

$$ X_N = N \left( X_1 e^{\alpha \left( 1 - N^{-1/3} \right)} \right)^N \approx N (X_1 e^{\alpha})^N $$ If \(X_1 < e^{-\alpha}\) there is almost no aggregates present. As the volume fraction increases and approaching \(e^{-\alpha}\) , aggregation must form as there is finite number of \(X_N\). This is called critical aggregation concentration where the aggregation starts to form.

docs.title: Aggregation of amphiphilic molecules
docs.text:
• Amphiphilic molecules are molecules with hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts and they typically make up of a spherical headgroup with carbon chain(s).

To form a spherical micelle, we have to fulfil several constraints. 1. Volume: \(4\pi r^3/3 = Mv\) 2. Surface area: \(4\pi r^2 = Ma_0\) 3. \(r \leq l_c\) $\(\frac{v_h}{l_c a_0} \leq \frac{1}{3}\)$ where \(a_0\) is the headgroup area, \(l_c\) is the critical chain length, \(v_h\) is the hydrocarbon volume and \(M\) is the number of molecules

docs.title: Critical micelle concentration
docs.text:
To form a spherical micelle, the number of molecules cannot be too small or too large and there is a simple way to model this: assume a minimum in \(\varepsilon_N\) i.e. when the \(N=M\), \(\varepsilon = 0\) and if \(N < M\) or \(N>M\), the condition is not fulfilled. Therefore the model is, by ansatz, a quadratic term: $$ \epsilon_N = \epsilon_M + \Lambda (N - M)^2, \quad \Lambda > 0 $$ We then find the fraction volume of aggregates $$ X_N = N \left( \frac{X_M}{M} e^{\frac{M (\epsilon_M - \epsilon_N)}{k_B T}} \right)^{N/M} = N \left( \frac{X_M}{M} e^{-\frac{M \Lambda (N-M)^2}{k_B T}} \right)^{N/M} $$ This is a Gaussian distribution with a variance \(\sigma^2 = \langle|N-M|\rangle^2 = k_B T/2M\Lambda\) .

ALSO, from the fact that $$ X_M = M \left( X_1 \, e^{\frac{\Delta \epsilon}{k_B T}} \right)^N $$ where \(\Delta \varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_1\) , the critical micelle concentration will be

[!note] $\(\phi_c = \text{exp}(-\Delta\varepsilon/k_B T)\)$

as, if \(X_1\) is below this amount, then the concentration is vanishingly small. Below this value the micelles start to form spontaneously when more molecules are added to the solution.

docs.title: Semiconductor Rydberg Physics   Review Paper
docs.text:
The binding energies of electronic states can be written in terms of principle quantum number. $\(E_n = -\frac{E_{Ryd}}{(n-\delta)^2}\)$

Rydberg atoms can be approximated to hydrogen-like systems, with usual Coulomb interaction energy. The Rydberg energy (unit of energy to ionise a hydrogen atom) is $\(E_{Ryd} = \frac{\mu e^4}{32\epsilon_0^2 \epsilon_r^2 \pi^2 \hbar^2}\)$ where \(\mu\) is a reduced mass of two charges.

docs.title: General differences between excitons in semiconductors and Rydberg atoms
docs.text: Feature Excitons in semiconductors Rydberg atoms Relative Permittivity \(\epsilon_r\) Greater than one (excitons in a medium that screens Coulomb interactions) 0 as they are treated as hydrogen-like systems Masses of Electrons and Protons Effective masses of electrons and protons are magnitude-alike but will be lower than free electron mass Usual electron's and proton's masses (and different magnitude)

docs.title: Implication of the differences
docs.text:
• Both effects (excitons) lower the Rydberg energy, and hence the binding energy
  • Reduction in Rydberg energy due to effective masses depends on materials, at least by a factor of 2
  • The dielectric constant of Cuprite scales with $\(\kappa \propto n^4\)$ where \(n\) is the refractive index (\(n\) = 2.7 for Cuprite)

The paper quantifies the reduction in Rydberg energy compared to hydrogen (on page 3).

docs.title: Differences between cold atoms and excitons
docs.text:
Feature Cold atoms Excitons Surroundings Individual entity that may be placed in vacuum Exist in semiconductor environment and impossible to decouple them from surroundings (defects like charged impurities and phonons). Open systems 1S state is the true ground state (is not open system) Necessarily constitute open systems (coupled to an environment) Confinement Easy to be confined (trapping Rydberg atoms in space with high precision) Randomly created in the light beam, harder to control the positions.

Note: Open systems are (a subsystem that is coupled to a larger, complex environment which defines its very existence and properties.)

Note: It's difficult to study a truly isolated state because the energy levels are close and phonons may cause them to transition

docs.title: What renders a material suitable to host Rydberg excitons
docs.text:
• High exciton binding energy (but binding energy scales as \(n^{-4}\), and max principle quantum number is \(n_{max} = \sqrt{E_B/k_BT}\) Materials with small binding energy have considerable amount of inhomogeneous broadening)
  • Peculiar band structure (same parity, no transition between states, giving high binding energy. Only P states can have direct dipole transition - that means no dipole emission at \(n =1\))

docs.title: Rydberg exciton blockade
docs.text:
• This is due to the interaction between Rydberg excitons
  • Energy required to create a second exciton in the vicinity of the first one becomes modified by their interaction energy
  • Energy shift may become larger than the linewidth of the laser.
  • Rydberg atoms have large polarisability which is described by the equation below (derived from the perturbation theory)

docs.title: Shell Model
docs.text:
The liquid drop model does not explain the phenomena in excited state. Therefore we are going to use the atomic physics knowledge to explain, even though it is less precise and smaller range of applicability.

There are some properties that can be explained using this model. For example, the magic numbers which require large amount of energy to transition and have larger binding energies

Just like atomic physics where when we are considering the Zeeman shift, we calculate the energy shift due to the magnetic field. Here, we consider the energy levels modified by the infinite potential well, Saxon-Woods potential and the spin-orbit coupling.

To do this, we have to make a few assumption: 1. The potential experienced by a nucleon is from other nucleons and it is spherically symmetry 2. The remaining \(A-1\) nucleons combine to have 0 total angular momentum (usually the case if \(A-1\) is even).

The potential (Saxon-Woods) experienced can be approximate to roughly follow the nucleon density in Form Factor i.e. $\(V(r) = -\frac{V_0}{1+e^{{(r-r_0)}/a}}\)$ Solve the Schrodinger equation to get the influence of infinite potential well + Saxon Woods potential.

What remain is the spin-orbit coupling, which is $$ H =V_{\text{LS}} = V_{LS}(r) \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S} $$

where it gives $$ \begin{aligned} \Delta E_{SO,nL} &= \langle V_{LS}(r)\mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S} \rangle |{J=L+1/2} - \langle V \rangle |}(r)\mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S{J=L-1/2} \ &= \langle V (L + 3/2 - (L - 1/2)) \ &= \langle V_{LS}(r) \rangle \frac{2L + 1}{2} \end{aligned} $$ and it correctly predicts the magic numbers. }(r) \rangle \frac{L + 1/2}{2 Intuitively, fully filled energy state is more stable and the binding energy is larger. Note that proton and neutrons are fermions. So they have to follow Pauli exclusion principle.

docs.title: Spin and parity of nuclei
docs.text:
Recall that the parity of a state is given by its eigenvalue under the operation \(\mathbf{P} : \mathbf{x} \rightarrow -\mathbf{x}\)

\[ \mathbf{P} Y_{L,m}(\theta, \phi) = Y_{L,m}(\pi - \theta, \phi + \pi) \rightarrow (-1)^L Y_{L,m}(\theta, \phi) \]

The composite states have parity equal to the product of their individual parities. The shell model can predicy the parity and total angular momentum for ground states in certain cases:

  1. If the number of protons and neutrons are even, the expect the parity to be \(+1\) since for every nucleon we can find another with the same parity. The net angular momentum is zero because they pair up.
  2. If the number of protons and neutrons are odd-even, the parity and angular momentum are determined by the unpaired nucleon i.e. \(P = (-1)^L\)
  3. Odd-odd number: no prediction

docs.title: Excited states
docs.text:
The transition between states can occur via emission or absorption of a photon. The essence for the nuclear selection rule lies in the conservation of parity and angular momentum.

The photons can carry away non-zero angular momentum \(\ell \geq 1\) and it is related to the multipolarity of radiation i.e. - Dipole: \(\ell =1\) - Quadrupole: \(\ell = 2\) - Octupole: \(\ell = 3\)

That means we have \(\mathbf{J}_i = \mathbf{J}_f + \vec{\ell}\) and that means the selection rule for angular momentum is $$ |J_i - J_f| \leq \ell \leq J_i + J_f $$ Note that if \(J_i = J_f =1\), we get \(\ell = 2\) it seems like there is no change in angular momentum but the photon carries non-zero momentum. This is because this is actually a vector equation, so even though it does not change in magnitude but it does change as vector.

There are two ways to change the angular momentum: 1. Spin change 2. Orbital angular momentum change

docs.title: Spin change
docs.text:
• Magnetic transition i.e. magnetic dipole/quadrupole/octapole
  • Labelled as \(M\ell\)
  • From matrix elements, the transition amplitude of magnetic transition is less than electric transition \(\implies\) less probable than electric transition.

docs.title: Orbital angular momentum change
docs.text:
• Electric transition
  • Labelled as \(E\ell\)
  • More probable than electric transition

The parity of the EM radiation is different electric and magnetic transition: $$ P_f = \begin{cases} P_i(-1)^\ell & \text{for } E\ell \text{ transitions} \ P_i(-1)^{\ell+1} & \text{for } M\ell \text{ transitions} \end{cases} $$ rearranging this gives $$ (-1)^\ell = \begin{cases} P_i P_f & \text{for an } E\ell \text{ transition} \ -P_i P_f & \text{for a } M\ell \text{ transition} \end{cases} $$

It is evident that the parity conservation will allow transition \(E(\ell \pm (\text{even number}))\) and \(M(\ell \pm (\text{odd number}))\)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
$$ \boxed{ \begin{aligned}

|J_i - J_f| \leq \ell \leq J_i + J_f \

\[1.5em]

(-1)^\ell = \begin{cases} P_i P_f & \text{for an } E\ell \text{ transition} \ -P_i P_f & \text{for a } M\ell \text{ transition} \end{cases} &

\end{aligned} }$$

docs.title: Soft Modes and Displacive Phase Transition
docs.text: In this section, we will combine the knowledge of measurement of phonons and look at displacive phase transition, involving the displacement of atoms i.e. amplitude of the phonons.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: SrTiO\(_3\) adopts the ideal \(Pm\bar{3}m\) structure at high temperature but undergoes a structural distortion below 105 K where extra peaks are observed in the intensity vs \(2\theta\) graph. After doing analysis (through Bragg's diffraction), we found that its structure turns from cubic to tetragonal. We can also analyse the modes.

docs.title: Phase Transition
docs.text: Here we will look specifically on displacive phase transition and investigate the temperature dependence of the amplitude of phonons. As usual, we define an order parameter \(\eta\). It can be any order parameter as long as it turn to zero from one above critical temperature. For example, for the ferroelectric phase transition of BaTiO\(_3\) will be the \(\Gamma_4^-\) mode which describes the polar displacements of Ti\(^{4+}\) cations.

docs.title: Soft Mode Theory of Phase Transition
docs.text:
We have considered that the displacements of atoms in the structure can be described by the phonon modes. Above critical temperature, the position-/time-averaged displacement is zero. Below critical temperature, the modes freeze and resulting in a net distortion. So the order parameter will be the mode frequency \(\omega\)

The soft mode theory of displacive phase transitions suggests if a material undergoes displacive phase transition, the mode frequency squared \(\omega^2\) must be dependent on temperature. The phonon instability (negative frequency) indicates that the high temperature phase is at maximum in potential energy with respect to this transition (?). ![[Pasted image 20260429221908.png]]

As the temperature drops, \(\omega^2\) decreases towards zero at the transition temperature i.e. this phonon mode is softened (restoring forces have weakened) and the equation is given by $\(\omega^2 = \frac{|\omega_0^2|}{T_c}(T-T_c)\)$ where \(\omega_0\) is the harmonic value (negative) calculated from lattice dynamics calculations.

docs.title: Spatial Coherence
docs.text: • Traverse coherence length is the lateral distance over which knowledge of phase can be predicted

docs.title: Van Cittert - Zernike Theorem
docs.text:
In this case, we cannot predict the wave front using time because it is corrugated. So we use Young's double slit to test spatial coherence.

For a narrow slit, coherence is greater than the separation between the two points in the second plane which gives interference.

What we observe is that as we increase the slit width, the visibility drops to zero and reappear again

and we also observe that the visibility graph is the fourier transform of the aperture function i.e. rect in this case. By ignoring diffraction, the on axis light is $\(\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{E}_1 e^{\frac{ikdx}{2z}} + \mathcal{E}_2 e^{-\frac{ikdx}{2z}}\)$ where \(d\sin \theta \approx dx/2z\) and the factor of two in the denominator is because we can take the angle from the top side of the single slit and bottom side of the slit.

If the slit is displaced by a distance \(x_s\), the terms above gain an additional phase and the we get $\(I = 4\bar{I}_s \cos^2 \left[ \frac{kd}{2} \left( \frac{x}{z} + \frac{x_s}{z_s} \right) \right]\)$ Each point in aperture gives cos squared fringes. To see the effect of the width of the single slit, we need to integrate the equation over all point and we get $\(I = 2\tilde{I} \left[ 1 + |\gamma_{12}| \cos \left( \frac{kdx}{z} \right) \right]\)$where $\(V = |\gamma_{12}| = \frac{\Gamma_{12}(k)}{\underbrace{\Gamma_{12}(0)}_{\text{max value}}} \quad , \quad \Gamma_{12}(k) = \underbrace{\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x_s) e^{-\frac{ikd}{z_s} x_s} dx_s}_\text{FT of the source}\)$ where \(f(x_s)\) is the aperture function. Therefore: Visibility of fringes = modulus of fourier transform of the source

** Another approach to see this is that, for a fixed slit width, the separation of the two pinole gives the visibility

The idea is that if the light from LHS slit diffracts and covers the area of the RHS slit, in QM, we don't know which one passes through, therefore there is no interference.

If the area of the light patch does not cover both slits, then in QM, we know which one goes through, therefore, no interference.

The size of the light patch on screen is \(\theta z = \lambda z/a_s\) so if we want to see fringes, we need $\(\frac{\lambda}{a_s}z > d\)$ The coherence length is then $\(\frac{\lambda z}{a_s}\)$ and the area is $\(A_c = \frac{(\lambda z)^2}{A_s} = \frac{\lambda^2}{\Omega_s}\)$ where \(\Omega_s\) is the solid angle subtended.

docs.title: Electron orbiting magnetic field
docs.text:
When moving in a circular orbit, the area sweeped is \(A=\pi r^2\) and the current produced is \(I = -ev/(2\pi r)\) where \(v\) is the speed. The magnetic moment produced is then $\(\mu_l = IA = -\frac{e}{2m_e}L\)$

In vector form $\(\vec{\mu_l} = -\frac{\mu_B}{\hbar}\vec{L}\)$ where the coefficient of \(L\) is replaced by Bohr magneton \(\mu_B = e\hbar / (2m_e)\)

The operator is then \((\hat{\mu_l})_z = -\mu_B \hat{L_z} / \hbar = -\mu_B m_l \hbar / \hbar = -m_l \mu_B\). This shows that magnetic momentum in \(z\) direction is quantised. Remember that \(m_l\) is magnetic quantum number and is dependent on \(l\), orbital quantum number.

docs.title: Hydrogen atom in a magnetic field
docs.text:
The magnetic potential energy is $$ V = -(\mu_l)_z B_z = m_l \mu_B B_z $$ and by differentiating it with respect to \(z\), gives $$ F_z = \left( \mu_l \right)_z \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z} $$ where \(\left( \mu_l \right)_z = -m_l\mu_B\) as shown above. So based on this, then \(m_l = 0\) then there should be no effect from the magnetic field, however we can see from Stern-Gerlach experiment that the beam splitted into two.

\(\implies\) there have to be another magnetic momentum which is not associated with orbital angular momentum and can 2 possible values rather than continuum of values (since it splitted into two).

docs.title: Spin magnetic momentum
docs.text:
We slightly modify the magnetic momentum equation by replacing the orbital angular momentum \(\vec{L}\) by \(\vec{S}\) and add a factor called g-factor to it $$ \underline{\mu}_s = -g_s \frac{e}{2m_e} S = -g_s \frac{\mu_B}{\hbar} \vec{S} $$ \(\implies\) the \(z\) direction force is then $$ F_z = \left( \mu_s \right)_z \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z} = -g_s m_s \mu_B \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial z} $$ Since the experimental result gives only two values, if we assume that \(m_s\) ranges from \(-s\) to \(+s\), like that of \(l\), then we must take \(s = 1/2\) and \(m_s = \pm 1/2\) because the steps must be an integer. Well, it simply means you can treat orbital angular momentum as spin. Everything is the same but different symbols.

[!IMPORTANT] \(m_s = -s, -s+1, ... , s+1, s\)

By working using \(m_s\) and spin magnetic moment, $\(S_z = \pm\frac{\hbar}{2}\)$

docs.title: Spin operators
docs.text:
We define \(\vec{S}\) as the angular momentum spin operator. Similar to that of orbital angular momentum, the eigenvalues are

[!important] \(s(s+1)\hbar^2\) for \(S^2\) \(m_s \hbar\) for \(S_z\)

except that their eigenstates are not spherical harmonics and not defined by any angles \(\theta\) and \(\phi\).

Instead for electrons, when it has a - spin up state \(s = 1/2 \implies m_s = +1/2 \implies\) eigenstate \(|\chi_+\rangle\) - spin down state \(s = 1/2 \implies m_s = -1/2 \implies\) eigenstate \(|\chi_-\rangle\)

docs.title: Formalism
docs.text:
[!note] $\(S_z | \chi_+ \rangle = \left( +\frac{\hbar}{2} \right) | \chi_+ \rangle \quad\)$ $\(\quad S_z | \chi_- \rangle = \left( -\frac{\hbar}{2} \right) | \chi_- \rangle\)$

We can merge them in a matrix and that matrix is called a Hermitian matrix $$ S_z = \frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} $$

We have also $$ \langle \chi_+ | \chi_+ \rangle = \langle \chi_- | \chi_- \rangle = 1 $$

docs.title: Spins State in Symmetry Properties of Wave Functions
docs.text:
Now we include spins in the symmetry properties in wave functions as discussed above. Recall that the wave function for bosons is $\(\psi(r, r') = rac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')+\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$

and for fermions $\(\psi(r, r') = rac{\phi_1(r)\phi_2(r')-\phi_1(r')\phi_2(r)}{\sqrt{2}}\)$

Now we want to include the spin state for each of the particles: $\(\psi(\vec{r})\alpha \quad , \quad\psi(\vec{r}) eta\)$ where \(\alpha, eta\) are spin-up(-down) vectors. For two electrons in an atom or molecule, they experience the attractive coulomb potential from the nucleus:

\[ v(\vec{r}) = - rac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \sum_i rac{Z_i}{|\vec{r} - \vec{R}_i|} $$ This is the general form of coulomb potential which accounts for molecules or solids where multiple nuclei are present. The Hamiltonian for each individual particle becomes $$ \left[ - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) ight] \psi_i(\vec{r}) = \epsilon_i \psi_i(\vec{r}) $$ The wave function can be replaced as $$ \left[- rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) ight] \underbrace{\psi_i(\vec{r}) \alpha(\sigma)}_{\psi_i(\vec{r},\sigma)} = \epsilon_i \psi_i(\vec{r},\sigma) \] \[ \left[- rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) ight] \underbrace{\psi_j(\vec{r}) eta(\sigma)}_{\psi_j(\vec{r},\sigma)} = \epsilon_j \psi_j(\vec{r},\sigma) \]

docs.title: Energy Levels of Two Electron Systems
docs.text:
Here the total Hamiltonian is $$ \left[ - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla'^2 + v(\vec{r}') ight] \psi(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = E \, \psi(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') $$ where we can separate (separable Hamiltonian) the total wave function into the ones above $$ \left[ - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla'^2 + v(\vec{r}') ight] \psi_i(\vec{r}, \sigma) \psi_j(\vec{r}', \sigma') = (\epsilon_i + \epsilon_j) \psi_i(\vec{r}, \sigma) \psi_j(\vec{r}', \sigma') $$ Or similarly we get $$ \left[ - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r}) - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla'^2 + v(\vec{r}') ight] \psi_j(\vec{r}, \sigma) \psi_i(\vec{r}', \sigma') = (\epsilon_j + \epsilon_i) \psi_j(\vec{r}, \sigma) \psi_i(\vec{r}', \sigma') $$ Recall that for fermions, we need antisymmetric wave function, so we separate the variables into spatial and spin wave functions like below $$ egin{aligned} \psi_i(\vec{r}, \sigma) &= \psi_i(\vec{r}) \chi_i(\sigma) \quad & \psi_j(\vec{r}', \sigma') &= \psi_j(\vec{r}') \chi_j(\sigma') \ \psi_j(\vec{r}, \sigma) &= \psi_j(\vec{r}) \chi_j(\sigma) \quad & \psi_i(\vec{r}', \sigma') &= \psi_i(\vec{r}') \chi_i(\sigma') \end{aligned} $$ and we arrive $$ \left[ \underbrace{- rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla^2 + v(\vec{r})}{H(\vec{r}, \vec{p})} \underbrace{- rac{\hbar^2}{2m} abla'^2 + v(\vec{r}')} ight) $$ $$ = (\epsilon_i + \epsilon_j) \left( rac{\psi_i(\vec{r}) \chi_i(\sigma) \psi_j(\vec{r}') \chi_j(\sigma') - \psi_j(\vec{r}) \chi_j(\sigma) \psi_i(\vec{r}') \chi_i(\sigma')}{\sqrt{2}} ight) $$}', \vec{p}')} ight] \left( rac{\psi_i(\vec{r}) \chi_i(\sigma) \psi_j(\vec{r}') \chi_j(\sigma') - \psi_j(\vec{r}) \chi_j(\sigma) \psi_i(\vec{r}') \chi_i(\sigma')}{\sqrt{2}

Here we can simplify this into shorter version i.e. Slater determinant $$ \psi(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = rac{1}{\sqrt{2!}} egin{vmatrix} \psi_i(\vec{r}, \sigma) & \psi_i(\vec{r}', \sigma') \ \psi_j(\vec{r}, \sigma) & \psi_j(\vec{r}', \sigma') \end{vmatrix} = rac{1}{\sqrt{2!}} egin{vmatrix} \psi_i(\vec{r})\chi_i(\sigma) & \psi_i(\vec{r}')\chi_i(\sigma') \ \psi_j(\vec{r})\chi_j(\sigma) & \psi_j(\vec{r}')\chi_j(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} $$

docs.title: Ground State
docs.text: Ground state occurs when the both electrons are in the ground state where the spins are opposite to each other: $$ \psi_{11}^{(s)}(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2!}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r}) \alpha(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}') \alpha(\sigma') \ \psi_1(\vec{r}) \beta(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}') \beta(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} = \psi_1(\vec{r}) \psi_1(\vec{r}') \frac{1}{\sqrt{2!}} \begin{vmatrix} \alpha(\sigma) & \alpha(\sigma') \ \beta(\sigma) & \beta(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} $$

docs.title: Excited States
docs.text:
There are four excited states: 1. down-down on ground and excited states 2. up-up on ground and excited states 3. up-down on ground and excited states 4. down-up on ground and excited states

\[ \psi_{12}^{(t)}(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r})\alpha(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}')\alpha(\sigma') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r})\alpha(\sigma) & \psi_2(\vec{r}')\alpha(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r}) & \psi_1(\vec{r}') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r}) & \psi_2(\vec{r}') \end{vmatrix} \underbrace{\alpha(\sigma)\alpha(\sigma')}_{|S=1, M=1\rangle} \] \[ \psi_{12}^{(t)'}(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r})\beta(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}')\beta(\sigma') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r})\beta(\sigma) & \psi_2(\vec{r}')\beta(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r}) & \psi_1(\vec{r}') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r}) & \psi_2(\vec{r}') \end{vmatrix} \underbrace{\beta(\sigma)\beta(\sigma')}_{|S=1, M=-1\rangle} \] \[ \psi_{12}''(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r})\alpha(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}')\alpha(\sigma') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r})\beta(\sigma) & \psi_2(\vec{r}')\beta(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} \] \[ \psi_{12}'''(\vec{r}, \sigma; \vec{r}', \sigma') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{vmatrix} \psi_1(\vec{r})\beta(\sigma) & \psi_1(\vec{r}')\beta(\sigma') \\ \psi_2(\vec{r})\alpha(\sigma) & \psi_2(\vec{r}')\alpha(\sigma') \end{vmatrix} \]

Note that for up-down and down-up states, the spin states cannot be factorised out i.e. not a eigenstate of the total spin \(S^2\). To construct an eigenstate of the total spin \(S^2\), we have to superpose the solutions:

docs.title: Electron Repulsion
docs.text:
So far we have not considered the repulsive force between electrons. We need first order perturbation to do so. The Hamiltonian is modified such that $$ H = \underbrace{h(\vec{r})}{H_0} + \underbrace{h(\vec{r}')}} + \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{1}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|}{V $$}

By applying the first order perturbation: $$ E_{\text{triplet}} = \langle \psi_{12}^{(t)} | H_0 | \psi_{12}^{(t)} \rangle + \langle \psi_{12}^{(t)} | V_{ee} | \psi_{12}^{(t)} \rangle $$ $$ E_{\text{triplet}} = \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2 + \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \int d^3r \int d^3r' \, \frac{|\psi_{12}^{(t)}(\vec{r}, \vec{r}')|^2}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|} $$

Same goes to singlet.

docs.title: Symmetry on Repulsion energy
docs.text:
For the triplet \(S=1\) states, note that the spatial wave function is antisymmetric, i.e. the electrons are avoiding each other, resulting in a lower repulsive interaction.

For the singlet states, the spatial wave is symmetric, resulting in a higher repulsive interaction.

Therefore the coulomb repulsive energies is lower for triplet states.

docs.title: Stability and Rigidity
docs.text:
Is ordered phase stable? We recall that when \(a(T) < 0\) then we have two minimum but are they stable?

Consider ammonia molecules with left \(|L\rangle\) and right orientated \(|R\rangle\), we form a Hamiltonian $$\begin{aligned} \hat{H}|L\rangle = E|L\rangle - U|R\rangle \ \hat{H}|R\rangle = E(R) - U(L) \end{aligned} $$where \(U\) is tunnelling probability.

From these two equations, we know that the state is actually in superposition as \(|L\rangle\) and \(|R\rangle\). We want to find a state where both states map back to themselves. So we set up an eigenvalue problem. From here we form Hamiltonian matrix. $$ \hat{H} = \begin{pmatrix} \langle L|H|L \rangle & \langle L|H|R \rangle \ \langle R|H|L \rangle & \langle R|H|R \rangle \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} E & -U \ -U & E \end{pmatrix} $$ and find its eigenvalues and eigenstates. The eigenvalues are $$ \begin{vmatrix} E - \lambda & -U \ -U & E - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0 ; \quad \lambda = E \pm U $$ we then find $$\begin{pmatrix} E - \lambda & -U \ -U & E - \lambda \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a \ b \end{pmatrix} = 0 $$ we then find $$ \begin{aligned} \phi_0 &= \frac{|L\rangle + |R\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} ; \quad E_0 = E - U \ \phi_1 &= \frac{|L\rangle - |R\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} ; \quad E_1 = E + U \end{aligned} $$ The idea is that the system oscillates between \(|L\rangle\) and \(|R\rangle\) at some frequency i.e. the ordered states are metastable. It depends on the tunnelling probability and the energy barrier.

docs.title: Rigidity
docs.text:
We want to find a formulation that describes rigidity i.e. when excessive amount of force is exerted on to an object, it breaks. We first consider [[Physics/Physics/Introduction to Soft Condensed Matter Physics|Hookean solids]] and we apply some force to stretch the square solid with length \(a\) by \(x\) amount $\(G = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \frac{F}{A}\frac{a}{x} \implies F = Gax \implies k = Ga\)$ where \(G\) is the Young modulus. As the energy of this stretch will be converted to heat energy, we use equipartition theorem to find the extension of the solid: $\(\frac{1}{2}(Ga)\langle x^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{2} k_BT \implies \langle x^2\rangle = \frac{k_BT}{Ga}\)$ so as \(G \rightarrow 0\), \(\langle x^2 \rangle \rightarrow \infty\) i.e. the solid breaks.

When we try to change order parameter, it costs a lot of energy $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Crystal:} & \quad E \propto (\Delta x)^2 \ \text{Ferromagnet:} & \quad E \propto (\Delta M)^2 \ \text{Superconductivity:} & \quad E \propto (\Delta \phi)^2 \end{aligned} $$ As Landau theory accounts for only mean field (treats the order parameter to be uniform throughout), we need to modify the model to $\(G_s(T) = G_N(T) + a(T) |\psi|^2+\frac{b(T)}{2}|\psi|^4 + c(\Delta \phi)^2\)$ and this is Landau-Ginzburg model.

docs.title: Statistical Mechanics for Semiconductors and Intrinsic Semiconductors
docs.text:
Since we mentioned in Electrons and Holes In Semiconductors that at finite temperature, some of the electrons are promoted to the conduction band. Here we want to quantify the number of electrons being promoted.

Using the statistical mechanics approach, the number of electrons in the conduction band will be $\(n = \int_{E_c}^{E_T} f_{FD} \ g_e(E) dE\)$ where \(f_{FD}\) is the Fermi-Dirac distribution. Similarly number of holes in the valence band will be $\(p = \int_{E_c}^{E_T} [1-f_{FD}] \ g_e(E) dE\)$ The density of state at finite temperature is hard to find. Since we are focusing on \(k=0\) region, \(k = 2\pi/\lambda \rightarrow 0 \implies \lambda \rightarrow \infty\), that means the electron wavelength is very large, which encompasses multiple ion cores. Therefore, we can approximate that there is no interaction between the electron and the ion cores, i.e. free electron behaviour which gives $\(g(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi^2} \left( \frac{2m}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2} \sqrt{E}\)$ (can be find here and here). Here, we have to tweak a bit the formula as

$$\begin{aligned} \text{CB: } g_e(E) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi^2} \left( \frac{2m_e^*}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2}}_{\beta} \sqrt{E - E_c} \

\text{VB: } g_h(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi^2} \left( \frac{2m_h^*}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2} \sqrt{E_v - E} \end{aligned}$$

where the shit in the square root is due to the fact that the energy curve is shifted up and down for CB and VB respectively. See diagram above. By doing the integration and assume that \(E_c - \mu \gg k_BT\) and \(E_T\rightarrow \infty\), we have $\(\boxed{ \begin{aligned} n &= N_c \exp \left[ -\frac{(E_c - \mu)}{kT} \right] \\[1.5em] p &= N_v \exp \left[ -\frac{(\mu - E_v)}{kT} \right] \end{aligned} }\)$

docs.title: Chemical potential
docs.text: For intrinsic semiconductors, we have \(n = p = n_i\), by rearranging the equations above, we get $\(\mu = \left( \frac{E_c + E_v}{2} \right) + \frac{3}{4} kT \ln \left( \frac{m_h^*}{m_e^*} \right)\)$

docs.title: Law of mass action (product of \(n\) and \(p\))
docs.text: $\(n_i^2 = N_c N_v \exp \left( \frac{-E_g}{kT} \right)\)$ Note that \(n_i\) is the concentration of electron in an intrinsic semiconductor.

docs.title: Electrical conductivity \(\sigma\)
docs.text: Recall from Metal 1 that the current density \(\mathbf{J} = qnv\), therefore the current density for the semiconductor is $\(\vec{J} = -en \vec{v}_e + ep \vec{v}_h\)$ where it has contributions from the electrons and holes. Using the fact that $\(\vec{v}_e = -\mu_e \vec{E} \quad ; \quad \vec{v}_h = \mu_h \vec{E}\)$ we can deduce that $\(\vec{J} = \underbrace{e(n\mu_e + p\mu_h)}_{\sigma} \vec{E} \quad \text{(Ohm's Law)}\)$ For intrinsic semiconductor we have $\(\sigma = e(\mu_e + \mu_h) n_i \propto \exp \left( \frac{-E_g}{2kT} \right)\)$ where the conductivity increases with temperature.

docs.title: Statistical definition of entropy
docs.text: \[S = k_B \ln \Omega\]

docs.title: Gibb's expression of entropy
docs.text: $\(S = -k_B \sum_i P(i)\ln P(i)\)$ where \(P(i) = \frac{n_i}{N}\), \(n_i\) is the number of microstates in macrostate \(i\) and N is the total number of microstates

docs.title: Physical interpretation of the statistical definition of entropy
docs.text:
• As more states are occupied, \(\Omega\) increases and so does entropy \(S\)
  • If states get closer in energy, more can be occupied increasing \(\Omega\) and there \(S\)

docs.title: Boltzmann distribution
docs.text: The probability \(P(r)\) of a given microstate \(r\) is $\(P(r) = \frac{n_r}{N} = \frac{e^{-E_r/k_B T}}{Z}\)$ where \(Z\) is partition function given by $\(Z = \sum_i e^{-E_i/k_BT}\)$

docs.title: Applying partition function in \(U\) and \(S\)
docs.text: \[U = -k_BT^2\frac{d\ln Z}{dT} = \sum_i P_iE_i = -\frac{1}{Z} \frac{dZ}{d \beta}$$ $$S = \frac{U}{T} + k_B \ln Z\]

docs.title: Heat capacity \(C_v\)
docs.text: \[C_v = k_B T \left[ 2 \left( \frac{\partial \ln Z}{\partial T} \right)_{\!V} + T \left( \frac{\partial^2 \ln Z}{\partial T^2} \right)_{\!V} \right]\]

docs.title: Bose-Einstein Distribution
docs.text:
Describes the probability of occupation for bosons (integer spin particles):

\[ f_{BE}(E) = \frac{1}{e^{\beta(E - \mu)} - 1} \]

Where: - \(E\) = energy of the state - \(\mu\) = chemical potential - \(\beta = \frac{1}{k_B T}\) (inverse temperature)

docs.title: Fermi-Dirac Distribution
docs.text:
Describes the probability of occupation for fermions (half-integer spin particles):

\[ f_{FD}(E) = \frac{1}{e^{\beta(E - \mu)} + 1} \]

Key differences: 1. Denominator sign: - BE: -1 (bosons can occupy states in unlimited numbers) - FD: +1 (fermions obey Pauli exclusion principle) 2. Behavior at low T: - BE leads to Bose-Einstein condensation - FD shows sharp cutoff at Fermi energy

docs.title: Strong Decays
docs.text:
Strong decays have to follow some conservation rules: parity and angular momentum

For example,

$$ \rho^0 \rightarrow \pi^+ + \pi^- $$

At lowest energy state and the total spin is \(S=0\) because the the spins are misaligned (\((u\bar{d}) \ \text{and} \ (d\bar{s})\)) , \(\pi^+\) and \(\pi^-\) has \(J=0\) and \(P=-1\) which \(\implies 0^-\)

But for \(\rho^0\), since it is \(u\bar{u}\), the spin is \(S=1\). If it's in its lowest state then \(1^-\)

It might have a problem because the angular momentum is not conserved. But we add a hypothetical angular momentum due to the rotation between pions

Tip: when the angular momentum is, by first glance, not conserved then see if there is some mutual orbital angular momentum to conserve both \(J\) and \(P\) i.e. be like a typical physicist, don't admit the math is wrong, just add the hypothetical stuff.

docs.title: Summation of Fields and Intensities in Coherence
docs.text:
Consider two fields with different electric field, frequency and phase $\({\varepsilon} = \varepsilon_1\cos\omega_1 t + \varepsilon_2\cos\omega_2t\)$ By using the standard relationship between intensity and field where \(\epsilon_{0} c E^2 /2\) , we get $\(I = 2I_1 \cos^2(\omega t + \phi_1) + 2I_2 \cos^2(\omega t + \phi_2) + 2\sqrt{I_1 I_2} \cos(\omega t + \phi_1) \cos(\omega t + \phi_2)\)$ Our detector takes measurements by considering the time-average. Therefore for cosine terms in the first and second term, it averages to \(1/2\). For the third term, as we allow the phase to vary randomly, the time-average becomes zero because

\(\cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2)\) \(\phi_1 - \phi_2 = 0\) \(1\) \(\phi_1 - \phi_2 = \pm\pi/2\) 0 \(\phi_1 - \phi_2 = -\pi\) -1

so if we average, it will be zero. That gives: $\(I = \langle I_1\rangle +\langle I_2\rangle\)$ for incoherent lights

docs.title: Condensed Matter Physics Project details (with reference to Microwave-optical coupling via Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide by Liam)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Quantum computers operate at a superconducting temperature (get rid of thermal noises since precise control over qubits is necessary) at a microwave frequency. However it is not feasible for quantum information to be transferred over a long distance, so it is necessary to convert microwave to optical (since we have the technology). The aim of this project is to create a microwave-optical converter.

  • Conversion using mechanical oscillators, nonlinear crystals and Rydberg atoms have been demonstrated but Rydberg atoms (electrons of atoms getting excited to a very high energy level, resulting in high quantum number, an unusual large atomic size and sensitive to external fields) show promises because of large dipole moment associated with transitions between Rydberg states of opposite parity (scaling \(n\) to \(n^2\)).

  • Finding:

    • Microwave field changed the absorption lineshape
    • Sidebands at the microwave frequency added to the coherent second harmonic
    • Complex dependence on principle quantum number and angular momentum
  • Details:
    • Introduction section
      • Rydberg atoms have to be held in place after they are produced. It involves laser cooling to reduce the temperature. But laser cooling produces lower temperature than millikelvin dilution refrigerator. Instead, excitons in cuprous oxide are used because it is already locked in lattice. We can just put it in dilution refrigerator.
      • The choice of cuprous oxide is because for low quantum number, the energy separation scales \(n\) to \(n^{-3}\). Combining with reduced Rydberg constant of excitons, the scaling means that the yellow series of cuprous oxide is accessible to microwave frequency.
      • Observe the coupling between electric field of microwave circuit (studied using one photon absorption spectroscopy and second generation spectroscopy) and the optical properties of cuprous oxide.
    • Experiment

docs.title: Superfluid and Superconductivity
docs.text:
The basics are in Introduction to Superconductivity. The four-fold symmetry is

Concept Mathematical Expression / Detail Description Order Parameter \(\Psi(\mathbf{r}) = \sqrt{n_0}e^{i\theta(\mathbf{r})}\) Description of the macroscopic wave function Rigidity \(\mathbf{J} \propto n(\mathbf{\nabla}\theta)\) Gives rise to the Supercurrent Defects Vortex lattice Topological defects in the phase field Excitation Bogolons Elementary excitations (Bogoliubov quasiparticles) The defect is vortex lattice i.e. Type II superconductor behaviour and the excitation is massive

but the excitations have no goldstone modes (theory: because global symmetry is not broken, local symmetry is broken and experimentally verified) because superconductors are described by a gauge theory (in gauge theory, goldstone modes vanish because of Anderson-Higgs mechanism). We will explore this more here.

docs.title: Gauge Theory
docs.text:
Recall the superfluid has a free energy$$ f = ( abla \phi)^\dagger \cdot ( abla \phi) - \mu^2 (\phi^\dagger \phi) + \lambda (\phi^\dagger \phi)^2 $$ This form of free energy tells us that superfluid has a certain symmetry i.e. invariant if \( abla heta = 0\) under the transformation \(\phi o \phi e^{i heta}\) .

What if we allow the phase to vary in space? Is it still invariant? We introduce a \( heta = \alpha(x)\), the gradient of phase becomes $$ abla \phi o abla \left( \phi e^{i\alpha(x)} ight) = e^{i\alpha(x)} ( abla \phi) + \phi e^{i\alpha(x)} (i abla \alpha(x)) $$ From here, if the \(\alpha(x)\) is a constant, the term \(\phi e^{i\alpha(x)} (i abla \alpha(x))\) is zero so the entire thing remain unchanged i.e. invariant and global symmetrical. But if it has a spatial dependent, then the entire thing is no longer invariant. This can be fixed using gauge theory.

We find an extra field to correct the local changes (because \( heta\) is not necessarily the same everywhere) in phase i.e. gauge freedom. Define $$ \hat{D} = abla + iq \mathbf{A}(x) $$ where $$ \mathbf{A} o \mathbf{A} - rac{1}{q} abla \alpha(x) $$ as \(\phi o \phi e^{i\alpha(x)}\). So the idea is to find a gauge field to fix the local changes in phase: $$ ({D}\phi)^\dagger \cdot ({D}\phi) o [{D}(\phi e^{i\alpha(x)})]^\dagger \cdot [{D}(\phi e^{i\alpha(x)})] $$ $$ o ({D}\phi)^\dagger \cdot ({D}\phi) $$

The example of magnetism is in Gauge Freedom I and Gauge Freedom II and it is this extra field \(\mathbf{A}\) that causes the gap in the dispersion curve.

docs.title: Superfluidity
docs.text:
Superfluidity is a state of fluid below critical temperature at ambient pressure. It has no viscosity i.e. defy gravity and flow indefinitely and anomalous specific heat capacity.

The collective superfluid can be described by a single macroscopic wave function \(\psi (\mathbf{r})\) where the 1. Number density of particles is $$ n(\mathbf{r}) = |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 $$ 2. Total number of particles is $$ N = \int d^3r \, |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 \quad \text{is total number of particles} $$

and the order parameter is $$ \psi(\mathbf{r}) = \sqrt{n(\mathbf{r})} \, e^{i\theta(\mathbf{r})} $$ where \(\theta(\mathbf{r})\) is phase field (phase of the wave function in space) and \(\sqrt{n(\mathbf{r})}\) is a constant (usually) number field. This implies that in disordered phase, \(\langle \psi \rangle = 0\) and in ordered phase \(\langle \theta \rangle = \theta_0\) in complex plane.

docs.title: Landau Theory
docs.text:
The Landau theory for superfluid is $\(f = -\mu\psi^\dagger\psi + \frac{g}{2}(\psi^\dagger \psi)^2 \quad \text{(Mexican hat potential)}\)$and this is analogous to the [[Setup/Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity|Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity]] with slight rewording i.e. \(\psi\) multiply to get \(\psi^2\). Here the \(\phi_1\) represents the real component and \(\phi_2\) represents the complex component of the wave function. The coefficient \(\mu\) is temperature dependence where it is negative for low temperature and positive for high temperature. For this reason, this equation can also be rewritten as $\(f = -\mu n + \frac{g}{2} n^2\)$ and the stable point is \(n_0 = \mu /g\) (which can be found by taking the derivative).

Analogous to [[Setup/Ginzburg-Landau Theory For Superconductivity|magnetism]] where the magnetisation is the same if it transfers from \(M\) to \(-M\), the order parameter for the superfluid is the same if we introduce a phase factor, $\(f(\psi, \psi^\dagger) = f(\psi e^{i\alpha}, \psi^\dagger e^{-i\alpha})\)$

docs.title: Rigidity
docs.text:
Here, we investigate the rigidity of superfluid in terms of phase space (instead of real space like solids). When we deliberately disorder the phase locally, it produces supercurrent., i.e. the rigidity is supercurrent $\(J = \nabla\theta(\mathbf{r})\)$ i.e. deforming order parameter gives supercurrent. We will be cover excitation in the future note, just to mention here

and the [[Vortices In Superfluids|defects]] will be vortices.

docs.title: Surfaces and Interfaces 2
docs.text:
This is the extension of Surfaces and Interfaces 1 where we will be dealing with fluid-fluid interfaces.

Similarly, we can balance the forces at the triple line where the fluid meet. This forms a Neuman triangle. What is special about this triangle is that it follows sine rule:

\[ \frac{\gamma_{13}}{\sin\theta_2} = \frac{\gamma_{12}}{\sin\theta_3} = \frac{\gamma_{23}}{\sin\theta_1} \]

We can also balance the horizontal forces to define the spreading coefficient, \(S\) which predicts if the lens will spread along the interface of fluid 1 and 3 to form a film. We get $$ S = \gamma_{13} - \gamma_{12} - \gamma_{23} $$ - If \(S>0\), we have complete spreading - If \(S <0\), the lens configuration is most stable - If \(S=0\), lens and spreading reach equilibrium (threshold)

docs.title: Capillary forces
docs.text:
• Ability of a liquid to flow in very narrow spaces without external forces
  • Originates from surface tension of liquids that are in contact with solids
  • Liquid molecules have a stronger bonds than gas so they pull the interfacial liquid molecules away from the interface
  • If the liquid surface is curved then there is a pressure inside the liquid. At equilibrium, there is a pressure difference across the interface.

For a more complicated case like a capillary bridge,

the pressure difference is dependent on the curvature. $$ \Delta P \equiv P_{in} - P_{out} = \gamma_L C = \gamma_L \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right) $$

where \(\gamma_L\) is the surface tension of the liquid and \(P_{\text{in}}\) is the Laplace pressure. If the liquid structures are large enough, then the influence of gravity (hydrostatic pressure) has to be considered: $$ \Delta P = \gamma_L \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right) + \rho gh $$

The threshold for considering the hydrostatic pressure is $$ x_c = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma_L}{\rho g}} $$ where \(x_c\) is the balance of surface tension against gravitational force. For structures much smaller than \(x_c\), influence of gravity can be neglected.

docs.title: Capillary rise
docs.text:
When a capillary is inserted into a liquid, the level of liquid in the tube is seen to go up or down by a height \(h\) with respect to the surface of the liquid.

We want to determine the change of \(h\). To do so, we have to consider when the free energy is minimum i.e. \(dG/dh = 0\)

The free energy is $$ dG = 2\pi r_c \, dh \, (\gamma_{SL} - \gamma_{SG}) + \pi r_c^2 \rho gh \, dh $$ $$\implies h = \frac{2(\gamma_{SG} - \gamma_{SL})}{r_c \rho g} = \frac{2\gamma_{LG} \cos \theta_{SL}}{r_c \rho g} $$

docs.title: Particles at the surface of a liquid
docs.text:
1. Small particles

    • Defined as particles which are not significantly influenced by gravity and buoyancy
    • If the contact angle is zero (fully wetting) then the particle sinks into the liquid
    • If the contact is larger than zero then it floats on the interface without miniscus.

  2. Large particles

    • Gravity and buoyancy has the ability to move the particle
    • Liquid deformed by the contact angle of the particle

To evaluate how stable the large particle is at the interface, we want to calculate the Gibbs free energy change before and after the particle is pushed into the liquid.

$$ \Delta G = 2\pi R^2 (1 - \cos \theta)(\gamma_{SL} - \gamma_{SG}) + \pi R^2 \sin^2 \theta \, \gamma_{SG} = \pi R^2 \gamma_{LG} (\cos \theta - 1)^2 $$ For \(\Delta G >0\), the particle sinks

docs.title: Homogeneous nucleation
docs.text:
• Supercooling of water.

Without any disturbances and impurities as the the nucleus, the freezing process involves two types of Gibbs free energy at equilibrium

docs.title: Solid-liquid interface
docs.text:
As mentioned in Surfaces and Interfaces 1 that the interfaces increase the energy in the system.

As the water begins to freeze, an interface is formed between solid and liquid.

This has a Gibbs free energy of $$ \Delta G_{\text{interf.}} = 4\pi r^2 \gamma_{\text{{SL}}}> 0 $$

docs.title: Volume free energy change
docs.text:
As the chemical potential (Gibbs free energy per particle) of the molecules in solid state, \(\mu_s\) is lower than in liquid state \(\mu_L\), there is a decrease of free energy proportional to the volume of the nucleus.

$$ \Delta G_{\text{phase}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho (\mu_s - \mu_L) < 0 $$ And the total free energy change of the system due to nucleation is

$$ \Delta G(r) = \Delta G_{\text{interf.}}(r) + \Delta G_{\text{phase}}(r) $$

There is an energy barrier opposing the transition, meaning that there is an unstable equilibrium between two transitions.

However, if there is external perturbation, it promotes growth of the nucleus and lowers the free energy of the system, leading to freezing. Or if there is a nucleus site, i.e. impurities, it lowers the interfacial energy (because in this case, the nucleation occurs around the impurity instead of costing energy to make a solid-liquid interface) which allows heterogeneous nucleation and it is why the ice forms from the edges of the pond.

docs.text:
As discussed in Optical Beats and Frequency Comb, the addition of waves of different frequency will give optical beats

$\(\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2} \mathcal{E}_0 \left[ (1 + e^{i 4 \pi \Delta \ell / \lambda_1}) e^{-i \omega_1 t} + (1 + e^{i 4 \pi \Delta \ell / \lambda_2}) e^{-i \omega_2 t} \right]\)$ As we add more light with different frequencies, some maxima will be suppressed

docs.title: Visibility of Fringes
docs.text:
When we plot the intensity graph,

we can quantify the visibility by $\(V = \frac{I_{max} - I_{min}}{I_{max} + I_{min}}\)$

Another approach is via the Winner-Winner-Chicken-Dinner-Kimchi-Einstein theorem. Realising that Michaelson has two time-dependent components so the time averaged intensity is: $\(\begin{aligned} I &= \epsilon_0 c \langle | \mathcal{E} |^2 \rangle \\[1.5em] &= \epsilon_0 c \langle [\mathcal{E}(t) + \mathcal{E}(t+\tau)]^* [\mathcal{E}(t) + \mathcal{E}(t+\tau)] \rangle \\[1.5em] &= \epsilon_0 c \langle |\mathcal{E}(t)|^2 \rangle + 2\epsilon_0 c \ \ \text{Re} (\underbrace{\langle \mathcal{E}(t)^* \mathcal{E}(t+\tau) \rangle)}_{\Gamma(\tau) = \text{autocorrelation function}} \end{aligned}\)$ Here we set another constant for the normalised autocorrelation function that compares \(\Gamma(\tau)\) with \(\Gamma(0)\) $\(\gamma(\tau) = \frac{\Gamma(\tau)}{\Gamma(0)} \quad \& \quad 0 \le |\gamma(\tau)| \le 1\)$

where \(\gamma =1\) means perfectly coherent. We rewrite time-averaged intensity in terms of \(\gamma\), giving: $\(I = 2I_0(1+ \text{Re}(\gamma))\)$ and it matches our expectation that \(I =4I_0\) in constructive interference in Michaelson interferometer. We then can find the relationship between \(\gamma\) and \(V\) by $\(V = \frac{I_{\max} - I_{\min}}{I_{\max} + I_{\min}} = \frac{(1 + |\gamma(\tau)|) - (1 - |\gamma(\tau)|)}{(1 + |\gamma(\tau)|) + (1 - |\gamma(\tau)|)} = |\gamma(\tau)|,\)$

Basically

[!Results] \(V = |\gamma(\tau)|\)

docs.title: Group Theory
docs.text:
As analogous to singlet and triplet states in QM, we can replace the spin up and down by up and down quarks. When we are transforming the quarks within their families like up to down, we are transforming the isospins. We want the physics to remain unchanged under the transformation so we need to put weak force to \(SU(2)\) group

For strong force, we have colour charge and we need a \(3\times 3\) matrices that describe this. So we need \(SU(3)\)

For EM force, it only couples to one thing: charge and anticharge so it has a symmetry of \(U(1)\).

docs.title: Cartesian coordinates
docs.text:
In real world, we have to consider three dimension so $\(T = \frac{p_x^2}{2m} + \frac{p_y^2}{2m} + \frac{p_z^2}{2m}\)$ and $\(V = V(x, y, z, t)\)$ \(\therefore\) the new form of Schrodinger Equation is $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 \Psi(\mathbf{r},t)+ V(\mathbf{r},t)\Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)}{\partial t} $$

Note that how initially \(x\) becomes \(\mathbf{r}\) because we consider 3D. The time independent is then $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \psi_n(x) + V(x)\psi_n(x) = E_n \psi_n(x) $$ where \(n\) is \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}\)

docs.title: Infinite potential square well
docs.text: In the time independent Schrodinger above, when we solve for \(\psi_n\), we need to consider the product in \(X,Y\) and \(Z\) directions, ie $\(\psi(x, y, z) = X(x)Y(y)Z(z)\)$ and the energy becomes $\(E_n = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{n_x^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{n_y^2}{L_y^2} + \frac{n_z^2}{L_z^2}\right)\)$ where \(L_i\) is the length of the well, not angular momentum in this case.

\[ x = r \sin\theta \cos\phi $$ $$ y = r \sin\theta \sin\phi $$ $$ z = r \cos\theta \]

and \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\)

The probability is then obtained from the volume integrals $\(P(\vec{r})dV = \psi^*(r,\theta,\phi)\psi(r,\theta,\phi)\,r^2\sin\theta\,d\theta d\phi dr\)$

The solution to the Scrodinger equation in spherical polar is called Spherical Harmonics \(Y(\theta, \phi)\)

docs.title: Symmetric nature of the inertia tensor
docs.text:
The inertia tensor is defined for a particular rigid body and for rotations of that body about a particular point.

The inertia tensor is represented by a symmetric matrix. We wish to know if there is a diagonal matrix representation of the inertia tensor.

docs.title: Principle axis theorem
docs.text:
\(\hat{I}\) is a symmetric tensor, represented by \(3\times 3\) symmetric matrix. We cna always find three eigenvalues and three orthonormal eigenvectors. The directions of eigenvectors determine the principle axes, labelled 1, 2, 3.

It s always possible to find a rotated coordinate system such that the representation of \(\hat{I}\) is diagonal. The diagonal elements are - principle moments of inertia (eigenvalues), - the coordinate system is set by the principle axes (eigenvectors) - a principle moment of inertia \(I_k\) (moment of inertia associated with rotation about the principle axis \(k\))

Rotating the coordinate system such that the representation of \(\hat{I}\) is diagonal is called principal axis transformation and it is always possible called principal axis theorem.

docs.title: Time dependent/independent Schrodinger's equation
docs.text: The time dependent Schrodinger's equation $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2 \Psi(x,t)}{\partial x^2} + V(x,t) \Psi(x,t) = i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi(x,t)}{\partial t} $$ simplifies to $$ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2} + V(x)\psi(x) = E\psi(x) $$

docs.title: Converting time independent to time dependent
docs.text: Since \(\Psi(x,t) = \psi(x)T(t)\) is separable, and \(T(t) = e^{iEt/\hbar}\), so to convert time independent to time dependent, $\(\Psi(x,t) = \sum_1 ^n \psi(x)e^{iEt/h}\)$

docs.title: Commutators and the Uncertainty principle
docs.text:
The origin of Heisenberg uncertainty principle is $$ \sigma_A^2 \sigma_B^2 \geq \left( \frac{1}{2i} \langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \rangle \right)^2 = \left( \frac{1}{2i} (\langle \hat{A}\hat{B} \rangle - \langle \hat{B}\hat{A} \rangle) \right)^2 $$ which gives $$ \sigma_x \sigma_p \geq \frac{\hbar}{2} $$

The uncertainty principle implies that there is a fundamental limit on the precision with which their corresponding observables can be simultaneously known.

Here, operators that are non-commutative implies that both observables cannot be measured precisely at the same time. This is because they don't have common eigenstates. Proof as below:

docs.title: Thermodynamic potentials
docs.text:
Tedious to just calculate the entropy like we have to calculate the entropy of the lake, of the metal, of the gas blabla so we introduce thermodynamic potentials.

$$dU = \delta Q + \delta w = TdS - pdV $$ $\(dU = \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial V} \right)_S dV + \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial S} \right)_V dS\)$ where \(U = U(S,V)\)

docs.title: Thermodynamics potentials
docs.text:
1. Enthalpy, \(H = U + pV\)
  2. Helmholtz, \(F = U -TS\), (constant volume)
  3. Gibbs free energy, \(G = H - TS\) (constant pressure)

The natural variables are derived by expanding the terms ie replacing \(U\) with \(TdS - pdV\). For example: This implies that \(H\) has the natural variables of \(S\) and \(p\)

[!note for enthalpy] If \(dH\) > 0, heat is added to the system, ie endothermic If \(dH\)< 0, heat is removed from the system, ie exothermic

[!note for Helmholtz] \(F = F(V,T)\)

[!note for Gibbs] Negative sign implies a spontaneous process

docs.title: Spontaneous processes
docs.text:
• Happens without the need of work
  • Direction of spontaneous change is governed by Clausius inequality $\(dS \geq \frac{\delta Q}{T}\)$
  • Spontaneous if \(TdS > dH\)
